This is the first fascicle of the *Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

One interpretation states that "practitioner" (*yogin*) has the meaning of "field. The preceding statement of taking refuge in and paying homage to the Buddha Jewel refers to the Great Sage at the stage of fruition;

here, clarifying the Sangha Jewel refers to paying homage to the various sages within the causal stage. This is intended to distinguish between these two types of sages: those of fruition and those of the cause.
Therefore, it is said that the assembly of noble ones (ārya-saṃgha) acts as a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).

Regarding those who adorn [the field] through the state of being learners (śaikṣa) and non-learners (aśaikṣa): although the term "assembly of noble ones" was mentioned above, it was not yet known which individuals are referred to as learners and non-learners.

Learners are those from the stage of patience regarding suffering (duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti) upwards, up to the candidate for arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka); these comprise the seven types of learners: those in the three fruits and four candidates.

These individuals, who fear [samsara] and seek to advance in their practice, are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*). Only those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship have ceased their efforts in the profound and vast [path];
having accomplished what was to be done, they are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). There are eighteen types of persons in training and nine fruits of those beyond training;
together, these constitute the twenty-seven noble ones (*ārya*). As for the four levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, they are termed "neither in training nor beyond training."
This meaning will be explained in detail separately later in the chapter on the Saṃgha.

Within the framework of the Bodhisattva dharma, first, that which has not yet attained the fruit of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is called "learning" (śaikṣa); from the attainment of the fruit of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas upward is "beyond learning" (aśaikṣa).
Second, within the path of effort (prayoga-mārga) it is called "learning," while the path of effortless spontaneity (anābhoga-mārga) is called "beyond learning."

Regarding "learner" (*śaikṣa*): if this is discussed in relation to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), the forty minds prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*) should be considered neither learners nor non-learners (*aśaikṣa*).
If explained in terms of cause and fruit, everything up to the ten stages is the learner, while only the fruit of Buddhahood is the non-learner.

Since the present section begins by separately paying homage to the Jewel of the Buddha, it does not discuss the fruit of Buddhahood as a non-learner. Regarding the "ornament": one explanation states:
This explains that these persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), possess superior virtues within and extraordinary appearances without;

as they mutually manifest brilliance and bring benefit to sentient beings, they are said to be "adorned. One interpretation states: it clarifies that such persons adorn their bodies externally with ethical discipline (*śīla*) and adorn their minds internally with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since these noble ones adorn their body and mind solely through ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom, it is so stated.
Adornment. Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that one is adorned by four kinds of necklaces (*vicitra-kaṇṭhika*);
these are called the "adornment of the necklace of ethical discipline" (*śīla-vicitra-kaṇṭhika*), and the same applies to the adornments of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding the phrase "those for whom the seeds of craving have been forever exhausted": one interpretation states that the first three phrases correctly clarify the abandonment of faults, which constitutes the quality of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*).
The final phrase subsequently clarifies the accumulation of qualities, which constitutes conditioned merit (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*).

Within the abandonment of faults, the first two phrases clarify the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*), while the final phrase clarifies the abandonment of karma and suffering (*karma-duḥkha*). In the first phrase, craving is abandoned; in the second phrase, [ignorance is abandoned].

[The text] says: "Views are the root of craving; that is to say, the afflictions arise from perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*). Since perception and feeling are also extinguished, it is said they have been 'removed.

Furthermore, the previous statement regarding 'being free from the three abiding grounds' means being free from the 'abiding ground of views' (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna-bhūmi*). 'Since what belongs to me has been extinguished' means being free from the 'abiding ground of self-attachment' (*ātma-grāha-bhūmi*).

'Since the roots have been removed' means being free from the 'abiding ground of ignorance' (*avidyā-bhūmi*). Moreover, the statement 'the seeds of craving for future existence are forever exhausted'—future existence (*punarbhava*) refers to..."

These are the three *bhava*s (existences). "The fruit-knot" clarifies that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the seed; this refers to the "seed-knot," which clarifies the raising of the afflictions belonging to the category of craving.
Although the *śrāvakas* (Arhats) have already severed the three fruits or exhausted them, they are forever without the seed-knot.

Although the Lesser Vehicle possesses the two cycles of afflictions—view and craving—their taking birth in the three realms and their departure from or remaining therein depend solely upon the craving for self (*ātma-tṛṣṇā*). Because craving is exhausted, [the cycle ceases]. 3.
The karma of the realms is destroyed; subsequently, one will no longer give rise to the various retributive fruits of existence within the twenty-five states of the three realms.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Only craving can cause the continuity of the various existences. Where there is craving for existence, there is birth; where craving is exhausted, there is cessation.

Since craving moistens and gives rise to birth, it is the root of all these existences. Speaking in terms of craving, it is called the "seed of future existence"; this merely mentions its [essential nature].
Regarding "love" (*rāga*): one should know that the five dull proclivities (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) are all extinguished together. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
"If one abandons even a single matter, I declare that you have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*. As for the fruit of *arhat*, both future and present fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eternally exhausted."

Although there may remain residual bodies and residual habits, these are not under discussion here. If one speaks of the three fruits and four stages of the path (the four candidates), each is distinct and exhausted in its own way;
however, here we speak specifically from the perspective of the ultimate point of final exhaustion. Therefore, it is called "permanently exhausted" (*yongjin*).

Furthermore, regarding both partial exhaustion and total exhaustion, all are eternally extinguished and will never arise again; thus, it is called "permanently exhausted. This does not refer to those who, like sand in a well, regress.
How is this known? Since this present context is a time for praising virtues, we take only the sense of "perpetual exhaustion" and not the sense of "retrogression.

The meaning and intent of terms each have their proper occasion; thus, within the context of the noble ones (*ārya*), one discusses them in order to distinguish between those who retrogress and those who do not.
However, in the present case, we take only the sense of "perpetual exhaustion" and not [the sense of retrogression].

This refers to the meaning of not being eternally extinguished. If we discuss the Bodhisattva, at the time of the first stage (*bhūmi*), the fruits of the three realms of existence are also eternally extinguished;

this present body was obtained as retribution for prior causes, and since the karma and afflictions of those prior causes have already ceased, one no longer speaks of receiving subsequent bodies of segmented birth.
Upon reaching the seventh stage, both types of birth and death are entirely forgotten; it is also said that...

It is eternally exhausted. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The wise should distance themselves from the two kinds of grasping that give rise to birth; these are the lack of vision and the four abodes.
These are acquired through the two types of karma—outflowing and non-outflowing—and result in the two kinds of birth-and-death.

One leaves these behind at the first stage (*bhūmi*). This meaning has been briefly set forth here. Later, the fruit and its conclusion will be explained separately. When future birth-and-death is exhausted, this is precisely what is meant by [nirvāṇa].

Wisdom has cessation as its object, as explained in the *Rājarṣi-sūtra*. Question: If there is no meaning of "partial exhaustion" regarding birth and death, is there also no meaning of "attenuation" regarding the afflictions?

It is not said that the remaining three [categories of afflictions] being severed is called attenuation; rather, the meaning is that the remaining three [categories] within the six realms of existence are called partial exhaustion.

Regarding the statement, "When 'mine' has been extinguished and the root has been removed," some say that "when 'mine' has been extinguished" refers to the afflictions of the view-division (*dṛṣṭi-bhāga*), while "the root has been removed" refers to the afflictions of the craving-division (*tṛṣṇā-bhāga*).

Now, in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, although the terms "indicating characteristics" and "not indicating characteristics" appear, they are not explained. Only in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is it explained, stating: "All greed and hatred..."

Alternatively, "manifesting" refers to external signs; thus it is called "indicating signs. Alternatively, "not manifesting" means that resentment is bound within the internal mind and does not take form externally;
thus it is called "non-indicating signs. Alternatively, what was previously explained as the seeds of craving refers to the afflictions belonging to the craving-portion (*tṛṣṇā-bhāga*).

Alternatively, that which has already been extinguished refers to the afflictions belonging to the view-portion (*dṛṣṭi-bhāga*). As for why craving was explained first and view was explained later: it is because craving was explained first.

Those who undergo existence do so solely because there is no "moistening" by craving (*tṛṣṇā*); thus, future existence (*punarbhava*) does not arise. Since karma and its fruit follow one another and their meanings are mutually interpenetrating, [craving] was explained previously.

Now, since this is explained according to the context of the occasion—and because it pertains to the time of exposition rather than the time of actual practice—it is explained later as a matter of seeing [the truth].
This does not undermine the meaning. One interpretation states: this is a praise of virtue; since it is difficult...

Excluding that which ceases last, one first extols its supreme virtues; thus, it is initially stated as "the exhaustion of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-kṣaya*), which establishes the meaning of praising its virtues.
As for "aversion" (*dveṣa*), it also extends to both views and craving. Even among those in training (*śaikṣa*), there is both [aversion] following views and [aversion] following craving.

Regarding the statement "now removed," this refers to the removal of these two types of aversion—both their partial removal and their permanent removal—and is therefore called "already removed. Long...

The Dharma Master then says, "The root has been eliminated. This clarifies that the three poisons are the root of all views; now that the three poisons are exhausted, all views have also perished. Therefore, it is said:

"Since 'I' and 'mine' have been extinguished, the root has been eliminated. Here, "I" refers to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and "mine" refers to the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Now it is clarified that both noble wisdom and [the objects of] perception are eliminated; hence, it is said they have "been extinguished. By mentioning only the view of self, [it implies the rest].
Because they know that the five types of gain and honor have been eliminated, it is said that "the faculties have already been removed.
They have already abandoned all worldly activities; birth and death constitute the worldly phenomena of conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*).

To create karma for the various realms of existence within birth and death is called "worldly activity. This clarifies that the assembly of noble ones will certainly never again create such worldly [karma].
One abandons the karma of the three realms of existence within birth and death, cultivating only the pure karma of supramundane *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that one "abandons all activities.
Furthermore, because one ultimately does not create the activities of the segmented, mundane cycle of birth and death, it is said that one "abandons all activities.
It is not that one still creates the karma of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) birth and death; however, at that time, since this karma has already emerged...

Because it pertains to the world of segmented existence (*paricchinna-loka*), it is said that "one does not perform worldly activities. Furthermore, "activity" (*vastu*) refers to suffering, while "action" (*karma*) refers to the karma that brings about suffering.
If one severs the afflictions (*kleśa*), the seeds of karma are naturally scorched, and the seeds of suffering do not continue. Therefore, it is said that "one has already abandoned activity.

According to another interpretation, "activity" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*); thus, it means one does not perform the karma of the five aggregates and so forth within the world.

Regarding the phrase "having relinquished worldly activities" and "the dwelling place of various merits": this assembly of noble ones is accomplished through the accumulation and adornment of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and the merits of knowledge and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*). It possesses immeasurable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

There are also immeasurable unconditioned merits; therefore, they are called "various. All these noble assemblies possess these two kinds of immeasurable merits, which serve as their place of reliance and abode.
The term "abode" (住) refers to that in which they dwell, in the sense of being supported by them, just like the meaning of a cause.
Taking merit as the support and the bodies and minds of the various sages as that which is supported, it is therefore called "that wherein one dwells.
The phrase "the most supreme among all multitudes" cites these virtues to manifest excellence, thereby establishing the meaning of the first sentence.
If one were to discuss the various paths, there are ninety-six kinds. Each of these ninety-six kinds has its own assembly of followers.
Among all these assemblies of noble ones, none surpasses this one; it is the most preeminent.
Therefore, it is said to be "the most supreme."
"Prostrating to the truly pure and virtuous Saṃgha": this single phrase serves both to cite their virtues and to conclude the section.

The preceding passage clarifying the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*) further establishes the meaning of "truly pure" within this context. This final summary expresses reverence for the *bhūta-saṃgha* (the real community).
"Truly pure" indicates that these noble ones, having realized the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and eliminated all afflictions (*kleśa*), are entirely authentic.
The assembly of purity, the great ocean of the assembly of supreme sages, thus fulfills the meaning of the "virtuous Sangha" within this context.
Because these afflictions will never arise again, it is called "truly pure. As for the "Virtuous Sangha," among all assemblies, the virtue of these noble ones is lofty and vast;
among all the assemblies of those on the various paths, the virtue of this Sangha is most preeminent. Therefore...

Regarding the term "Venerable Sangha" (*bhadanta saṃgha*): one explanation states that because they have fully accomplished the meritorious qualities of both conditioned and unconditioned wisdom and cessation, they are called the "Venerable Sangha.
Question: Since the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), why does he pay homage to the various lower-ranking Śrāvaka monks?
Answer: "Sangha" means "assembly. It is like a person who, although possessing a hundred years of seniority...
If there is a Dharma seat, even if there are only junior bhikṣus present, one must still pay homage. Why?

Because I fundamentally revere the assembly, not the individual person. Although these śrāvakas are said to be "junior," out of reverence for the assembly, one should pay homage to Nāgārjuna alone as being in accord with the Dharma.
One version states: Śākyamuni has no separate community of bodhisattvas; [the assembly] consists of bodhisattvas...
When entering the assembly of bhikṣus, one must still rely on the sequence of the Saṃgha to perform all ritual activities.
Within this assembly, both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas are present together; therefore, Nāgārjuna ought to pay homage [to the Saṃgha].
Regarding the phrase "having single-mindedly paid homage to the Triple Gem": the meaning of the Triple Gem should be explained in detail here.
From this point onward is the third section, the specific homage to the Saṃgha Jewel, which consists of two parts: first, the homage to the three individuals who represent the provisional Saṃgha;

second, the homage to the teacher Maitreya and the two authors of the treatise. This opening line serves both to conclude the preceding section and to introduce the following one, clarifying that the author of the treatise [first]...
Having already completed the general expression of reverence toward the Triple Gem, we now wish to pay particular homage to three individuals. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"With a single mind, having paid reverence to the Triple Gem. This is why Nāgārjuna stated that "to pay reverence to the Triple Gem with a single mind" clarifies that whatever actions Bodhisattvas undertake, they never harbor distracted thoughts;
even in their homage to the Triple Gem, they do not allow the mind to wander until [enlightenment] is attained.
Out of reverence, it is said that he was "single-minded. One interpretation states that he was single-minded solely because he wished to compose this treatise so that the Dharma might be propagated;

since he did not have any other purpose, it is called "single-minded. Another interpretation states that the reason the Buddha taught this Dharma was to cause sentient beings to believe and understand it, and to rely upon the teachings to practice;
I now follow the Buddha’s intention in composing this treatise, and it is likewise the same. With...
The Buddha’s mind does not differ [from that of others]; therefore, it is called "one mind. The Master further cites the explanation of King Aśoka’s coming to recite incantations.

Since Nāgārjuna was a great Bodhisattva, the reason he took refuge in and honored the Saṃgha is that, as his traces appeared during the Semblance Dharma (Śāsanā), he wished to manifest that the virtues of all people were superior when the Buddha was in the world;
thus he took refuge in and honored them. This clarifies that during the time the Buddha was in the world, Sudatta...
He used ten billion *jin* of gold to purchase land for the Buddha and establish a vihāra. King Aśoka appeared one hundred and sixteen years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
He became the king of Jambudvīpa and ruled over the spirits dwelling one *yojana* beneath the earth and the spirits dwelling one *yojana* above the earth.
As an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (*cakra-vartin*), he reigned over the entire world. He asked his ministers: "When the Buddha was in the world..."
At that time, who was most renowned for having performed the greatest merit and possessed the most excellent reputation? The ministers replied, "We have heard that there is only Sudatta;
he has performed the most excellent meritorious deeds by spending ten billion gold pieces, and this is beyond compare. King Aśoka said, "I am the king of Jambudvīpa, ruling over the entire world.
Why is it that the fame of my own meritorious deeds does not spread as far as his? It is not even equal to that of a minor [person]."
The young son of the elder immediately dedicated all his possessions toward meritorious deeds.
When the time of his death arrived, he calculated them and found he possessed only nine hundred and forty million gold pieces, lacking sixty million.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the merit of a great iron-wheel-turning monarch was not equal to that of the elder while the Buddha was still in the world; furthermore, during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were six...
The dignified conduct and rules of the community of bhikṣus were even superior to those after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such as that of the great arhat Upagupta.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, wishing to manifest the excellence of the Saṃgha while the Buddha was still present and to inspire longing for that time, must today, despite being a great bodhisattva himself, pay homage [to the Saṃgha]. Therefore, it is said:
Regarding the phrase, "Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, as well as to Maitreya and the other Saviors of the World": this sentence serves to introduce the following inquiry. Question:

Since Maitreya is already included within the Jewel of the Sangha and has thus been honored within the homage to the Triple Gem, why is he mentioned again here with the words "as well as to Maitreya and the other Saviors of the World"?
The commentary states: Since Maitreya is one who will appear in the future, he is here called "the Successor to the Honored Position"; therefore, he must be separately paid homage.

As for the term "Savior of the World" (*jagad-trātṛ*), it clarifies that the sentient beings of the world wander through birth and death within a great darkness, creating karma without end and suffering from the maladies of afflictions.
If the Buddhas did not appear in the world to bestow the medicine of the Dharma and preach the various Mahāyāna and Triyāna teachings, [they would remain lost].
The sublime scriptures, the Dharma of liberation, and so forth, which save sentient beings—yet those beings are perpetually submerged in the world, having no means of escape.

It is by the power of the Buddhas' compassion and their original vows that they appear in the world, preaching the Dharma to teach and transform the beings of the world, causing them to attain the supramundane fruit of *nirvāṇa* at a distant time. Today, Śākyamuni, having already fulfilled his great original vow...

The power of compassion resides in the present; as the Teacher who saves the world, Maitreya shall come in the future to succeed to the Buddha’s place, just as the present Buddha is the Teacher who saves the world.
For this reason, one takes refuge and pays homage. To exalt his virtues and manifest his person, it says "Maitreya, the Savior of the World," and so forth.
One interpretation states that if [the text mentions] Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others, this should be understood as a separate expression of homage to these two.
As for a person such as Maitreya, it is not that one should take refuge in and revere Maitreya alone. How is this known? A verse states:
"And all the World-Saviors, Maitreya, and the rest. Since it says "and all the World-Saviors" and further mentions "Maitreya and the rest," how could this refer to only one individual?
This clarifies that the path of all Buddhas is the same. Today, the Master of the Treatise intends to compose this treatise to widely propagate the Three [Baskets].

The Buddha-dharma of the world is entrusted solely to this sutra to clarify this single principle. Since it is thus for the Buddha-dharma of this one lifetime, so it is for all that which has been taught by all Buddhas.

Today, we specifically clarify our taking refuge in and paying homage to all those throughout the ten directions who occupy the place of the Buddha, such as Maitreya and others who act as teachers for the salvation of the world and succeed to the venerable position; we pay homage to them all—how could it be otherwise? Not only [to Maitreya] alone.
It refers to Maitreya alone. This is why it is said in the verse "and all the World-Saviors," and also "Maitreya and the others.
If one were revering only a single individual, how could it be said "and all the World-Saviors"? How could it be said "and the others"? One explanation states:
"And all the World-Saviors" refers to the two masters of the sūtras, while "Maitreya and the others" refers to three persons. How is this known to be so?
Since names are specifically mentioned here and reverence is paid [to them], one should not discuss other persons.
Regarding "Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom, the one who practices non-contention and emptiness," etc.: from this point downward, it clarifies the separate homage paid to two masters of the sūtra.
Whether they be the *pāramitās* themselves or [the masters who teach them], since these are the true realization of emptiness and equalizing wisdom, there is no...

Consider this: among the disciples of the Buddha, none surpasses Śāriputra in being foremost in wisdom; none surpasses Subhūti in constantly cultivating the contemplation of emptiness and being foremost in the practice of non-contention.
For this reason, the Tathāgata commanded these two to expound the Prajñāpāramitā in dialogue, thereby manifesting the two types of Dharma-gates:
the wisdom of emptiness and the wisdom of non-contention. Today, the Master of the Treatise intends to understand the sutra by means of this [commentary].

The treatise provides an explanation. Therefore, it separately pays homage to the principal figures who respond [to the Buddha]. Although one knows they are those who respond, if their virtues are not known, how can one cause sentient beings to give rise to deep respect and faith?
Thus, it cites their virtues to manifest these individuals, saying, "Foremost in wisdom," "those of non-contentious conduct," and so forth;
this is the specific clarification of the homage. Second, it clarifies that since these two individuals are śrāvakas, the Tathāgata...
Regarding the fact that the Prajñāpāramitā is taught here to these two individuals today, one might harbor the doubt that this Prajñā is a teaching of the Hīnayāna.
To dispel such a suspicion, the author of the treatise—being a Bodhisattva of the Dharmakāya—nevertheless pays special homage to these two.

One should therefore know that these individuals are not actual Śrāvakas, and what they have spoken is not a teaching of the Hīnayāna. Thus, at the beginning of the "Chapter on Exhorting to Speak," it says: "The Buddha..."
He addressed Subhūti: "You should now expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas.

The Master of the Treatise (the author) now wishes to sweep away the traces [of worldly manifestation] to return to the fundamental, and to sever the doubts of future generations; therefore, he mentions their names and extols their virtues as a distinct expression of homage.
Furthermore, these two venerable ones were both past Buddhas who, having served as the shadow and echo of Śākyamuni, manifested their traces as śrāvakas to provide instruction.
For the sake of his disciples, he elucidated this principle of *prajñā*, which is profound and subtle; were it not for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, it could never be exhausted.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly investigate it. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"Only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Therefore, the preceding verse says: "The ocean of the Great Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Buddha has exhausted; as..."
Because he intends to preach this profound and subtle Dharma, he summons these two individuals.
Since these two were Tathāgatas in the past, the Master of the Treatise now wishes to sever this doubt; for this reason, he pays special respect to these two Venerable Ones.
Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Internally they conceal their bodhisattva practice, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas, possessing few desires and being weary [of saṃsāra]."
Birth and death are, in truth, the purification of the Buddha-way for oneself; yet one manifests the presence of the three poisons to the multitude and further displays the marks of heterodox views.
My disciples act in this manner as skillful means to deliver sentient beings. Today, among the assembly, how many can be taught through such marks?

It concerns precisely two people; therefore, the Tathāgata commands that they be explained. This is why they are separately accorded reverence. The causes and conditions for the establishment of the names of Śāriputra and the others are as follows [in the subsequent section].
Commentary on the Text:

Regarding my current desire to expound this treatise according to my ability, these two lines of verse constitute the fourth major section of the homage, clarifying the purpose for composing the treatise, requesting that [the audience] listen, and entreating the Noble Ones to grant their assistance. Therefore, in all [traditions] of the Western Regions...
In all that we do, we should entirely take refuge in and pay homage to the sages, requesting their holy assistance. Nowadays, those who practice this Dharma method in these parts are very few;
even those who practice it to some extent do not compare to those in the Central Kingdom. As for my current efforts, they are according to my capacity.
The teaching of the true mark of *prajñā*—the great wisdom of equality—is exhausted only by the Buddha. Its principle is profound and remote, beyond the reach of ordinary meaning.
[The Master] said: "However, since I now wish to proclaim and disseminate this Dharma, I shall expound these indications according to my knowledge, to the best of my ability and capacity;
therefore, it is said: 'the power of suchness,' and so forth."
Regarding the meaning of "the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the great wisdom's other shore": "great wisdom" is precisely *mahāprajñā*.
Therefore, it is said that "the other shore of great wisdom" is the *pāramitā*. "Ultimate reality" is precisely the eternally abiding *prajñā*. "Meaning" refers to the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
There are three kinds of "other shores," as already explained in the opening of the sutra. What is now referred to is the "ultimate reality of the other shore."

"Meaning" (yi) refers to the other shore where there is neither "this" nor "that. Although these three types of waves on this shore are also clarified herein, the reason the Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach them is solely to enable understanding of that which is beyond verbal expression.
The essential intent of today’s sūtras and śāstras is to elucidate the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth), the signless *prajñāpāramitā* (perfection of wisdom).

The "other shore" (pāra) is the eternally abiding, wondrous principle of intrinsically pure *nirvāṇa*. However, as for the other three types of *siddhāntas*, since they have not yet reached the ultimate limit, they are not what is clarified by the primary intent;
they are merely illuminated incidentally. Now, that which I wish to distinguish is solely the *dharmatā* of the true mark (*tathatā*), which is the other shore;
therefore, it is called the "meaning of the true mark. Taking birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as this shore and *nirvāṇa* as—

Regarding the "other shore" (*pāra*): if one were to categorize it according to cause and effect, then from the present stage up until now, because there still exist meanings such as residual afflictions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, it is also called this shore.

Only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, when the *upāya-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (the nirvana of purified skillful means) is perfectly fulfilled—distinct from the *visadṛśa-lakṣaṇa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of dissimilar characteristics)—is it called the other shore. This is the general classification. However, this is merely the perspective of the śrāvakas.
Taking this to be the definitive meaning, the subsequent treatise states: "In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, there are the 'this shore' and the 'other shore.

If one says that these two types of birth-and-death constitute the 'this shore' and the cessation of these two types of birth-and-death constitutes the 'other shore,' then from the seventh stage upward is the other shore, while from the sixth stage downward is the this shore. If explained according to its figurative meaning, it is based on the sequence..."

Furthermore, regarding the practitioner’s discourse: since those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) have not yet attained true realization, they are said to "sever birth and death" only nominally; thus, this stage is called "this shore.

Since those on the stages have truly realized the truth and definitively severed birth and death, it is named the "Mahāyāna entry into the stream of *nirvāṇa*," analogous to the meaning of "entry into the stream" for the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) in the Hīnayāna.
Therefore, it is called "the other shore. If one considers the attainment of the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhāga*).

Regarding the phrase "for those who [attain] the noble embryo (āryagarbha) and so forth": this refers to those from the stage of the *śikṣamāṇa* (cultivated seeds) upward. Having already entered the Buddha-way and accomplished the meaning of deliverance (*tāraṇa*), they also attain the state of the "other shore" (*pāra*).

If one is prior to the stage of the cultivated seeds, having not yet attained the noble embryo and being unable to diminish or thin out birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one is therefore called "this shore" (*apāra*).
If speaking in terms of those Śrāvakas who have turned their minds (*cittavivarta*) to enter [the Mahāyāna], it refers to those from the stage of "light hair" (*laghumaṣi*) upward.

There is also the sense of attaining this "other shore" (pāra), which shall be explained in detail. Second, it is said that the six defilements constitute this shore, while the Buddha-way constitutes the other shore.

If one bases the meaning of "attaining the crossing" (*tīrṇa*) upon the Buddha-way, then from the stage of the "nature of practice" (*śikṣamāṇāgotra*) upward, one attains a semblance of the meaning of crossing;
this is a semblance of the Buddha-way and the attainment of a semblance of the other shore. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, [it is the actual attainment].
The true Buddha-way is the true Buddha-way; it is the true other shore. Regarding the term *kṣetrika* (苦提), in this context it is called "the path.
Thus, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "That which is abandoned by the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom regarding the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).

The meaning of this is that, among the paths of the three vehicles, this belongs to what is abandoned by the wisdom of the Buddha-way. The wisdom of the Buddha-way is precisely the wisdom of the Mahāyāna path. This is based on...

This is spoken from the perspective of the causal stage; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-way" (*buddhamārga*). When one reaches the fruit, that is the "Buddha-fruit" (*buddhaphala*), not the Buddha-way.
Since the Buddha-way refers to the cause, one should know that the wisdom from the first *bhūmi* upward is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha-way.

One should know that from the first *bhūmi* upward, ignorance (*avidyā*) is severed; whereas the Buddha has severed it completely, exhausting even the subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The *srotāpanna*..."
A person is also called a Buddha. Why is this? Because one who has attained perfect awakening (samyak-saṃbodhi) perceives the Path and thereby severs the afflictions (kleśa).

Although there is giving prior to the stage of the cultivated seed (śikṣā-bīja), since it has not yet achieved the meaning of "crossing over," such giving belongs to the middle of the river; it does not yet belong to the crossing, nor is it called the Buddha-way.
The six corruptions and other obstacles keep people on this shore. However, once one reaches the stage of the cultivated seed and above, all [acts of] giving attain [the state of crossing].
To cross the river of giving by means of what is similar: those who have already given in the past have not yet crossed the river of giving;
they are still called "those on this shore" until their minds turn [toward liberation], as explained above. Third, regarding "taking neither 'this' nor 'that' as the other shore":
taking 'this' and 'that' as "this shore" means that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are taken as "this shore," such that there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. As for... [as explained].

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are explained as having four types: first, the portion of merit (*puṇyabhāga*); second, the portion of liberation (*mokṣabhāga*); third, the portion of certainty (*niyāmabhāga*); and fourth, the untainted (*anāsrava*).

If one’s birth-attained or acquired [faculties] are dedicated toward the three realms of existence, they constitute the portion of merit. If they are dedicated toward [the cessation of] suffering, they are the portion of liberation.
The roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are the portion of certainty. The patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth are the untainted.

The first two, "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, although they belong to stages from which one may fall back, necessarily require this wholesome [root]; therefore, they are designated as "definite" (*niyata*).
Now, it is said that "if one possesses these dharmas," one possesses the "part of certainty" (*niyāmāvakrānti*). If one lacks these dharmas, one is devoid of these four types;

such a person is one who has severed the roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*). The above various explanations have been distinguished; thus far, they have been explained repeatedly. It is not... [text ends].

Within the explanation of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), there are two parts: first, the exposition [of the seven factors] themselves; second, the analysis of their essential natures through questions and answers.

Regarding the statement that "the seven factors of enlightenment are as explained in the *Prakāśa*," this refers to the explanation given within the *Prakāśa* concerning the sequence of the seven stages—prior, posterior, and intermediate. Among these analytical distinctions, first...

Question and subsequent answer: Because the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*), they are formless (*arūpa*). Because they do not belong to the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), they are invisible (*anidarśana*).

Because they do not possess resistance (*apratigha*), they are non-obstructive (*apratigha*). Because they are free from the two bonds (*bandhana*), they are untainted (*anāsrava*). Because their characteristics are subject to change, they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Because they arise by depending on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they are said to be "produced by causes and conditions. Since these are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are subsumed within the three periods of time (*tryadhva*).

Because it is not form (*rūpa*), it is included within the [mental] aggregate (*skandha*). Because it falls within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it is included within the external spheres (*bāhyāyatana*). Realizing it through wisdom (*prajñā*) is called the "essence of wisdom.
Because it is not a defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it is not something to be abandoned by means of antidotes; thus it is called "not abandoned by the view.

Because it is not a defilement of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) and cannot be severed, but rather increases clarity and illumination, it is called a "cultivated dharma" (*bhāvanādharma*). Its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), so it is called an "untainted dharma" (*anāsravadharma*). From the perspective of vision...

The Path arises; it is called "having this as its fruit" because it can attain the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Because its substance is not form (*rūpa*), it cannot be pierced or split; thus it is called "not subject to sensation" (*anupādāna*).
It is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) and is produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). There is a superior dharma above Nirvāṇa, which is called "having a superior" (*sottara-dharma*).
Because it does not follow the two types of existence (*bhava*), it is called "without existence" (*anuttara*). Because it is a mental factor, it is a "associated cause" (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). 2.

Regarding the inclusion of the factors of awakening within the categories of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*): the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), while the remaining six are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Since the seven factors of awakening do not exhaustively encompass all wholesome qualities, they are referred to as "factors" (*pakṣa*). The remainder of the text is clear.

In the explanation of the Right Path, there are two parts. First, the essential characteristics of the Eightfold Path; second, from "The Eightfold Path has two divisions" onwards, the classification of its nature through three aspects.
Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, a brief reference to the preceding explanation; second, from "Right Speech" onwards, a detailed clarification of the various types.
Regarding the statement "Excluding the four kinds of wrong livelihood, which comprise verbal action," there are five kinds of wrong [livelihood].
Regarding the types of livelihood: the first is subsumed under bodily action (*kāyakarman*), and the latter four are subsumed under vocal action (*vākkarman*).

Since all of these can arise from a mind of greed, if one’s livelihood is wrong, then any other bodily actions arising from hatred (*dveṣa*) or delusion (*moha*) are termed "wrong actions" (*mithyākarma*), as they can likewise arise from hatred and delusion.
This is called "false speech. Now, wishing to explain "right speech," I fear there may be confusion; therefore, I shall clarify and exclude [the other categories].
By removing the greedy mind, one can give rise to speech. There are four types of false livelihood, which are removed by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

As for abandoning the remaining false actions, this refers to abandoning the four types of false speech that can arise from the minds of hatred and delusion; thus it is called "right speech. Regarding action, one likewise removes the greedy mind.
One may abandon the three types of wrong bodily action that arise from wrong livelihood; therefore, it is called Right Action (*samyak-karmānta*).
One abandons the five types of wrong livelihood that arise from outflows (*āsrava*); therefore, it is called Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). Question:

Since the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) does not sever the causes [of afflictions], how can there be Right Speech and the others? Answer: It is explained that at this stage, one severs the causes of the motivating impulses (*samutthāna*).
Therefore, regarding the various types of "pseudo-life" (*jīvitaka*), the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
first, feigning eccentricity; second, seeking intimacy; third, inciting agitation; fourth, alternating between suppression and exaltation; and fifth, seeking profit through profit.

The first [type] is a physical action (*kāyakarman*), while the latter four are verbal actions (*vākkarman*). The first and the fifth are similar to those mentioned here, whereas the remaining three differ. [The second type,] "seeking intimacy,"...
[One who] acts as a kinsman to others; one who incites [desire] by showing others desirable things and manifesting signs of greed;

and one who disparages and exalts by speaking of others' stinginess to reveal oneself as a holy person. Among the three types of conduct, those that constitute the factors of concentration (*samādhi*) are mindfulness, concentration, and diligence.
Those that constitute the factors of wisdom (*prajñā*) are right view and right thought. Question:

Other treatises clarify that diligence (*vīrya*) is a form of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), because within the aforementioned seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), it is further termed "arousing" (*samuttejana*).

Here, it is subsumed under the category of concentration (*samādhi*). There are two meanings to be understood regarding diligence: first, in terms of its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); second, in terms of its capacity to exert (*pragraha*).

If considered according to its characteristic, its nature is one of movement and arousal, and it would be judged to belong to the category of energy (*vīrya*). However, here it is based on exertion; because it exerts concentration, it is proximate to it, and thus it is placed [here].

They are subsumed under the category of "determined" (niyata-bhāgīya). Within the analysis of the precepts, they are subsumed under the single category of the wholesome portion. As for the three types of right [action], these belong to the wholesome portion of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
Because they do not exhaustively encompass all [factors], they are termed "portions" (bhāga). The remaining categories can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement that these thirty-seven factors are fully present in the stage of the first dhyāna: from here below, they are distinguished according to the stages of dhyāna.
As for the thirty-six factors in the *anāgamya* (preparatory) stage, because it is unstable due to its reliance on preparatory means (*upāya*), there is no joy (*prīti*).

As for the thirty-six factors within the second dhyāna, because right practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) is itself a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), [the others] are not included. The rest is self-evident. Question: Regarding the three [liberations], what...?
Regarding the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpadhyāna*), how can the four factors beginning with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) exist there? The explanation says:

if judged according to their status (*avasthā*), the eightfold noble path belongs to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and since the three formless absorptions (*ārūpyadhyāna*) do not give rise to the path of vision, they should likewise lack [the path of vision]. However, in terms of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they do indeed possess them.

As for the twenty-two [factors] within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), these exclude the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path; this is because the factors of enlightenment and the path are non-existent [there].

Because they are subject to outflows (*āsrava*), the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) lacks them. Question: The four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) do not contemplate the matter of lower stages, and in their own respective stages there is likewise no such matter.

How, then, can the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) exist within the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*)? Answer: If one follows the perspective of the superior Dharma (*dharmaviśeṣa*), then even in the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, there is no application of mindfulness to the body.
However, according to our current interpretation, although one cannot contemplate the matter of lower stages [in that state], [the application of mindfulness to the body is still established].

It is with outflows (*sāsrava*). One attains the outflow-free state at the limit of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) through the contemplation of the four *dhyānas*. Question: What is the method of contemplating phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*)? Answer:

Regarding the discourse on the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are two types: first, the distinct contemplation of impurity; second, the skillful means of the contemplation of the truths (*satya-anupaśyanā*).

What is here called "existence within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) refers precisely to the inclusion of the objective field of the body within the truths; it is not a distinct [contemplation] from what was previously mentioned regarding existence.

Contemplating impurity. As for the "expedient means" mentioned above, it does not refer to a distinct stage of practice outside of the Truths (satya) for the purpose of establishing the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

Because it is not the fundamental basis of rational contemplation, it is called an "expedient means. Regarding the question of why there is no foundation of mindfulness of the body [in certain contexts], yet there is no mention of right speech, action, or precepts:
the answer is that they are absent because we are speaking in terms of the objects of contemplation; these objects extend across both the higher and lower stages.

One can observe from afar. The untainted (anāsrava) states of the lower stages are [absent here], because they serve to prevent wrongdoing according to their respective stages; thus, the factors of those stages do not exist [there].

In the Desire Realm and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), if one relies on the sequential order of the stages, there are likewise not twenty-two types [of mental factors], because the four minds such as "Heat" (uṣmagata) must arise based upon the six dhyānas.
Furthermore, in the Desire Realm and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, one cannot attain right effort (samyak-vyāyāma) as desired.

As for the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), what is now called "existence" refers to their occurrence within the path of practice (*caryā-mārga*). According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, there is no meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

therefore, [supernormal powers] such as the power of transformation (*rddhi*) cannot exist there. However, according to the Venerable Ghoṣaka, there is meditative concentration in the desire realm. Since the author of the treatise agrees with Ghoṣaka, the power of transformation and so forth do exist there.

As for the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not reside in the desire realm. This is consistent with...
This is identical to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*. Thus, the *Sūtravarga* states: "In the second dhyāna there are thirty-six; the same applies to the *anāgamya*.
In the third, fourth, and intermediate dhyānas, there are all thirty-five. For the first dhyāna it is said [to be] thirty-four; in the formless realms there are thirty-two;
in the highest [attainment] there are twenty-two; and the same applies to the desire realm. This is for those within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas; taken collectively—

This concludes the [section on] the bonds. From here below, we proceed to the explanation according to the Mahāyāna. First is the question, followed by the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts: first, the specific clarification of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*);

second, the discernment of the benefits of contemplation. Within the former, there are five sections; the first concerns the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

There is one section for a general synthesis, followed by four sections for individual explanations; thus, there are five gates in total. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, an explanation of the *sthāna* (bases);

second, a categorized explanation of the meaning of *samyakpradhāna* (right efforts) and *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power). Within the first of these, the four *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) are explained individually, constituting four subsections.
Within the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are two parts. First, a detailed explanation of the contemplation of the internal body;

second, the classification of the two bodies. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, a detailed analysis of the practice of contemplation; second, from "The Bodhisattva thus contemplates the true mark of the body" onwards, the benefits of such contemplative practice.
Within the first of these, there are three sections: first, the contemplation of the five aspects such as impermanence; second, the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the body...
Thus, knowing that it is not the characteristic of one's own body, one proceeds downward to enter the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Third, knowing that the body is without action and without an agent, one proceeds downward to enter the contemplation of the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Within the preceding section, there are five parts: first, clarifying the contemplation of impermanence and suffering;

second, clarifying the contemplation of impurity through the passage "impure and without outflows" (*aśubha-anāsrava*); third, clarifying [the cause] through the passage "due to the causes and conditions of having previously received tainted karma" (*sāsrava-karma-hetu-pratyaya*).

The contemplation of non-self and the contemplation of impermanence. Fourth, from "the bodily characteristics are not to be found within the body" onwards, it clarifies the contemplation of emptiness.

Fifth, from "the eighty thousand families of worms" onwards, it further clarifies the contemplation of suffering. Within the third contemplation, regarding the statement that the matter of the body is formed through the causes and conditions of two lifetimes:
the afflictions and karma of previous lives serve as the cause, while the parents of the present life serve as the condition. Proceeding from [this perspective]...
Within the gate of contemplation on arising, it is said that "one knows the body has no agent. This clarifies that by tracing from the origin to the end, [the self] is dispelled.
As for the statement, "it merely arises from the causes and conditions of various dharmas," this refers to the causes and conditions for the formation of the present body.

The phrase, "these various causes and conditions perform such and such [actions]," clarifies that this body arises from conditions and reveals that it is not real. It further states that it also arises from false and inverted [conceptions].
"Past" refers to the causes and conditions for the formation of the present body; it also arises from past afflictions (*kleśa*).

Within these causes and conditions, there is no characteristic of "causes and conditions" itself: within these causes and conditions that form the present body, there is neither past affliction nor karma capable of forming the causes and conditions for the present body. This is the characteristic of arising produced by these causes and conditions.
This refers to the bodily characteristics produced by present causes and conditions, which likewise cannot be apprehended.

Within the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), there are two parts: first, the question; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, a detailed clarification of internal feeling.
The subsequent section classifies the two types of sensation (*vedanā*). The preceding section has two parts: first, the actual exposition of the contemplative practice;

second, from "knowing thus" onwards, the conclusion regarding the benefits of the contemplation. The first part has three sections: first, performing the contemplation of the three aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*);

second, from "having contemplated these sensations of the three periods of time" onwards, transitioning into the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); third, from "also contemplating all arising and ceasing" onwards, transitioning into...

Regarding the contemplation on the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda-dvāra*), within the section on the benefits of concluding the contemplation, it is said: "The mind does not receive" means it does not receive suffering;
"it does not cling" means it does not cling to pleasure; "it does not rely on the correct" means it does not rely on that which is neither painful nor pleasant.

Regarding the explanation of the mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are two parts: first, the question; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, the explanation of internal contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*);

second, the categorization of the two types of mind. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the detailed analysis of the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-caryā*); second, from "By means of this, the mind becomes pure" onwards.
Regarding the benefits of concluding the contemplation, there are two parts in the preceding section: first, the practice of the three modes of contemplating impermanence;
second, from "having realized that the characteristics of the mind are non-arising" onwards, the transition into the contemplation of non-arising.

Within the conclusion on the benefits of the contemplation, the statement "by this, the essence of the mind is pure and cannot be defiled by adventitious afflictions" clarifies that the substance of the mind is free from defilement and cannot be entangled by various delusions.
Question: Since afflictions exist together with the mind, why are they called "guests"? Answer: The mind pervades the three natures and exists at all times;
thus it is called the "host. Afflictions, however, pertain only to two of the natures and are absent within the wholesome; they arrive temporarily and can be dispelled.
This is called being a "guest. The remaining textual passages are self-evident; let the student reflect upon them for themselves.

Within the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there are two parts: first, the question, and second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two further sections: first, the detailed explanation of internal phenomena.
The subsequent section follows the same pattern as the previous two. The first part is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the contemplation of specific characteristics;

second, from "When contemplating in this manner" onwards, the summary of the completion of the contemplation. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the internal contemplation of the three emptinesses;
second, from "Because it is non-active, one does not see dharmas arising or ceasing," the transition into the contemplation of non-arising.

Regarding the explanation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), there are two parts. First, a brief presentation of the two gates of contemplation and cultivation. Second, a detailed explanation of these two gates. Within this, there are two sections:

first, an extensive explanation of the cultivation of the five faculties; second, from "The bodhisattva, having attained these five faculties and thoroughly knowing the faculties of sentient beings" onwards, an explanation of the preceding gate of contemplation.
Within the former, the detailed explanation of the five faculties is divided into five segments, each one [addressing a faculty].

Within each of these, there are three parts: first the introduction, next the explanation, and finally the conclusion. According to the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, there are seven sections concerning the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), whereas for the "non-practice of all dharmas" (*sarvadharmāpracāra*), there is only one section.
Regarding the statement, "With faith as the foremost, one abides well in the upholding of precepts," this refers to the purity of non-decline regarding the precepts (*śīle 'vetyaprasāda*).
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), taking the precepts as the object, the ability to believe that the precepts are indestructible is called [the faculty of faith].
Purity. If one follows the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya*, untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts are indestructible; they are not pure because they are subject to destruction.
Rather, it is through the arising of faith regarding their objective sphere that they are now considered pure. Here, the Master of the Treatise agrees with the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya*.

Regarding the phrase "relying on the retribution of karma," this refers to the indestructible faith in the Buddha, clarifying that the Tathāgata attains retribution based upon untainted karma. This is distinct from all heterodox views.
"Seeing" refers to not relying on the wrong views of non-Buddhist ascetic practices, such as [the fruit of] the *kaṇḍa* plant;

furthermore, one does not believe in other teachings, but accepts only the Buddha-dharma—this is the indestructible purity (*aveccappasāda*) regarding the Dharma. To say that "the Saṅgha dwells in the path of reality" is the indestructible faith in the Saṅgha.
Within the explanation of the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*), "skillfully knowing the objects of perception" means skillfully knowing the five kinds of objects.
First is the condition of name; second, the condition of meaning; third, the condition of mental characteristics; fourth, the condition of the characteristic of exertion;

and fifth, the condition of the characteristic of equanimity. To discern and thoroughly understand these five types is called "skillful knowledge. Regarding the five types of decline, they are termed "deteriorating conditions.

This continues through the textual descriptions of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), which are easy to understand. When a Bodhisattva attains these five faculties and skillfully knows the faculties of sentient beings, from this point downward—

The faculties (*indriya*) are not fixed; through the sixteen [aspects], one knows the faculties of the assemblies of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Having explained the bodhisattva’s practice regarding these five faculties, the following clarifies the five powers (*bala*). Within this, there are two parts: first, an analysis according to the dharmas; second, a correlation with persons.
Based on the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, the explanation of the five powers consists of eleven sections; here, it is presented in extreme brevity.

Regarding the explanation of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), there are two parts: first, a brief explanation of their names and meanings; second, a detailed explanation through questions and answers. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, the citation [of the topic], followed by the explanation. Regarding the explanation, according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there are three stages for understanding the meaning of the seven factors of enlightenment.

Now, regarding the explanation of the seven factors of enlightenment, this is precisely what the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Those who do not enter the triple world observe that the essence of the triple world is empty, and thus they differ from ordinary beings.
Those who do not destroy the characteristics of the dharma-realm observe that the essence of dharmas is empty, and thus they differ from those of the two vehicles."

That sutra states directly: "One does not grasp at the characteristics of the triple world. Because one thoroughly destroys the characteristics of the triple world, it appears as if the latter [explanation] serves to clarify the former two lines, which have no distinction.
Within the extensive clarification of the question and answer, there are two parts: first, a brief indication of the four types of awakening; second, an extensive clarification of the three.
The textual structure is easy to understand.

Within the Eightfold Noble Path, there are two parts: first, the restatement [of the headings], and second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, explaining by referring to the preceding categories;
second, an extensive explanation of the latter four. This explanation consists of four segments. Regarding the explanation of Right Thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), there are three parts:

first, the presentation; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, extensively citing the erroneous to manifest the correct; second, the Bodhisattva’s faith in this manner.

The section on "Right Reflection" below clarifies the characteristics of right practice. Within this, there are two parts: first, a brief clarification of the two types of practice—erroneous and correct;
second, from "Why is this? onwards, an explanation of the meaning of erroneous and correct [practice].

Regarding the first part, the statement that reflecting upon *nirvāṇa* and reflecting upon the Buddha are both erroneous reflections refers to the fact that loving the Buddha and loving the practice of *bodhi* is called "right reflection. If one relies on the ten...

The *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Stages) explains the four stages in the "Chapter on the Path. The current exposition of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) appears to correspond to the eighth stage and above.

As explained previously regarding the five powers (*pañca-bala*), it is also said that one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, as stated below, one enters the rank of a bodhisattva. Thus, the overall meaning is difficult to definitively establish.
If one relies on the extensive explanation in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it is briefly clarified in the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa Sūtra*. Within this present text:
This is largely identical to the *Apraṇihita-sūtra*.
Regarding the explanation of right speech (*samyag-vāc*), there are two parts: first, the presentation of the topic; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two sections:

first, an explanation by way of meaning; second, a citation of the sūtra. Within the former, there are two points: first, clarifying that the Bodhisattva knows all speech to be determinate; second, the practice of the Bodhisattva.
From "Right Speech" onwards, it clarifies that which can constitute right teaching.

Within Right Action, there are three parts: first, the introduction; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. In the explanation, there are three sections: first, a brief explanation of Right Action;
second, a refutation of attachments through question-and-answer to reveal Right Action; and third, [the section on] how all Bodhisattvas enter into all actions.

Below, it clarifies that the equality of the right and the true constitutes right action (*samyak-karmānta*). Regarding the second section, the refutation of attachments, there are four questions and answers.

The first question and answer refutes the attachments of the Śrāvakas to clarify the emptiness of karma. The subsequent three questions and answers refute the attachments of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to clarify that karma has no fixed nature.
These three questions and answers successively refute attachments; within the first of these, the question comes first and the answer follows. Within the question:
In the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the "Examination of Going and Coming" (*Gatāgata-parīkṣā*) contains twenty-five verses. Within it, an objection is raised:
"The world perceives with its own eyes that activity exists in the three times—what has been gone over, what has not yet been gone over, and the time of going.

Because activity exists, one should know that phenomena exist. The intent of this question is largely the same as that [of the previous objection]. In the response, it is clarified that the essence of all actions is empty and lacks the distinction of these three [times]; therefore, regarding...

In the three times, it is clarified that there is no action (*karman*). Thus, that treatise states: "The answer is: in what has already gone, there is no going; in what has not yet gone, there is also no going;

apart from what has already gone and what has not yet gone, in the process of going (*gamyamāna*), there is likewise no going. The prose commentary explains: "In what has already gone, there is no going, because it has already gone.
If one were to claim that there is the action of going apart from [the state of] having gone, this is not so. In what has not yet gone, there is also no going..."

Because there is the phenomenon of going (*gati*). The "time of going" (*gamyamāna*) is called half-gone and half-not-yet-gone, for it is not separate from what has already been gone over and what has not yet been gone over.
In the second question-and-answer section, the intent of the question is identical to that of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*; thus, the text states: Question: Where there is motion, there is going.

Herein there is the time of going, which is neither what has already been gone over nor what has not yet been gone over. Therefore, going occurs during the time of going. The prose commentary explains this as follows:
It is said: Wherever there is the locus of an action, there must be going. For one observes that at the time of "presently going," the action is present;
in that which has already gone, the action has ceased; and in that which has not yet gone, the action does not yet exist. Therefore, going exists at the time of "presently going.
[This] removes the action from the single response; now, the locus of going cannot be found. This is according to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, which states: "Apart from going..."
The time of going (*gamyamāna*) cannot be apprehended. The dharma of going (*gamana*) would have to exist within this time of going;

the act of going would have to exist within this time of going. As that verse says: "How could there be a dharma of going within the time of going? If one is separated from the [act of] going, the time of going cannot be apprehended.
The prose commentary explains: "The claim that 'there is going within the time of going' is untenable. Why? Because it is separated from the dharma of going."
It cannot be apprehended. Now, as for the statement that if one were to remove action, the locus of going could be apprehended—this refers to the second alternative:
if there were a time of going apart from the act of going, then there would have to be going during that time of going, like fruit inside a vessel.

In the response to the second [alternative], it is said that there would be two acts of going at once; this is the logical explanation of the meaning: a locus does not abide in itself, but depends upon...
When action (*karman*) is distinguished, its locus (*sthāna*) is not fixed; yet action does not act of itself, but relies upon a locus to be distinguished.
Thus, when action is not fixed, it is merely a conventional designation for a locus based on the harmony of causes and conditions, and a conventional designation for action.

However, the outsider’s view is that both locus and action each possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Yet, a locus does not become a locus of itself; there must be the action of going for a locus to exist.

Regarding the statement that "one who has already departed" and "one who is currently departing" both exist, they are situated in the middle; therefore, it is said that there are two acts of going (*gati-karman*).

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* also states: "First, there is going because of the time of going; second, there is going within the time of going. However, an act does not act by itself; it exists through [the agent].

Since there are thus three acts, there must be two [distinct agents]. If there are two [agents], then when one person is in the process of going... [text missing] ...it would follow that [there are two goers].
"The goer has departed. He replied: "The 'goer' who is said to have departed cannot be apprehended. This is the answer based on the middle [section].
Furthermore, to provide a brief citation of the first section from that text: "If one is separated from going, the phenomenon of going cannot be apprehended.
Since the phenomenon of going does not exist, how can there be a goer? This is called true wisdom; it is precisely the correct [view].
As for "action" (*karmānta*): it refers to that which resembles the essence of right action; it is actual wisdom.

Furthermore, it is the action that can arise based on actual wisdom, yet without perceiving "wrong" or "right," that is properly termed "right action. If one perceives there to be wrong or right, all such [perceptions] are termed "wrong.
Regarding "not creating": one does not create wrong action. Regarding "not performing": one does not perform right action. The remainder of the text is understandable.

The explanation of right livelihood has three parts: first, the introduction; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, manifesting pure livelihood in relation to conditions;

second, manifesting pure livelihood in terms of reality, beginning with "Abiding in the wisdom free from conceptual proliferation. The aforementioned factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) constitute the practice for the definitive cessation [of afflictions].

In the twentieth treatise, the following three samādhis are the gateways through which one enters into practice; the four dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are the basis upon which practice relies;

and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and those below them are the skillful means for initiating practice. Furthermore, this is divided into three parts: first, the elucidation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); second, the elucidation of the excellence of nirvāṇa.
Practice. The accomplishment of practice must necessarily enter through a gateway; therefore, the second [section] clarifies the three samādhis as the gateways to nirvāṇa.

A gateway does not open of its own accord, but by means of the superior practices of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). For these superior practices to be established, skillful means (upāya) are required;
therefore, the third [section], from the four dhyānas down to the nine notions (navasaṃjñā), contains eight types of practice that clarify the skillful means that assist superior practice.

The Method for Opening the Door: These three and four [categories] all discuss what is called "self-proclamation. Regarding the term *śūnyatā-samādhi* (emptiness-concentration): these three types differ in their nomenclature;
some call them the "three samādhis," others the "three gates of liberation" (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), and still others the "three gates of emptiness.

As for the term *samādhi*, it is the correct phonetic transcription from the Western Regions (India); here in this land, it is translated as "wholesome mind" (*kuśala-citta*), referring to the continuous succession of the mental nature.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: Question: For what reason is it called "samādhi"? Answer: It is named samādhi for three reasons:
first, by means of correctness; second, by means of gathering; and third, by means of continuity. Regarding "correctness":
since beginningless time, afflictions, evil conduct, false views, and inversions have caused the mind and mental factors to become turbid and disturbed. Thus, it [the samādhi] causes them...

That they are upright is due to the power of samādhi. Regarding what is called "gathering," it means that from time immemorial, the mind and mental factors have been scattered among sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas; therefore, they are gathered so as not to be dispersed.
That they abide in the middle is due to the power of samādhi. Regarding what is called "continuity," it means that the mind and mental factors give rise to three kinds of mind in succession.

Next, regarding their sequential arising: because one is able to abandon two kinds of mind and cause only wholesome states of mind to continue in succession, all of this is due to the power of *samādhi*.
Possessing these three meanings, it is called *samādhi*. There are three different types of *samādhi*: namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
As for "emptiness," the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) being devoid of self and what belongs to self is termed emptiness; this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

The meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with this wisdom is calm and stable; it is free from distraction, disciplined, and upright. Possessing these three meanings, it is called *samādhi*. Regarding "signless" (*animitta*):

because one takes as an object that which is free from the ten signs, and because signs such as male and female are entirely non-existent, it is called signless. The *samādhi* is the same as before. Regarding "wishless" (*apraṇihita*):
because one no longer forms any further volitional constructions regarding the causes and effects within the three realms of existence, it is called wishless. The *samādhi* is the same as before.

The same as before. These are all explained according to the Hīnayāna. If one proceeds from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, the suchness (*tathatā*) of the essence of all phenomena is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
That emptiness has no substantial form or characteristics is called signlessness (*animitta*). Because it is signless, there is no further seeking or wishing;

this is termed wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Thus, these are designations for the union of mind and object: emptiness, signlessness, and so forth are the objects, while that which is called samādhi is the mind.
Regarding the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*): that which is the aforementioned absence of self and what belongs to self (*anātman-anātmīya*) is called "emptiness.

Since one takes emptiness itself as the gate, it is named the "gate of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-mukha*). As for "signlessness" (*animitta*): the absence of the ten factors such as male and female is called "signlessness.
