By severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the fourth dhyāna, one attains the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Regarding these three types of skillful means (*upāya*), their number is not fixed across the sūtras and śāstras;

for instance, in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), only the second skillful means is present. Thus, that treatise states: "That which transcends all perceptions of form" refers to transcending the eye...

Regarding "by means of consciousness and perception": "extinguishing all perceptions of resistance" refers to the extinguishing of the perceptions associated with the conjunction of ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses.

"Not attending to any perceptions of diversity" refers to not attending to the perceptions associated with the conjunction of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is mental consciousness alone that discriminates all phenomena;
thus, it is described as the perception of diversity. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, only the latter two [perceptions] are clarified, while the former ones are not discussed.
Among these, the first two are present, while the last one is missing. The method for wearying and destroying [the object] has already been explained in the section on the higher dhyānas;
therefore, it is not discussed here. What is now referred to as "transcending the characteristics of form" refers to visible and resistant form (*sanidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*).

"Entering the cessation of the characteristics of resistance" refers to the five sense faculties and four sense objects, which are invisible and resistant form (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*). "Not recollecting the characteristic of distinctness" refers to...
Non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is invisible and non-obstructive form; it is merely divided into three locations due to differences in the pedagogical approach (*upāya-mukha*).
There is no sequence of priority or posteriority in its cessation. This concludes the first preliminary skillful means for the conceptual cessation of form.

The second question and answer. The question comes first, followed by the answer. The intent of the question is: since all taught dharmas each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even if one performs contemplation, how can they be extinguished?
The answer contains three parts: first, clarifying the contemplation of falsity and unreality; second, further clarifying the contemplation of impermanence and signlessness;
third, further clarifying the contemplation of relinquishing the inferior to seek the superior.

Regarding the third explanation, there are two instances of citing a sūtra; the former is understandable. In the second instance, it says that because the eye sees the destruction of forms (*rūpa*), it is called "transcending forms" (*atīta-rūpa*).

This next passage clarifies the second type of mental application: the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-vyupaśama*). It states that "transcending forms" means the cessation of the perceptions associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna-saṃprayukta-saṃjñā*).
Since this should have already been transcended at the time of becoming detached from the desire of the first dhyāna, why is it only now that "transcending forms" is mentioned?
According to the explanation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are three kinds of faults (*doṣa*): first, the basis of the fault; second, the range of activity of the fault;

and third, the dwelling place of the fault. Regarding the basis of the fault, there are further two types: first, the support of the fault; and second, the objective basis of the fault. This occurs at the time of departing from desire for the first dhyāna.

It transcends the basis for the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). "Basis" refers to eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*). When one becomes free from desire for the fourth dhyāna, it transcends the basis for the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*).

"Basis" here refers to the eye [and its faculty]. Furthermore, there are two kinds of "range of activity" (*gocara*): first, that which is transcended by what is abandoned; second, that which is transcended by the range of activity itself.

When one becomes free from desire for the first dhyāna, it transcends the range of activity. "Range of activity" refers to the afflictions associated with the perception of eye-consciousness; these are associated with what is to be abandoned.
Bondage. When one is free from the desire for the fourth dhyāna, there is the transcendence of active functioning (*samudācāra*).

Active functioning refers to the fact that although visual consciousness is absent within the fourth dhyāna, perception (*saṃjñā*) may still manifest by borrowing the consciousness of the first dhyāna. Because one has left the fourth dhyāna, even the mind that borrows this consciousness ceases.

Furthermore, the transcendence of the dwelling place (*sthāna*) is of two kinds: first, the transcendence of desire-attachment; second, the transcendence of the dwelling place itself. This refers to being free from the desire of the first dhyāna.

At that time, one transcends the perception of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*). "Sensual desire" refers to the conceptualization and binding of eye-consciousness. When one leaves behind the desire for the fourth dhyāna, one transcends the "abode" (*sthāna*). "Abode" refers to the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).

As for the statement "one transcends the perception of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*) up to the destruction of the perception of cognition": this means that from the ear and sound up to the mind and mental objects, these are called perceptions of resistance because they are subject to decay and destruction.

This refers to the cessation of the perceptions associated with the nose, ear, tongue, and body. However, the perceptions associated with the consciousnesses of the nose and tongue have already ceased when one is free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The perceptions associated with the consciousnesses of the ear and body have already ceased when one is free from desire for the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*).

Why, then, is their cessation mentioned only now? According to the *Vibhāṣā*, it is as previously answered. That which is called "cessation" refers to the cessation of the activities [associated with them]; all such activities...
That which is capable of producing the perception of resistance (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*) is entirely extinguished when one becomes detached from the desire for the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding the statement "in two kinds," the first is the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), and the second consists of the four [subtle] particles. The remaining forms are the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), and the "innumerable forms" are unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

To clarify the perception of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the fourth [dhyāna], it is called "diverse perception" (*nānātva-saṃjñā*) because it takes these eleven bases as its cognitive objects. This refers to the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Since they have already abandoned [them], it is called "mindfulness. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason does one cultivate various perceptions?

Because one takes the various bases (*āyatana*) as objects. Those that are defiled take ten bases as objects; those that are non-defiled take twelve bases as objects. If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:

The characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. This characteristic of form is precisely that which possesses resistance and obstruction (*sapratigha*).

The characteristic of difference (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to things such as bells and drums. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-nirgrantha-sūtra*, the characteristic of form refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four objects (*viṣaya*).

These alone constitute the characteristics of resistance and difference; there is no separate dharma [beyond them]. That sūtra considers the four great elements and the four objects to be what is called "form."
Since this is the root [text], I shall clarify it alone.

Regarding the statement that "four of the formless [realms] are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*)," this constitutes the second section, the analysis of their essential nature (*svabhāva-vibhāga*).

Within this, there are eighteen distinct sections, which together comprise thirteen main headings. The first concerns whether they are with-outflows or without-outflows (*anāsrava*); the second concerns whether they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

3. With retribution and without retribution; 4. Cultivated and uncultivated; 5. Defiled and undefiled; 6. Existence and non-existence; 7. Associated and dissociated; 8. The four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are five gates: 1. Wholesome (*kuśala*); 2. Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); 3. Tainted (*āsrava*); 4. With outflows (*sāsrava*); 5. Without outflows (*anāsrava*).
These all consist of four propositions. 9. The three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*); 10. Mental association and non-mental association; 11. Concomitant with the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).

The four propositions regarding the correspondence of practice (*caryā-saṃprayukta*). Twelve [categories] are distinguished by three propositions based on the cause of the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

Thirteen [categories] are distinguished by the four conditions (*pratyaya*), which constitute four separate propositions; thus, there are eighteen gates. Now, within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there are five kinds of four aggregates (*skandha*):

first, obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); second, non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); third, wholesome through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*); fourth, wholesome acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*); fifth, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The outflows are wholesome. Now, they shall be analyzed in detail through various Dharma-gates. Regarding the statement "one is to be considered as having outflows," this is based on the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (or *Saṃyutta-nikāya*).
Previously, there were three gates such as the formless realm (*ārūpya*) and so forth; here, the one that "is to be considered as having outflows" is omitted for brevity.

This refers to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), because the Great King of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) does not dwell in a peripheral region. Regarding the "three that are to be analyzed": as for the outflows of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*)...

There are four kinds of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*). Those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) are the untainted four aggregates. When it is said that "all are conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), it is because they have not yet been exempted from the nature of transition.
When it is said that the wholesome tainted sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) "has retribution" (*savipāka*), this refers to the two kinds of the four aggregates:

innate wholesomeness (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) and acquired wholesomeness (*prāyogika-kuśala*). That which is neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted has no retribution; these are the two kinds of neutral [states] and the untainted.

Regarding the four aggregates (*skandha*), within this framework of various matters, there are further five gates such as "arising from causes and conditions" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As for the statement that "wholesome formless states are to be cultivated":

the three types of wholesome formless states—those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), those produced through application (*prāyogika*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*)—possess the sense of being able to be increased, clarified, and progressively practiced;

therefore, they are to be cultivated. As for the statement that "the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are not to be cultivated": this refers to [the indeterminate states] consisting of fruition (*vipāka*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Because two types of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) have ceased, there is no sense of further progress, cultivation, or increasing clarity. Regarding the term "disappearance," it refers specifically to the disappearance of one type of the four aggregates;

as for those that do not disappear, they are the remaining four types of the four aggregates. According to the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (or *Kṣudraka-vastu*), within this context there are still the four gates such as "this fruit" and so forth.
As for the statement "one existence" (*eka-bhava*), it means that the essence of the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) is contaminated (*sāsrava*).

Bound [to existence]. There is not a single [state] that exists; the remaining three may be understood accordingly. Regarding the statement that dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*):

this refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), acquisition (*prāpti*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), the category of sentient beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and so forth.

Regarding the statement that there are dharmas that are not among the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) nor included within the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless realm: this refers to the two lower realms.
The four aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are wholesome but not formless (*ārūpya*). In the fourth clause, space (*ākāśa*) is not exhausted by knowledge;
it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and is therefore neither a wholesome dharma nor formless. As for those among the unwholesome dharmas that are not mutually subsumed:
In the higher realms, there is no unwholesome [dharmas]. Therefore, they are not subsumed [by the unwholesome]. Regarding the statement "one outflow (āsrava) and a portion of two outflows":

the one outflow refers to the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava); the two outflows refer to the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava) and the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava). Since these all exclude the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu), they are called "a portion."
These are the outflows (*āsrava*), yet they are not formless (*ārūpya*). Regarding the statement that the outflows do not include the four formless states:

this means that within the formless realm, retributive neutral states, innate wholesome states, acquired wholesome states, and untainted (*anāsrava*) states are all not outflow phenomena; therefore, it is said that they are not included.
Regarding the statement "neither outflows (*āsrava*) nor the four formless [aggregates]": because the essence of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is not affliction, it is not an outflow;

because it is form, it is not among the four formless [aggregates]. Regarding the statement "and those not included among the outflows or the formless aggregates, which consist of the four aggregates":

this refers to the two types of wholesome states—the self-purifying (*svabhāva-śuddha*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)—of the two lower realms, as well as the four untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates. These various dharmas are, first, not included among the outflows, and second, not included among the formless [aggregates].
[Included]. However, among the various statements, those that say "not included in the formless" (*ārūpya*) all refer to dharmas of the lower realms. Question:

What is the difference between "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*), such that two sets of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are required? Explanation: Outflows are exclusively afflictions (*kleśa*);

being with-outflows extends to both afflictions and non-afflictions. This is the distinction. According to the *Saṅgītiparyāya*, regarding the fourfold propositions of the formless realm, [the latter... remains.

There are three gates, such as the three time periods. Regarding the phrase "a portion of the three formless [aggregates]," it means that within the three formless [realms], there are five kinds of four aggregates;
however, one takes only the untainted (anāsrava) four aggregates. Because these are not taken in their entirety, they are called "a portion. This is because they are untainted.

Regarding the fourfold classification of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*): when it says "one formless realm," this refers to the tainted state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and a portion of the three lower formless realms.
It is called a "portion" because the untainted four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) are excluded; the rest may be understood by reflection.

Regarding the phrase "among those that follow the mental feeling (cittānuparivartin)," the expression "excluding those formations dissociated from mind that follow the mind" means excluding the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) of the feeling and the mind themselves.
These are excluded because they are about to be categorized as non-concomitants; therefore, they are removed first.
The phrase "the remaining formations dissociated from mind" refers to the other mental factors (caitasika-dharmas), whose four characteristics do not follow the mind, and...
Regarding the association with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*), according to the *Saṃgītiparyāya*, following these [points], there are still two further sections concerning vitarka and vicāra.

As for the statement that "proceeding from the cause of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it does not again act as a cause for the self," the author of the treatise intends to formulate the first proposition;

thus, he first excludes the second proposition without specifically pointing out the first. That which is distinguished [as the first] refers to the non-universal proclivities (*asarvatraga-anuśaya*) found within the category of the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) throughout the three periods of time.
In the cultivation of the path of cessation, one abandons all afflictions (*kleśa*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*), such as the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

These arise solely from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) acting as a pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*); they cannot, in turn, give rise to the view of a self-identity. Why is this so? Because it is not a pervasive latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it cannot function as a pervasive cause.
Because it is of a different category, it is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*). Because it belongs to a different class, it is not an associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).

Regarding the cause: the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) can function as a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). However, because one wishes to establish three categories [of causes], it is not analyzed in terms of the productive cause.
As for that which is a cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and, in turn, acts as a cause for the view of a self-identity:

these are the remaining factors mentioned above, namely, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the lower realm (the desire realm) pertaining to suffering in the past and present, along with their associated mental factors (*caitasika*) such as the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the pervasive underlying tendencies of the lower realm pertaining to origination in the past and present, together with—
These associated factors coexist with such dharmas. Arising from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they in turn act as causes for that very view of a self-identity.

When the view of a self-identity is considered in relation to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the category of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it acts as both a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); when considered in relation to those of the category of origin (*samudaya-satya*), it acts only as a pervasive cause.
Among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), if they are universal (*sarvatraga*), they act as two causes to produce the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

If they are not universal, they act only as their own respective cause. Regarding the universal latent dispositions of the lower realm that produce the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), they act only as universal causes.

As for the production of the view of a self in the past and present, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not mentioned because they are omitted. Furthermore, regarding the exclusion of the view of a self within the future time, it is not that the view of a self is excluded; rather—

Excluding the factors associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and its concomitants, because these can function as associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) with the view of a self-identity due to being co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Furthermore, if one were to say that there are also homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) within the future time, then one must exclude the view of a self-identity;

this is because a future view of a self-identity can serve as a cause for [a present] view of a self-identity. If that were so, then regarding the afflictions of the suffering category in the future time...

The afflictions (*kleśa*) and the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the lower realms, when compared to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), all possess their own respective pervasive causes (*svabhāva-sarvatraga-hetu*).
Why, then, are they not excluded? The explanation states: In the future, there truly exist homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* says:

"Furthermore, some teachers state that within the future time, there also exist similar causes and pervasive causes. As for why the various masters [state this], it is because of the similar cause (*sādṛśya-hetu*).

Because the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is not yet exhausted, it is designated as a cause; however, that which has the power to give and take its fruit—when considering the future in relation to the future—is unable to give or take its fruit, and therefore it is not mentioned.

As for the statement "also excluding the arising, aging, duration, and cessation of the view of a self" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), this refers to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the future view of a self and its associated factors (*paryavasthāna*);
these also function as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the view of a self.

Because of this reason, since the previous sentence has already stated "future," this sentence does not state it separately. Furthermore, another interpretation is that this excludes the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) across the three time periods.
Thus, the future four characteristics, in relation to the view of a self-identity, possess only the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

The past and present four characteristics, in relation to the view of a self-identity, universally possess both the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*). If this were the case, [regarding] the past and present view of a self-identity and...

Regarding associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*): why are they not excluded? The explanation states that because they pertain generally to the present and are included among those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are not excluded separately.
As for the phrase "stainless space" (*vimalākāśa*), this refers to the retributive neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), the two types of wholesome, and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
According to the *Saṅgītiparyāya*, there are still two categories here: karma and retribution. Within the section on the four conditions (*catuḥ-pratyaya*), it mentions the Arhat.

Regarding the phrase "at the time of cessation after [the preceding moment]," because the subsequent mind and mental factors arise from the immediately preceding mind, this sequence does not further project a subsequent consciousness;
therefore, it is not a *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition), and it should also not be the *manodhātu* (mind-element). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* explains:

"The elements (*dhātu*) are established by way of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the conditions (*pratyaya*) are established by way of their function (*karma*); thus, their meanings are not analogous.
