The passage beginning with "Why is this so? explains and resolves the preceding objection. The meaning is that [the effect] cannot be apprehended in any way;

this constitutes a specific refutation of the four conditions according to the Exegetical School (*Vyākhyāna-vādin*), clarifying that while the "disease" (the misconception) is removed, the "dharma" (the causal condition) is not.

Since the Questioner school raises the objection that the dharma must be removed, this initial section first establishes two logical alternatives to refute it. If one were to say that the effect pre-exists within the cause, then since the effect already exists, [it would follow that...]
It is not necessary to establish the principle that an effect exists without a cause by means of production from causes. Therefore, the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states:
"If the effect were to exist beforehand—just as parents are the cause and the child is the effect—if the effect were to exist beforehand, then it would have to exist simultaneously with them."
If both exist simultaneously, they would be like brothers. If the fruit did not previously exist, what would serve as the cause for this fruit?
Furthermore, for what reason could that cause be designated as a "cause"? To say that it produces a fruit is like saying that when water and milk are together, there is no curd;
yet, by that logic, the curd should also be obtainable from the water alone.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, from the absence of a cause" and below constitutes the objection regarding the fulfillment of the argument.
If one were to say in empty words that this effect did not previously exist, then this effect could likewise arise without a cause. Why? Because the effect is absent within the cause.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover, having seen that the effect arises from a cause," the underlying intention is as follows:
Since one observes that an effect arises from a cause and thus designates it as a "cause," if the effect did not previously exist, how could one designate the cause by the name of the effect?

For example, because one sees milk produce curd, milk is called the "cause of curd. If you say [the effect] does not exist [in the cause], then it likewise does not exist in water; consequently, [curd] should also arise from water.
It emerges. One should know that it cannot be said to have been previously non-existent.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning "If the effect arises from a cause," this clarifies that if this effect arises from a cause, it then belongs to that cause.
Since a cause is dependent upon conditions and lacks self-mastery, it might follow that the effect could also arise from other causes.
If this were so, why do you say only that the effect arises from this cause and not from others? This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, following the previous section on past minds and mental factors, we now proceed to refute the second [type of] sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Above, it was clarified that for an Arhat, with the exception of the final mind of the present moment, all past and present minds can only be considered "sequential" in name;

because they have completely ceased and are without further mentation, they cannot act as conditions to produce subsequent sequential minds. If this is so, then these various minds are likewise [incapable of producing subsequent conditions]. This concludes the point.
There is the sense of total cessation. The sense of cessation is called "non-existence.

Since non-existence is a non-entity, how can it be said that past minds and mental factors can serve as the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) for the existence of present minds and mental factors?
Furthermore, if the past mind were to exist, it would not be a "past" mind; if it does not exist, it cannot function as an immediately preceding condition to produce the present.

Mind. If that were so, then there would be no present mind. The same logic applies to the arising of future [dharmas], which shall be explained below in the section beginning with "All dharmas are without marks and without objects.

Next, the meaning of the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) is refuted. Since it was stated that the mind takes an object as its condition, and these two—mind and object—are spoken of together, they are called the "object-condition";
yet, since it has already been said that all dharmas are without marks and without objects, [there can be no such condition].
Because there are no characteristics, there is no object; because there is no condition, there is no mind. If this is so, what meaning does "conditioning" have?

From the passage beginning with "If all dharmas have no belonging," it clarifies that since all dharmas are equal—having neither belonging nor reliance—what meaning does "predominance" (adhipati) have within the dharma of equality?
Yet it is said that when one dharma arises, the ten thousand dharmas do not obstruct it.
Therefore, one takes all phenomena as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for oneself. This will now be explained.
The answer begins with: "You do not know the characteristics of Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth.

The meaning of this is that within Prajñāpāramitā, when it is said that the four conditions cannot be apprehended, this merely eliminates the disease [of false attachment] and does not eliminate the phenomena themselves. That is to say:

Within the profound waves of the Prajñāpāramitā of the illumination of Dharma, there is nothing that can be abandoned; since there is nothing to abandon and nothing to destroy, form itself is emptiness, and afflictions themselves are bodhi.
Therefore, it is said that the four elements and empty space are distinct, yet the nature of the four elements is itself the nature of empty space.
All of this is the emptiness of the illumination of Dharma, which does not obstruct the diversity of phenomena. You—
That which is attained is spoken of as the "Dharma of Destruction. To say it is "unattainable" would be an obstruction; it should rather be explained thus:
the passage beginning with "those of little wisdom" clarifies that because ordinary people cling to views, these must be removed.
If such clinging ceases, then the myriad dharmas present no obstruction. It is like being lost, whereby the four directions appear disordered; once awakened, all is vast and empty.
Since the sides are already aligned and thus achieve rectitude, how could emptiness be attained only after removing phenomena? You instead destroy phenomena, claiming that emptiness is pure;
this is called "seeing forms with one's eyes while being like a blind person. If one can remain unattached to forms, then as for the various objects before one: [they are empty].
It has no concern with my own affairs. It is called "empty" because it is unimpeded with respect to me; it is called "existent" because it is impeded for those who are attached.
However, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are empty. Since emptiness itself is not a [substantial] phenomenon, there is truly nothing to be refuted.
This concludes the clarification of the meaning of the non-disruption of dependent origination. Third, the six causes are used to explain the four conditions in detail.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as mental phenomena arise from the conjunction of internal and external bases and conditions," which was previously stated would be explained extensively later regarding the meaning of the five causes—
it is precisely from this point onward that they are explained in detail. Since the *saṃprayuktaka-hetu* (associated cause) is to be explained first among these,
the text first clarifies the principle that although all phenomena arise from internal and external causes and conditions, they are deceptive and do not exist without such causes and conditions.
Arising is like the moon in water; although it is unreal, it nevertheless relies upon the moon in the water as a causal condition, yet it does not produce a stone moon.
All phenomena are likewise: though the mind is like an illusion, it is not devoid of the correspondence of causal conditions.
Just as dream-events, though unreal, arise because of dreams, so too are the mental factors (caitta-dharma) and other such things, for they lack a fixed nature.

Because they are unreal, they arise from the mind and function in conjunction with the mental factors (*caitasika*). "The king of the mind" refers to the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); "factors" refers to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

Thus, among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), only three factors are mentioned. As for the statement that there is "one form and one mind," this is done for the sake of those sentient beings who harbor doubts regarding the factors;
thus, for those who doubt form, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are taught, and for those who doubt both form and mind, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) are taught.

The meanings of the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth shall now be explained. Thus, when the mind intends to take form (*rūpa*) as its object, sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and the others likewise follow that object, just as a minister follows his lord.

This is the case when intending to take sound (*śabda*) and so forth as objects. These—sensation, perception, volition, and the rest—belong to the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-citta-dharma*).

Although there are five categories, they do not exceed the general and the specific. The general refers to the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), while the specific refers to the five classes.

Because the universal factors extend vertically through the three realms and horizontally through the five classes, they are termed "general" in number. The specific, meanwhile, refers to those within the five classes.
There is also a sense in which they pervade all three realms; however, the wholesome factors do not pervade the unwholesome, and the unwholesome factors do not pervade the wholesome.

This is unlike the "great ground" factors, which universally pervade both the wholesome and the unwholesome. These [factors] merely maintain their own respective categories, and for this reason they are called "distinct.

According to the Abhidharma, there are ten pervasive factors: perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), joy (*prīti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), volition (*cetanā*), as well as liberation (*vimukti*) and attention (*manasikāra*).
Regarding the samādhi of the objective sphere and its associated sensations, there is a specific purpose for clarifying only three categories here.

Within the ten categories, the two categories of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) each constitute one category; because the category of volition (*cetanā*) is extensive, it is divided into eight categories.

Thus, when explained extensively, they are ten, but when abbreviated, only three are mentioned. This is merely a distinction between the extensive and the abbreviated; it is not that some are being clarified while others are not.
This is exhaustive. If one were to discuss the nature of the mind, there are only three categories: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
As for why the number is five, this arises from the specific intent behind establishing those numerical categories; it is simply so according to their respective purposes.

Generally speaking, the broad principle of establishing numbers is that there are cases where the essence is identical while the numbers differ; therefore, one must follow the distinction in number and establish them as three categories. There are also cases where the numbers are identical.

As for those that differ in substance (*dravya*), they are distinguished merely by their different natures rather than by their numerical categories; therefore, they are not established separately. What is the meaning of this?
For example, although the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the independent [unwholesome] are of the same substance, the category of the unwholesome arises solely from seven [mental factors].

Excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), since these two views belong exclusively to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the unwholesome *anuśayas* and so forth do not arise from them.
As for the ignorance (*avidyā*) that arises separately as a "solitary" (*mūla*) [defilement], it is because these unwholesome *anuśayas* likewise do not arise from ignorance.
Regarding the twenty-one unwholesome solitary [defilements], they do not accompany the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), just as...
There are no [factors] such as solitary killing; these belong exclusively to independent (*mūla*) ignorance (*avidyā*), which arises separately in twenty categories.

These arise solely from ignorance. As for the category of unwholesome (*akuśala*) factors, they include associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*). The meaning of "associated ignorance" applies to both contexts.

If it is the category of defiled (*kliṣṭa*) factors, they arise only from the two views of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and belong to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Separately, there is...
The nineteen categories are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). There are twelve categories;
within the neutral, there are these two types: obscured and non-obscured. As for their numerical counts, they differ from one another.
Although these two types—unwholesome and neutral—are identical in kind, because their counts differ, although their essence is one, they are both unwholesome and neutral.
Because they are distinguished by their specific enumerations within the category of mental factors (*caitasika*), each is established as a separate number in two categories of mind.

Regarding the wholesome [factors], there is only the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Since they equally possess twenty-two factors without difference, their names are based on the distinctness of their essence;
thus, although the numbers are the same, they are not established separately. Therefore, for the three natures of mind, they consist of only five categories of factors; such is the intention. Now...

This is because they are distinguished by their numerical categories. As for "distinction by number," it means they are separately established through division; it is not for the sake of clarifying a difference in substance.
Therefore, where substances differ but numbers are the same, there is no division. The meaning of these numerical equivalences shall be explained in detail separately later on.

For now, let us discuss this matter at length in this manner. Therefore, it is said that sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth, are mental factors (*caitasika*).
In this section, the Dharma Master generally refuses to provide a detailed explanation of this meaning. Why is this? The Master says: "This is the doctrine of the *Abhidharma*.

Now, the primary purpose here is to clarify the general outline (*mahā-uddeśa*), which is why it has been set forth. If one were to explain it exhaustively, the meaning would become overly diffuse; only then can it be understood.
Regarding the meaning of "enumeration" (*saṃkhyā*): it is simply because sentient beings have, throughout immeasurable kalpas, possessed weak roots for the Mahāyāna.

If they were to hear an extensive exposition, their minds would consequently become distracted and lose the essential direction of the Mahāyāna; therefore, there is no need for a detailed explanation. As for "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):

this clarifies that since both the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the mental factors (*caitta*) share the same nature as mental phenomena, they are said to possess common characteristics. As for "common objects" (*sālambana*): this clarifies that when the mind takes an object, the mental factors...
Thus, they follow conditions; hence it is said that they "share the same object" (*samanālambana*).

Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "is called the associated cause" (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Sharing one and the same object, their activity is likewise always associated.

This clarifies that since the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*) act as mutual causes and arise in association, they are termed the "associated cause. As for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*)...
Regarding those that should be associated: among the three aggregates, they pertain only to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), being associated through correspondence;

they do not pertain to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), because the latter is material (*rūpa*). Furthermore, they pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) and to both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
Since they clarify only mental phenomena, they are termed exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and cannot pertain to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

For example, regarding the passage beginning with "just as a close friend or acquaintance": in discussing the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it is intimate; in the case of the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it is distant. Why?
Because the meaning of an "acquaintance" (*vidita*) serves as an analogy for the associated cause, while the meaning of "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) serves as an analogy for the co-arising cause.

The Master says that a "close friend" (*mitra*) refers to a companion: those who share the same teacher are called "companions" (*mitra*), and those who share the same aspiration are called "friends" (*suhrd*). One who has known another is called an "acquaintance" (*vidita*); this distinguishes them.

"Kindness" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since these individuals share the same teacher and the same aspiration, they know one another intimately; this mutual relationship is more significant than that between brothers.
Therefore, the Master clarifies that the meaning of the "associated cause" (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is intimate, and thus he illustrates it by means of the analogy of friends.
This is because it is explained that the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*) cannot arise if they are not associated. Such is the reason for saying so. It shall now be explained.
Regarding the "co-arising cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*) mentioned below, it is also called the "common-functioning cause" (*sahakāri-hetu*).

If the aforementioned "associated cause" (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) refers only to mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth—being termed "associated" because they are closely linked and subtle—then this co-arising cause is more remote and extensive, as it applies universally to all things that arise together, whether material (*rūpa*) or mental (*citta*), and everything belongs to this cause.
For example, when visual consciousness arises, it necessarily requires the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Only when factors such as dharmas arise together can they be produced; therefore, it is called a "co-arising cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Since this cause is said to be co-arising, it applies universally to all phenomena of the three natures, the three categories, and those that are out-flowing (*sāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); however, it does not apply to that which is unconditioned.

The phrase "like brothers" and so forth serves as an analogy because, just as brothers mutually support one another and can only stand by means of each other, so too must form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and objective spheres (*viṣaya*) arise together.

This reason is cited to demonstrate that [the unmanifest] applies to all three aggregates (*skandha*); since the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) belongs to the aggregate of form, it is directly related to the sense of being a "co-arising cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*).
As for the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the fourteen non-associated [factors], they do not apply here.

Regarding formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth: because they belong to the category of that which is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), if one were to regard them as co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) based on this, they would merely receive the name "co-arising" by virtue of arising together with other factors such as form and mind; therefore, this interpretation is remote from the truth. The Master said, "So it is. This shall now be explained.

The section beginning with "self-seed cause" (*svabīja-hetu*) is also called the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*). This is clarified in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*: "Good [dharmas] arise from their own kind, and evil [dharmas] arise from their own kind;
therefore, they are called 'self-seeds'. The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The term 'natural cause' (*svabhāva-hetu*) is like when chestnuts are sown;
later, the fruit arises of itself without requiring instruction from another; hence it is called 'natural. This translation is incorrect," says this Meditation Master.
In the midst of the assembly, he said, "My younger brother has come from across the South Sea.

Because of this single phrase, which set him apart from the rest of the group, he was driven out and fled, stopping at Mount Luyuan at the residence of Dharma Master Jingxing. This should be explained as being called the "pseudo-reason" (*sādharmya-hetu*).

Now, it is said that one’s own seed constitutes "good. For example, beans produce only beans and chestnuts produce only chestnuts; this refers to the meaning of belonging to the cause of one's own seed.

Since the meaning of the cause of one's own seed applies to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), if one speaks of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), they are termed "one's own seed" because they follow matter and mind.
Furthermore, since [the term] is extremely remote [in such cases], it is stated here that it applies to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).

Since it is stated that this [cause] pervades all phenomena, one should know that it applies to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), unlike the causal condition of habituation (*abhyāsa-hetu*), which refers only to the mind.

Regarding this cause and the causal condition of habituation, there are distinctions in terms of presence, identity and difference, pervasion and particularity, and breadth and narrowness. Why is this?

For example, as in worldly dharmas, [the dharma of suffering] acts as the causal condition of habituation for the "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), yet it is not its own specific seed-cause (*bīja-hetu*). Why is this so? Because...
Because there is a distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the first outflow-free mind arises from only three causes:

namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the non-obstructing cause (*avighna-hetu*). Thus, it lacks its own seed-cause (*sva-bīja-hetu*). If this is so, then while the habituated cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) is universal, the seed-cause is specific.
If one says that the habituated cause refers only to the mental continuum, whereas the seed-cause applies to all phenomena, for each phenomenon has its own respective seed.
"Category" refers to its own seed (*svabīja*). "Its own seed" carries the meaning of being its own cause. It further includes the cause of cultivation (*vāsanā-hetu*).
Other points, such as the fact that the subsequent specific causes pertain to all three time periods, shall be explained separately.
Regarding the section beginning with "The pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)," the following explains the nature and characteristics of the pervasive cause in relation to the pervasive cause itself.

As for the defilements (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), if one were to discuss afflictions (*kleśa*) exhaustively, there would be five categories; however, here we speak only of those afflictions abandoned through the two modes [of perception and conceptualization], which are termed "pervasive causes.

These are so called because, when taking the two truths of suffering and origination as their objects, they belong to the category of impure objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and are capable of universally producing all outflows (*āsrava*) and afflictions.

Because they cause affliction, these are termed "pervasive proclivities" (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*). If they were to take cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their objects, they would belong to the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere and could not universally generate tainted (*sāsrava*) afflictions.
Now, since pervasive and non-pervasive proclivities are distinguished according to whether they take tainted or untainted objects, it is only said here that these two [truths] [are the objects].
The *Vibhāṣā* explains: Question: How many are pervasive proclivities and how many are non-pervasive proclivities? Answer: Thirty-three.

There are universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and sixty-five non-universal proclivities (*asarvatraga-anuśaya*). Within the suffering (*duḥkha*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten proclivities;

in the two higher realms, there are eighteen. Thus, across the three realms, they constitute twenty-eight proclivities. Within the origin (*samudaya*) of the three realms, there are nineteen proclivities. Combining those of the suffering and origin of the three realms, there are one hundred and forty-seven proclivities.
Now, the reason why it is stated here that only thirty-three proclivities within the two [truths of] suffering and origin are universal is as follows: [the remainder are not].

Regarding the "proliferating latent tendencies" (*paryavasthāna-anuśaya*): although there are ten such tendencies within the suffering of the desire realm, the four types—craving, aversion, pride, and ignorance—belong to the category of afflictions associated with craving;
these are "tendencies directed toward objects" (*vastv-ālambana-anuśaya*) and are also called "tendencies with distinct objects" (*viśeṣa-ālambana-anuśaya*).

Now, the "universal tendencies" (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are taken only as those that take the thirty-two truths as their object and arise from delusion regarding the principles (*dharma*). Although ignorance (*avidyā*) extends to both the categories of views and craving, it likewise belongs to the universal tendencies.
The universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) comprise [the first three]; the remaining three proclivities belong only to specific conditions.

A mind of greed cannot give rise to hatred, and at the time of a mind of hatred there is no pride; because they cannot universally produce all proclivities, they are not called universal proclivities.

Since these three proclivities are excluded from the category of suffering in the desire realm, and these same three proclivities are likewise excluded from the category of origin in the desire realm, the remaining four proclivities constitute the eleven universal proclivities. Because...

These eleven universal proclivities (*paryavasthāna*) pervade all three realms; thus, they constitute thirty-three. Therefore, there are thirty-three that belong to the category of universal proclivities.

The remaining sixty-five are non-universal proclivities. If the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising under the two truths of suffering and origin are produced by taking conditioned, outflowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena as their object, they are further able to universally produce the outflowing phenomena of the five destinies; the cause is likewise affliction, and the fruit is likewise [affliction].

They are also afflictions (*kleśa*). Because they are capable of producing the fundamental roots of *sāsrava* (outflowing) existence and are profound, they are established as pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).

As for the afflictions arising from the lower levels of the Truths of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*), these arise by taking unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas as their objects; they do not arise from conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas. Therefore, they are not established as pervasive latent tendencies.

Only within the two truths [of Suffering and Origin] are pervasive latent tendencies explained; it is said that those [afflictions] arising from the Truths of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and Origin (*samudaya-satya*)...

Regarding "the severance of fetters" (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*): this refers to the essential nature of the pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*). As for the phrase "the cause of all defiled phenomena" (*sarva-kliṣṭa-dharma-hetu*): it specifically expresses the meaning of being a cause.

Regarding the discussion of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*): this cause pertains to two natures. Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those that take everything as their object belong to the unwholesome (*akuśala*), with the exception of the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).

In the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), the pervasive [proclivities] are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and outflowing (*sāsrava*), and consist solely of a collection of mental factors (*citta-kalāpa*).
This is capable of universally producing all the five types of lower latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Therefore, it is called the cause of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).

The Master says that, according to the *Bhāryāsūtra*, it is said to arise from the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) and is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*); its mental object (*ālambana*) consists of the higher afflictions.

Regarding "the mind taking higher afflictions as its object": this refers to the various afflictions of the higher stages of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), such as the dhyānas, all of which belong to the ground of abiding in the three types of craving (*trṣṇā*) and are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

In this way, from ignorance (*avidyā*) arises craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*); from craving for existence arises craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*); from craving for form arises craving for desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*);
and from the arising of craving for desire, there first arise the afflictions of the ground of abiding in a single locality (*ekadeśasthāna*) of views. This is the root text.
The Sūtra also merely states that the four inversions arise from the three inversions; this statement is general and remains difficult to understand. This treatise, however, explains it clearly:

the inversion of mind arises from the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*); the inversion of mind gives rise to the inversion of views (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*); and from the inversion of views, the four inversions arise.
As for "the four inversions arising from the inversion of views," this means that the afflictions categorized as views are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Perception...
Perverted mind and perverted views belong to the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Afflictions are abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

As for the previous statement that afflictions abandoned by the path of cultivation arise from ignorance (*avidyā*), these too are exclusively part of the category of craving. These sūtras and śāstras all state that views arise from craving;
however, what is currently being taken up—the pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—as well as the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and other texts, state that they arise from the category of views.
Regarding the section on craving (*tṛṣṇā-bhāga*), the sūtras and śāstras are as stated above. How are these conflicting meanings to be reconciled? The Master says:

As for the human sūtra, it states that there are two kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*): first, the "afflictions of the dwelling grounds" (*sthiti-bhūmi-kleśa*), which refers to the afflictions of the five dwelling grounds;

second, the "arising afflictions" (*utthāna-kleśa*), which refers to the afflictions produced and activated upon the five dwelling grounds. Here, the discussion is based on the ground where the afflictions dwell.
In the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), it is said that they arise sequentially; thus, it is stated: "From ignorance arise the three abodes of craving (*trṣṇā-vāsabhūmi*);

from the three abodes of craving arises the abode of views in a single place (*ekadeśa-dṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*). However, the intention here regarding the pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) does not concern the sequential arising of one stage from another.
This is because they arise through association and co-arising; thus, craving can arise from views. Question:

If craving can arise from views because they arise through association and co-arising, then by the same logic of association and co-arising, one cannot say that craving for the form and formless realms is the root.
For when one abandons craving for the lower realms through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the fundamental craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted.
Therefore, even though this branch of craving still arises, one should likewise not say that it does so. The commentary states:

Although the meaning of the arising of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is not explicitly clarified within these Three Piṭakas, this [present] meaning is intended to facilitate an understanding of that meaning of the arising of the underlying tendencies.
This is why it is so. Now, since the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) involve the confusion of the meanings of "arising" and "mutual production," they arise accordingly;

or rather, [the distinctions between] lightness, heaviness, views, craving, and so forth are simply indeterminate. One interpretation of the intent of the teaching on pervasive latent dispositions is as follows:

based on the analysis according to the Truths (*satya*), pervasive latent dispositions are established within the two truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origin (*samudaya*). Since they pervasively give rise to afflictions under the five categories of existence, they thus universally produce both views and craving.
Because the principle of mutual generation is broad and pervasive, craving arises from views; such is the intended meaning of the teaching.

However, there is also the principle that the heavy arises from the light. Now, regarding the classification of afflictions, based on their types and their mutual generation, this passage clarifies only that craving gives rise to further craving.

It does not function as a pervasive latent tendency (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*). This clarifies the meaning of the sequential arising of the [afflictions]. Therefore, it takes only the subtle craving (*anunaya*) of the upper realms as its root;
from the subtle arises the gross, and when the gross is severed, the subtle remains, and thus it continues to arise.
From the section beginning with "The cause of retribution" (*vipāka-hetu*) onwards, it clarifies that contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karma can bring about future fruits;

therefore, it is called the "cause of retribution. It receives its name from the fruit. The treatise states: "In relation to the cause, it is called the 'fruit'; in relation to the conditions, it is called 'retribution. Therefore, one speaks of 'causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions.

When analyzed according to the three natures, the two types—wholesome and unwholesome—possess both manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karman*), through which they obtain future fruits. Thus [it is said].

It belongs to the category of retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*). The unconditioned (*avyākṛta*) possesses only active karma (*kriyā-karma*) and lacks non-active karma (*avijñapti-karma*); because it does not yield future fruit, it is not a retributive cause.
This is like the unconditioned acts of walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and so forth—all such things are merely active karma within the category of the unconditioned;

therefore, the Sūtra refers to them as "unconditioned karma. If one analyzes this according to the three aggregates (*triskandha*), non-active [matter] is form (*rūpa*), and because it can also yield retribution, it is included therein.
The retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) also extends to the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*); it is exclusively impure (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The Master said:

Although retributive fruits (*vipāka-phala*) are immeasurable, they do not exceed five types. First, as it is said, wholesome and unwholesome karma that results in suffering, pleasure, and so forth is called the retributive fruit.

Second is the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): for example, when one cultivated goodness in a previous life, today’s goodness arises again in dependence upon that previous goodness; this is [the concordant fruit].

The meaning of the cause of practice (*abhyāsa-hetu*) is explained as the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*). The three fruits of liberation (*vimukti-phala*), beginning from the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) up to Buddhahood, are all supramundane fruits;

therefore, they belong to liberation. As in the Chapter on the Eightfold Path and other such categories, one must cultivate these path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) and so forth to attain them, and because they further enable the attainment of various fruits, the treatise states that "these fruits also have fruits," and both [the path and its fruits] belong to liberation.

[This refers to] liberation. Regarding the four fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*): they are like a man who seeks employment and obtains a salary, or a farmer who sows fields and obtains grain, and so forth.
The fifth is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). For example, when a single dharma such as visual consciousness arises, there is light and space;

because color-form and the eye do not increase [in magnitude], it is able to arise. When this one dharma arises, all other factors neither obstruct nor hinder it; therefore, they [all] [arise together].
This belongs to the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). In the *Bhūmivastu*, all fruits are subsumed within these five fruits. The Master said:
"For example, when Śāriputra saw a defiled land and Śikhin saw a pure land, these were the same location, yet they perceived different qualities due to disaster and purity.

This is what is induced by the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*); because of the power of karma, that [land] appears as empty to him, while it appears as real to me. Because it accords with me, what I see is not false."

The same applies here. That empty space does not obstruct one another; it all belongs to the color of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment). Long storerooms, crows, white [objects], and so forth, belong to the color of the *sambhoga-vipāka* (retributive body).

If one argues in this manner, then among all phenomena, all internal forms—including mountains, rivers, and the great earth—are none other than retributive colors (*vipāka-rūpa*). This shall be explained in detail.
The five causes above constitute the summary.
Regarding the phrase "because the mind and mental factors proceed in succession without interval," this next explains the *samanantara-pratyaya* (condition as immediate antecedent).

As the *Bhagavad-viśeṣa-sūtra* states: "The mind arises and ceases only moment by moment, with intervals. How, then, is it explained here that there is no interval? [This is the question to be resolved.]
It is said: This was stated in order to eliminate the two views of annihilationism and eternalism held by sentient beings.
Because sentient beings do not understand that when these aggregates cease, three other aggregates continue in succession, they give rise to the view of annihilationism regarding form (*rūpa*).

Seeing that the mind arises here and arises there, they give rise to the view of eternalism regarding the mind (*citta*). That sutra, in order to eliminate this view, states that the mind is merely subject to arising and ceasing with intervals.

Regardless of the meaning of "uninterrupted continuity," here it is explained as the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Because there is no interruption in the successive arising of preceding and succeeding moments, it is called "uninterrupted.
The meaning of the condition of immediate succession has already been explained previously; this [condition] is exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This applies to both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), and pertains to the meaning that [these] pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and exist only within the mental aggregate (*cittakalāpa*).

This will be explained later. Regarding the passage "the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) arise because they take objects (*ālambana*)," etc., this next section explains the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

This clarifies that the mind is the primary subject that takes an object, while the preceding realm is the actual substance of the object; because the mind and the object are spoken of together, it is called the object-condition. This applies to...
The three aggregates consist of the conditioned, the unconditioned, and the three natures such as the contaminated (*sāsrava*), and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "When all phenomena arise, they do not obstruct one another," this should have stated here that they constitute the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

yet it says instead that they are "non-obstructive. This is because the author of the treatise intends to clarify that the four conditions are identical in meaning to the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*). Therefore...

Thus it is said. Since this principle applies universally to all phenomena (*dharma*), and because it is most fundamental, it also extends to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, the three natures, the three aggregates, and so forth. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from the passage "Next, the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions" onwards, the fourth section clarifies that phenomena arise from conditions.
It explains that since these minds and mental factors are associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), they arise from causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because the minds and mental factors arise in successive order, they arise from sequential conditions (*anantara-pratyaya*). At the moment the mind arises, there must necessarily be...

Because it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it arises from the object-condition. Because when one dharma arises, the ten thousand dharmas do not obstruct it, it arises from the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This shall now be explained.

Regarding the passage "The signless concentration and the cessation concentration arise from three conditions," and so forth: this clarifies that these concentrations must be cultivated before they can be attained;
thus, they belong to that which arises from causes and conditions. Since these concentrations are dharmas of cultivation, as for the meaning of cultivation itself:
It must reside in the mind. This concentration arises from a preceding moment of mind; therefore, it is said to arise from the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
However, because it ceases at the very moment it is present, it is said to arise from the immediately antecedent condition. It is a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

Since all phenomena do not obstruct its arising, it is said to arise from the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Generally, when discussing the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one must necessarily speak of the union of mind and object.

In discussing the meaning of the mind taking objects as conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), since the mind has ceased and subsided at that time, one cannot say that [the subsequent state] arises from the object-condition. Question:

If, because this meditative absorption is without mind, it cannot arise from the object-condition, then for the same reason—that it is without mind—it also cannot arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Answer: The meaning of the object-condition refers merely to the relative correspondence between the mind and its object at that specific moment.

Thus it arises. For this reason, they are collectively described as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). At that time, since there is no mutual confrontation of minds, one cannot say that it arises from the object-condition as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Although these are mental factors, the meaning of the sequential condition is not discussed solely in that context;

rather, it is based on the principle of successive arising between preceding and succeeding moments. At that time, although this meditative absorption and so forth are without mind, they cannot arise in isolation.

It is not that it cannot arise from the preceding mind, for it can indeed arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This concentration has existed within the preceding minds up until the present moment;

however, because it ceases as soon as it reaches the present, it lacks the functional capacity of a condition. Therefore, there is certainly no sense in which it arises from an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This shall now be explained.
Regarding "the remaining formations dissociated from mind and form" and below: according to the *Amṛtarasa-Abhidharma*, there are seventeen dissociated formations;

according to others, there are only fourteen. The previously mentioned non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are these two dissociated formations.
Having already explained that [these] arise from three conditions, one now wishes to explain the remaining ten or twenty-five.

Regarding the meaning of "arising from conditions" for the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and so forth, it is said that these other non-associated formations are not like the two aforementioned meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), which must be attained through long-term cultivation starting from the mind;

therefore, they do not arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Furthermore, because they are neither material nor mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), they do not arise from the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). This...
When a phenomenon arises, it does not do so without a basis for grasping, nor does it arise without the principle of co-arising; thus, it arises from causes and conditions.

When this phenomenon arises, because other phenomena do not obstruct it, it arises from the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding "form" (*rūpa*), there are two kinds of form.

There are two kinds of matter (*rūpa*): first, matter as primary retribution (*vipākaphala-rūpa*); second, matter as secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhānika-rūpa*). Because matter is neither mind (*citta*) nor mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), it does not arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Since the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is explained based on the conjunction of mind and its objects, and matter is merely an object and not itself an object-condition, it cannot arise from an object-condition.

When this matter arises, it necessarily co-arises with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and various acquisitions (*prāpti*). Therefore, it is said to arise from causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
When this form arises, because the myriad dharmas do not obstruct it, it arises from a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

According to the Abhidharma, while the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) exists within the four sense organs and ten types [of objects], one should know that the body-organ (*kāya-indriya*) consists of nine types.

The remaining eight are said to be "fragrance" (*gandha*) and "possessing fragrance" (*gandhavat-bhūmi*). This refers to external forms and so forth; because they lack the various sense organs, they merely possess the subtle locus of fragrance. Thus...

They possess eight subtle elements (*anu*). For example, within the eye, there are the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of intrinsic nature and four subtle elements; furthermore, the eye faculty possesses the body faculty.
Since this applies equally to the ears, nose, and tongue, these four faculties each possess ten subtle elements.

However, within the body faculty itself, there are only the four primary elements of intrinsic nature and four subtle elements, and no other faculties besides the body faculty, as is the case with the eyes, ears, and so forth; thus, it possesses only nine subtle elements.
This meaning has already been explained previously; it shall be discussed in detail separately below.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The mind and mental factors born of retribution arise from five causes," the fifth section clarifies the phenomena that arise from causes.
There are two kinds of mind: first, the resultant mind; second, the causal mind. The causal mind is precisely the preparatory (upāya) mind. That is to say:

Regarding the various minds of good and evil, the "resultant mind" (*vipāka-citta*) is precisely the retributive mind. This refers to coarse and subtle minds, as well as sharp and dull minds, and so forth.

What is here termed the "retribution-born mind" specifically refers to this [type of] mind. Because this mind arises solely as produced by a retributive cause, it belongs to that which is born from a retributive cause.
Furthermore, because this mind and its associated mental factors arise together, they belong to the category of association (*samprayukta*).

It arises from causes. When this mind arises, there must necessarily be four characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*), because it arises simultaneously with various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth; thus, it belongs to the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Because the minds and mental factors produce one another, they belong to the self-seed cause (*svabīja-hetu*). Because when one dharma arises, ten thousand dharmas do not obstruct it, it belongs to the designation cause (*nāman-hetu*).
The essence of affliction (*kleśa*) is a defiled dharma; as it belongs to the obscured category, it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This retributive mind is not...

These afflictions (*kleśa*) are not defiled dharmas (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*), because they belong to the category of non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Therefore, they do not arise from a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).

Regarding the passage "the various afflictions also arise from causes" and so forth, this clarifies the five types of causes (*pañcahetu*). Because afflictions are not uniform, the term "various afflictions" is used. As for the definition of afflictions:
since they must necessarily arise together with the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), they belong to the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*). Thus, afflictions arise...
At that time, because it must arise simultaneously with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*), it belongs to the co-nascent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Although afflictions (*kleśa*) are immeasurable, they merely give rise to greed from greed and hatred from hatred; thus, in the sense that each arises from its own kind, they belong to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
When a single dharma arises, ten thousand dharmas do not obstruct it; therefore, it belongs to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). As for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it only...

Regarding the fact that the mind associated with feeling and form is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), whereas afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed obscured and defiled phenomena (*nivṛtakaṣāya-dharma*) and not retributive phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*):
therefore, the cause of retribution is excluded. Although afflictions generally belong to the category of obscured phenomena, there are some that belong to the neutral class (*avyākṛta-pakṣa*).

Specifically, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as the afflictions of the two upper realms, all belong to the category of obscured-neutral phenomena. As for the desire realm...

As for the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*), although they are obscured phenomena (*nivṛta-dharma*), they are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); rather, they belong to the category of the unwholesome (*akuśala-pakṣa*). This shall be explained later.

Regarding the statement that "matter born of maturation (*vipāka*) and the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arise from four causes," the previously mentioned "mind born of maturation" refers to a collection of mind (*citta-kalāpa*).
The present mention of "matter" refers to a collection of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*). As for the "non-associated formations," these are neither matter nor... [mind].

The "mental aggregate" (citta-kalāpa). This clarifies that the six causes can produce the three types of aggregates. To clarify this: the record of this resultant form (*vipāka-rūpa*) must necessarily repay the records of good and evil karma;

therefore, it belongs to the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*). When this form arises, there are necessarily the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, which arise together in mutual accompaniment like shadows;

therefore, it belongs to the cause of co-arising (*sahabhū-hetu*). As for form producing form, it is like the preceding form giving rise to the subsequent form; therefore, it belongs to [the cause of continuity].

Regarding the cause of its own seed (*svabījanimitta*): when a single dharma arises, the myriad dharmas do not obstruct it; therefore, they are categorized as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*). There are two kinds of form (*rūpa*):

the forms of the two retributions, namely the environment and the body. All of these arise entirely from these four causes. They do not belong to the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*), for the meaning is as explained in the treatise.

The retribution-cause (*vipākahetu*) consists of obscured phenomena (*nivṛtadharma*), whereas retribution-form and the like are non-obscured phenomena (*anivṛtadharma*); their essence is not affliction (*kleśa*). Therefore [they are not associated causes].

Excluding the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Regarding the various formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there are two types of formations: first, those associated with mind (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra*); second, those dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

As for the formations associated with mind, these refer to mental factors (*caitta*) and various karmic formations. As for the formations dissociated from mind, they are either fourteen or seventeen; these shall now be enumerated. They are:

the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the absorption of non-characteristic (*ānimitta-samādhi*), [the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),] the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the acquisition (*prāpti*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the birth (*jāti*), the aging (*jarā*), the duration (*sthiti*), the impermanence (*anityatā*), the name-set (*nāmakāya*), the phrase-set (*padakāya*), and the syllable-set (*vyañjanakāya*). [The remaining items are] the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*); the designations of names, phrases, and syllables; the nature of sentient beings; the life-span of sentient beings;

and the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*). Since these are neither form (*rūpa*) nor mental factors (*cittadharma*), they are called "conditioned factors dissociated from mind" (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).

These two types of formations (*saṃskāra*) are all impermanent phenomena; therefore, the Mahāvadāna Sūtra states: "All formations are impermanent. Thus it is with these dissociated formations and the like.

Since it is neither a form nor a mental factor (*citta-dharma*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is excluded. Since it is born of retribution (*vipāka-ja*) and is a dharma of retribution, it belongs to the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
because it is not a dharma of affliction or defilement (*kleśa-mala*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is excluded.

When these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they arise together in mutual reflection and harmony; therefore, they belong to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). Each of these conditioned phenomena possesses its own specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because they possess the characteristic of arising, these non-associated formations belong to their own seeds as causes. Furthermore, they are all retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*).
Since cessation arises simultaneously with matter and mind, and is non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it belongs to the category of retributive causes.
"Defiled matter and the various formations dissociated from mind also arise from four causes," and so forth.

Having previously explained the meaning of resultant mind, and subsequently having completed the explanation of the meanings of resultant matter and resultant formations dissociated from mind, [the text] now explains the meanings of matter produced through effort (*prāyogika*) and the various formations dissociated from mind produced through effort. Regarding "defiled matter," this refers to that which is produced through effort.

This refers to form (*rūpa*). For example, within a temple or a stupa, if someone enters there with the intent to commit theft, their coming and going and their movements constitute "unwholesome form" (*akuśala-rūpa*).
If, however, someone enters there for the purpose of practicing the Way or performing prostrations, the various actions they perform are called "wholesome form" (*kuśala-rūpa*).
Furthermore, there may be someone who neither intends to steal nor practices the Way or performs prostrations, but simply... [text truncated]

Regarding the statement that "the states such as recording the mind, coming, entering, moving, and so forth, once they have been manifested, are indeterminate matter (*avyākṛta-rūpa*)," this matter is not produced by the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
Rather, it is a matter of skillful means (*upāya-rūpa*) arising upon the basis of retributive matter; it belongs to the category of causes.

Because these dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and so forth also follow along with this matter, they are said to be concomitant. Furthermore, they are all likewise produced from the four causes.
This matter (rūpa) and the non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra), etc., belong to the co-arising cause (sahabhū-hetu), because they mutually reflect upon and arise together.
They belong to the self-seed cause (svabīja-hetu), because matter gives rise to matter, and various formations give rise to various formations, and so forth.

As for the aforementioned retributive matter and retribution-born non-associated formations, they all ultimately belong to the category of non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) nature; they are alike in being retribution (vipāka).

Because it is a dharma, it belongs to the category of the dharma-cause (*dharmahetu*). Now, defiled matter (*rūpa*) up to the matter of preparatory effort (*prayoga-rūpa*) does not arise as a maturation of a prior retributive cause;

rather, it is a defiled dharma (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). Since the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is the cause for all defiled dharmas, although these are matter and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), they can nevertheless arise from the pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*). This is just like the case of non-associated formations and so forth. Although...

Furthermore, it is neither matter nor mind, because it belongs to the category of non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). It can arise from a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), as its nature is similar [to that of maturation].

This applies to all other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), with the exception of the initial untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) mentioned below; the above clarifies the arising of minds and mental factors born of maturation.

The explanation of the meaning of "number" is concluded. Next, we wish to clarify the arising of the various provisional means—the primary minds (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), namely those that are wholesome or unwholesome, as well as those such as understanding (*prajñā*) and so forth; thus it says, "the remaining minds.

Regarding the previous explanation of the arising of the various afflictions within the three natures of mind, the explanation of the arising of both unwholesome and neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds has already been fully contained therein. Now, herein we shall provisionally rely upon...

This refers to wholesome states of mind and mental factors, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*). Because these minds are not uniform, it is also said to refer to "all other minds and form," excluding the first untainted mind.

Since the mind of *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* (the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering) is the first untainted mind, this mind arises from the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
While the mundane dharma is with outflows, the receptivity (*kṣānti*) is without outflows; it does not arise from its own seed.

Because they arise from causes, they are eliminated. If it is the second moment of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-citta*), it arises immediately from the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).
Being likewise untainted (*anāsrava*), it possesses the sense of arising from its own seeds as a cause; at that time, it first arises from four causes.

When these tainted or untainted wholesome minds and so forth arise, they must necessarily be accompanied by mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); therefore, they belong to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). These...

When the mind arises, there must necessarily be four characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*), because they arise together with the various acquisitions (*prāptis*) and so forth. This pertains to arising through the co-nascent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). There are many types of acquisition;
there is the acquisition of causes, the acquisition of fruits, and the acquisition of form. When any dharma arises, it is invariably bound by this rope of acquisition.

Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because the consciousness and acquisition of one in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) still exist, such a person is still called a sentient being."
This meaning shall now be explained. Because each of these wholesome minds and so forth possesses its own specific characteristics and the principle of arising, they have their own seeds as causes.
When a single dharma arises, if there were obstructions, it could not arise; however, because the myriad dharmas do not obstruct my arising, [it does so].
I am able to attain birth; therefore, this is called the cause (*hetu*). This is a wholesome mind and not a defiled mind; thus, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is excluded.

This is a causal mind and not a resultant mind; because it is not a dharma that is a result of the non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and so forth, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is excluded.

Regarding the other mental non-associated factors—namely, matter and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) discussed below—the previous explanation concerning how the retribution-born mind, matter, and so forth arise from four causes is now complete.

Next, the explanation of the defiled formations and the expedient means regarding matter and the formations dissociated from mind, which are also said to arise from four causes, is likewise concluded. Now, I wish to explain *bhava* (existence).
Regarding the conditioned factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that are outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*), outflow-free (*anāsrava*), or wholesome (*kuśala*):

within these wholesome minds and so forth, some possess their own seeds as causes while others do not. For this reason, these distinct entities—the dissociated factors and so on—are presented here by way of two categories.
Those that possess their own seeds as causes arise from three causes; those that lack them arise from two causes. Hereafter, [the text proceeds as follows]:

The *Chuyun* (Emergence from the Clouds) initially presents the matter of form (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) within the untainted (*anāsrava*). This section begins the explanation of these two categories.

It clarifies that although these non-associated formations and so forth also follow the dharmas in terms of the number of causes they possess, there are masters who hold that among the untainted wholesome states, some are complete with their own seeds as causes while others are not; this is just as in the case of an initial tainted mind.

Among these, [the factors] such as right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these material and mental phenomena and so forth—possess no seeds as their cause, because they are neither mind nor mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*).

Furthermore, because they are merely cultivated (*vaipākika*), they lack a corresponding cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). Because they are not defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), they lack a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Regarding these wholesome forms, they belong to the category of forms produced by application (*prayoga-rūpa*); being merely forms caused by effort, they are not forms born of retribution (*vipāka-rūpa*), and thus they lack a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Since this is the first instance of untainted (*anāsrava*) matter (*rūpa*), arising for the first time from that which was tainted (*sāsrava*), it lacks its own seeds as a cause.

At that time, this matter lacks these four causes. However, because when this matter arises there are the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the various acquisitions (*prāpti*), and the activity (*karman*), which arise together with their shadows and harmoniously, it possesses the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Because when this dharma arises, other dharmas do not obstruct it, it possesses the non-obstructing cause (*an-āvaraṇa-hetu*). It also possesses the... [non-obstructing cause].
Regarding the obstructive cause (*āvaraṇa-hetu*): these dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) associated with this form (*rūpa*) likewise possess only these two causes;
therefore, it is said that "if they lack their own seed-cause (*svabīja-hetu*), they arise from two causes. If they do possess their own seed-cause, then they possess three causes.

As for the various dissociated formations associated with tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome mental factors (*caitta*), because they are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the [obstructive cause] is excluded.

Regarding the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*): because these are not defiled phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is excluded. Because they are neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is excluded.

When these formations (*saṃskāra*) arise, they necessarily arise together with their shadows and companions; therefore, there is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). These formations possess the characteristic of producing their own marks;
therefore, there is the self-seed cause (*sva-bīja-hetu*). When these formations arise, all phenomena do not obstruct them; therefore, there is the non-obstructing cause (*an-āvṛti-hetu*).

Therefore, it is said that if there is its own seed, it arises from three causes. Within the category of contaminated wholesome states of mind (*sāsrava-kuśala-citta*), there are both those that arise through homogeneous production (*jāti-nirvṛtti*) and those that arise through non-homogeneous production.

If it is a case of homogeneous production—excluding the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—it arises from four causes; this includes the associated mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-saṃskāra*) as well as the concomitant dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Since the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) must already have been excluded, [the dharma] can arise from only three causes.

If it is not a case of arising through the production of its own kind (*jāti-sabhāga*), then the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) that accompany it can arise from only two causes, as explained above.
If it is the first untainted wholesome mind (*anāsrava-kuśala-citta*), because it is a mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), it possesses an associated cause; when this mind arises, then—

There are four characteristics. Because all acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise simultaneously [with their respective dharmas], acquisitions have a common cause. When a single dharma arises, the myriad dharmas do not obstruct it; therefore, it is able to arise.
If there were obstructions, this dharma would not be able to arise. Since it does indeed arise, [it follows that there are no such obstructions].

There is the non-obstructing cause (*anāvaraṇa-hetu*), because it first arises from that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). There is no self-seed cause (*svabīja-hetu*), because the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth arise simultaneously.
There is the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because all dharmas do not obstruct its arising. It is called the "attainment cause" (*prāpti-hetu*).
Therefore, it is said that the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) arises from three causes.

Regarding the statement that "in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), matter (*rūpa*) and the various formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arise from two causes," this has already been explained above.
However, although the initial untainted mind arises from three causes, the dissociated formations it carries can only arise from two causes.
This is because they are neither mind nor mental factors (*caitta*); thus, they lack a corresponding cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). Furthermore, they lack their own seeds (*svabīja*).
The meanings of the causal cause (*hetu-hetu*), the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and so forth, are all the same and shall be explained below.
The passage beginning with "There is not a single dharma that arises from a single cause" clarifies that the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is weak and inferior;
this is stated in terms of their causes. If the minimum number, they arise from two causes; if the maximum, they arise from five or six causes. As for those arising from six causes, then...

This is a general discussion on the beginning and end of all phenomena (*dharma*), establishing the principle that they arise through the four conditions (*pratyaya*). The same applies to the principle of arising from conditions:

there is no phenomenon that arises from a single condition, because the six causes (*hetu*) are themselves the four conditions. Thus, it is said that "if there are six causes, these are called the four conditions";
this is the summary. Question: In the previous discussion on phenomena arising from conditions, you mentioned mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), yet only five causes were stated.
The explanation states: Although the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*) are identical to the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*), the meaning of "condition" is broader, as it encompasses all causes.

Since the meaning of "arising from conditions" is general, one may say they arise from the four conditions; however, since the meaning of "arising from causes" is specific, it is said that they arise from the five causes.
It is said to be "pervasive" (sāmānya) merely because it is broad; though pervasive, it is not loose. Previously, it was not clarified that phenomena arise from six causes.
Why, then, is it said here: "If they arise from six causes, this is called the four conditions"? This is a hypothetical statement.
To arise from five causes is precisely to arise from the four conditions; to arise from the four conditions is simply to arise from the six causes.

From the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā contemplates the four conditions in this way and the mind becomes unattached," the sixth section clarifies that the Bodhisattva understands the characteristics of the four conditions as unreal, like the moon reflected in water, yet sentient beings falsely cling to them.

I shall explain each point in detail when we encounter the relevant passages in the text. However, the point that "what is to be rejected is the graspable, not what is visible" clarifies that one merely eliminates the disease of attachment, rather than eliminating the phenomenon itself.

Question: If one wishes to know the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*) in detail, one should study the Abhidharma, and so forth. (The following) seventh section clarifies the refutation [of the four conditions] based on the Abhidharma.

This point means that "Abhidharma" is named for its analytical discernment of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Within this, the meaning and characteristics of the four conditions are explained at length.
If one studies the four conditions, one ought to study the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); yet within the Perfection of Wisdom, there are no four conditions.
[The section on] Characteristics. What is meant by "exhorting to study"?
The answer follows below; it shall be explained one by one as we encounter the text.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that all phenomena depend upon causes, and those causes depend upon the four conditions—what, in turn, do these four conditions depend upon? This is precisely to refute [wrong] attachments.
Regarding the meaning of the four conditions (*pratyaya*), because one seeks them out without ceasing and yet finds them unattainable, wrong views arise.
Those who study the *pāramitās* as causes will be free from this delusion; each shall now be explained in turn.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If one wishes to know all phenomena as they are, according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)," why are these three dharmas explained immediately after the four conditions?
Above, it was clarified that emptiness is itself dependent origination; therefore, eighteen types of emptiness were taught first, followed by the explanation of these four conditions.
Now, it is clarified that the meaning of conditions is itself quiescence; thus, these three dharmas are explained after the four conditions. If a bodhisattva wishes to act in this manner...
Conditioned, unconditioned, and neither-conditioned-nor-unconditioned. One who penetrates these three dharmas should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the statement that "a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in this manner," it means that if a bodhisattva can penetrate the characteristics of these three dharmas of all phenomena and abide in *prajñā*, they should abide by means of non-abiding. This is the scriptural text; what follows below should [be understood accordingly].

The commentary explains the various dharmas, beginning with the passage "There are two kinds," which constitutes the exegesis. Within this section, there are two main intentions: first, citing the scriptural text;
second, providing the commentary. Within the commentary itself, there are further ten intentions. The first is the establishment of the treatise, which begins by establishing two gates.
There are seven points: first, clarifying that [all things] are like the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) and so forth; second, explaining the similarities and differences among the three meanings;

third, clarifying the sense that the *dharmatā* is common to all three vehicles; fourth, clarifying that the three periods of time are equally suchness; fifth, correctly explaining the meaning of *dharmatā* and its transcendence of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*);
sixth, clarifying the three types of the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*); and seventh, clarifying the presence of the name "dharma" within the nine matters.
As for "according to the meaning" (*yathārtha*): the eighth [section] clarifies the three dharmas from the perspective of the meaning of the defilement and purity of sentient beings;

the ninth explains the meaning of the three dharmas from the perspective of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); and the tenth clarifies the meaning that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is immeasurable and not known by the mind.

Now, this first [section] first clarifies "suchness" (*tathatā*) from the perspective of distinct characteristics (*pṛthag-lakṣaṇa*), and secondly clarifies suchness from the perspective of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is said there are "two kinds."

The passage beginning with "As the earth has the characteristic of solidity" clarifies that these dharmas each possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). These specific characteristics are themselves suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is said that they each have their own respective characteristics.

The section beginning with "The true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) previously explained the meaning of suchness specifically within the context of these respective characteristics. Now, next, we shall proceed from [the perspective of] these respective...

Within these characteristics, reality cannot be found when sought; even their individual characteristics do not exist. Since there is not a single characteristic at all, it is said that they are indestructible.
Because there is nothing to be grasped or discarded and one is detached from a recipient [of experience], it is said that they are without fault.
The passage beginning with "In the emptiness of suchness" has already been refuted therein.
