Regarding the phrase "practicing the six pāramitās, etc., without skillful means," this appears to refer both to the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths) and to the sixth bhūmi;

thus, one should know that it encompasses these two meanings. How is this known? The subsequent treatise states: "Because they have not yet attained the fire of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), they are 'unripe' and are therefore called 'birth.

One should know that [this state] resembles the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformity-patience) within the *mārgajñatā*, for therein one gives rise to craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), which constitutes an obstruction."

The first stage (*bhūmi*) is the summit of the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, it is called "the arising of the Dharma. Because one has reached the summit from which there is no falling back, the text states:

"Without employing skillful means, one practices the six *pāramitās*, enters the three samādhis, yet does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), nor does one attain entry into the rank of a bodhisattva.

This inverted phrasing appears to refer to the distinction between the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrvamga*) and the first ground itself. On the stage prior to the grounds, one possesses the "patience of conformity" (*anuloma-kṣānti*).

Because one has not yet attained the skillful means of non-arising on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one gives rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). This obstructs non-arising and causes one to fall from the summit (*mūrdhan*).
According to the subsequent treatise, it further states that attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and increasing its firmness is called the Bodhisattva stage.
Upon entering this stage, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and all the hosts of Māras cannot shake one; this is also termed the dharma of the patience of non-arising. [From the] Sūtra.

Furthermore, it is said: "If one practices the six *pāramitās* without skillful means (*upāya*), enters the three samādhis, yet does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) nor enter the stage of the arising of the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, one consequently falls from the summit (*mūrdhan*). This is the first reversal of meaning explaining skillful means.
This appears to be the skillful means of non-arising (*anutpāda*) of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

Because one has not yet attained this skillful means of non-arising of the seventh stage while within the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*) on the sixth stage, one gives rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). Consequently, one violates the equality of the seventh stage and thus falls from the summit (*mūrdhan*).
If, in the scriptural text, it were merely intended to clarify the meaning through this first instance alone, the subsequent treatise would have only two points of interpretation.
For this reason, one should know that the scriptural passage herein contains both types of "summit" (mūrdhan) meanings as well as the two types of "conformity-patience" (anulomikī kṣānti).
Within the summits of these two locations, there are again two types of summit meanings in one location: the first is the summit based on the state of correct position (samyaktva-niyāma).

Thus, both cases are based on the absence of arising (*anutpāda*). In the second case, both are based on the two [aspects]. The patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) takes the intermediate stage as its "summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Now, when it is said that one "falls from the summit" because dharmas arise, this clarifies that "arising" refers to the occurrence of attachment to dharmas (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*) within the stage of conforming patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*);

because one has not attained the great summit-stage of the patience regarding non-arising, it is called "falling from the summit. Furthermore, this also possesses the twofold meaning of "falling. Why?

It is so. Because within the stage of "patience in accordance with reality" (anulomikī-kṣānti), one gives rise to attachment to dharmas (dharmatṛṣṇā), it opposes the "patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Consequently, one cannot enter the summit of the bodhisattva stages; one falls back into patience in accordance with reality and cannot abide between patience in accordance with reality and the patience of non-arising.

One ought to take up the path of the Buddha, which is the patience of non-arising; therefore, it is called "falling from the summit. In the subsequent treatise, these two meanings are present. Thus, it is as fully explained.

Because these two meanings are lost, it is called "falling from the summit. Therefore, the commentary below explains: "That which ought to be attained is not attained; hence it is called 'falling' (patita).
From the passage beginning with Śāriputra’s question onward, he correctly asks for the reason why it is said that [the bodhisattva] is "born" (jāti). After Subhūti has replied...

The lower section contains two points. First, it answers by way of the three samādhis. It states that taking emptiness and so forth as dharmas means that because the Bodhisattva receives and becomes attached to this emptiness-samādhi as a teaching, they accord with the dharmas such as the emptiness-samādhi, giving rise to attachment to dharmas (dharmatṛṣṇā) and producing a state of receiving and being attached.
Since this attachment is as manifest as the attachment of evil afflictions, it is said to "accord with the Path."
Attachment to dharmas arises; therefore, each is examined through the dharmas one by one, and in every case it is said that one "accepts, attends to, and clings.
This shall now be explained. Second, attachment to dharmas is clarified through the gate of quiescence (*śamatha*); its meaning is as explained above.

From the passage "this suffering should be known" onwards, thirdly, attachment to dharmas arises through the gate of the analytical discernment of all dharmas. Each of these shall be explained in turn. This...

A "mature Bodhisattva" refers to one who has attained the fire of the outflow-free (anāsrava) true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa). One who is not a mature Bodhisattva refers to one who has not yet attained the fire of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The section beginning with "Question: explains the four matters from the initial intent of the seventh division above. The section beginning with "Answer:
clarifies that these are elucidated by means of the three roots of goodness.

Regarding the statement that those whose craving and so forth are attenuated enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): this refers to the fact that meditative concentration can sever craving.

Regarding those whose anger and so forth are attenuated and enter deeply into the mind of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*): this refers to the fact that the four immeasurable concentrations (*catur-apramāṇa*) eliminate the poison of anger.
These four, when based on the twelve gates of meditation, are designated as "meditation. If they are based on the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*), these four are merely derived from meditation.

Birth cannot be called a "ground" (*bhūmi*). The meaning of "non-delusion" shall now be explained. Regarding the statement that "the summit (*mūrdhan*) is the station of the Dharma (*dharmapada*)," the previous treatise explained that the station of the Dharma is also called the station of the bodhisattva, also called the summit of the bodhisattva, and also called the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Since this has already been explained above, why is it stated again here?

attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) within the context of non-arising dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma*) is termed an affliction (*kleśa*). Since afflictions pertain to arising dharmas, they are described as "arising" even within the context of non-arising dharmas. As for ordinary beings...
The term "middle" (*madhya*) is also called "excellent" (*sādhu*).

From the passage on the three liberations lacking skillful means (*upāya*) downward, it explains the preceding text concerning falling from the summit due to conceiving an attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) because of a lack of superior skillful means.
One does not attain true wisdom; it is like a clay vessel that, having not been fired by fire, is unfit for holding water.
Because one does not apprehend the dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*), it is called "arising" by virtue of being contrary [to that realization].

If one attains true wisdom, like a vessel that has been fired, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*) and contains the water of the true characteristics; because it cannot be destroyed, it is called "matured.
From the intermediate stage of the patience of non-arising downward, this is a distinct kind of "summit" (*mūrdhan*); its meaning is as explained above.

Question: From "As follows" onwards, the intent of the question is as follows: Since it has been stated that this intermediate stage is the "Summit" (mūrdhan), one who dwells above this should properly advance toward the Buddha-way and no longer fear falling back.
If the Summit has not yet been attained, there would be no Summit to follow; if the Summit has already been attained, one should no longer be following it.
Now, why is it said here that one "follows the Summit"? Answer: From "As follows" onwards, it means that one is about to attain the Summit and arises [from that state].

Regarding "Affection" (*āsvāda*): it should not be said that this merely follows the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). It shall now be explained. As for what is termed the "Bodhisattva Stage" (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), this is a treatise on a single principle that correctly explains the summit of the Bodhisattva stage;
this has already been examined and discussed above. It shall now be explained.

Furthermore, from the section beginning "Based on the wisdom of arising and ceasing" (*shengmie zhihui*) below, the Master extensively cites various schools to explain the meaning of the two obstacles (*er-zhang*) and clarify the differences in the transformation and reversal of consciousnesses (*zhuan-shi*).
He states that according to one school’s interpretation, citing the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces), it says:

"The Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue pusa*) is not different from the Buddha-Dharmakāya; they differ only in terms of arising and ceasing. Therefore, the transformation of consciousness continues until the Vajra [stage]. Furthermore—
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "For the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), there exists at this point an obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents mastery.

To counteract this obstacle, the Buddha-stage (*buddha-bhūmi*) is taught. Thus, the obstacle to knowledge persists through the tenth stage. Regarding this, one school of interpretation says: "The first stage is like stone from which gold is extracted;

therefore, the arising and ceasing of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which are false and illusory, are exhausted at the time of the first stage. My teacher now offers this explanation: [text continues].

Formerly, Emperor Taizu of the Zhou dynasty sent men to the country of Qi to invite Dharma masters. Over ten people arrived, but they were only able to lecture on the Vinaya and the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā).
Taizu said, "I wish to propagate the Mahāyāna," and thus asked, "Where is there a Mahāyāna master? They replied, "There is one in the palace.
He immediately dispatched Prince Liang to go and invite him. That country then sent Āryadeva to come; although...

Not understanding the local dialect, he began by asking through an interpreter: "The *Aksayamatinirdeśa-sūtra* states that the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) ceases upon reaching the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

Yet, here it further says that one enters the 'stage of dharma' (*dharmatā-pada*), where the Bodhisattva of Non-arising Patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) possesses wisdom free from arising and ceasing.

This accords with that treatise. Since it is said that one relies on wisdom free from arising and ceasing to depart from inversion, this is precisely the cessation of the evolving consciousness. Departing from arising...
Regarding "because wisdom is extinguished, there is no arising": this refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This accords with the *Shenji lun* (Treatise on the Auspicious Spirit);

it shall be explained extensively in the relevant passage. The Master said: "According to the teachings received from my teacher, even light feathers can perceive their nature and attain the function of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, in the subsequent commentary explaining the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is stated that from the first stage up to the tenth stage, all are called 'knowing the stages.'"

This refers to having already transcended the "light feathers" (trivialities). Therefore, one is called a Bodhisattva. Because those of the Two Vehicles cannot perceive their nature, they are not Bodhisattvas.
The Master says that there are two kinds of inversion: first, the universal; second, the particular. If one views the four [realms] as distinct, the various afflictions are the universal.
Here, it is said that one leaves behind the universal inversion. Regarding "leaving behind the wisdom of arising and ceasing," this means by means of the True [Nature].
"Consciousness" here excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). "Attaining the non-arising and non-ceasing" means attaining the true wisdom of non-birth (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

This principle of non-arising is difficult to believe and difficult to maintain; this Bodhisattva is able to endure and receive it. He should enter the unimpeded, immovable, and non-retrogressive state.

Therefore, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). By extinguishing all contemplative dharmas, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, it is called a "stage" (*bhūmi*).
If it is not thus, it is called "attachment to dharmas" (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*). This shall now be explained.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Three Kinds of Provisional Designations" within the "Section on Non-Attachment": by means of this non-attached wisdom, one eliminates ignorance and all other afflictions.
Here, "ignorance" refers to the fifth dwelling-place (*vihāra*), and "all afflictions" refers to the four dwelling-places.
Therefore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "The afflictions such as vexation and so forth are called the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Just as one speaks of a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) who does not attain the various dhyānas or the cessation of dhyāna, this refers entirely to the nine meditative absorptions (*navasamāpatti*).

One should know that here, when it says 'ignorance and other afflictions,' it refers exhaustively to the five stages of existence (*pañcavihāra*). If this is the case, it appears there is no distinction between the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*)."

This refers to the removal of the four abodes (*catur-vihāra*) as well as the fifth abode. As for the term "knowledge of arising and ceasing" (*utpāda-nirodha-jñāna*), this is stated in reference to the removal of specific inversions (*viparyāsa*).
However, since this stage is based merely on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and has not yet been truly realized, it is described as "arising and ceasing.

How is this known? The original treatise explains the aforementioned "removal of the four [abodes]"; the scriptural text should not deviate from that explanation. Yet, it speaks of being "free from arising and ceasing."
"Wisdom" here refers to the wisdom prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) that has not yet realized the truth; therefore, it is said to be subject to arising and ceasing.

When the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) arises, one departs from this wisdom and thus attains non-arising (*anutpāda*). Because one receives the rank of a bodhisattva for the first time, it is said that "one departs.

It is precisely because they exist only in the fruit that this is so. Next, it is the same regarding the gate of quiescent extinction (*śānti*); in all cases, it is said that one is attached to this attachment to the sensations and mindfulness of quiescent extinction.

From Subhūti’s speech onwards, it clarifies how Subhūti (Śāriputra) proceeds through each phenomenon one by one to answer and clarify the meaning of non-arising.
This first section proceeds sequentially through the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) to engage in a dialogue based on the principle of non-perception. Furthermore, Śāriputra...
From "Not so, Śāriputra" onwards, the second section provides a sequential exposition of the dharmas, answering and explaining by means of the gate of non-recollection (*amanasikāra*).
From "In this way, Śāriputra" onwards, it clarifies the explanation of the three kinds of mental fetters (*citta-saṃyojana*).
"By what reason? and so forth below, correctly explains the essence of mind revealed above.
One should know that the *ālayavijñāna* mind is like the "store of a tree" (*vṛkṣagarbha*); it does not refer to wisdom (*jñāna*). Therefore, the statement here—"For what reason?

This mind is not mind, because the characteristics of mind are eternally pure"—should be understood as referring to the mind of self-nature purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*), the mind that is the store of the tree. If...
Is this "knower" not the mind? This meaning shall now be explained in detail.
From the passage where Śāriputra speaks to Subhūti onwards, this constitutes "deriving further discussion from the current topic.

Since the Venerable Subhūti (Śāntideva) has already explained that "this mind is no-mind" because the characteristics of the mind are fundamentally pure, Śāriputra (Śariputra) immediately questions him on this basis.

Subhūti’s speech concludes with the following response: "If a bodhisattva knows that this mental state is neither conjoined with nor separated from lust and so forth, one should know that this refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure mind. Therefore, the commentary explains: "O virtuous one, reflect well;
you should answer by means of the mind of true reality (*dharmatā-citta*). This refers to the mind that is real in its essence, not the mind of analytical wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). If...
Regarding the statement by the *Jñānavatī* (The Wise One): "How can it be said that if a bodhisattva knows the characteristics of this mind, [it is not wisdom]?

Since these characteristics of the mind are elucidated based on what is known (*jñeya*), one should understand that they are not wisdom itself; rather, the treatise merely discusses their actual substance.

As for the statement that these characteristics of the mind do not conjoin with lust and so forth, this is based on the fact that the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* is primordially pure and its self-nature (*svabhāva*) is pure. This is as stated in the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*.
It is said: "Mind and mind do not touch afflictions; afflictions do not touch the mind. How can a mind that does not touch phenomena become defiled?
This is precisely the meaning. Speaking from the perspective of their essential nature (*tattva*), they do not conjoin.
Regarding the phrase "not separated from the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)": this is based on the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*. It refers to the sense of being enveloped;

since it refers to the aforementioned essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is said that they do not combine. Now, specifically based on the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* while speaking of the sense of being enveloped, it is said that they are not separated.
Therefore, that sutra states: "The *tathāgatagarbha* is enveloped by the storehouse of immeasurable afflictions."

This is precisely its meaning. Thus, it is said that one does not depart from the various *paryavasthānas* (entanglements); this refers to the sense of being "unstained yet stained," which is difficult to comprehend and sever.

If one speaks of the meaning of the Tathāgata, it is discussed in terms of the fruition (*phala*). If one speaks of the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is discussed in terms of the time when it is within entanglements.

As for the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is discussed in terms of the time of natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). These merely clarify the meaning according to specific occasions; they do not [contradict one another].
Because there is a risk of confusion, it is necessary to distinguish them. This shall now be explained.

From the passage beginning with “Śāriputra said to Subhūti” onwards, the treatise correctly elucidates the meaning of the non-existence of mental characteristics (*citta-nimitta*). The commentary explains this very clearly;
each point will be explained in detail as we proceed. The section beginning with “One should not ask” concerns the existence or non-existence of the internal and external.

Both [the mind and its characteristics] are non-existent. Why, then, do you ask about the meaning of the existence of mental characteristics (citta-lakṣaṇa) or the non-existence of mental characteristics? Therefore, this is not a valid question.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having offered praise... onwards, constitutes the second major section of this chapter:
the meaning of Śāriputra’s eulogy and exhortation to study. This will be explained in the main treatise.
The commentary beginning with "The explanation states" below clarifies the meaning of equality and mutual non-perception within the eighteen kinds of emptiness mentioned above.
The passage beginning with "Some say" below clarifies that in order to clarify non-existence, one first establishes the existence of phenomena; therefore, the words "some say" are set forth.
The four external great elements refer to food, drink, clothing, and so forth, which can augment the four internal great elements;

therefore, it is said that they enter into the body and become internal. When the body dies, it returns to belong to the external earth, water, fire, and wind; therefore, it is said that they are external.
From "All dharmas" onwards, it clarifies that they are empty and devoid of the meaning of coming and going. It clarifies that all dharmas fundamentally have no coming or going.

If there were an external [existence], then there could be an internal [existence]. Now, since the external itself is non-existent and there is nothing to fear as an internal [existence], one does not perceive internal emptiness within external emptiness. The same applies to all other cases.

Furthermore, from "There are also bodhisattvas who have already [attained]" onwards, the text next explains the passage concerning not being mindful of the six pāramitās and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
From the question "Having asked about bodhi" onwards, it first explains the meaning of the three types of mind. There are many further subdivisions; the intention is to explain each one individually.
This shall be explained when we encounter the relevant text. The answer follows below. According to the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, there are four types of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
The first generation of the mind is like the new moon; the second, the generation of the mind through practice, is like the moon on the fifth day;

the third, the generation of the mind of non-retrogression through the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), is like the moon on the tenth day; and the generation of the mind by a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage is like the moon on the fourteenth day.
The sun and moon are perfected in the Buddha, like the moon on the fifteenth day. This means that the moon of the first day is not non-existent; it is simply not seen because it is small.
By using the moon as a metaphor for seeing the principle, one attains a constant understanding of the meaning:

one should know that a Bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is already constant, just as the moon of the first day becomes the full moon. It is not that the full moon is a separate wisdom. Since the sutra provides this clear textual evidence, the meaning is established accordingly.
This is explained extensively; therefore, it is said here that this bodhicitta resembles the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "because the cause resembles the fruit," this clarifies that both cause and fruit are eternal. As for the Buddha’s response to Nātha regarding the rag-robe, when he said, "In my Buddha-dharma, although the cause is impermanent, the fruit is eternal," Śreṇika’s intention was that even though the cause is merely a solid mass, the fruit nonetheless exists.
It is likewise a mere lump [of insentience]. Therefore, they claim that both cause and effect are eternal.
The Buddha, wishing to refute this view, taught that because birth possesses growth and gradually increases in clarity, the cause is impermanent; yet it is not truly subject to extinction.

In the "Section on Additional Benefits" (*guṇavardhana*) of the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, it says: "Because the Dharma-body is the eternal body and the wisdom-body, how could the Dharma-body itself possess impermanence?

It is merely that because [the other bodies] are partially eternal, they increase as fruits; however, because [the Dharma-body] is perfectly eternal, it remains unimpeded. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, following the sections on *dāna* (generosity) and *śīla* (ethical discipline), the next section addresses these three types of mind in relation to the six *pāramitās*.

The first *pāramitā* is established as the stage of the bodhicitta; the middle two are the "unequaled" mind (*asamasama-citta*); and the latter two are the "great mind" (*mahācitta*). This shall now be explained.
If one can practice in this manner—this "single practice" being the beginning—it constitutes the bodhisattva’s wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); otherwise, it does not.
"Named 'arising'" refers to attachment to dharmas. "The mind neither exalts itself nor deprecates others" is a general explanation of the meaning of the non-arising mind not being exalted.
"Like the characteristic of empty space," and so forth, serves as a metaphor for the meanings such as the fundamental, the cause of understanding, and so on.
"Should be explained.

From "Question" onwards, this explains the reason why Śāriputra posed his inquiry. From "Answer" onwards, it clarifies that the question was asked because many lesser bodhisattvas give rise to numerous attachments.
The phrasing within this section is clear and can be seen for oneself, point by point.
This should be explained according to the preceding sutra passage.
As for the question, "Why is bodhi also deceptive? it must be asked in order to clarify the fears of those lesser bodhisattvas who have questions.
Therefore, the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra says to the lesser bodhisattvas: "Emptiness is [the ultimate], while non-emptiness is..."
Regarding the Great Parinirvāṇa: if it were taught for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas, then both the city of Kapilavastu would be empty and the Great Parinirvāṇa itself would be empty.
It is because those who are here—namely, the lesser Bodhisattvas—fear hearing of non-arising that they have asked this question. Furthermore, as for that which arises from falsehood:
if this Dharma were merely the Buddha’s *pratyaya-hetu* (causal condition), it would simply manifest the essence [of reality] and nothing more; it would not concern itself with...
Regarding "arising" (*jāti*): according to the report concerning the Buddha, since it arises from conditions in relation to the cause of arising, it is said to arise from the false and deceptive.

In this context, the explanation that the fundamental existence (*mūla-sat*) constitutes the causes of arising, cessation, and conditions is also excellent. If arising is understood through conditions, the essence of these three causes is not different;
they are merely distinguished by being spoken of in accordance with their respective meanings. As for the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*), it refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Regarding "nature" (*dhātu*): it is now appropriate to explain this by correlating the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*) with the "counter-cause" (*pratipakṣa-hetu*), and the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) with the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*).
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Śāriputra, having offered praise... onwards, the second major section is explained;
it consists of the text in which Śāriputra recounts his praise and exhorts others to study. The reason the Buddha sighed in approval was because he intended to validate what Bhadrika had said, and...

This is the meaning of Śāriputra’s eulogy. Regarding the phrase "born from the Buddha’s mouth," this explains the preceding words of praise. It should simply be said that the teaching is the Buddha’s word;
however, now Subhūti has given rise to understanding through that teaching and practices according to it, exactly as the Buddha spoke, such that what he says is without error.
Therefore, it is said that he is "born from the Buddha’s mouth. Now, this [phrase] is used to describe him; hence, it is said that he "has... (the text here appears incomplete).
This is what people say. People claim that the Brahmā King was born from among the four castes of sentient beings:
the Kṣatriya was born from his crown, the Vaiśya from his navel, and the Śūdra from his feet;

now, because the Brāhmaṇa was born from the vicinity of his mouth, he is noble and thus the foremost among the four classes of sentient beings. Now, Śāriputra is likewise so; for this reason, he is praised in such a manner.
"Furthermore, those who have not yet attained the Way," and so forth, explains the meaning of "not taking a share of the wealth" mentioned above.
"The fourfold faith" refers to faith in the Three Jewels and the precepts. "Śāriputra and others," and so forth, explains the passage from the *Shushuzan* (Description of Praise).
Since there is no pure practice in the ultimate sense, this is clarified by citing the four great śrāvakas.

Regarding the passage "this samādhi" and below, if explained according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), it is said that this *amala-samādhi* arises from five locations, namely the four dhyānas and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The treatise here speaks only of its arising from the four fundamental dhyānas; however, because it functions within the desire realm, it is [also] described as such.
This is the fifth section.
From the question below, the text next explains the words of Śāriputra’s exhortation to study. Above, Śāriputra stated:

"Those who wish to attain the state of a bodhisattva, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and so forth, should study the *prajñāpāramitā* and practice according to its teaching. Now, the intent of the question here is as follows: if...
If one discusses the Mahāyāna, then the five vehicles arise; yet if one discusses its actual substance, it concerns only the affairs of the Bodhisattvas.
Why, then, is it that here one relies solely on the three vehicles to clarify the study of Prajñā?
The answer begins as follows: It is said that, just as in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the five vehicles are produced;
however, the practice of those in the three vehicles is all for the sake of *nirvāṇa*. Now, this is spoken according to the supramundane perspective, hence it refers to the "three vehicles.

This must refer to the secret path, wherein it is discussed how the three vehicles equally abide in the true mark (*dharmatā*) and enter pure *nirvāṇa*. Here, we speak only of this true mark and purity.
[The Master said: "Because its nature is taken as *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), it is said to be 'identical' [to that]. The Master further stated:

'If the wisdom of the Three Vehicles and the state where afflictions (*kleśa*) have been severed are absent, it is called *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); the point at which birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are exhausted is called *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

Now, based on the fact that for those of the Three Vehicles birth has ended, their merit and *dharmakāya* merge their virtues with emptiness; therefore, it is said that all people of the Three Vehicles [attain this]."

They are equally [attained] as *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. When Dharma Master Daoping read this sutra, seeing that it causes those of the three vehicles to study together in the *prajñāpāramitā*, he composed the *Wushi jiaoyi* (The Meaning of the Teachings of the Five Periods), wherein he categorized this sutra as a "Common Teaching" (*tongjiao*).
If one were to name it a "Common Teaching" because it gives rise to the three vehicles, then since all Mahayana sutras give rise to the five vehicles, they too should [be called Common Teachings].

These are all part of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*). This sutra states: "Those who wish to attain the status of the four castes, beginning with the Kṣatriya, up to the six heavens, as well as the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, should study Prajñāpāramitā.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "By entering the Samādhi of the Afflicted Eye, one can cause immeasurable sentient beings to leave the three evil paths;
immeasurable sentient beings to obtain the happiness of humans and devas; and immeasurable [sentient beings to...]"
Those born with the capacity attained the fruits of the Two Vehicles; immeasurable humans and devas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The *Bhagavati-sūtra* states:
"Just as the eight rivers flow forth from Lake Anavatapta, so too does the Mahāyāna give birth to the wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, both mundane and supramundane.
What is called "mundane" refers to the vehicles of humans and devas; what is called "supramundane" refers to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.
One should know that all Mahāyāna teachings give rise to the five vehicles; there is none that does not contain the universal teaching—how much more so this very sutra?

This sutra indeed propagates the birth of the five vehicles, yet now it speaks only of three. The Master said: "Prajñā is precisely the ālayavijñāna, the true mind of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
The pure wisdom of the two vehicles is merely a transformed consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); without attaining this wisdom, how could one..."
The statement "one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*" refers to the fact that the three vehicles equally contemplate the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This is spoken with reference to the eternally abiding *prajñā*, not to discuss true wisdom (*jñāna*). True wisdom is not attained by those of the two vehicles; as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"The contemplation of the two vehicles does not perceive the Buddha-nature. Now, some say that the statement "not perceiving nature" is based on the path of manifest realization (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the statement that they "see the nature" (*dharmatā*): according to the secret path, because true wisdom is identical therein, they are made to study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
therefore, it is said that they equally attain the single, ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

However, within the path of manifestation, it is said that the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) do not possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and thus they do not see the *prajñāpāramitā*. Such is the distinction.
There are two meanings. These are clearly stated in the sūtras and śāstras; they can be understood by inference. This meaning shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "Next" onwards, this single "furthermore" (*punar-aparaṃ*) provides one interpretation regarding the beginning and the universal basis [of the same...].

[The phrase] "attaining the Way and nirvāṇa at the beginning" refers to the various preceding meanings. This is based on the *Guhyamārga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Secret Path) and does not refer to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). This, moreover...

Next, regarding the "intention": the preceding discussion was based on the objective realm (*viṣaya*). This shall now be explained. Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Moreover, Śāriputra" onwards, the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā* are clarified;
as this has already been interpreted in the previous text, what follows here merely exhorts those training in the three vehicles.

The forty-second fascicle of the *Śāstra*, the ninth chapter, is titled "The Chapter on Accumulation and Dispersion" (*Saṃcayavibhaṅga-parivarta*). This constitutes the third major section within the "Division of the Response to the Command.
From this point onward, Subhūti receives the command and begins the formal exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Within the text of this formal exposition, there are many...

There are four parts. First, from the "Chapter on Characteristics" (*Lakṣaṇaparivarta*) to the "Chapter on Practice" (*Caryāparivarta*), these three chapters clarify the gate of the three kinds of understanding and explain *prajñā*.

Second, from the "Chapter on the Meaning of Phrases" (*Padārthaparivarta*) down to the "Chapter on Bondage and Liberation" (*Bandhanamokṣaparivarta*), this section concerns the "Great Person" (*mahāpuruṣa*);
because they have already realized the Great Dharma through their engagement with *prajñā*, they are called "Great Persons. Third, from the "Mahāyāna... [chapter].
From the chapter below this down to the "Chapter on Reaching the Essence of the Assembly," there are seven chapters of sūtra text. Next, regarding the Great Dharma:

since *prajñā* has already been explained as that which is known by great beings, it is called the "Great Dharma. From the fourth [chapter], the "Ten Non-existences" chapter and the "Non-arising" chapter, these two subsequent chapters arise.
The former clarifies the elimination of arising, while the latter clarifies the dispatching of dharmas; therefore, they are categorized according to the aspect of dispatching.
Chapter on the Collection and Dispersion of All Dharmas. To clarify this, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one does not perceive the collection or dispersion of all dharmas.

As for the current title "Chapter on the Collection and Dispersion," Master Xingzhuang’s commentary on the intent of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "In reality, it is for the purpose of refuting arising, yet it is named the 'Chapter on Arising.
It refutes dependent origination, yet it is named the 'Chapter on Dependent Origination. Furthermore, Master Zhizheng’s commentary on the intent of this sūtra states: "This [title] raises..."
The objects to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*) serve as the categories, while the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) are cited to establish the title of the sūtra; thus it is said.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, this constitutes the first major section among the three chapters.

First, regarding the three gates of liberation, this clarifies *prajñā*. Within this first section, the first chapter, there are further three parts concerning the purpose [of the treatise], all of which are the master’s own topical headings. This initial part concerns the gate of requesting and indicating.

The first section, from the beginning up to the "Gate of Humility and Refusal," clarifies *prajñā*. The second section, from "Furthermore, World-Honored One" onwards, clarifies Subhūti’s formal exposition;

this is the "Gate of Non-Abiding," which clarifies *prajñā*. The third section, from the forty-third chapter onwards, likewise correctly elucidates the essence and characteristics of *prajñā*. Within the first section, the Gate of Humility and Refusal, there is furthermore...
There are two intentions. The first states: "I do not perceive, I do not obtain a bodhisattva," and so forth; this explains *prajñā* with respect to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
The passage beginning with "O Bhagavat, I do not obtain the gathering or dispersing of any dharmas" and so forth, next explains *prajñā* with respect to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This shall now be explained.
"World-Honored One, I do not perceive any dharma as having accumulation or dispersal," and so forth.
This constitutes the second section, which addresses the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) by elucidating *prajñā* through the gate of non-abiding.

Although the Master of the Treatise provides various interpretive explanations regarding the meanings of "accumulation and dispersal" and "non-abiding" within the subsequent scriptural text, when one examines its underlying intent, this chapter states that all dharmas are without arising.
There is no accumulation; because there is no cessation, there is no sense of dispersal.
As for those who might feel regret: since all these are merely conventional designations established by the three types of conceptual constructs, both the Bodhisattva and his name are unobtainable.
In reality, there is no Bodhisattva. If I were to say that there is a Bodhisattva and declare, "This is a Bodhisattva," it would be for the sake of teaching them Prajñāpāramitā.
What I have thus spoken would contradict the true nature of dharmas and incur the offense of false speech; it might even lead to regret, rendering my teaching ineffective.
Therefore, I shall now speak of the reality: that there is no bodhisattva. This alone accords with the true mark of reality (*dharmatā*).
From the passage "The World-Honored One, these words do not abide" onwards, each point is clearly explained through both mundane and supramundane phenomena to clarify the meaning of non-abiding;
this shall be discussed in detail according to the text. The subsequent treatise is also explicit on this point.

Although the Master of the Treatise employs various interpretations to explain these meanings from "these words do not abide" onwards, its general intent is solely to clarify that the Dharma requested is fundamentally non-existent, because of the Dharma... [text ends].
Because there is no [dharma], it is called "having nothing to rely upon. Originally, names were used to summon dharmas; names were established for the sake of dharmas.

Since there are no dharmas, there are likewise no names. Because there are neither dharmas nor names, it is said that "this character does not abide. Because it originally does not abide, there was a state of "not non-abiding.
Now, since there is no longer even non-abiding, there is therefore also no "not non-abiding. Thus, the Sūtra asks: "What is it?"
This is because there is nothing that exists. All such meanings are likewise so. "World-Honored One, I do not obtain it.

From the section on "gathering and dispersing" (*saṃcaya-vikṣepa*) onwards, each point shall be explained individually. This will be clarified by examining the dharmas, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the six perfections (*pāramitā*) within the context of cause and effect;
these shall all be interpreted as they arise in the treatise. Regarding the "gathering and dispersing of the exhaustion of ignorance," in comparison with...
In the preceding text, among the twelve links of dependent origination, only this single phrase is added. It should be explained:

why is it that the term "bodhisattva" is used? The Master says: this is the meaning of expressing disdain and yielding. Therefore, the text here contains three or four sections that clarify this point. It should be explained.

Question: If that is so, since these same words also appear at the beginning of the three preceding chapters on the provisional (prajñāpāramitā), should they not also be understood as the "gate of yielding out of disdain"?
Answer: No. In those other instances, the words "Subhūti" are used merely to request an exposition of prajñāpāramitā;

however, because the Buddha spoke these words to confirm and complete the meaning of the teaching for bodhisattvas, they do not constitute the "gate of yielding out of disdain" when clarifying the meaning of prajñāpāramitā. It is only here [in this current context] that it truly begins.
Because Subhūti speaks correctly, this is the "gate of censure and yielding" that clarifies the meaning of *prajñā*.

From the passage beginning with "I do not perceive [anything] like a dream," this single point serves to resolve doubts regarding the Tathāgata; this shall be explained in the main discourse. Regarding the passages such as "detached from cessation, non-arising, and non-demonstration," these shall each be explained in turn in the main discourse.

Regarding the statement, "I do not attain [anything] such as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and so forth": although the three provisional designations and other categories in the preceding sections clarify the state of emptiness and the dharmas, these three phrases were not present there.

As for why they are clarified here, the Master explains that in the preceding sections, the meaning was mostly elucidated from the perspective of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and therefore those phrases were not mentioned. Now, however, this section deals with the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

In discussing the meaning, the two truths are clarified together and the true nature (*dharmatā*) is skillfully expounded; therefore, their characteristics are explained here at the outset. There is one interpretation which says:

"In the preceding chapters on the three types of provisional designation (*prajñapti*) and so forth, the meanings of both emptiness—of phenomena and of arising—and the two truths are likewise clarified together.
Why, then, are they not present above? The reason they are clarified here is that within the section on the analysis of names, there is both the extensive and the concise; whereas above..."
The preceding two chapters were merely brief expositions; they did not explain the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in detail, and therefore those matters were not discussed.

Now, this section marks the beginning of the "Exposition" (*pravibhāga*) division within the "Instruction" (*deśanā*) division, wherein the characteristics of phenomena are explained more extensively; it is from here that they are first elucidated.

Question: Regarding the passage "already below in the previous chapter," the meaning is as follows: In the preceding three chapters on the provisional designations (*prajñapti*), it was clarified through Subhūti’s words that he does not see a bodhisattva or the term "bodhisattva," and that the term "bodhisattva" does not exist within, without, or in between.
Why do you say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is taught for the sake of bodhisattvas? Now, why is it further stated here that "I do not perceive" and so forth? For whom is this being taught?
The answer follows below. The reason these four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are enumerated here is precisely to clarify that craving for the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is difficult to eliminate;
therefore, three types of craving are cited as precedents to counter it. Because it is so difficult to eliminate, they are stated repeatedly in order to cause one to abandon craving for the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the section following the previous "upper" teaching, the intent of the first "successive" (or "repeated") explanation was that there is no fault in restating it. Now, this single point asserts that it is not a repetition;
it specifically states "not seeing," whereas here it says that because all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, they are neither perceived nor attained.
This is explained through the two gates of "non-perception" and so forth; how could it be the same as the explanation in the previous "gate of non-seeing"? Moreover, above...
He showed that [the Dharma] was not seen, and thus requested an exposition. The present statement, "not awakened," and so forth, is based on the quiescence of phenomena;

it means that because they are not awakened, they do not attain [realization]. This is not due to a lack of intellectual power. Since the previous passage was based on the fact that [the Dharma] was not seen due to a deficiency in wisdom, he requested an exposition. There are such meanings as these.
"Different intention" means "different.
The question that follows asks: Regarding the statement that there are no bodhisattvas now, does this mean that there are no bodhisattvas even before they have begun their practice?

It is not that the Bodhisattva is produced only at the time of practice. If one were to say that the Bodhisattva exists [in potential] within the light, but only upon reaching the practice of Prajñāpāramitā does one then say they do not exist, then the Bodhisattva would be something that originally existed and is now non-existent.
If the Bodhisattva already existed prior to practicing Prajñāpāramitā, why then say that one does not see a Bodhisattva practicing Prajñāpāramitā?
The answer begins below. This clarifies that it is within the very nature of phenomena (*dharmas*) that one speaks of primordial great quiescence; therefore, it is said to be "non-existent.

If, while practicing Prajñā, one were to first eliminate phenomena so as to make them non-existent, one would destroy the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "For example, the eye and so forth," since one intends to explain that there is neither accumulation nor dispersal, it first clarifies this by establishing the dharmas, and only afterwards does it clarify their negation.
For now, we shall discuss this in terms of the eye; the same principle applies to all dharmas. There are various underlying intentions for these explanations, which shall be stated one by one.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "observing the cessation-truth (nirodha-satya) of the world," the Master says: "This is based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."
This concerns the discussion of the mundane world.

When it says, "One should speak," and so forth, from the phrase "there is no conventional discourse" onwards, there are two intended meanings. This is explained by way of connecting with the meaning of the worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*).
It is not that they do not abide; it is not that they do not abide through the conjunction of names, causes, and conditions.

If it were otherwise, there would be no conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as a provisional existence, and all phenomena would consequently cease to exist. It is precisely within conventional reality, in contrast to conventional reality, that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is said to exist.
If conventional reality did not exist, the ultimate truth would likewise not exist. If this were so, then regarding—
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), both truths are absent; thus, all worldly phenomena fall into great disorder. Therefore, Dharma Master Tanyan said:
"The two truths are the proximate designations used to interface with the mundane."

Furthermore, from "Next, herein" onwards constitutes the ultimate explanation. As stated above, from "having already departed from the two characteristics" onwards, each and every point explains the meanings of the various dharmas being quiescent, unborn, unceasing, non-indicative, and so forth; these shall all be explained in accordance with the text as it proceeds.
From "There are two kinds of quiescence" onwards, the preceding section has clarified all dharmas by way of the gate of departure (*viyoga*).

The exposition on the meaning of the nature of words being devoid [of intrinsic reality] is complete. Now, proceeding by way of the gate of quiescence (*śānti*), we shall explain the aforementioned meaning by observing that all phenomena possess the characteristic of *nirvāṇa* and have been quiescent from the very beginning.
From "not produced" onwards, the text next explains the meaning of the non-arising of all phenomena. Since phenomena are fundamentally unproduced, they likewise do not cease now.
First, regarding "the unconditioned of the future," this refers to the unconditioned state to be attained in the future.
Regarding the statement "there are three kinds of non-extinction," this clarifies the meaning of the three types of extinction (*nirodha*).

Why, then, is it said that there are three kinds of non-extinction? It is because one now wishes to clarify non-extinction; therefore, the three types of extinction are first cited by way of their contrast.

Thus, they are called "three kinds. To explain these differences: if a Vaibhāṣika were to explain it, they would say that they are called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because their temporal characteristics differ. If...

The *Tattvasiddhi* states: "That which is apprehended by the reckoning of true wisdom is called 'conditioned by reckoning' (*saṃkhyā-ālambana*); that which is not apprehended by the reckoning of true wisdom is called 'not conditioned by reckoning' (*asaṃkhyā-ālambana*).

Thus, "conditioned by reckoning" and "not conditioned by reckoning" mean respectively "conditioned by wisdom" and "not conditioned by wisdom"; it is merely a difference in the terminology used by the translators of the scriptures.
As for the explanation in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it agrees with the *Renwang jing*. One should now rely on this [the *Vibhāṣā*] for the discussion. The *Mahāvibhāṣā*...
It is said: For a person who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the severance of the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) without remainder is termed "conditioned by wisdom" (*jñānapratyaya*).
Why is this so? Because this cessation is attained through severance by means of what is conditioned by wisdom; therefore, this cessation is called "cessation conditioned by wisdom.
If a person of the first fruit is of the most dull faculties, they have at most seven more births; these seven births belong to the cessation conditioned by wisdom, which is without remainder.

Nirvana. Apart from these seven births, all other future births within the cycle of death and rebirth (*saṃsāra*) and the three miserable realms (*trāya*), which are no longer experienced, are termed "cessation not through the condition of wisdom" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Why is this so? At that time, this wisdom merely severs the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the afflictions are absent, future births and deaths are naturally not undergone. These births and deaths do not depend [on anything else].
Because cessation is attained through the condition of wisdom, it is said that the limit of birth and death is "cessation not through the condition of wisdom" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Thus, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: "When a Bodhisattva dwells in the first stage of patience (*kṣānti*), the immeasurable births and deaths of the future are extinguished spontaneously without depending on the condition of wisdom;
this is called 'extinction not through wisdom. It has the characteristic of signlessness and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). For this reason, [it is so designated].

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that for a *sakṛdāgāmin* who has abandoned six grades of the afflictions of the realm of thought, this constitutes cessation through the condition of knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Once the births involving coming and going between the human and celestial realms have been eliminated, the remaining births of saṃsāra that do not arise and are extinguished belong to cessation not through the condition of knowledge (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The Anāgāmin has severed ninety-two *anuśayas*; this constitutes cessation through the condition of wisdom (*prajñā-pratyaya-nirodha*). For the humans, devas, and those born in the three miserable realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), their births are exhausted;

this constitutes cessation not through the condition of wisdom (*a-prajñā-pratyaya-nirodha*). For the Arhat, whose births in the three realms are exhausted, it belongs to cessation not through the condition of wisdom.

Having severed the ninety-eight *anuśayas* such that there is no further place for them, this constitutes cessation through the condition of wisdom. Within the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), all that exists in these two types belongs to the category of characteristics.
It is like the cessation not conditioned by wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This shall now be explained.
Regarding "cessation through impermanence" (*anityatā-nirodha*): it does not depend upon an antidote, but ceases spontaneously.

If none of these three types of cessation exist, then that which is contrary to them is designated as belonging to the unarisen and the non-ceasing. As for "not being shown," the *Lotus Sūtra* says this:
The Dharma cannot be shown, for its verbal characteristics are quiescent. This accords with the "Exposition on Going" (*Gatiparikṣā*).
From the question below, this section further briefly examines the aforementioned meaning, yet accepts only one side while rejecting the other.
Because it does not admit of one-sidedness, [the text] poses a question. "It shall be explained" refers to the following answer:

It states that this suchness and so forth truly have no gathering or dispersing; however, when its function is attained, it is termed "gathering," and when it is not attained, it is termed "dispersing.
This true mark (dharmatā) cannot be lost; it is only because its function is not being attained that it is called "lost."
From "Just as empty space" onwards, the explanation of the ten metaphors above is identical in its textual content. The intended meaning is as follows:

empty space itself has neither accumulation nor dispersal. For example, if a house is filled with empty space, yet its perimeter is not opened by doors, one cannot utilize the space within that house.
However, if one hews out a door or opens windows and shutters, one can enter within and thus obtain the use of that space.
Because it is utilized, it is called "accumulation" (*saṃcaya*). If, when the door is closed, it cannot be used as empty space, it is called "dispersion" (*vikiraṇa*).

Therefore, it is said that empty space possesses accumulation and dispersion. Now, since empty space is also fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, one can say that it neither accumulates nor disperses.
The same shall be explained for the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth.
From the passage beginning "World-Honored One, when the causes and conditions of all dharmas have harmoniously combined" onwards, the author of the treatise provides his own topical outline, stating:
"Above, by means of the 'gate of non-abiding,' he has clarified *prajñā* and completed the explanation of the meaning that the Bodhisattva and the word 'Bodhisattva' are unobtainable.
Now, for the second time, by means of a different gate, he refutes the notion that the Bodhisattva and the word 'Bodhisattva' are unobtainable, thereby clarifying *prajñā*. This is why..."

Regarding "different names," this shall be explained in the formal discussion. For instance, even when one forcibly designates it as "space," there is no dharma within it that can be described as being "space.
In this way, each point returns to reiterate the meaning of the preceding text; thus, the Dharma clarifies it. This shall now be explained.
The commentary beginning with "The explanation below" clarifies the master’s intention regarding the structural divisions of the treatise. The section beginning with "Why is this so?
explains the meaning of the term *paryāya* (alternative formulation). Above, [the author] refuted [the opponent's position] by means of such categories as the gate of neither abiding nor non-abiding.
Now, by examining and refuting [the opponent's position] through the equal characteristics among the five aggregates and so forth, it is called a "differentiation" (paryāya). It shall be explained:

since inhalation and exhalation belong to the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), they do not belong to space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, the sphere where form ceases (*rūpakṣayadhātu*) is also not space.
Because it is the limit where name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases, space is unobstructed. Since form is obstructive, it is the opposite [of space].
Thus, there would be no space at all, but only a mere name.

Question: From "The following [passage]... onwards, this also merely accepts one side; therefore, it constitutes a "gate" (dvāra). This shall now be explained. Answer: From "The following [passage]... shall be explained," onwards, it means that such a matter is not so.
As observed above, the characteristic of earth (*pṛthivī-lakṣaṇa*) is further non-existent. If one takes meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*) as...

[The opponent] says: "If [the opponent] claims that all meditative objects (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are real, the Buddha has also said they are empty; they are merely the characteristics of earth. Since these things are not real, the three great elements (*mahābhūta*) are likewise so.

Therefore, it is said: 'This matter is not so. From the passage beginning with 'As the four great elements constitute the body' onwards, it clarifies the emptiness of successive transmission (*paramparā-śūnyatā*).
Since the body is the basis, when the body does not exist, one should know that everything practiced upon the body is likewise entirely non-existent."
In this manner, one proceeds step by step until reaching the fruit of Buddhahood. From "For this reason" onwards is the concluding explanation.
The meaning of the nature of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) shall be explained in the relevant passage.
Furthermore, from the words "Next, the World-Honored One" onwards, the Master of the Treatise himself provides a topical outline.

Having already completed the explanation of the meaning according to the section on "Abiding in Neither Abiding nor Non-abiding" within the preceding Gate of Attachment and Aversion, this current passage constitutes Subhūti’s formal exposition, which proceeds next to clarify Prajñāpāramitā by means of the Gate of Non-abiding.
Within this text, there are three major points. The first clarifies non-... by means of the Gate of Non-abiding.
The one who abides attains [the goal]. The second statement—that a bodhisattva abides in form without skillful means—clarifies the fault of such an abider.
From the third section, concerning Śreṇika and those below, it clarifies the principle of using the small to illustrate the great.

Now, by taking these as the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), elements (dhātus), and the twelve links of dependent origination, they establish the aforementioned meaning; thus, they are analyzed and distinguished concisely. This shall now be explained.
Regarding the statement, "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form," the Master said: "This clarifies the meaning of mutual identity (*yiji*). Now I say:
if the two truths were two distinct things, they would not be identical; if they were one, they would likewise not be identical. Rather, within a single dharma there are two meanings.

Because we grasp their single essence, it is called 'identity. It is said that form arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature; therefore, it is described as non-existent. This is what is meant by 'lack of intrinsic nature' (*niḥsvabhāva*)."
The non-existence of this [intrinsic nature] is precisely the existence of dependent origination, because it is taught as the dependent origination of form (*rūpa*).

To say that there is this existence of dependent origination, and that this is precisely the non-existence of intrinsic nature arising from conditions, and thus to claim that the two truths are mutually identical (*paraspara-saṃbheda*), is not something seen stated as "mutually identical" in the sūtras or śāstras.
Rather, they only state that "form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. This, however, is merely the sense of "itself" (*eva*) in the phrase "is itself."
This is not an "identity" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the sense of two distinct phenomena being identical; therefore, it is called "mutual identity.

However, people see these two meanings discussed interchangeably and redundantly speak of "mutual identity," subsequently causing everyone to transmit this view. Now, it is precisely because they are neither one nor two that their identity is discussed;
there is no "identity of identity. If one were to speak of mutual identity, there would have to be two phenomena conjoined, which could then be so described.
This refers to identity as characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, it is only identity as suchness (*tathatā*) that is intended; one cannot discuss it in terms of characteristics.

This meaning shall be explained in detail below, up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). The Master said: "The preceding portion of the sūtra enumerates various dharma-gates, all of which conclude here.
Now, within this gate of non-abiding, [it includes] everything up to the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and immeasurable dhāraṇīs."
Regarding the dharmas such as the "gates" (*mukha*) and so forth: it should be understood that they are explained according to their respective underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This may be so. The section beginning with "The commentary states" (*śeṣa ucyate*) is the first instance where the Master of the Treatise himself outlines the structure of the text.

Now, from the passage beginning with "Subhūti," although this is part of the "Section on Entrusting the Teaching" (*parindana-bhāga*) starting from the beginning of this chapter, it constitutes the formal exposition by Subhūti (*Sujāti*). However, the preceding portion [is based on]...

The section on "Humility" (謙讓門) was merely an introductory preface; it was not yet the formal exposition. Now, at the beginning of this second section on "Non-abiding" (不住門), the formal exposition truly commences.

Here, Subhūti is the primary speaker and the World-Honored One acts as the interlocutor; since it is appropriate for him to expound upon Prajñāpāramitā, the text says, "Furthermore, the World-Honored One... (復次世尊).
From the passage "If there are various names for *pāramitā*," etc., this first section begins from the perspective of the practitioner (*yogin*) up to "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*).

It merely provides a brief enumeration of seven gates to show that the names differ. One must proceed to the formal treatise to list and explain the text, starting from "practice" (*caryā*) and concluding with "non-abiding," covering as many as twelve gates.
These shall be explained one by one, so that sentient beings may rejoice upon hearing these various names and explanations.

Because of this joy, it is necessary to provide explanations using multiple names. This is like the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), which pervades both the upper and lower levels of cause and effect.

Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, there is one practice; this is the practice of the Tathāgata. Since one must maintain mindfulness of this, it is necessary to differentiate [the teachings].
Although *prajñā* (wisdom) is itself free from differentiation, this explanation follows the path of establishing dharmas; therefore, it must be done in this way.

[The section] beginning with "Question: is a brief inquiry intended to clarify the preceding meaning. [The section] beginning with "Answer: clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s affection for the Dharma is profound;

because their wisdom and love for the Dharma are great, they fear that this attachment may obstruct the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma*). Since this attachment is difficult to eliminate, he further teaches the state of "non-abiding."

From the "Samādhi of Neither-Existence-nor-Non-existence" (*anupalambha-samādhi*) onwards, it clarifies that when a Bodhisattva enters this samādhi, although there is nothing observed, the mind is not extinguished;

thus, it differs from entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Consequently, he is able to abide in existence while following the locus of concentration on emptiness to transform others externally, and within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he simultaneously illuminates both truths (*satyadvaya*). All of these are the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva.

Question: From "It is asked" onwards, it clarifies that the mind necessarily follows conditions. Now, since the Bodhisattva does not believe in the various mental objects and the mind is already quiescent, why does he not enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?
Answer: From "It is answered" onwards, the author of the treatise again cites the words of Subhūti, using the sūtra to provide the explanation.
Furthermore, from the words "Next, the World-Honored One" onwards, the Master of the Treatise provides his own explanation. This passage is spoken for the sake of two types of bodhisattvas;
while it is intended to discuss each individual bodhisattva as fully possessing these two [qualities], it now speaks only by following these two meanings, and therefore refers to them as "two types."
Because Bodhisattvas who study the scriptures are often attached to words and phrases, [the Buddha] teaches them the gate of non-abiding in words.

Because they possess the penetration of dhyāna, for those practicing meditative concentration, he teaches the non-abiding in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This will be explained in detail in the main treatise.

The commentary states: The following section formally enumerates the two types of bodhisattvas. Regarding the "single-character gate" (ekākṣara-mukha), this clarifies the secular convention of the Western regions [India]:
for every single phenomenon (dharma), there are ten names; these names differ from one another, such that a single phenomenon may have ten, five, three, two, or one name.
If one explains the meaning according to the single-character gate, the term for "earth" (pṛthivī) is simply expressed as *bu*. Only.

It is named by means of a single syllable. Regarding the "two-syllable gate," it is like a single entity such as water, which may have a name consisting of two syllables, or names consisting of three syllables and so forth; this shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from this point onward, as I now wish to explain the meanings within the Buddha-dharma, I first cite the secular customs of the Western Regions (India) to serve as a starting point.
Next, I clarify how the gateways of words (*padamukha*) in the Buddha-dharma correspond to those in secular usage.

Now, I shall explain that when a Bodhisattva hears a single gateway of words, they immediately enter into the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). For example, upon hearing the syllable "A"—which is also called "the beginning" and also called "non-existence"—they hear it thus.
At the time of the gateway of the letter A, one should form this understanding, saying: "All phenomena have been ultimately empty and quiescent from the very beginning;

there is no arising. Yet, one does not abide in the letter A. This clarifies that within the Buddha-dharma, by hearing the meaning of the gateway of a single letter, these forty-two letters likewise enter into the single letter A, and each letter A likewise enters into the forty-two letters.
"Duḥkha" means "suffering. If one hears this name, one gives rise to great compassion and does not dwell upon the syllable "duḥ.
Such is the meaning of hearing these two gates of letters.

*Anitya* means "impermanence" (*múcháng*). If one hears this term, one enters into the practice of the sages; one knows that the syllable is empty and quiescent. Such is the meaning of hearing these three gates of letters.
Therefore, it causes the Bodhisattva not to dwell upon the gates of letters. Thus, by means of the gate of non-dwelling on letters, one clarifies *prajñā*.
Furthermore, names serve as gates; a "gate" has the sense of "passage. Through letters, one explains the principle. There is...

Because it is the functional application of that Path, it is designated as a "gate of letters" (*akṣaramukha*). Since the Bodhisattva knows that the nature of letters is detached and fundamentally empty, he does not dwell upon what he hears.
From the words "other letters" onwards, this is for the practitioner of seated meditation; this is the meaning of this *dhāraṇī*.
This shall be explained below.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning "Moreover, World-Honored One," because the attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is difficult to eliminate, the meaning of the preceding text is restated.

Moreover, each of these various dharma-gates further clarifies the sense that one should not dwell upon the contemplation of dharmas and so forth, thereby elucidating *prajñā*. This shall be explained.
"Quiescence" (śānti) is precisely nirvāṇa; it refers to the purity of intrinsic nature (prakṛti-viśuddhi).
From the passage beginning with "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without skillful means," and so forth.
The second section concerns the gate of abiding (*sthiti-mukha*), wherein the meaning of "loss" is clarified, and each individual dharma is explained accordingly; this shall now be discussed.
As for the passage beginning with "Why is this? and so forth, it returns to explain the reason why one who abides in various dharmas fails to attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

It should be explained that since this fruit is a fruit that is signless and free from dwelling or attachment, one cannot attain this signless fruit by means of practices characterized by dwelling and attachment or practices characterized by signs. Therefore, it must be taught.

The commentary states: "From 'already explained' onwards," this first section provides a general summary and points toward the explanation of the aforementioned noble practices (*ārya-caryā*), such as non-abiding in the impermanence of form (*rūpa-anityatā*), as well as the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*) and so forth.
The question asks: "From 'the question' onwards," those of like mind say: "As for what is called 'non-abiding,' among the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), one can only abide in [one of them]."
Regarding defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*): because of these faults, what further fault do the other two natures (*svabhāva*) possess such that they do not abide [in the ultimate]?
The answer follows below, wherein the Master of the Treatise himself cites and explains the scriptures. "If one practices by grasping at signs, one does not reach the other shore;
therefore, it is called 'incomplete practice. This concludes with the phrase "up to the gates of *dhāraṇī*. Within this [passage]:
[The text] below resumes by citing and explaining the scripture once more.

From the question "If this were so" onwards, it asks: since the meaning of this form (*rūpa*)—namely its impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth—is a fault, one could simply avoid experiencing it.

For what reason, then, does [the Buddha] further refute this form and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)? It is, for example, like a gold ball; [it is not the gold that is the problem, but the specific form].
Because it was hot, he did not take it; this was not for the purpose of removing the gold ball. Why, then, does one now break up the five aggregates as if casting away a gold ball?

The answer follows below: it clarifies that in order to become free from attachment to views, one must eliminate the dharmas such as the five aggregates; this is for the purpose of casting away craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
The section beginning with "Question" explains the meaning that the samādhi of non-acceptance is not shared with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

The section beginning with "Answer" here appears to explain it by way of revealing the Path (*mārga*). The section beginning with "The two vehicles have residual habituation" will be explained in the chapter on the Threefold Wisdom (*trividya*).
The section beginning with "As in the case of Mahākāśyapa" cites evidence for the meaning of the residual habituation of the two vehicles. Furthermore...
Next, regarding the passage "This is the samādhi of non-apprehension, which only the Buddha knows universally," etc., the intent of this subsequent section is as follows:

it appears similar to the Secret Path (Guhyamantra) in its explanation that the samādhis of the two vehicles are not different; however, because they differ in their inferiority, it is said that [the Buddha's] are "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).

Question: From "The question says, 'Below this... onwards, it clarifies why one employs this wisdom of the eighteen emptinesses to contemplate all phenomena as empty, yet does not grasp at those phenomena.
Answer: From "The answer says, 'Below this... onwards, herein the Master of the Treatise again cites the preceding scriptural passage to provide an exegesis.
From "Even down to the subtle characteristics of existent dharmas that might be grasped... onwards, it clarifies that the Master provides an interpretation based on this very [scripture].
The practice can be grasped, yet the meaning of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) cannot be attained. Furthermore, the subsequent scriptural passage arises immediately;
that which is revealed by the preceding passage applies equally to "digging. This is solely because it does not arise from the scriptural passage.
From the passage concerning the Brahmin Śreṇika onwards, this is the third section, which clarifies how the small [vehicle] serves as proof for the great.
Although the text of this single sūtra speaks of using the small to prove the great, it appears to be a secret path;

its intent clarifies that although many teachings within the Hīnayāna do not speak of the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they nevertheless employ the emptiness of phenomena according to the Hīnayāna to prove the Mahāyāna’s non-abiding in all phenomena.
Setting aside the meaning of "detachment from craving for dharmas," this Śreṇika was originally a follower of non-Buddhist paths who attained a minor fruit;
it was solely because he did not grasp at the characteristics of dharmas that he came to have faith in the Buddha-dharma.
"Regarding 'What is faith? and so forth: this explains the essence of faith. 'Abiding in the practice of faith' does not refer to the practice of faith within the sixteen moments of mind;
rather, it refers to the practice of faith that enters into the Buddha-dharma. Regarding 'For what reason? and so forth: this explains the meaning of being able to be without attachment.
Regarding 'Because it is not attained through internal contemplation' and so forth: this clarifies that Śreṇika attained the realm of wisdom."
