"Both are severed," because both the internal and external are forgotten. This can be understood through the principle of non-abiding, which the subsequent treatise itself explains.
As for the passage beginning "For what reason," it explains how Śreṇika was able to thus forget both the internal and external:

it is because he had attained the two kinds of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*). The section beginning "In this state, his mind attained" clarifies that Śreṇika had achieved liberation.

This is the locus. Regarding the phrase "because this shore and that shore are not crossed": it clarifies that from this shore and that shore one reaches the further shore where there is neither "this" nor "that," wherein there is neither anything to be crossed nor anything to be transcended.

The section beginning with "Question" clarifies that the master of the treatise himself concludes the scriptural text. The section beginning with "Answer" correctly explains the intent of the topical outline (*ko-wen*);

it uses small-scale instances to corroborate the great meaning. For example, the passage beginning with "The Brahmin Nāya" and following can be cited here because it serves to corroborate the meaning of Śreṇika’s attainment of faith.
From "This Great Teacher of the Multitude" (*mahāsaṃghika-śāstṛ*) onwards, it sets forth the meaning of distinguishing the heterodox from those who can be predicted as Buddhas.
From "After Śreṇika’s Question" onwards, it correctly sets forth the fundamental meaning of Śreṇika’s arising of faith. From "Śreṇika said" onwards...
This section describes what may be questioned. The preceding passage explains how the six heretical teachers gave different records than the Buddha’s teaching;
it should be understood that this returns to the wish to clarify the points where the records of those six teachers differ from the text.

From "The Buddha addressed Śreṇika" onwards, his heterodox mind is subdued and he is brought to submission. From "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, it describes the height of the faith he has generated.
From the passage beginning "The Buddha questioned the brahmin" onwards, it clarifies that the Tathāgata knows the eternalist views he holds regarding the two types of self (*ātman*).

He conceives of the body-self as being like a vessel, and the eternal self as being like the fruit within that vessel. Therefore, the Buddha wishes to question him in return, saying: "Is the self identical to the transmigrating being?

The meaning of "identical to the transmigrating being" (*yāvad-gatam*) will be explained in the following section. From the response onwards, it clarifies that he possesses a slight degree of insight.

This is the true nature of the Dharma; therefore, he replied, "No. Since you have already expressed your resolve by saying "no," how could you possibly give rise to doubt or seek for a fixed characteristic within the Buddha-dharma?

The passage beginning with "The answer says" clarifies his vows and understanding; therefore, it states that [the claim] is incorrect. From "The Buddha told Śreṇika" onwards, the text explains the aforementioned meaning of why the Tathāgata can grant different predictions (vyākaraṇa).
It clarifies that since a person of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has only severed eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), seven more births remain;
thus, it is said that they still have birth. A person of the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) has merely eliminated six grades of the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

There are four *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) that lead to rebirth through coming and going; therefore, it is said that there is "birth. An *anāgāmin* (non-returner) has severed only ninety-two *anuśayas*, yet because the remaining [tendencies] still exist within the higher realms, it is said that there is "birth.
The great disciples, by following [the path], attain the superior fruits, and thus the three realms are either exhausted or [partially] eliminated.

Therefore, it is said that there is "non-arising. Yet, the statement that this is "due solely to the residue of self-conceit" (*māna*) clarifies that conceit is an affliction belonging to the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Rebirth among humans and devas occurs solely through the category of craving; as for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), they mostly give rise to conceit based on contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*).
Because śrāvakas frequently engage in such activities, the present discussion regarding craving refers specifically to conceit.
The passage beginning with "Having heard this, Śreṇika... explains the meaning of his realization and attainment of the Way. This sutra was spoken by the Buddha five years after his enlightenment;

since it already clarifies that Śreṇika attained the Way, one should know that those who first claim he became a sage in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* were not actual persons who attained the fruit only later in their lives.
The same applies to King Ajātaśatru. Thus, the *Yayue jing* (Sutra on the Night Moon) says:
When King Ajātaśatru saw the bright moon, he asked his ministers, "What day is this? They replied, "It is the fifteenth day. On the fifteenth day, one ought to perform repentance;
thus, by riding upon the night moon, one may go to the Buddha to repent and thereby attain the extinction of transgressions.

You should know that the Twin Trees (Śāla Grove) is not the actual [location]; it is merely because of preceding events that it is called the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candrāloka-samādhi*). Thus it was made.
These are merely explained through alternative names; they are simply the teachings of the secret path. [The self] clarifies that I am the sovereign lord.
Since there is no self, then there are no dharmas to which it can belong.
The section beginning with "Question" below analyzes and explains the meaning of why Śreṇika could have remained without answering as previously stated.
The section beginning with "Answer" below presents the first point of interpretation: that he could have remained without answering based on his state of bondage.
Furthermore, from "Below this" onwards, the explanation proceeds by first addressing the Brahmin’s attainment of realization.

This initial section shows that when one seeks [the self] within the causes themselves—both in terms of its presence and its absence—it cannot be found, and thus realization and awakening arise; hence the answer, "No, indeed. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "The Brahmin, having investigated... onwards, it likewise follows the Tathāgata’s method of counter-questioning; the fourfold meaning within the response is as follows, and it says:

To seek it in these four locations is to investigate the "self" both in terms of identity with and separation from form (*rūpa*). One asks: "Is the *gati* (the one who goes) identical to form? He replies: "No. "Is the *gati* separate from form? He replies: "No.

The same applies to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Is the *gati* identical to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? He replies: "No.

"Is the *gati* separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? He replies: "No. Thus, there are two propositions for each of identity and separation; within these four [locations]...

Seeking it within the various realms, one does not find it; thus, knowing that there is no fixed characteristic, one enters the gate of emptiness. This wisdom is precisely what is called the wisdom of attaining the Way.

From the passage "having observed one's own body" onwards, the text next clarifies the contemplation of existence (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*). Although this is indeed wisdom, one does not thereby attain the Way.
That is to say, observing the five aggregates of one's own body is internal observation; observing the five aggregates of another's body is external observation;

observing the five aggregates of both oneself and others collectively is internal-external observation. If one clings to the view that these three types of internal, external, and equal dharmas are what is observed, this wisdom is not called attaining the Way.
Nevertheless, even though this is so, if one lacks wisdom, one likewise cannot attain the Way. However—
One must forget them; do not allow wisdom to be lacking.
Furthermore, from the section "As for the internal" onwards, the meaning of internal and external is clarified in relation to the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and so forth.

Because phenomena have no fixed nature, one employs wisdom to contemplate them, thereby establishing the preliminary conditions for various meditative observations. If things possessed fixed characteristics, then...

One must not engage in [discursive] observation, for that would constitute an obstacle to the various practices of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); to do so would mean that speech lacks the function of wisdom (*jñāna*). This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from the passage "this wisdom" onwards, it clarifies the correspondence between the object and the wisdom. Wisdom fundamentally arises in accordance with the Dharma;

since the Dharma has no fixed nature, one should know that wisdom is likewise without fixed nature. For example, when something is designated as a "thing," this is merely a provisional establishment of a "Dharma" for the purpose of explanation.

"Name" refers to that which designates an object; this clarifies that phenomena (dharmas) ought to have names. "The two things mutually depend upon one another" clarifies that there are no names apart from objects, and no objects apart from names.
Since this is so, one should know that because names are posterior, phenomena are likewise provisional; because names are provisional, there is no name;
and because phenomena are provisional, there is no phenomenon.
Regarding "those with immeasurable numbers of knowledges": this clarifies that immeasurable categories of knowledge are all skillful means for the Path.

Within these skillful means, they all pertain to cessation through the condition of knowledge (*jñānapratyaya-nirodha*), which is also termed cessation through counting (*gaṇanāpratyaya*). This shall be explained in the following text.
Regarding the contemplation of the characteristics of the immeasurable dharma-nature: it clarifies that this dharma-nature is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
the true mark is *nirvāṇa*; *nirvāṇa* is the *tathāgatagarbha*; and the *tathāgatagarbha* is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Therefore, it is also called the nature of *nirvāṇa*, and it is also called the nature of bliss (*sukha*). The nature of bliss is the Buddha-nature. As the treatise says: "Dharma is named *nirvāṇa*. One should know this.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is itself the nature of nirvāṇa. Since it is stated that "the Tathāgatagarbha is the pure nirvāṇa by nature," one should know that the nature of nirvāṇa is identical to the nature of the garbha, and the nature of the garbha is identical to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Thus, the meaning of the statement here that "Śreṇika contemplated the immeasurable nature of phenomena" can be understood. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "below this" onwards, the meaning of neither grasping nor abandoning explained above is expounded. Herein, first the meaning of "no abandoning" is explained.
From "this and that not being crossed over" onwards, the meaning of "crossing over" from the preceding text is explained. "Not dharma" means that no dharma can be apprehended.
"Nor is it non-dharma" means that even non-dharma does not exist. One interpretation states that "not dharma" refers to the perspective of the *tathatā* (suchness).
Discourse: Because no dharma can be apprehended, it is called "neither dharma nor non-dharma. This is spoken according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
it does not mean that this dharma does not exist.
(Exegesis from the forty-third fascicle of the *Śāstra*).
Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, O World-Honored One" constitutes the third major division of the *Sañcaya-parivarta*. It elucidates three meanings:

the essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Prajñāpāramitā, the name of Prajñāpāramitā, and that to which Prajñāpāramitā belongs. The treatise itself categorizes these as: first, the essence; second, the name; and third, that to which it belongs.
The specific textual meaning of each point shall be explained in detail according to the text itself. Moreover, since the treatise is extensive...
Commentary: There is no need for the trouble of further explanation.

From the passage beginning "Śāriputra, form-dharmas are non-existent" onwards, the preceding section should have proceeded by means of the six *pāramitās* and so forth to clarify the meaning that there is nothing that can be or is obtainable.
Now, this section further expands upon those dharmas to clarify the meaning that they can be and are obtainable.
That the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is ultimately non-existent and unattainable refers to the meaning of *tathatā*, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and the two truths.
That "characteristics are also devoid of characteristics" refers to the characteristic of the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); even this characteristic of ultimate reality does not exist.
This is the *tathatā* of phenomena and the two truths, as can be explained above.
From "Form and so forth" onwards, it clarifies that because all phenomena are empty, they can be understood through such meanings as non-arising and non-attainment.
Because one trains in this way, one attains the three kinds of purity. From "Not giving rise to a defiled mind" onwards, the sutra itself explains the meaning of the aforementioned purity of mind.
From "Not being born from a mother’s womb" onwards, it explains the purity of body.

This is the meaning of purity. When awakening (*bodhi*) is attained, the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and so forth are precisely the explanation of the aforementioned meaning of the purity of marks.
Regarding the section beginning with "Question" (*praśna*), the intent of the question is as follows:

In the preceding portion of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* where the Tathāgata himself commanded Subhūti to speak, this current chapter’s main text extensively clarifies the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) through such gates as modesty, deference, and non-attachment.
The benefit is immeasurable. Now, why is this the opening section? What is *prajñā* (wisdom)?

The answer follows below, which correctly clarifies the Master of the Treatise’s own topical outline (*śāstra-vibhāga*) regarding the meaning of the scriptural text in three parts within this chapter.
Herein, the primary intent is to extensively set forth the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the eternally abiding essence of *prajñā*; thus, it is appropriate to pose these questions.
Regarding the passage "Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, [the Dharma] abides eternally" and below: others claim that this sutra does not clarify permanence.
However, if one explains the meaning according to the text itself, every single sentence of this sutra clarifies the meanings of permanence, the Buddha-nature, the purity of nature, and nirvana.
Why is this so? As the treatise itself states: "Prajñā is the true mark of all dharmas and is eternally abiding. Such is the intent of this sutra.
Taking the true mark (*dharmatā*) as its central tenet, every sentence therein elucidates *prajñā*. Is this not to say that every sentence clarifies the permanence [of the Buddha]?
If one intends to argue that all three Buddhas are permanent, why does this text state that *prajñā* is eternally abiding regardless of whether a Buddha appears or not?

Since it speaks of the absence of a Buddha, one might conclude that the Buddha is subject to impermanence. To explain: this is based on the historical traces of the transformative teaching (*nirmāṇa-dharma*).
Regarding the statement: "As for the *puruṣa*, its traces do not manifest; only when there is a response does it cease to exist in the world.
This is based on that statement. The passage beginning with "It is not that the Buddha and others created [it]" explains the meaning of its permanence.
Furthermore, following the section "Having departed from these two extremes," the next part explains the wisdom of contemplative insight (*prajñā*).

Since one might argue that there is a "middle" because there are two [extremes] to be discussed, and now that both extremes have been abandoned, there is likewise no middle—why, then, is it called the "wisdom of middle-way contemplation"?

If one asks what constitutes *prajñā*, the explanation is as follows: since there is neither duality nor even a "middle," it is merely designated as the "middle" in reality because one does not grasp at duality for the sake of countering it;
furthermore, there is no middle way to be observed. Taking this wisdom of signlessness (*animitta*) as *prajñā* is the interpretation of Master Ying.
Regarding the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, it is said that this treatise is capable of acting as an antidote to [false] doctrines.
This is precisely why [the text] can be treated as chapter headings. The meaning of the subsequent passages is likewise so.
Furthermore, from the passage "having departed from existence and non-existence" onwards, the explanation of the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) has been completed.

Now, we shall explain the essence of the *prajñā* of true realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) by means of three dharma-gates. The Master said: "Whether it be the *prajñā* of the true mark, if one relies upon its wisdom..."

Regarding the term *prajñā*, if it is not considered to be either mind (*citta*) or mental factors (*caitasika*), then according to true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), it is the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaracitta*), which is the direct cause of Buddhahood (*tathāgatagarbha*).
This is the wisdom of authentic realization. If, however, one says that *prajñā* consists of mind and mental factors, then it is designated as "contingent illumination" based on its causal nature;
this *prajñā* would then belong to the consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and their associated dharmic wisdoms.
The meaning of the text from "impermanence" (*anitya*) onwards is exhausted here. However, the Master says:

"That the followers of the Two Vehicles do not see the Buddha-nature means that they simply do not perceive this wisdom of the *ālayavijñāna*. If this were the case, it would follow that they would have attained wisdom and would be seeing wisdom."

Furthermore, it constitutes wisdom as the object. If this knowledge of reality (*tathatā-jñāna*) is itself the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), yet one speaks of a Bodhisattva seeing the Buddha-nature, it further establishes the Bodhisattva.
Moreover, there is another wisdom of vision; this true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) further constitutes two kinds of *prajñā*.
Examining the opening of the treatise, it clarifies only these two. This meaning shall be explained extensively elsewhere. This is the explanation.
This is the essential meaning of the *prajñā*.
Furthermore, from "next" onwards, it again cites the sutra to provide an explanation. Furthermore, from "that which is non-existent" onwards, it likewise cites the sutra to explain it.
Furthermore, from "the eighteen emptinesses" onwards, it concludes and explains the preceding section concerning Śāriputra. All of the above [is as follows].
This is a section of the sutra text. Why is it that from the passage "Why is it named Prajñāpāramitā" onwards, it explains the previous question, "What is meant by wishing to give birth to Prajñā?
This is because the following portion provides an explanation; thus, a doubt is raised.

Question: From "The question says, 'Below this... onwards, the intent of the question is as follows: Previously, when first presenting the *prajñā* of veneration, it was clarified that the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) is eternally non-different.

Why, then, is the *prajñā* of practice and exposition now said to be supreme? This question arises because the two kinds of *prajñā* are about to be presented next in order to examine their characteristics.
Answer: From "The answer says, 'Below this... onwards, the Master of the Treatise explains the emergence [of the answer]. Entering into non-duality.

Since there is neither duality nor unity, and as for that which is the single characteristic within each individual phenomenon, how can it be said that one enters non-duality simply because of the absence of characteristics?
For this reason, from "Your objection is not [valid]" onwards, the preceding section clarified the meaning by establishing the doctrine;
now, within the context of the two dharmas of cause and effect, the two kinds of *prajñā* have been explained. Now, we shall clarify the meaning through a middle-way approach.

Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that can be maintained. Why, then, do you ask about the difference between the two types of *prajñā*? Furthermore, from the section beginning with "Furthermore, the world...

onwards, because one wishes to explain the superiority of the *prajñāpāramitā*, three kinds of wisdom are enumerated, starting from the inferior and proceeding to the superior, gradually clarifying them.

From "Detached from birth" (*vivekaja*) onwards, it clarifies the mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) of the various *dhyānas*. The mundane wisdom of the first *dhyāna* arises from detachment from desire.
In the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), wisdom arises detached from form; therefore, it is said that "wisdom arises through detachment.
Furthermore, from the passage "this wisdom" onwards, it clarifies that wisdom is cultivated in successive waves (*taraṅga*).

Because there is progressive excellence [in this cultivation], it is described as "arising and abiding," rather than in the sense of impermanent arising and ceasing; thus, the term "ceasing" is not used. The Master [Vasubandhu] explains that this refers to the transformation of the causal conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

"Consciousness-prajñā" refers to the wisdom of arising and ceasing; this shall now be explained. The passage beginning with "Who is it that... and following serves to explain the textual phrases pertaining to the aforementioned prajñā.
Regarding "no self and no mine," this takes emptiness as the meaning of "no self," which is precisely the sense of "no self" within the three types of two truths.
Since it has already been stated that although ordinary beings may be free from desire, they still possess an attachment to the mind of "I" and "mine."

Regarding those who act out of desire, it should be understood that although they attain the stage of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), their views have not been eliminated. How, then, can it be said that they sever the underlying realm (*dhātu*)?

As for those who cannot fully attain the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Master says this clarifies that the two vehicles possess only the *prajñā* of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) as its conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), but lack the *prajñā* of true wisdom (*jñāna*) as its direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); therefore, it is said they cannot attain it in its entirety. Thus says the treatise.

However, only two kinds of prajñā are established. Furthermore, it is said here that [the former] cannot be fully perfected; this is not because gold does not exist, for there is an underlying intention.
This shall now be explained.
Question: From "The following" onwards, one might briefly examine the preceding scriptural passage; why is it that the six *pāramitās* are now presented at the beginning? Answer:
From "The answer is as follows" onwards, it is explained that this is done for the sake of describing what is easy to understand.
The five *pāramitās* are merely explained without reference to the [previous] intention. The subsequent explanation from "Then, continuing the discourse" onwards, clarifies the second intention.

"Śāriputra, as for 'form and so forth'" and below—that is the scriptural text. "Once the bodhisattva has entered this gate" and below—this is the subsequent explanation of the scriptural text on "attaining understanding and being without fear. "Śāriputra asked" and below—this explains the scriptural text on "not arising and not being accomplished."
The passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva can practice in this way" explains the preceding scriptural text regarding the purity of the three aspects of body, mind, and marks.

While the *dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya* (body born of the nature of phenomena) is in reality never born again, it is nevertheless called a "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) from the perspective of its capacity to manifest in accordance with what is appropriate, its great power of vows, and its non-abiding in *nirvāṇa*. In truth, however, its internal body does not require transformation.
They constantly see the Buddha and perform immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable acts of worship and buddha-work therein.
This is because they are not merely able to make offerings to a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); thus, it is said here that they are never separated from the Buddha.

The tenth chapter is titled "Chapter on Characteristics and Practice" (*Lakṣaṇagatiparivarta*). It is the second division within the first major section, consisting of the authentic exposition by Subhūti.

Following this, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are elucidated through the gateway of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamukha*) to clarify *prajñāpāramitā*. Since the Master of the Treatise intends to provide an explanation and commentary, he introduces it as "the commentary on the tenth chapter."
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha" and continuing through this chapter, there are five major sections.
The first clarifies the meaning of a bodhisattva practicing the *pāramitās* without skillful means (*upāya*), characterized by objective signs (*nimitta*).
The second, from the point where Śāriputra asks Subhūti, "How should one know... and so forth, clarifies that because the bodhisattva possesses skillful means, they practice the *pāramitās*.

If it is not characterized by asceticism, the third section clarifies that although Śāriputra’s questions do not depart from the *asaṃprajanya-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-appropriation), they nonetheless lead to the meaning of swiftly attaining bodhi.
From the fourth section, where the Buddha praises Subhūti onwards, it clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation.

Within this confirmation, there are further two parts: first, the initial confirmation; second, the confirmation that the bodhisattva possesses skillful means in their practice of *prajñāpāramitā* without attachment.
The Meaning of Practice. Second, beginning with the description that completes the first section on the meaning of practice characterized by attachment due to a lack of skillful means (*upāya*).
From the passage "Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies both the gain for those who possess skillful means and the loss for those who lack it.

This initial portion specifically elucidates the first point: how a bodhisattva, due to a lack of skillful means, engages in the practice of giving while remaining attached to the characteristics (*nimitta*) of the act.

"Skillful means" refers to the skillful application of non-realization. Because this bodhisattva now pursues and clings to conditioned phenomena, it is said that he lacks skillful means and possesses faults.
This applies to all subsequent points, such as "not attaining the noble path," which follow the same principle.
From the passage "If form is... onwards, it clarifies that since form is itself neither-form-nor-non-form, how could there be any such concepts as permanence or impermanence, suffering or pleasure?
If a bodhisattva perceives and attends to form, this is precisely forgetfulness and misunderstanding.
If one acts toward form, one will not be able to escape birth, old age, and death; this is the great fault of having the characteristic of "having-outflows" (sāsrava).
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "How should one know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not practice?

From here below, the second [section] clarifies the meaning of the bodhisattva’s attainment through skillful means (*upāya*) while practicing *prajñā* without the characteristics of practice (*anupalambha*).
Herein, the text returns to the preceding phrases and applies them by analogy: "Form (*rūpa*) is itself..."

"Emptiness" refers to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). "Emptiness is itself form" is based on its dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The principle that form is not separate from emptiness and that emptiness is not separate from form applies to all such meanings.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is this Prajñāpāramitā, which is able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In the preceding section on practicing Prajñā through skillful means (*upāya*), the faults of attachment in practice were clarified; therefore, by practicing in such a manner, one cannot even attain the fruits of the Two Vehicles, let alone Unsurpassed Bodhi.
Now, in this section, it is clarified that when one practices Prajñā with skillful means, there is no attachment.
Because one practices this practice, it is said that one "surpasses" and attains bodhi.
From the phrase "the practice is also not received" onwards, only two lines were clarified in the first chapter; the same applies to the second chapter.
In the third chapter, three propositions were clarified; here, although one intends to clarify four propositions, by including "neither accepting nor not accepting," five propositions are formed.
This is for the sake of those attached to existence, who neither practice nor accept [the teachings], and for those who stagnate in nihilism.
To say that one neither practices nor does not practice is for the sake of those who cling to both existence and non-existence.
To say that one neither practices nor does not practice is for the sake of those who cling to that which is neither existent nor non-existent.

To say that one neither practices nor does not practice, and even that one does not accept this [position], is to further eliminate the fourth alternative. When one no longer clings to the fault of that which is neither existent nor non-existent, one is likewise free from the four alternatives. Thus it is.

It is further established because the preceding four phrases have all been exhausted; thus, this fifth phrase arises, which is precisely the meaning of the selflessness of dharmas (dharmānātman) within True Suchness (tathatā).
The passage beginning with "For what reason... asks why [the Buddha] did not accept [the previous position]. For these reasons, Śāriputra...
The following section clarifies that the sutra itself provides a general explanation of the aforementioned meanings, such as "non-acceptance" (anupādāna). Why is this?

Because the subsequent portion must return to explain what was stated above. Regarding the "samādhi of non-acceptance" mentioned above, it refers to the samādhi of non-acceptance within the context of the gate of emptiness (śūnyatā);
however, in the present passage, it refers to the samādhi of non-reception within the gate of signlessness (animitta). This samādhi is not separate from the swift attainment [of awakening].
"Bodhi" (Awakening) here clarifies that it transcends time, not that it transcends practice. The following is the author's own commentary on this.

From "The commentary states" onwards, the author himself outlines the structure of the treatise. From "If a bodhisattva lacks skillful means" onwards, the text generally explains the first point mentioned above;
each of these shall be explained in turn. From "As if with a mind of anger" onwards, it clarifies all phenomena (*dharmas*).
This is the meaning of "indeterminate. "Originally without marks" means that from the beginning there have been no marks.
"Contrary to the above" is a concise summary; it explains the second part of the preceding scriptural passage concerning "non-practice.
"Not departing" explains the meaning of "not departing from such [practice] while practicing in *prajñāpāramitā*," which leads to the attainment of *bodhi*.
Regarding "one who enters this samādhi," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* provides an analogy: when a bodhisattva of the sixth stage enters this samādhi, it is like riding a boat on dry land;
this is called the path of effort (*prayoga-mārga*). In the seventh stage, it is like a boat in the great Ganges;

in the eighth stage, it is like a boat in the great ocean. This shall now be explained. The passage beginning with "at times, having transcended" below explains the meaning of "swiftly attaining bodhi. This is...
"Transcending time does not mean transcending practice. This shall be explained in detail.

From the passage beginning with "Śāriputra said: 'But it is not apart from the samādhi of non-reception'" onwards, the third [section] addresses the doubts of certain people who claim that within the Buddha-dharma there is only this samādhi of non-reception that can swiftly lead to the attainment of Bodhi; therefore, they equate it with Subhūti.
Śubhūti extensively [attained] the one hundred and eight samādhis, beginning from Śūraṅgama and extending to those such as "Detachment from Attachment" and "Unstained by Space.
He was able to swiftly attain all that had not yet been answered. The meaning of the one hundred and eight samādhis shall be explained one by one in the Mahāyāna Chapter.
Regarding the passage "Having attained the immeasurable," etc., it clarifies that although only the one hundred and eight were briefly mentioned, they actually comprise the infinite.
The samādhis of measure can all cause a bodhisattva to swiftly attain bodhi. It is not only these samādhis;
there are also immeasurable gates of dhāraṇī that can cause one to swiftly attain it. This demonstrates that within the Buddha-dharma, skillful means are immeasurable.
“Āyuṣmān Subhūti spoke in accordance with the Buddha’s mind” is a phrase used by the author of the sūtra.

It clarifies that once Śrīgupta (Subhūti) had received the command to speak, his words were no different from those of the Buddha; therefore, it is said that he “spoke in accordance with the Buddha’s mind.

Regarding the passage beginning with “He was thus instructed,” and so forth, above it was stated that Śrīgupta himself said, “I spoke in accordance with the Buddha’s mind. As for this samādhi: by means of... [text ends]
The Buddhas bestow predictions of enlightenment upon them; yet now, when Śāriputra asks about this, Subhūti immediately says "no. Why is it so?

It is clear, Subhūti, that he explains the meaning of the prediction with a mind free from attachment, and thus there is no characteristic of prediction. Now, however, Śāriputra acts with a mind attached to characteristics.
Because he asked about the meaning of the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), [the Buddha] replied, "No. This was not a contradiction of his previous statement. From the words "Why is this?
onwards, he again explains the meaning of why it can be said "no": it clarifies that the person is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the person;
therefore, there is no characteristic of a prediction being bestowed. Regarding the phrase "How is this known," Śāriputra asks: "If one says 'person'..."
Regarding the meaning of "the identity of dharmas" (*dharmasamatā*): why is it said that a bodhisattva knows the samādhi of the equality of all dharmas?
If that were so, there would be a distinction between person, dharma, object, and wisdom; how then can they be said to be identical? The passage beginning with Subhūti’s reply [addresses this].
The commentary states: "This refers to a person who has no entry entering the mark of non-entry.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying, 'Excellent! onwards, the fourth section clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation.

It is because the preceding discourse by Subhūti on the presence or absence of skillful means—spanning two cycles of the sūtra text—might cause the assembly to doubt that Subhūti does not possess omniscience.

What has been stated may contain errors because it does not accord with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The Tathāgata’s recounting and praising clarifies that what the Buddha has raised is not in vain;
he approves of what was said as being well-consonant with principle. This is the first [point], which is the very first within the section on "recounting and establishing" (*anujñāna*).
First, this clarifies the exposition that completes the second section on the meaning of non-attachment in practice; it constitutes one full cycle of the sūtra’s text.

From the point where the question is posed below, this is the treatise’s explanation of the intent of the preceding text; each [point] shall be addressed in correspondence with the characteristics of the aforementioned sūtra text.
This shall now be explained. The "three matters" refer to the bodhisattva’s samādhi and prajñā.

When Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, after a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has trained in this manner," and so forth, the following section serves to explain and establish the meaning of the second scriptural passage above—that which is not practiced. This shall be explained point by point. Why?
From "This is ultimate purity" onwards, the Sūtra explains this through four gates: non-emergence, non-arising, non-attainment, and non-action;
the Treatise shall now explain these. When the Buddha says that all phenomena are non-existent, it means that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics.
"Existing in this way" refers to being forcibly described as existing within the context of conventional designations. "Non-existing in this way" [refers to the same].
"Ownerless. This single phrase serves as a summary and explanation. It means "the sense of non-existence. Regarding the statement, "If one does not know this matter":
if one does not know that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are thus ownerless, this constitutes ignorance (*moha*); therefore, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Following Śāriputra’s address to the Buddha, the scriptural text of the second section is described and established, as well as the meaning of the "samādhi of non-appropriation.

Having concluded this, the text now further intends to extensively explain the meaning of "non-existence," which constitutes the second part within the fourth section on "describing and establishing" the meaning of the practices performed by bodhisattvas who lack skillful means.
Furthermore, when Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this manner, yet does not train...
and so forth, this constitutes the fifth major section. It elucidates, in pairs, the gains and losses of practice with and without skillful means.
This is the meaning. It shall now be explained.

Regarding the commentary below: first, it clarifies that the Master of the Treatise cites the preceding scriptural passage because he intends to generate the intent for the subsequent scriptural passage;
thus, he sets forth the reason for Śāriputra’s question. This shall be explained: all samādhis within Prajñāpāramitā are equally named "signless" (animitta).
Because it is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is said that *prajñā* raises up its partial characteristics within all the *samādhis*.
Regarding the section beginning with "ultimately pure" (*atyanta-viśuddha*), this explains the meaning of the ultimate purity of the four preceding gates of dhyāna.
The first two gates establish the thesis and explain it; the latter two phrases, however, provide successive mutual explanations to clarify that all phenomena do not arise from causes.
Because it arises from conditions, it is called "non-emergence. Furthermore, because it does not arise solely from the side of conditions, it is called "non-arising.
Because the dharma of causes and conditions is quiescent, it is termed "non-emergent and non-arising. The phrase "the fixed characteristic of arising is unobtainable" is a summary explanation.
The phrase "because it is non-emergent and non-arising" transmits the meaning of its being unobtainable. Because it is unobtainable...
This transmits and explains the meaning of "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Question: From the passage "The Bodhisattva, by means of this ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), studies the six *pāramitās*" onwards, [the text] provides an exposition that establishes the middle way.
The second turn is the textual passage on practice without skillful means.
From "Now, how do all dharmas exist... onwards, it explains the previous question by Śāriputra regarding the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.

In the preceding sutra, it was stated, "How does the true reality of all dharmas exist? Since the true reality itself had not yet been explained [in that context], [this section now provides the explanation].
"It exists. This meaning is difficult to understand. Now, the explanation here states that when Śāriputra asked how all phenomena exist, it becomes intelligible.
However, Śāriputra’s underlying intention was actually directed toward all phenomena; he merely used the *dharmatā* (true nature) as a pretext for his inquiry.
How is this known? The words spoken by Subhūti did not originally contain such phrasing; rather, he spoke of the *dharmatā*.
It exists. Now, one should not ask whether the true mark (lakṣaṇa) can be attained. This treatise explains that this refers to the initial mark.
As for "losing the light of wisdom," it is not that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) attain it and then lose it; rather, it is that which should have been attained but was not. Therefore, it is said:

This is a failure. It is because bodhisattvas who lack skillful means (*upāya*) are attached to dharmas that they cannot enter the Noble Path and fall into the category of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
therefore, there is a failure.
From the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva practices in this way," Śāriputra asks [the following] to explain the fifth point above: having skillful means but lacking wisdom.
"Skillful means and the absence of skillful means" refers to the scriptural passage concerning the attainment of [the fruit].
If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it is a practice attached to signs; because they are practicing with [mere] prajñā, they do not attain bodhi.

From the section beginning "He then explains the causes and conditions," the text reveals those who lack skillful means—those who engage in discriminative and attached practice and are unable to relinquish their actions, thereby failing.
Furthermore, that which is contrary to this explains the meaning of the skillful means of the bodhisattva’s practice mentioned above.

Regarding the explanation of the eleventh chapter of the forty-fourth fascicle of the Treatise, it is titled "The Chapter on Illusion" (Māyā-varga). This is the third [section] within the first part of the correct exposition by Subhūti.
Regarding the gate of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), this chapter is titled the "Eleventh Chapter" because it is now intended to explain Prajñāpāramitā.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti... and following, there are two major divisions within this text; the first is named...

This is the meaning of the illusory person being fundamentally empty and without activity. Second, it clarifies that this principle is difficult to believe and requires both internal and external conditions.
The internal condition refers to skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The external condition refers to the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This first point clarifies that the illusory person is fundamentally empty because they lack the characteristics of a mind; they are, therefore, utterly without grasping or activity.

There is no practice, nor is there anything to be attained, because there is no characteristic of attainment. Therefore, he raises an easily understood object in order to reveal that which is difficult to understand;

this is why it is raised as a question. As for why Subhūti raises the example of an illusory person to question the Buddha, and why the Buddha in turn questions Subhūti to prompt an answer—these matters shall be explained in the subsequent discussion.
World-Honored One, because the clarity, form, and illusion are all of one and the same reality, it is said that they are not different;
this meaning is indeed evident. This has already been explained above by way of the gate of non-differentiation; now, this is explained by way of the present gate.
The passage beginning with "If dharmas are neither born nor extinguished" clarifies that it is so because of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Since the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), they are forcibly named "Bodhisattva," yet in reality there is no Bodhisattva. Thus, this anticipatorily explains the meaning of the defilement and purification of the five aggregates of clinging.
If a dharma exists as nothing more than a name, then it lacks substantial reality (*bhāva*). Because it lacks substantial reality, it is not [a real entity].
These three karmas are neither defiled nor pure; this is to clarify the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Therefore, it is necessary to clarify them by means of karma.

Regarding the passage "if one can thus study these dharmas" and below, it clarifies that if one studies all dharmas such as being without defilement or purity in this manner, then because there is nothing to be attained, it is said "no.
Regarding the passage "the six sense-faculties are the five aggregates" and below, the treatise will now explain the practice (*caryā*).

[The section] beginning with "Question" below correctly explains the meaning of Subhūti’s initial inquiry above; the principle that practitioners cannot [attain it] is easy to understand. Why, then, does he ask?
[The section] beginning with "Answer" below correctly presents the origin of this scriptural passage. It follows the question posed by Śāriputra above;
the Buddha replies, "If all dharmas have a single characteristic, then illusion is not different from reality. Reality enters first...
One attains Buddhahood; this is not like a phantom person for whom cultivation is not accomplished. Why is it "one"?
Because of this doubt, the example of a phantom person is raised as a question, which serves as the title of this chapter.
Question: [The following] shall be explained below. Answer: As explained below, it is clarified that these are called "practices" (saṃskāra) only because they are perceived by the ignorant.
For example, at the four crossroads, a conjurer might create an illusory person who goes forth as a renunciant, or acts as a Buddha saving beings, emitting light and shaking the earth.
Having created this illusory person, he then strikes another illusory person, yet the illusory person remains patient. When people see this, they perceive it but do not understand it.
Regarding "emptiness and reality": the Bodhisattva is likewise without any [inherent] agency. Subhūti, suspecting that the Bodhisattva was not so, asked;
the Buddha then answered him, saying they were no different. From the words "The answer says" onwards, this is merely an explanation based on Subhūti’s own commentary (*vyākhyā*).
Question: [The passage] beginning with "It is asked" means this: A phantom person possesses form; thus one may say that form is not different from the phantom. However, a phantom person has no mind;

therefore, it should not be that the four assemblies are not different [from the phantom]. Answer: The following will explain. Even one who has truly attained the eye of wisdom cannot be deceived by the five aggregates.
It is only because they fail to attain what they ought to attain that they are said to be deceived.

From the point where Subhūti has formed this thought onwards, [the text] explains his underlying doubt. To speak in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one cultivates practice to become a Buddha;

to speak in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is neither cultivation nor attainment. Since Śāriputra (Śubhagata) has raised a doubt regarding the ultimate truth based on conventional truth, [the text] clarifies this.
The Buddha replied: "The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are deceptive.

From the passage "In this provisional designation... onwards, it explains the "provisionally named Bodhisattva," which includes the text stating that they lack the three types of karma (*tri-karma*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Within this, there are also name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so on," the *Śāstra* commentary explains: "The five aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are called the member of consciousness (*vijñāna-anga*); [this refers to] the intermediate state's..."

[It is] the ear. Because it pertains to the dharmas such as the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). This is precisely the six sense faculties; the six sense faculties are themselves the five aggregates.

Regarding the phrase "because they are not yet mature," this clarifies that the five aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are merely a provisional skillful means (*upāya*) belonging to the category of the manifest aggregates (*dṛṣṭadharmika-skandha*); therefore, it is said that they are "not yet [mature]."

This is why it is designated solely by the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). However, the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* states that the very first moment of consciousness within the present existence is called the "limb of consciousness.
This clarifies that when the three aggregates (*skandha*) continue and the parents unite, this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body first begins to approach for the sake of rebirth;
at the time it enters the womb, it is termed the "limb of consciousness. It is based on this that it is said to be the "initial" [moment].
Once one has entered the womb, one immediately belongs to the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). There is no such thing as consciousness (*vijñāna*) traveling alone;

this is the meaning of the term "link of consciousness. If there were a solitary consciousness that did not depend upon form, then the continuity of the three aggregates (*skandha*) would be impossible.
This is like the analogy of a seal stamping clay: when the seal meets the clay, the impression is formed within it. Why would there be only the clay alone?
Since there is no seal, these aggregates likewise do not exist; yet, as this aggregate ceases, that aggregate arises.

Now, within a single moment, the twelve links of dependent origination naturally possess the sense of being complete in terms of their long duration, their oppositions, and their coarse and subtle categories.
This is because they possess the sense of being fully present when viewed over the course of a lifetime. As the Mahānidāna Sūtra states: "The consciousness of the present life may be described as..."
Regarding birth in a future life, what prevents the five aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) from being subsumed under the present member of consciousness (*vijñāna*)?

The statement that "from consciousness arise the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)," indicating that the five aggregates exist during both periods, clarifies that the five aggregates are present at the time of the member of consciousness and likewise at the time of the six sense bases; thus, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, they exist throughout all these stages.

"Because form (*rūpa*) is established": this clarifies that because there is form, there are the five sense organs; thus it says "because form is established," they are called the five feelings (*kāya*).
"Because name (*nāman*) is established":
this clarifies that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself the mind organ (*manas*); thus it says "name is established," and therefore it is called the feeling of the mind (*manaḥ-kāya*). 6.
"Sentient faculties do not depart from the five aggregates" clarifies that when the six faculties are complete, there are the five aggregates;
therefore, it is said they "do not depart. "For this reason" indicates that the Master of the Treatise establishes the doctrine according to conventional truth.
Having completed the explanation of this first cycle of meaning, he concludes it.
Question: [The section] below shall be explained. Answer: [The section] below clarifies that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the basis of the present existence.
At the time of the parents' union, it is necessary for this intermediate body to arrive and take recourse in the present existence; if consciousness does not arrive, conception cannot occur.
Therefore, it is said that when the parents meet in their intimate union, even the intermediate body is able to follow.
Entering from outside, there is no obstruction, like a seal impressing its mark upon clay. How could one allow the Buddha’s wondrous form to be described as obstructive?
Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) must necessarily have a basis for their support, form does not exist in isolation;
it must be joined with the other three aggregates—feeling, perception, and formations—as explained in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, from the passage "Next, the Buddha knows that after five hundred years... and below, it clarifies the refutation of false views.

If one were to take a single consciousness as a constituent factor (*aṅga*), then it would be subverted accordingly. The phrase "this dharma cannot be found within internal emptiness" and above is an explanation that accords with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Establishing the dharma to explain it, we now proceed to discuss it according to ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*). This is the initial explanation.
From the passage beginning with "Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, this constitutes the second major section of the chapter.

It clarifies that this principle is difficult to believe and requires both internal and external causes and conditions to hear the profound Dharma without giving rise to fear. Furthermore, within this text there are two parts:

first, clarifying the meaning of hearing [the Dharma] without fear when one possesses both internal and external causes and conditions; second, clarifying [the case of] not possessing both internal and external [conditions].
This is the causal condition (*nidāna*). Because he has heard the meaning of fear, he raises this question. Each point shall be explained in turn.

From "The Buddha said" onwards, it is because there is no such thing internally or externally that there is terror. From "Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, this concerns the meaning of the vehicle;
it is both a question and what is termed "a discussion arising from a discussion. This shall be explained. "One who accords with the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience)" refers to this.
It clarifies that by means of the signless true mind, one practices *prajñā* without grasping at any phenomena, thereby becoming in accord with the Buddha;
thus it is said, "it demonstrates all meanings clearly. From the phrase "This is called" onwards, it clarifies that there are two kinds of *prajñāpāramitā*:

first, according to its essence; second, according to skillful means (*upāya*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of skillful means: first, the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*); second, the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Regarding these...
Regarding "expedient means": because among the two types of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme, the text concludes by establishing the meaning that the gift of Dharma is ungraspable;
this constitutes the *dānapāramitā* of the bodhisattva. The passage beginning with "not with the mind of a śrāvaka, etc.

clarifies that although the precepts of a bodhisattva are immeasurable, if one gives rise to the mind of the two vehicles (*yāna*), it constitutes the foremost violation of the precepts and an obstruction to the Path. Therefore...
Not giving rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles constitutes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Regarding "enduring desire and pleasure" and below:

there are two kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) to be discussed—first, patience toward sentient beings (*sattva-kṣānti*), and second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). Since patience regarding phenomena is superior here, the superior one is cited to conclude [the section].
By enduring desire and pleasure and so forth, it constitutes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Regarding "not abandoning and not ceasing" and below, this clarifies bodhi...
Because one diligently cultivates various contemplations without attachment, it is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

From the passage "not giving rise to the mind of the śrāvakas and so forth" onwards, it clarifies that if a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of the two vehicles, it constitutes a great confusion of thought, which is no different from the unwholesome;
thus, it is concluded as the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). From the passage "not because of emptiness or form, it is empty" onwards, it clarifies...
The wisdom of a bodhisattva deeply understands that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself empty; it is not a wisdom of emptiness that forcibly renders them empty.
Therefore, it is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.

From the passage beginning with "Subhūti addressed the Buddha," this question arises from the preceding discussion regarding whether there are internal and external conditions (*pratyaya*) for a bodhisattva,

and whether there are internal and external causes (*hetu*) for a bodhisattva. Since the meaning of the correspondence between the external cause and the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) has been established,
and one now wishes to clarify the essence of these internal and external causes and conditions, he poses this question.
From the passage beginning with "The Buddha told Subhūti," the meaning of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth is correctly set forth. Regarding the spiritual friend:

they are the external condition (*bāhyapratyaya*), whereas the wisdom of *prajñā* is the internal condition (*adhyātmikapratyaya*). Therefore, Ānanda said to the Buddha: "As for the spiritual friend..."

This is called "half of the holy life" (*brahmacarya*). Why is it said so? Ānanda’s intention was that internal wisdom constitutes half of the holy life, while external spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) likewise constitute half of the holy life;
through the causal conditions of both the internal and external, one attains the complete holy life.
Therefore, he said that this is indeed the principle. However, because the Buddha wished to praise spiritual friends, he spoke of them as such—thus he spoke of "knowing."
"One who is skilled in discernment" is another name for the complete holy life (*brahmacarya*). To further explain this:

the internal wisdom is all obtained through the guidance and teachings of external spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); without them, it cannot be attained. Therefore, the "spiritual friend" is called the complete holy life. As the sutra states:
"The spiritual friend is a great causal condition," meaning that they lead people to behold the Buddha.

From "not turning toward the paths of the two vehicles" (*na dvayayānamārgeṣu*) onwards, although many sections of the preceding sūtra clarify non-attachment to all phenomena, they do not mention dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Now, within this section, for the first time, this single phrase is added at length; it is added because its purpose is to clarify the factors of virtue (*kuśalāṅga*).
There is the merit of instruction, for it serves as the conclusion of these three gates of liberation.

From the question "It is asked" (*iti pṛcchati*) onwards, this initial master of the treatise intends to provide an explanation; first, he sets forth the purpose of the arising of the scriptural passage.
From the answer "It is replied" (*ity ucyate*) onwards, it clarifies that Subhūti heard above that all dharmas are like illusions and that everything is empty by its own nature.

There is no other reason. Fearing that people might not understand, I now wish to clarify the facts of the matter. This question arose because two groups hold opposing views regarding the practice and non-practice [of the Way].
The Buddha then answered by means of internal and external causes and conditions. It shall be explained: those who are not born in the Middle Kingdom find it difficult to attain awakening.

As the Book says, "Ritual (*li*) originates from the four barbarian tribes (*siyi*). Here, it is said that ritual originates from outside the four barbarian tribes; this refers to the [practices] of the four barbarian tribes.
Internally, they are not transformed by ritual propriety; therefore, they are not of the Central Kingdom. Furthermore, they are difficult to transform.
Each of these points shall be explained in correspondence with the preceding text, as can be understood.

From the passage beginning with "Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies the extensive exposition of the meaning of evil associates (*pāpamitra*). There are ten further sections (*daśa-paryāya*) that shall now be explained.

Regarding the phrase "one who has abandoned the mind of omniscience" (*sarvajñatā-citta*): the preceding section clarified that, through the fulfillment of causes and conditions, one accords with the Buddha-mind.
Now, it is explained that being close to evil associates (pāpa-mitra) means not possessing the attachment to signs (nimitta), yet one's conduct contradicts the Buddha’s mind;

because one does not attain the Buddha, it is said that one is "separated from the mind of omniscience" (sarvajñatā-citta). If one teaches sentient beings the doctrines of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), all such instances constitute being separated from omniscience;
these are called evil associates. From the passage "following evil associates" onwards, it clarifies that if one teaches sentient beings the two vehicles...
To understand through mere intellectual comprehension is not the Mahāyāna; to be devoid of the various perfections (pāramitās) is called a bad friend (pāpamitra).

Furthermore, regarding the "bad friends" mentioned below: whereas the preceding section spoke of difficulties concerning humans, this section speaks of difficulties concerning devas. There are various explanations regarding the difficulty of dual confusion in form and speech.
If a person first studies the Lesser Vehicle and later returns to study the Lesser Vehicle again, this is simply the Lesser Vehicle.
Furthermore, one does not open the way for demonic activities (*mārakarma*). If one first studied the Great [Vehicle] and then abandons the Great to study the Small, this is sent by Māra;
however, if one first studied the Small and then abandons the Small to study the Great, one is then encompassed by the Mahāyāna.

The commentary states: Below, the treatise itself provides its own topical outline (*śāstra-vibhāga*), which shall be explained one by one. "Māra" means "the Harmer"; he is King Pāpīyān. This shall be explained.
As for the twelfth chapter, it constitutes the [specific] major section within the "Section on the Proclamation of Life" (*jīvita-nirdeśa-bhāga*) concerning the Bodhisattva. Regarding the Great...
Regarding the person: by means of the clear *prajñā*, the first three chapters explain it through the gate of "as-it-is-ness" (*yathābhūta*).

To speak of *prajñā* in this way is to clarify the basis for the virtues of a bodhisattva. Next, we clarify that such a person is called a "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*) because they practice the Great Dharma;
therefore, *prajñā* is explained in relation to them. Within this section, there are further two parts, and this first chapter clarifies the bodhisattva.
The meaning of "bodhisattva" (*sattva*). Next is the "Chapter on the Mahāsattva," which clarifies the meaning of a *mahāsattva*.

Now, in order to clarify the bodhisattva by means of the meaning of the terms (*padārtha*), this is called the "Chapter on the Meaning of Terms. Since the present treatise intends to provide an explanation, it is cited as the twelfth chapter of the commentary.

From the passage beginning "At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, although all of the preceding sections constitute the portion on the entrustment of the teaching (*parindanā-bhāga*), within the actual discourse delivered by Subhūti himself, Subhūti speaks only of one chapter and a half of the sutra.

The chapter on the Accumulation and Dispersion (*Saṃcaya-vyavakiraṇa*) is spoken entirely by Subhūti, as is the first half of the following chapter; all the remainder consists of questions posed by Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others to the Buddha, and the Buddha’s responses.
This shall now be explained. At the beginning of this chapter, because Subhūti has already asked his question, the Buddha further explains the ten kinds of non-arising (*anutpāda*) below;
furthermore, this entire section is spoken by Subhūti. Within the scriptural text of this single chapter, there are again two parts:
the first part clarifies the Bodhisattva through the meaning of the phrases, and the second part proceeds from the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*) to the supramundane (*lokottara*).
Regarding the "intermediate outflows" (*sāsrava*) and so forth: from the six pairs and twelve gates below, the virtues of the Bodhisattva are elucidated.

This matter refers to the first section of the sutra; as it is intended to set forth the words of the inquiry by Subhūti, it says, "At that time, Subhūti himself may inquire," and so forth, which shall be explained in the treatise (*śāstra*).

From the passage beginning with "The Buddha told Subhūti" onwards, within this first section, there are two further points: first, an explanation by way of the Dharma; second, an explanation by way of analogy.
Now, it clarifies that the nature of words is detached from words and is ultimately empty; therefore, it says that "the absence of phrases is the phrase-meaning of a bodhisattva.
From the passage beginning with "For example, like a bird flying," within the analogy, there are again two types: the first...

This means: first, using a phenomenon to illustrate the Dharma; second, following from the analogy. From the passage "As suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)" onwards, it clarifies returning to the Dharma by means of the analogy.
This initial section is precisely the use of a phenomenon to illustrate the Dharma; the subsequent passages will explain this accordingly.

From the passage "Just as the Buddha-eye has no location" onwards, it clarifies that because the Tathāgata possesses the five aggregates (*skandhas*) which are eternally abiding, he is likewise said to possess the sense-bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth;

yet in reality, these do not exist at all. This shall now be explained. From the passage "Within the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-svabhāva*), there is no nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-svabhāva*)" onwards, although this single point is expressed through the negation of the phrase "unwise understanding" (*avidyā-pada-artha*), within the very state of existence, there has been from the beginning no [unconditioned nature].

This constitutes its nature; therefore, we approach it to clarify the meaning of original non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*). For instance, from the passage beginning "When the sun rises" onwards, we next approach the counteractive [teachings] to clarify the meaning of the phrase "non-existence."

"Neither conjoined nor dispersed" clarifies that all dharmas are not conjoined because they are not identical, and not dispersed because they are not different; they are non-existent, being without form, without objects, and so forth.
"One mark" clarifies that although all dharmas possess various characteristics, from this point onward they are all equally the single mark of ultimate emptiness;
therefore, it is called the "one mark," which is to say, the markless.
Nor is there even one; it is the mark of ultimate emptiness. One interpretation explains that all phenomena are identical to suchness and fundamentally not different.
Therefore, it is said that the "one mark" is what is called the "markless. This "marklessness" is also the single mark of suchness.
Question: From "It is asked" onwards, this first section provides the formal explanation for the reasons behind Subhūti’s inquiry.
It clarifies that since [the three provisional designations] were already refuted above, why are they discussed again? Answer: From "It is answered" onwards, the explanation states:

Previously, Subhūti initially established the three provisional designations in order to specifically refute dharmas such as the "Bodhisattva" and the "name Bodhisattva. The Buddha does not now refute those; rather, he speaks of the ultimate nature of all dharmas.
This is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is inherently non-existent because it does not depend on the removal of an opponent.

When the Buddha answered Subhūti, saying, "The meaning of 'non-phrase' is the meaning of 'Bodhisattva,'" he did so precisely because the term "Bodhisattva" is a mere provisional designation (*prajñapti*) without substantial reality. Thus, the Buddha spoke in advance of the provisional name as being non-existent; therefore, [the teaching] is not undermined.
Furthermore, from the passage "The Buddhas have already... onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable.

Having previously explained *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the three provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) and so forth as being empty, Subhūti now wishes to hear the Buddha himself explain the true nature of the words and syllables of the bodhisattva—that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is fundamentally empty—and thus he poses his question.
Furthermore, from the section below, this single point clarifies the reason for the inquiry:

because the Tathāgata’s voice is subtle and wondrous, all beings delight in hearing it, and it is capable of bringing immeasurable benefit; therefore, it must be asked about. Now, [the text] explains the Buddha’s voice.
There are indeed infinite adornments; however, this is merely a partial explanation based on one direction.
The passage beginning with "those who have not yet resolved their minds" sets forth matters that are beneficial. This is because Subhūti possesses immeasurable causes and conditions.
Question: This has been a brief explanation of the general meaning.
From the passage where the Buddha tells Subhūti that there are no words or meanings (*pada-artha*) onwards, the preceding sections have not yet explained the scriptural text itself;

rather, they have concluded by explaining the causal conditions for why Subhūti (Śāriputra) posed his question. Now, we shall explain the scriptural text, interpreting it through the two kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Therefore, when presenting [the term] for exposition, it must be explained.

The question beginning with "What is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'? and so forth, having already clarified that there is no such thing as a "term-meaning," seeks to establish the essence of the term-meaning;
thus, the formal question is posed. The answer beginning with "It is said" and so forth clarifies the linguistic conventions of India by means of various characters.
A word (*pada*) consists of a single syllable; a phrase (*vākya*) consists of multiple words; and four phrases constitute a verse (*gāthā*).
For example, the two characters "Bodhisattva" must first be combined to form a single word, which is "bodhi.

As for "sattva," when the two-character word "bodhi" from above is joined with the two-character word "sattva," they form two words of four characters total, which together constitute a single phrase. It is also called a "collection" (*saṃghāta*).

"Arising" (*sheng*) is a reverse explanation (*fan-shi*). For the sake of supreme wisdom (*anuttara-jñāna*), that which brings forth the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) is precisely what constitutes the meaning (*artha*) beneath the phrase;

thus it is called "meaning. Herein, two reverse explanations are provided: first, it is called "supreme wisdom," and next, the reason for this is explained as the "meaning of the supreme path" (*anuttara-mārga-artha*).
Because they are established in such a sequential manner, this is termed [the reverse explanation].

It constitutes the "various characters. When the various characters form phrases, and beneath each phrase the meanings such as the "Great Mind" are brought forth, this is called the "meaning of the Bodhisattva-phrase.
If one explains the section beginning with the character "yi" (亦), it clarifies that since names are provisional, so too are phrases.
Therefore, it is said that there is "no fixed location. As for the statement that *pada* has various meanings, this refers to meanings such as long phrases, short phrases, and categories of speech.
The following response clarifies that it is precisely because the inclinations of sentient beings differ that the Buddha taught the twelve [links of dependent origination].

The twelve divisions of the scriptures—such as the *nidāna* (causal origins), *itivṛttaka* (past events), *avadāna* (parables), and so forth—are excellent because they are suited to various capacities for hearing and lead to different modes of awakening;
therefore, the holy teachings are not uniform, yet this does not mean they are not in accord with reality.

By this principle, one knows that all twelve divisions of the scriptures are teachings for the purpose of transformation and instruction. Just as the Buddha’s emanations arise from conditions, they are thus provisional and illusory.

As in the section on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) below, the preceding portion up to this point—the commentary on the extensive passage concerning the various types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states, such as defilement and purity—is now complete.

The reason why the text on these thirty-seven factors has been introduced here is to explain the aforementioned passage on the "purity of the four foundations of mindfulness" (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), which was only briefly mentioned there by simply stating "the purity of the four foundations of mindfulness. Now, the treatise intends to provide a detailed exposition of them.
Therefore, it is said: "It is like the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Each point shall be explained in accordance with the preceding scriptural text.
From the passage where Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what are all dharmas? onwards, this constitutes the second major division of the chapter;
it is precisely the gateway of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics). This serves to clarify the Bodhisattva. Above, based on the meaning of the phrases, the Bodhi [was clarified].

"Sā" (Sa) refers to the gate of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). This clarifies that, within this context, by means of six pairs and twelve gates, the dharmas known by the Bodhisattva are explained;
hence it is called the gate of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which elucidates the meaning of "Bodhisattva. This is the text of Subhūti’s question.

From what do they arise? They arise from the aforementioned statement that all dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed, and that they arise from that which is formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive.

Since Subhūti has heard the preceding teaching stated in this way, he now asks about the emergence of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) with the desire to clarify the Bodhisattva by means of the gate of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); thus he poses this question. This accords with principle and benefits transformation.
Those that accord with principle and benefit others are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). Those that contradict principle and harm others are called unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*).

Those that cannot produce a fruit-retribution are called indeterminate dharmas (*avyākṛta-dharma*). Both mundane and supramundane, as well as contaminated and uncontaminated, possess these two meanings in their entirety;
they shall each be explained according to their respective stages, categories, and so forth.
Regarding "that which should be studied and that which should be known": previously, the Venerable Subhūti posed two questions.

Now, from this point downward, we shall first explain the first question—namely, "What are all phenomena?"—and the second question—"How should one understand the unimpeded correspondence within all phenomena?"—which will only be fully explained at the end of this chapter. For now, the Buddha briefly provides a summary conclusion here.
This is not a combined explanation of both gates.
Regarding the passage beginning with "What are the worldly virtues," and so forth, from here on each point will again be discussed in relation to the six pairs of scriptural passages mentioned above.
The Buddha himself explained each point one by one. This first section constitutes the pair [of questions] regarding the mundane.
Since supramundane wholesome dharmas are clarified in the chapter on the mundane and supramundane, the question here asks only:
"What are the mundane wholesome dharmas?"
From "filial piety and obedience" onwards, one wishes to discuss the practices of a bodhisattva. Such virtues as these are all signless (*animitta*) and can all be termed supramundane.
However, for the sake of those ordinary persons who practice only minor deeds, this classification of the Dharma has been made according to such provisional distinctions.
Among these, the nine signs (*navasaṃjñā*) are the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) within the five gates; thus, they belong exclusively to the five gates. One.

Because they are subsumed under the gates [of the mundane], they are called mundane dharmas (*laukika-dharma*). As for the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), these belong to the supramundane (*lokottara*);
this shall now be explained.

From this point below, regarding the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), it is clarified that the twelve gates of dhyāna (*dvādaśa-dvāra-dhyāna*) are practiced by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) to increase their attainment of the Brahma-heaven paths;
therefore, they belong to mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*). The ten recollections (*daśa-anusmṛti*) also belong to the mundane; these two categories will now be explained.
