Regarding the section beginning with "The indeterminate bodily and vocal karmas, etc.," below: while the treatise intends to discuss the three types of karma, the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth—including their exhaustion, the path, and the three natures—for now, within this section on the indeterminate, it speaks solely from the standpoint of what is indeterminate. Therefore, it simply says "the three types of indeterminate karma, etc.

The meaning of these categories, such as the single nature and the five aggregates, has already been explained in the first chapter; thus, the words of the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) are established.

Regarding the statement that "good and evil do not exist within the nature of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*)," this refers merely to the single principle of indeterminate form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and so forth;

it is not something that can be fully understood [without further context]. From the section on the three samādhis below, these three samādhis are also identical to the *dhyāna*s and so forth, with no difference. For what reason, then, [is there a separate mention]?

This is called a supramundane dharma (*lokottara-dharma*). To explain: among the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), there are those characterized by attachment to flavor (*āsvādana*), those that are pure (*śuddha*), those that are the result of retribution (*vipāka*), and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).

The previous passage referred to the first three, and thus stated they belong to mundane dharmas (*laukika-dharma*); the present passage refers to the untainted, and therefore speaks of them as supramundane.

"Clarity" refers to the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*). "Liberation" refers to the two kinds of liberation. "Wisdom" refers to the ten knowledges (*jñāna*). "Right mindfulness" refers to the wisdom of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Because the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) are attained only by noble ones (*ārya*), they belong to the supramundane.

In the first chapter, the Master [Vasubandhu] has already cited these terms from this section and explained them above. As for the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*), they pertain only to...

Regarding the eight dhyānas: although they are generally attained by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), one cannot enter them sequentially and without interval; therefore, they are not termed "sequential.

Now, because only noble ones (*ārya*) attain them, they are categorized as supramundane (*lokottara*) dharmas. However, in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they belong only to the category of tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas.
As for the noble ones' ability to explain and relinquish them, the Buddha spoke solely on the basis of these meanings regarding the dhyānas attained by noble ones.
Therefore, this explanation is made.

Regarding the passage beginning with "What are the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)": if one refers to the stage [of practice], then from the perspective of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) no longer arise.

If one refers to the phenomena themselves, they consist solely of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) belonging to the three realms, as well as all tainted meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth. What are the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?
Below this, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*): if spoken of in terms of their nature (*dharma*), they belong to the supramundane (*lokottara*);

if spoken of in terms of their stage (*avasthā*), they belong to the contaminated (*sāsrava*). As for why the present sutra states that they belong to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "The supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)."

Although these are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are able to destroy conditioned phenomena and outflows. Now, because they resemble the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), they are directed toward the outflow-free;

they destroy the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages associated with outflows, and because they involve both affection and exertion, they are now taken solely for the purpose of destroying, resembling, and directing toward [the outflow-free], and through such exertion.
Thus, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) receive the name "outflow-free" in this superior sense. Question: If it is said that they destroy...

Regarding the statement that "because it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is called 'similar to the outflow-free' (anāsrava)": it is also said that because it destroys the conditioned (saṃskṛta), it is called "similar to the unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta).

The explanation says: by analogy, this too is a portion of the permanent [nature] that is subdued; or, there may be cases where it is not obtained, as this "similar knowledge" takes the unconditioned of cessation (nirodha-asaṃskṛta) as its object.

"What are the conditioned? and so forth. Here, both types of the conditioned are explained together: one based on the three marks of the conditioned, and the other based on the conditioned as the performance of an action.
Now, the sūtra-master wishes to encompass all phenomena through these various categories so that they are fully exhausted.
Therefore, both types are clarified. Regarding the passage beginning with "What is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

and so forth, this also relies on the two kinds of unconditioned states—such as the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśakṣaya*)—and designates them as the unconditioned state of cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As for the passage beginning with "As it is not different," and so forth, this clarifies the unconditioned state of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Both shall now be explained.
Regarding the section beginning with "What are the common dharmas?": this clarifies the twelve gates, such as dhyāna and so forth, which represent what ordinary beings and sages alike lose or gain.

Regarding the section beginning with "What are the uncommon [dharmas]? and so forth: this clarifies the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and other such factors. Since these belong to supramundane dharmas, they are not attainable by external worldlings;
rather, they pertain to the practice of those who resemble sages. Therefore, they are called "uncommon."
"From 'A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not become attached to these dharmas that are empty of self-characteristics' onwards,
this is the Buddha’s correct explanation herein of what Subhūti [the Second Questioner] previously asked regarding the meaning of entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality and so forth."
It shall now be explained.
The following section, beginning with the question, constitutes the commentary’s detailed explanation of the six pairs and two gates of the sutra.

First, it clarifies the underlying intent of the initial inquiry: "One who first knows the characteristics of the world" refers to one who understands both the mundane and the supramundane wholesome [dharmas].
This is the characteristic. From "The wholesome dharmas of the world" onwards, the preceding explanation of the reason for asking [the question] first is complete.
Now, the text itself will be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "There are [retributions] in this life and in future lives," the reason why the past is not mentioned is to clarify that the causes and effects of the past have already been [established].
This has already been explained and need not be discussed here. Now, we are specifically discussing the meaning of attaining the fruit; therefore, we shall only discuss the present.
As for the future, it will be treated in accordance with the principles of the three types of retributive karma and so forth, and thus the past will not be discussed here either.
The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: "Regarding the twelve divisions of the sūtras, if one believes only six divisions and does not believe the other six, this is called 'incomplete faith.
Therefore, one must have clear and firm faith. This refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), and thus it pertains to mundane goodness (*laukika-kuśala*).
The prohibitions of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others consist in the joyful training in the wholesome conduct of body and speech according to the household laws.
If one were born and lived for seventy years, eating only once a day, it would amount to only thirty-six thousand meals in a single lifetime of one hundred and twenty years;
this is why it is so. It is the same for bhikṣus. As for rice gruel, it does not count as food. Bo Jiqi said: "Venerable sir."
"Brother and sister" refers to the elders. Regarding those who cultivate the family law (*jiafa*): "law" (*fa*) here means the codes (*dian*).

If one were to consider scriptures outside of the [Confucian] canon as belonging to the national codes, yet the descendants within the household transmit them and constantly practice them in this manner, such applications of the law are termed "family codes" (*jiadian*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Having generated merit through skillful means": practices such as performing the five dharmas morning and evening every day do not deplete one's wealth or strength, yet they enable the acquisition of immeasurable merit.
Since this is merit obtained through clever application, it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).

Although the principle of practicing emptiness while remaining unattached to emptiness and so forth should pertain to supramundane goodness, these words were spoken here specifically to clarify the meaning of skillful means.

Regarding the statement "this is the foundation of mindfulness of the body": previously it was stated that the four foundations of mindfulness belong to supramundane dharmas; now, however, this is explained according to the mundane good.

As for the phrase "is precisely" (*jìshì*), it refers to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) among the five gates [of meditation]; thus it is called the "foundation of mindfulness of the body," following the terminology of that specific context.
Therefore, it is called "wholesome thought.
That which is contrary to wholesome dharmas—namely, being unfilial toward one's parents, disrespectful toward elders and superiors, and so forth—is therefore called "unwholesome.
It should be explained that herein, these are also termed unwholesome because failing to practice them results in the loss of merit, as in the *Mahā*... [text fragment].
This sutra states: "One who does not perform prostrations is not called 'good,' just as one who does not practice the ten recitations and so forth;
yet this does not necessarily mean that they have committed evil or unwholesome acts."

Regarding the section beginning with "unconditioned phenomena" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): herein, the deportment (*iryāpatha*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), the fourteen transformations (*nirmāṇa*), and so forth are clarified.
Because the nature of this mind is not evil, yet its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) function in such a way, it is designated as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

For example, when one maintains the precepts and restrains one's deportment, the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*) involved is indeed wholesome; however, the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of the deportment itself is—

Because it is a resultant phenomenon (*vipākadharmatva*), its nature is neutral (*avyākṛta*). However, as for the teaching that this is a defiled phenomenon (*kleśadharma*), it belongs to the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*);
whereas as a resultant phenomenon, it belongs to the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding the phrase "and the bodily and vocal karmas arising from this," it clarifies that these three types of karma pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

Since we are currently explaining the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), we take only the three types of indeterminate karma; thus, it is said as such. Having thus clarified the indeterminate.

Therefore, it is said that one excludes the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. This clarifies that the five aggregates all encompass the three natures (tri-svabhāva).

Within the indeterminate (avyākṛta), there are the five aggregates consisting of deportment (airyāpathika), craftsmanship (śailpasthānika), transformation (nairmāṇika), retribution-born (vipākaja), and so forth. Within the wholesome, there are the five aggregates consisting of mundane and supramundane wholesome states.

Furthermore, there are two types: those of fragmented birth (*pariccheda*) and those of transformation (*pariṇāma*). These are further divided into two: the unwholesome (*akuśala*), which is unique, and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) that are eternally abiding.

Thus, there are ten kinds of aggregates in total. This shall now be explained. As for the "remaining five aggregates," these refer to all aggregates excluding the wholesome and unwholesome five aggregates, and so forth.
The remaining indeterminate five aggregates and so forth are therefore referred to as "the rest.

As for space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): if one explains the meaning according to the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, among the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), only cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is considered wholesome;
the unconditioned phenomenon of space belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Since [this] is based on time...

Because it is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is also categorized as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus, the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states: "Because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Since the Buddha-nature is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is virtuous (*kuśala*); therefore, it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This passage reflects the perspective of the Hīnayāna:

since the Buddha-nature is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, it is simply an unconditioned state like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is virtuous. It is not [unconditioned in the sense of being] non-virtuous.
This is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is not the same as space (*ākāśa*) or cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Therefore, it is said that because this is wholesome (*kuśala*), it is not unconditioned. If one discusses the three unconditioneds according to the Mahāyāna, they are exclusively wholesome dharmas. Thus, the *Renwang jing* states: "The Buddha attains the fruit of the three unconditioneds.
Taking the space of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-ākāśa*) as the unconditioned of space, it is therefore a wholesome dharma. [Regarding] the future...

The exhaustion of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and so forth are likewise wholesome dharmas. Since it is said that the Buddha attains the three unconditioned fruits (*asaṃskṛta-phala*), how could these be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), such that they would cause the Buddha to attain indeterminate fruits?
As for "worldly dharmas" (*laukika-dharma*), this clarifies that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the three realms are all permeated by the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
Regarding the statement that "among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and four are of three kinds":

although the five aggregates (*skandha*) are identical to the bases and elements (*dhātu*), the five aggregates are general and concise dharma-doors; therefore, they are not subdivided. If they are wholesome, all five belong to the wholesome;

if unwholesome or indeterminate, likewise, they all pertain to the three natures (*tridharmatā*). Now, since the bases and elements are doors of detailed classification and are extensive doors, [they are so categorized].
They are divided for the sake of clarifying their meanings. Eight are categorized as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while four pertain to all three natures. The "eight" refers to the five faculties;
these are merely faculties of retribution that function in conjunction with consciousness and have no other use, and thus they are exclusively indeterminate.
By adding the two objects of fragrance and taste to the five sense objects, they become eight. As for the two objects of form and sound, they pertain to all three natures. For example:
The body belongs to retributive form (*vipākaja-rūpa*). The body that is retributive form, and the form of the retribution-body (*vipāka-kāya*), are invariably indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

However, when one performs prostrations or other wholesome deeds, such forms belong to wholesome form; when one commits evil, such forms then belong to unwholesome form. For this reason, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) all encompass the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
This is precisely why the teaching is a skillful means (*upāya*): form, sound, and so forth can themselves belong to either the wholesome or the unwholesome. As it is said:
Sounds acquired through retribution—such as those that are broken, clear, turbid, long, or short—are categorized as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

However, sounds such as those used for reciting scriptures or praising the Buddha are categorized as wholesome (*kuśala*), while sounds such as those of harsh speech or abuse are categorized as unwholesome (*akuśala*); therefore, they pertain to all three categories.

Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there are generally seven types of phenomena. Among the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, one is wholesome, as explained above; the other two belong to the indeterminate, as explained above.
It is said that feeling, perception, mental formations, and so forth, if they belong to the category of maturation (*vipāka*), are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

however, from the perspective of their application through effort (*prayoga*), they belong to the wholesome or unwholesome, and thus pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). As for other physical forms and so forth, they likewise pertain to all three natures.

Within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), if there is non-manifest form (*avijñapti*) or matter, it pertains only to the wholesome; within the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), if it is the mind born of maturation, it is indeterminate, whereas the mind arising from effort...
Their inclusion [within the categories] depends on whether they are wholesome or unwholesome; thus, there are these four types of inclusion, which apply to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
In the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, there is a general enumeration with further analytical explanations: among these twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), how many are wholesome, and how many are unwholesome?
How many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? How many are retributions (*vipāka*)? How many are not retributions? Such are the meanings [to be examined].

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), eight are indeterminate, no differently than in the case of the twelve bases (*āyatana*). The remaining six consciousnesses, together with the mind-faculty (*manas*), are termed the seven consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
If the retribution-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) is indeterminate, then the functional consciousnesses (*prāyogika-vijñāna*) and so forth belong to the two categories of wholesome and unwholesome.

As for their nature: while the remaining [elements], such as the material elements, sound, and the dharma-element, pertain to all three natures, the meaning of these three natures is also as explained in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*.
Therefore, it is said that eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and ten pertain to all three kinds.

Regarding the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) and below, the treatise itself states: "This is based on ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who, having accomplished these [practices], obtain such benefits but are unable to transcend [saṃsāra];
therefore, they are called 'worldly dharmas' (*laukikadharma*). This does not concern the noble ones (*ārya*). This shall now be explained.

The section beginning with "That which transcends the world" (*lokottara*) is explained by the passage beginning with "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Among the eleven types of knowledge, there is also conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), which belongs to worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*).
However, because the intention here is to speak according to the majority rather than the minority, it is called "transcending the world.

Regarding "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*): it clarifies that reaching the correct [state] constitutes being a sage (*ārya*). Only the principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) can give rise to noble wisdom; therefore, it is named "correct principle" (*samyak-naya*). Now...

Because it accords with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is called "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*). For example, one who contemplates the body according to its nature is contemplating the true nature of the body and so forth.
This enables one to become skillful; thus, it is said that right mindfulness is the root of wholesome dharmas, for it causes wholesome dharmas to be eternally firm.
Furthermore, from "the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and so forth" onwards, this is also explained in the *Śāstra* itself; it is also extremely clear.
From "receiving the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) and so forth" onwards, [this] is divided into two paths.

Although these belong to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and are with outflows (*sāsrava*), because one takes the single mind as the path, these are the merit and wisdom within the skillful means (*upāya*) and have no other business; therefore, they belong to the supramundane (*lokottara*).
Furthermore, from the section on "the liberations" (*vimokṣa*) onwards, the Master himself explains the reason why these are termed "supramundane" (*lokottara*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Although mindfulness and wisdom (*smṛti-prajñā*) and right recollection (*samyak-smṛti*) are of two kinds," "mindfulness" refers to the ten types of mindfulness, which may pertain to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

"Wisdom," however, consists of the eleven types of knowledge (*jñāna*), which can only be attained by noble ones. As for the statement here that there are "two kinds," [it refers to the following distinction].

However, among the eleven knowledges, there is one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that is common to both ordinary beings and sages. For now, speaking in accordance with their general characteristics, it is said that there are two [types].
This is also similar for those within the stage of the "right mindfulness" of the inner ordinary beings (*antara-pudgala*), as they too contemplate the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
thus, they also possess these two.

Regarding "the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)," the explanation below is as above. Since the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are similar to the untainted (*anāsrava*), according to this one sense, they are taken as being untainted, supramundane (*lokottara*), and so forth; this is also explained as above.

Regarding "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and below, there are two [meanings]. First, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), four aggregates, and so forth, which are bound to the three realms, are called "conditioned" because they possess the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*).

Second, from the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the Buddha and others, all belong to conditioned phenomena produced by volitional effort (*abhisamskāra-saṃskṛta*), rather than being conditioned by way of the three characteristics.
The sūtras and śāstras themselves provide this analytical explanation; one should know that the applications of mindfulness [are] the dharmas of wisdom.

Because the body and so forth all possess parts and do not transmigrate, the preceding scriptural passage is explained as merely stating that there is arising and abiding, without mentioning that there is cessation.

Regarding the section beginning with "When one explains that conditioned phenomena are contrary [to the unconditioned]," there are also two meanings: it clarifies that the three poisons and other such factors are afflictions, and their abandonment belongs to wisdom.

Because the characteristics of the five aggregates and so forth that are non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) do not continue, they are based on the cessation of birth and death; thus, they belong to the category of non-conditioned phenomena that are not objects of cognition.

This stands in contrast to the three aforementioned types of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) meanings, such as the "dharma-characteristic" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). To be "unconditioned" in this sense is to stand in contrast to the aforementioned meaning of conditioned phenomena as "constructed" (*kṛtaka*).
Question: From "The following" onwards, the meaning of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*) will next be examined; this shall be explained herein. Answer:

From "The answer says, from 'onward," although the minds of the sages also know that form (*rūpa*) is real—this being because they have realized the Single Truth—it is simply for the sake of the present analysis that the ordinary person and the sage are contrasted and divided.
Because ordinary beings do not attain the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of form, they each speak by relying exclusively on one side;
this is not the case for the noble ones (*ārya*), who know only the true mark of form and do not [conceptually] know form. The subsequent passages and so forth shall all be explained accordingly.
From "The signless, the unimpeded," etc., down to this point, the explanation of the Buddha’s answer to Subhūti’s first question is complete.
From here onward, up until the entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality, the explanation of the answer to the second question shall be set forth.
Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Scroll Seventeen.
Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Scroll Twenty-one.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiying of Qianshan Temple in Tongzhou, Shu Province.

Regarding the thirty-sixth chapter of the fifty-ninth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, it is titled "The Chapter on the Comparative Measurement of Śarīra. In all the preceding chapters, the virtues were first elucidated, followed by their comparative measurement;
since this chapter begins by specifically taking the comparative measurement of śarīra as its primary focus, it is so named.
Now, as I am about to provide an explanation, I shall introduce it by stating: "The Commentary on the Thirty-Sixth Chapter.
From the passage beginning with "The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra" onwards, the text proceeds to correctly clarify the comparative analysis of the *Śāriputra-parivarta*.
The meaning within this section is indeed immeasurable; however, to discuss it in broad terms, there are three cycles of comparison. First, [it] introduces...
The first [comparison] is the comparison of the śarīra filling Jambudvīpa against the sūtra scrolls; the second is the comparison of the śarīra filling the trichiliocosm against the sūtra scrolls;
and the third is the comparison of the śarīra filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges against the sūtra scrolls.
This first instance is precisely when the Buddha, wishing to perform this comparison, addressed the Lord of Devas.
This shall now be explained.
As for the passage beginning with "Why is this? and so forth, its intent is to explain that while the *śarīra* (relics) are merely traces, Prajñāpāramitā is the very essence of the Buddha;
therefore, one should prefer Prajñāpāramitā. For instance, as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "The *śarīra* [are the fruit] of the six pāramitās..."
Because they are permeated by the merit of honey, they should be paid homage. This shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Śāriputra asked... onwards, it clarifies how Śāriputra further engages in discussion on this basis. This shall now be interpreted.
Regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason... and extending from "not for the sake of grasping" to "purity," there are five pairs that clarify the meaning of emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*).
These shall be explained one by one as they arise.

The passage beginning with "not giving the dharmas of the Buddhas" clarifies the invitation to the Buddha. Because the dharmas such as the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*) are unattainable, they are not grasped;
because the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth are likewise unattainable, they are not abandoned. All cases are to be understood by this analogy.
From "In this way, in this way" onwards, it clarifies that the Lord of Devas restates his questions as answers.

From "At that time, the Buddha praised him" onwards, it clarifies that because the Lord of Devas is able to rely upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he speaks of the non-dual characteristic (*advaya-lakṣaṇa*).

Relying on the One Sovereign (*eka-īśvara*), he makes distinctions and comparisons; how could one not choose Prajñā? Its meaning encompasses the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and enables future attainment.
Therefore, the Tathāgata offered high praise and composed this work to bring it to completion. This shall now be explained:

regarding Prajñā and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), since both object and wisdom are equally merged in stillness and lack two distinct characteristics, it is said that they are not separate. All meanings are thus.
From the passage beginning with "Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies that Śāriputra’s discourse was explained by the Lord of Devas (Indra) and validated by the Tathāgata.
This section on the meaning having concluded, he now wishes to return to the primary subject to provide a comparative evaluation; for this reason, he addresses the Buddha.

The passage beginning with "For what reason... constitutes the second intention within the first section; it clarifies the specific meaning of why *prajñā* (wisdom) is superior to *tyāga* (renunciation).
This will be explained in the main treatise. The "Hall of Good Dharma" (*Saddharmakūṭa*) is used as a metaphor for the scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra. This is appropriate.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Moreover, World-Honored One" onwards, this is the third intention: it clarifies that within the Dharma of Prajñā, the ability to give rise to fearlessness is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon;
therefore, [the opponent's claim] is not so. This shall now be explained.
"From 'For what reason? onwards explains the meaning of why there is fearlessness.
From 'It should be said that this person does not follow the evil paths' onwards constitutes the fourth point, which provides a comparative evaluation to clarify its superior significance."
It shall now be explained.

Furthermore, from the passage "Next, the World-Honored One filled the trichiliocosm" onwards, this is the second section of the chapter, which uses the śarīras filling the great trichiliocosm as a standard for comparison.
As for the phrase "For what reason," it explains the underlying cause. Rather... [the text continues].
One should grasp the meaning of *prajñā*. It is clarified that while *prajñā* can give birth to the relics (*śarīra*) of all Buddhas, it cannot give birth to the Buddha himself.
Therefore, the reason one obtains superior fruits by making offerings to the relics is solely due to *prajñā*.
However, if the relics were not permeated and cultivated by *prajñā*, how would they differ from other bones? For this reason, one should rather grasp *prajñā*.
"By what reason? and so forth below explains that Prajñā-wisdom is itself the Buddha; therefore, it is said there is no difference.

Regarding the question "As for what follows," each point shall be explained in turn. As for the passage "filling Jambudvīpa" and so forth, this clarifies that the śarīra relics are not equal [to the Dharma];
hence the word "fill. Because Prajñā is superior, it refers simply to the "scriptural volume"; even a single fascicle or a single scroll of the sutra is superior.

Furthermore, regarding the passage "As for those who have left the household life" and below, this section is explained again by means of the "Great Path" (Daimoku) interpretation. This is because it distinguishes between the differing dispositions of the monastic and the lay;
such is the reason. It shall now be expounded.

Even down to the size of a mustard seed, it clarifies that when the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa* and passed away, he entered the Vajra-like Samādhi and spontaneously shattered his own body into eight *hù* and four *dǒu* of *śarīra*.
The Buddha’s body was only one *zhàng* and six *cùn* in height; it is because the [relics] such as those [from the *dhātu*] were added to the *śarīra* that they became so numerous.
If they are bone *śarīra*, their color is reddish-white. As for the [other] *śarīra*, their color...
It was then crimson-red. The eight kings divided it, each receiving one *hu*. There were only eight *hu* in total;
however, when the person measuring the relics used honey to coat the measuring vessel and scraped it clean, they obtained four more *hu*, which is why it is said there were eight *hu*.
These relics were of wondrous color and substantial essence, surpassing even diamond (*vajra*). Formerly, Kang Senghui came to the presence of the Ruler of Wu to translate scriptures.
"It is well said that the Buddha-dharma is inconceivable. Sun Quan said, "If this is so, why not allow me to see it?
Senghui immediately requested one śarīra on his behalf. When the śarīra was placed upon a copper tray and a depression appeared, he called for someone to place it on an iron plowshare and strike it;
it sank into the plowshare, and after searching carefully, it was recovered. Thereupon, Jianchu Temple was established. At [that time]...
This is the intermediate offering. From here on, each passage shall be explained in accordance with the meaning of the text.

Regarding the section beginning with "At that time, the Buddha praised [him]": if one relies upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all phenomena are identical to suchness (*tathatā*), and thus there is no *prajñā* superior to the *śarīra*.
If one relies upon worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), then the *śarīra* cannot be equaled. What the Lord of Heaven has now spoken is excellent and worthy of being followed.
Regarding the two Emperors, they were thus praised by the Buddha; this shall now be explained.

From "using one's own body as a metaphor for the Buddha" onwards, the second point above shall be explained. The "Hall of Good Dharma" (Sudharmā) is a metaphor for the scriptural text; this shall now be explained.
"Having seen no fear" and below explain the scriptural passage concerning the third meaning mentioned above.
"Not following the evil destinies" and below explain the scriptural passage concerning the fourth meaning mentioned above.
Having increased [the number] to three thousand for the sake of all sentient beings, the following section of the second major division of the scripture is produced.
This is also the scriptural text for the first two points within the explanation of the second intention; it shall now be explained.

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Next, World-Honored One" onwards, within the second major section, is the third comparison of intent. This clarifies that the Buddha-nature is capable of abiding;

it demonstrates the manifestation of three matters to transform sentient beings and the preaching of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, which is no different from upholding and expounding the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The phrase "For what reason? and following explains the meaning of why there is no difference. Regarding the "manifestation of the three matters," these refer to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), preaching the Dharma, and knowing the minds of others.

This is also called the manifestation of the three karmas for the benefit of sentient beings; it is also called the three secrets (*triguhyaka*), and it is also called the three wheels (*tricakra*). These shall now be explained.

Furthermore, from "Next, World-Honored One, the Buddhas of the ten directions... onwards, the preceding section compared [the Buddha] to Śākyamuni in terms of three matters of benefiting sentient beings.
Now, for the fourth time, this section compares him to the Buddhas of the ten directions in terms of their abiding in three matters. These shall all be explained in the main treatise.
Furthermore, from "Next, World-Honored One" onwards is the fifth [section], which compares [the merit] with that of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "Next, World-Honored One" onwards is the sixth [section], which compares it according to the underlying intent. Above, there was merely a direct clarification of the merits;
now, the textual meaning herein is brought forward because it serves as a comparative evaluation against what preceded, and is not a mere repetition. This shall now be explained.
Commentary:

Furthermore, from "Next, the World-Honored One... onwards, the seventh section provides a further parable of the person who reproaches others, which serves to compare and evaluate the contents of this sutra scroll.
This shall be explained in the main treatise.
Furthermore, from "Next, the World-Honored One... onwards, the eighth section provides a comparison using the analogy of a mani-jewel to correspond with the sutra scroll;
this will be explained in the main treatise.
From "Having produced various colors... onwards, it clarifies that because Prajñā is signless (animitta), it has no fixed color; this shall also be explained.
The section beginning with "At that time, Ānanda... and following concerns those who have left the household life through the power of the Bright Jewel (Maṇiratna).

The section beginning with "After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored Buddha" and following is the ninth [section], which generally clarifies the power, function, and ultimate significance of Prajñā.
This shall now be explained.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, after you have measured out the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems filled with śarīras and placed them [in this scripture], this constitutes the third major section of this chapter.
Next, by using the śarīras of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, one shall weigh the merit of creating this scripture;
this is what should now be explained. At present, even a single śarīra cannot be found, let alone filling ten [worlds].
As for the experts in these matters: because ordinary people do not understand, they exclusively value the *śarīra* (relics).

Thus, the aforementioned treatise states that those who have left the household life mostly seek wisdom and the fruit of liberation, and therefore cherish the scriptures; whereas worldly people mostly seek mundane pleasures, and therefore delight in honoring the *śarīra*.
Therefore, the Lord of Devas said above: "It is not that I slight the Buddha’s *śarīra* that I speak in this manner."
Now, because I wish to cause those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds to deeply understand this principle, I shall evaluate it according to reality:
it would be better to take up even a single scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. This is because its merit is supreme and its Way is vast; such is the reason for this.
Within this third section, there is furthermore a further intention.

From "The World-Honored One" onwards, [the stage] is superior because it involves the immeasurable comparison of the first intention regarding its retribution, as well as the entry into the bodhisattva-dharmapada (the station of the dharma of bodhisattvas), and so forth.
This shall now be explained. Herein, since the sutra states "the bodhisattva-dharmapada," they have already attained the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva;
for the sake of sentient beings, they take on bodies from one buddha-field to another, according to what is appropriate for each. Or...

Regarding the statement that "the manifestation of transformation is produced by responding to conditions," one should know that this is not a karmic retribution. One should know that the Dharma-body merely appears according to what is appropriate for beings to see;
it is not something that arises through active effort or movement. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, regarding the passage beginning with "There are people who wish to see the immeasurable [buddhas] of the ten directions" and so forth:
this is the second intention, which shall now be explained by means of comparing the two kinds of *dharmakāya* that appear.

Furthermore, from "The Buddha, having manifested through the three modes of appearance" onwards, this first section clarifies that the Master of the Treatise must cite the preceding scriptural text before he intends to explain it. Regarding the question "Why is this so?

and so forth, the intent of the question is as follows: Since the Buddha has already fully expounded the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), why does he [the treatise] then say...?
"A person who upholds, recites, and studies the *Prajñāpāramitā* is no different from the Buddha.
The following response states that among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the most significant. This is a general statement;
however, it clarifies that all Mahāyāna sūtras are of one kind and possess no superiority or inferiority. To say that the *Prajñāpāramitā* is great is simply...
Among these twelve divisions [of the canon], the Vaipulya (fangdeng) is the greatest; it encompasses eleven of the twelve divisions. Therefore, the scriptures of these eleven divisions—
This is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. A single division, the Vaipulya, is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Because within the Vaipulya sūtras there are twelve divisions, all of which are termed the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, it is referred to here as "one division.
Within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, because the Bodhisattva-piṭaka does not exist, it is said to consist of eleven divisions. Now, because the Vaipulya is vast, it is said that the Prajñā is also vast.
The passage beginning with "Why is this so? clarifies that these are *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas who exclusively teach *prajñāpāramitā* and exhort others toward the Mahāyāna;
thus it says, "many have resolved their minds on bodhicitta. As for the others, they preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*).
This is because those who have newly resolved their minds [on awakening] frequently teach *prajñāpāramitā* and generate the great resolve; this shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "the manifestation of the three matters" onwards, this is the general synthesis of the meaning;
it explains the four points mentioned above—the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth—and serves as a comparative evaluation of the scriptural text. This shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "Just like a person taking responsibility" explains the seventh point above by employing the metaphor of taking responsibility, thereby evaluating the scriptural text.

The reason for using the metaphor of taking responsibility is to clarify that if this *śarīra* (relic) were not perfumed by the cultivation of *prajñā*, it would continue to undergo various retributive responses pursued by the causes of karma from previous lives;
however, through the perfuming cultivation of *prajñā* now, those karmic responses from the past are forever avoided.
Because it is determined that [the merit] shall receive offerings, this analogy is thus employed.
Now, from the passage beginning with "the mani-jewel" onwards, the meaning of the eighth section on comparative measurement (*tulanā*) in the sutra is explained.
Within this, there is both a general explanation and a specific explanation. This first part briefly sets forth its power and its majestic influence. It shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "Question" (問曰) below intends to clarify its source. Regarding the [vajra], it must be struck by Śakra alone for it to break;

this will be explained in the relevant context when we encounter the text. As for the "liberation of the three vehicles," this refers to the *pariśuddha-nirvāṇa* (pure nirvāṇa) attained through skillful means (*upāya*).
In the Hinayana teachings, there is only the extinction of phenomena (*vastu-nirodha*) and the pure [nirvāṇa] of skillful means, because the Arhat [attains it] at the ninth...

The wisdom of liberation is the conditioned fruit. The non-existence of the ninety-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the unconditioned fruit, etc., is precisely the meaning of purification through skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*).

The "ash-like body" is the meaning of the cessation of phenomena. Because it does not clarify that the fundamental nature of all dharmas is inherently pure, there is no "purity of non-nature" (*abhāva-viśuddhi*).
In the Mahāyāna, these are the three [purities]. This shall now be explained. As for the root of the four illnesses, they are wind, heat, cold, and their combination.

These are called the "equal portions" (*sabhāga*). Third, regarding illness, it is spoken of in terms of its partial manifestation; regarding the equal portions, it is based on the three types of origination.
Fourth, there are four meanings, which have already been explained above.
"Furthermore, it can eliminate the eighty-four thousand roots of illness," and so forth. Here, the explanation is based on the predominance of the three poisons;

thus, there are sixty-three thousand [afflictions] arising from them individually. Those that arise as a combination of equal proportions constitute twenty-one thousand. Therefore, they total eighty-four thousand.
This is why the *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra* explains the eighty-four thousand [dharmas]. From the light-shining [perfection] onwards, all the pāramitās...
The *pāramitās* (perfections). Ultimately reaching the *pāramitā* of distributing the *śarīra* relics, there are three hundred and fifty *pāramitās* in total.

Within each of these *pāramitās*, there are further six *pāramitās*, which results in two thousand one hundred. Within each of these, there are ten wholesome deeds (*daśakuśala*), which results in twenty-one thousand *pāramitās*.
When these are divided by means of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*), they become eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*. This is the system of other schools.
One might take ten dharmas from the *Avataṃsaka* to supplement this, but the Master said, "I fear this is not correct.

Since each individual *pāramitā* already contains these ten dharmas, they total twenty-one thousand. When these are applied to the afflictions arising from the four types of illness, they become eighty-four thousand;
thus, the various *pāramitās* are called the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates. Therefore, within this...
It is said that Prajñāpāramitā can eliminate the eighty-four thousand ailments. This point has already been touched upon previously, so it cannot be explained in detail here.
Regarding the four fundamental ailments: greed, delusion, and their equal proportions each comprise twenty-one thousand varieties.
These are discussed in terms of the afflictions that arise and obstruct the various pāramitās, or which constitute the eighty-four thousand gates of worldly defilement (*kleśa*). Now...

Furthermore, regarding those who come with greed and other afflictions, which are removed by the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): these four contemplations correspond only to the four fundamental ailments and do not discuss other meanings. This shall now be explained.

The passage beginning with "Once the jewel has removed the heat" (珠除熱已下) synthesizes and explains the aforementioned meaning of being able to eliminate the four hundred and four diseases, such as those caused by wind, cold, heat, and their combinations;
these shall be explained one by one in the relevant sections of the text. The sun-jewel belongs to the essence of Yang, while the moon-jewel belongs to the essence of Yin.
If there were only the moon, all things would become damp and rot; if there were only the sun, all things would wither and dry up.
Therefore, these sun and moon bring about the transformation of all things through the interplay of Yin and Yang: because of the moon, all things are moistened;
because of the sun, all things grow. As for the claim that cold and heat are like the vapors of Yin and Yang, this is the fourth month.
When the six yang lines arise simultaneously, why is it not extremely hot? When the six yin lines arise simultaneously in the tenth month, why is it not extremely cold?

In this present age, because the sun travels the southern path during winter, the days are short and cold; because it travels the middle path during spring and autumn, day and night are equal, and heat and cold are temperate and balanced;
and because the sun travels the northern path during summer, the days are long and hot. Such is the principle of serving Heaven.
Each point shall be explained in combination. It clarifies that by means of *prajñā*, one practices the relinquishing of all [attainments], such as the fruit of *srotāpanna* and so forth;
therefore, unimpeded *prajñā* can mutually accord with them. This shall now be explained. Regarding the sixth, the light-blue color (*pīta-varṇa*):

based on the aforementioned meanings of relinquishing all fruits and so forth, this is contrasted with the five colors. It specifically designates the color of the "spiritual void" (*ākāśa-varṇa*), which is merely perceived from afar.

Space (ākāśa) appears as a blue color; thus, it is called "azure" (pīta). This very color is used to harmonize with the meaning of the cultivation of emptiness, which is why it is mentioned separately. This shall now be explained.

From here on, the following shall be explained by way of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). What has been discussed up to this point is also called "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and "equal analogies";

it combined [the analogy] to explain the meaning of *prajñā*. From this point onward, it is also called "specific characteristics" and "exceeding analogies," as it combines [the analogy] to explain *prajñā*.
This shall be explained one by one. Regarding how *prajñā* can eliminate two things: it can also eliminate both ghosts and devas.
It is also a demonic affliction. It is a disease of the mind that neither devas, nāgas, spirits, nor deities can cure.

As for the statement, "Since beginningless time, it is a disease never before cured," this refers to the diseases of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*). Each of these shall be explained in turn.

Regarding "associated ignorance" (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*), this is the ignorance that arises concomitantly with the nine underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Regarding "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇika-avidyā*), this is the [ignorance] of the tenth...
Regarding "the proclivities": this refers to the ignorance that arises separately from the various proclivities.

Furthermore, regarding "the delusion and darkness of non-comprehension within all phenomena," this refers to the analytical ignorance within all forms of knowledge and vision, which exists because one fails to penetrate the correct principle.
Some distinguish this by explaining it as "lack of understanding. From the following text onward, each point shall be explained in turn. Regarding these two poisons:
they refer to the internal poison of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the external poisons such as toxic drugs. They can cure the eye of wisdom, causing it to attain clarity and purity.
"Leprosy of the mind" refers to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) and other such offenses.
Question: [The following] provides a detailed analysis. This shall now be explained. A jewel can only cause water to become clear, whereas worldly objects and the like undergo transformation.

If waves can cause the "water of the mind" to become clear, this refers to the inquiry regarding the wholesome mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with the mind. Regarding the "six perceptions" (*ṣaḍ-vijñapti*):

these refer to the perceptions of desire, wisdom, harm, kinship, decline, birth, and immortality. This shall now be explained. [This concerns] those who experience worldly and supramundane happiness, Śāriputra.
And so forth. Because they are all precious, they differ from the pearl caskets and boxes; this shall be explained.

Having thus completed the explanation by means of analogies for both the general and specific characteristics, next follows the summary conclusion. The question regarding "below" shall be explained there.
The meaning of this has already been explained above. From here on, throughout the majority of the intermediate sections of the third part, the sūtra texts have been largely omitted;
since their meaning has already been covered above, they are referred back to the previous explanations.

Furthermore, from the passage "Next, World-Honored One, there are two kinds of dharma-characteristics" onwards, this constitutes the final intent within the preceding third major section, the *Viniścaya* (Analysis).
Each point shall now be explained in turn.

Regarding the passage beginning with "This is called the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma-lakṣaṇa*)," herein all mundane and supramundane wisdoms that proceed toward liberation are subsumed under conditioned virtues because they are produced by effort; thus, they are termed "conditioned phenomena.

From the phrase "from non-arising" (*anutpāda*) onwards, because these are not produced by effort, they are explained as the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Each of these shall now be explained in turn.

From the passage beginning "At that time, the Buddha said" onwards, it clarifies that since the Lord of Devas was not the one who initiated [the discussion], the assembly might find it difficult to believe;
therefore, the Tathāgata confirms and completes [the teaching]. This shall now be explained. As for the phrase "not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)," this refers to what has been stated above:

although it was said that there is neither defilement nor purity, and no grasping or abandoning, these [teachings] are still subsumed within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If, however, within the ultimate truth...
There is no such fascicle [in the canon]. As for the statement that the two Emperors encompass all phenomena exhaustively, this is spoken by way of conventional metaphor.

Taking form (*rūpa*) and so forth as the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth as the ultimate (*paramārtha*), it is thus because these are terms used to bridge the conventional.
If one discusses the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), in reality there is nothing encompassed. This shall now be explained.
"Knowing the minds of all sentient beings yet not apprehending those minds," and so forth, clarifies the meaning of the twofold illumination of the two truths;
this shall be explained.
"Does one not practice the other pāramitās? and so forth, shall be explained one by one.
This should be explained by way of analogy, such as "the various trees beneath Jambudvīpa.
From the passage beginning with "Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha," it clarifies that the Lord of the Devas further praises Prajñāpāramitā using five phrases;
this also should be explained by way of analogy.

Regarding the section beginning with "giving to others" and below: since the preceding portion has not yet compared giving to others, from here downward, the subsequent comparison will clarify the superiority of giving to others. Each point shall be explained in turn.
Regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason...": this sutra was spoken by the Buddha between the fifth year of his enlightenment and twelve years prior [to the present].
The Buddha now explains it for the sake of others; because it concerns the victory over others, he speaks of it in advance. He provides the event of the shattering of his body as proof.
As for why he caused it to be shattered in such a manner, it was solely because he desired that many other people might attain [realization]. This shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "After I have made offerings to this Dharma" clarifies that the Dharma is what all Buddhas take as their teacher.
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. This "Dharma" refers precisely to *prajñā* (wisdom); this is what is meant. Therefore, the Tathāgata pays homage to it.

As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the Buddha also prostrates before the *śarīra* (relics) for the sake of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). This paying of homage to the *śarīra* pertains to [the practice of] the various...
The *pāramitās* do not reside in the relics; herein, the Buddha himself takes his own person as witness.
If even the Buddha himself honors and reveres *prajñā*, how much more so should others? It is because its benefit is great that it causes people to know deeply where merit is cultivated;
thus it is so. This shall now be explained.
The question [beginning with] "As for 'below'" shall be explained. The answer [beginning with] "As for 'the following'" shall also be explained.
Regarding the passage "Having already existed, it returns to non-existence" and so forth: this is not the same as the non-existence of cessation (*nirodha-nāstitva*).

Because it has fundamentally attained all modes of arising and now attains its great function, it is called "present existence. Since this arising is itself quiescence, it is said to be "present non-existence. This is [consistent with]...
Regarding the aforementioned contradiction: it clarifies that [the dharmas] were originally non-existent and yet are not non-existent now. It shall be explained:

when it says "conditioned wholesome dharmas are the sphere of practice," this refers to their function; when it says "unconditioned dharmas are the locus of reliance," this refers to their essence, which is precisely the meaning of relying on the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *dharmakāya*. It shall be explained.

This refers to those of newly awakened resolve and below; it clarifies that for newly practicing bodhisattvas who have not yet been able to penetrate deeply into the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), such distinctions are therefore made.
It is not so for bodhisattvas of the stage of non-arising forbearance (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). Each point should be explained in correspondence with the preceding text.

The answer begins as follows: Since the shadow is fundamentally the darkening that obscures light, and its substance (rūpa) is no different from that of the object itself, it is therefore definitively one with it.
One does not define the meaning of "shadow" by its size; thus, this question is unnecessary.
From the phrase "This matter is difficult" onwards, the text next explains the scriptural passages concerning the comparison between oneself and others. Each point shall be explained in turn.
Because the Buddha’s merits are complete, it is said that they are "not required."
"From 'one should explain its meaning' onwards is the explanation of the preceding passage concerning the subsequent comparison; it shall be explained one by one.
Listen with a single mind to what is received, for this belongs to the supreme offering of the Dharma. This is what should be explained.

Regarding the thirty-seventh chapter of the third volume of the Commentary on the *Śāstra*, it is the ninth chapter within the section on Comparative Evaluation (*tulanā-bhāga*); it should be titled "The Chapter on the Gift of Dharma" (*Dharma-dāna-paṭala*).
Because it first elucidates the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), it is named accordingly as the "Chapter on the Ten Wholesome Actions.

Having completed the comparative evaluation of merits, this commentary is presented here for the purpose of providing an exposition; thus, it is designated as the "Explanatory Commentary on the Thirty-seventh Chapter."
After the Buddha had addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, this chapter proceeds to provide a comparative evaluation of the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*) to clarify the supreme meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.

Within this text, there are generally four major sections of comparison. The first compares the act of teaching a person in Jambudvīpa to practice the ten wholesome paths of action, the twelve gates of dhyāna, the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth, with the act of teaching a person even a single verse [of the Prajñāpāramitā]. The latter is shown to be superior.

The Prajñāpāramitā is compared with other sūtras as mundane virtues: second, teaching the people of a single Jambudvīpa so that they attain the four fruits of the śrāvaka is not equal to giving another person a sūtra scroll and teaching them the Prajñāpāramitā; this is the comparison as supramundane virtue.
Third, it is compared with teaching others so that they attain the state of a pratyekabuddha. Fourth, [it is compared] with oneself [practicing] the various Mahāyāna...
Regarding the sequential comparison of stages and practices, within the first section on the comparison of worldly virtues, there are three cycles.
The first raises the teaching on the practice of the ten virtuous actions for comparison; the second raises the four dhyānas and the twelve gates of meditation for comparison;
and the third uses mutual interpenetration for comparison. Of these, the present passage is the first. Although there are also four [subsections] within it...
The meaning of "fruition" (*phala*) and so forth merely follows from the momentum [of the previous discussion] and is not a second intended meaning. This shall be explained point by point.
As for the passage beginning with "Why is this? and so on, it explains the reason why one obtains greater merit than others; this shall now be discussed.

To teach a single person and cause them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is superior to teaching all the people of a single Jambudvīpa, because [the former] eternally separates them from the three miserable realms (*durgati*).

The ten wholesome actions cannot permanently separate one from the three miserable realms; thus, the inferior teaching that enables a person of Jambudvīpa to attain all four fruits of the path is still not equal to the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā, which causes one to resolve their mind for enlightenment.
"By what means? and so forth explains the reason why teaching people to resolve their minds toward enlightenment is of supreme significance;
this shall now be explained. "Setting aside Jambudvīpa," and so forth—this section below further employs a progressive analogy; each point shall be explained individually.

A "small thousandfold world system" refers to one thousand suns and moons, one thousand Mount Sumerus, one thousand sets of four continents, and so on. The "intermediate [thousandfold world system]"... [text continues].
Regarding "thousand": taking one of these small thousand-fold worlds as a single unit and counting up to a thousand of them—this is the thousand within a thousand;

therefore, it is called the "Middle Thousand. Regarding the "Great Thousand": taking one of these middle thousand-fold worlds as a single unit and again counting up to a thousand of them—this is the great among thousands;
therefore, it is called the "Great Thousand. Each of these shall be explained in turn. Although this teaching of transformation primarily grants much merit to many people, because...
It is like giving a single person a scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and causing them to uphold it.
Having established [the comparison] from the four dhyānas downward, the second and third intentions among the worldly virtues shall now be explained in conjunction with this calculation.

Regarding "right mindfulness": it is precisely because one does not employ the duality of "is" and "is not," nor the non-duality of "neither-is-nor-is-not," when upholding, reciting, and studying the *Prajñāpāramitā*, that it is called "right mindfulness.
Because one does not recite it with a mind of attachment and discrimination, it is called "not employing the duality of dharmas.
Furthermore, because one does not cling to emptiness, it is called "the non-dual dharma. All other meanings are likewise; these shall all be explained accordingly.
"From 'One should not contemplate by means of two marks' onwards, the meaning of *prajñā* is explained through a comparison with the gift of Dharma;
this shall be explained point by point.
From 'Having thus expounded the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*' onwards, the method for giving the gift of Dharma is clarified. Thus [it is said].
To "speak" is what is first called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Each of these shall now be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "What is the semblance [of it]? and so forth: this question is posed in order to clarify the distinction between what constitutes the gift of Dharma and what does not.
If it were as previously stated—that this is called a semblance of the gift of Dharma—it would not be the gift of Dharma. This shall be explained one by one according to the text.

From the passage "explaining that form is impermanent" onwards, it clarifies that [the teaching] is for the purpose of counteracting the inversion of permanence; thus it says "form is impermanent" up to the point of "contemplation."
Once form is understood to be impermanent, even the contemplation of its impermanence is relinquished; this is called true *prajñā*.

If one does not relinquish the contemplation while seeking the impermanence of form, it is termed a semblance and is not the gift of Dharma. Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "This is the perception of impermanence."
It is able to eliminate craving for desire, form, and the formless realms, as well as ignorance, pride, and the perception of impermanence. The remaining meanings are all likewise;
they shall be explained one by one.

From the passage beginning with "Having addressed the Buddha... onwards, it clarifies that the Lord of Devas wishes to cause those in future generations to be free from semblances and to attain true *prajñā*.
Therefore, this question was raised. The Tathāgata answered it: "The nature of form (*rūpa*) is inherently empty; how could there be such meanings as permanence and so forth?
This is what is called "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*), which differs from the aforementioned "erroneous contemplation. This shall now be explained.
As with the "similar contradictions" mentioned above, here too one should list and clarify each of the dharmas individually, as was done in the section on the similar.
However, to avoid excessive prolixity, I have merely stated it thus; I shall now explain it.

The section beginning with "The commentator says" below explains the scriptural passage from the initial exposition on the comparison of worldly virtues. This shall be explained point by point. The section beginning with "First, this...
differentiates worldly virtues, clarifying the various fruits as well as the underlying intent and significance of what was previously and subsequently elucidated.
These are different meanings, and each shall be explained in turn.
The answer below clarifies the practices of upholding, reading, reciting, and so forth. However, one who possesses great merit and correct mindfulness is able to fulfill both;
therefore, they are mentioned separately, which effectively includes upholding, explaining, and the rest.

From the passage beginning "First, by means of the excellence of the sūtra scrolls" onwards, the Master of the Treatise (śāstrakāra), wishing to explain the subsequent section on comparative evaluation (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of teaching the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) to others, first sequentially recounts the preceding sūtra text to introduce the intent of what follows.

He clarifies that although one’s own correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and so forth are superior, they remain unknown; therefore, in order to make them known to others, he makes this statement. This shall now be explained point by point.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if one were to teach all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa so that they all attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and below—
this constitutes the second section of this chapter, which measures the supramundane wholesome teachings such as the four fruits of the *śrāvaka*.
Each shall be explained individually.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In this context, why is each [so]? and following, all shall be explained one by one; the reasons for their being the ultimate meaning (paramārtha) will be discussed as they arise in the text.
To teach sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the four [fruits] of the Śrāvaka...
As for the fruit: although the merit of this master of emanations is immeasurable, it does not equal that of teaching others the Prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this? This shall be explained one by one below. Regarding the passage "having caused them to attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha" and so forth, this is the third section of the chapter, which uses the Middle Vehicle as a point of comparison; this too shall be explained one by one.

"Once you have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*... and so forth. This is the fourth section of the chapter, in which one evaluates oneself according to the sequential stages of practice within the Mahāyāna.
Here, it is first clarified that although one may teach others to resolve their minds toward enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), this is not equal to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Each point shall be explained in turn.

Furthermore, from the passage below, it is clarified that teaching the *prajñā* of sentient beings in a single Jambudvīpa who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind—even extending to those in the ten directions—is not as effective as teaching the *prajñā* of a single *avaivartika* bodhisattva. This shall now be explained. Regarding "non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) unsurpassed enlightenment":
this refers to having emerged and reached enlightenment. If one were to teach [the *prajñā*] to as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges throughout the ten directions...

The prajñā of all the *avaivartika* bodhisattvas in the world is not equal to that of a single *avaivartika* bodhisattva who, according to the teaching, swiftly attains *bodhi*. This shall now be explained.
"Turning and turning closer" and below clarifies that although the Bodhisattva’s tracks of practice become increasingly sublime, they must still accord with the teachings;

therefore, within each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there is the fruit of setting forth toward the goal. One requires wise teachers to instruct in the practices of the higher stages and to cultivate the karmas of purifying the stages.
This applies even to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, as these also extend throughout the ten stages. Thus it continues until the tenth stage.
The Buddhas of the ten directions have now arrived to rain down the Dharma like clouds; this shall be explained point by point.

From the words "Excellent, excellent" onwards, it clarifies that after Subhūti saw the Lord of Devas conclude the section on the comparative analysis, he offered praise in order to encourage those newly set out in training and to cause them to properly understand the principles. This shall now be explained.

The following section begins with the words "The commentator says. If, within the preceding discussion on the middle [level], one had separately used the Middle Vehicle as a single point for comparison, then here at the outset, the Master of the Treatise now intends to explain the scriptural passages concerning the two subsequent meanings—the second and the third.

He shall now explain: "These dharmas, their true reality" (*dharmāṇām bhūtalakṣaṇam*). This clarifies that Prajñāpāramitā is itself the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since the arising of the function of wisdom-illumination is itself real, it is said: "These."

Furthermore, from the section "The Perfectly Enlightened One" (*samyaksambuddha*) onwards, this clarifies that the Buddha is most supreme, while bodhisattvas are slightly inferior; pratyekabuddhas and arhats are, in turn, inferior to bodhisattvas.
It is by means of such comparisons that those such as the *anāgāmin* are shown to be progressively inferior. This is how it should be understood.
Commentary: From the passage "having loved, cherished, and made offerings" onwards, it clarifies that if one recites and makes offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā* with an attached mind,

although the [dharmas] are indeed such as the marks of reality (*lakṣaṇasamatā*) and so forth, one will only obtain worldly fruits of honor and nobility, such as rebirth among the gods or within great clans of the Kṣatriyas.

This shall now be explained. Furthermore, regarding the passage from "teaching one Jambudvīpa" down to "the people in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," this next section explains the fourth major division of the upper part;
it is a comparative analysis of the scriptural text based on the position of the Mahāyāna itself.
Question: This shall be explained below.
Answer: As follows. Regarding "there are three kinds": if one includes the Buddha, these two kinds of bodhisattvas also constitute three.

If one excludes the Buddha and instead includes an ordinary person who is a Dharma teacher capable of expounding the *prajñāpāramitā* according to the sūtras and śāstras, they likewise constitute [three].

There are three types [of bodhisattvas]. Here, the statement that "Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas are neither born nor die" is made from the perspective of the Dharmakāya while it still functions conventionally.
If one were to discuss the merit of the *janmakāya* (birth-body) Bodhisattva, their Dharmakāya would likewise be immortal.
However, the present statement is made solely with reference to the stage and practice of the *saṃsāra* karmic retribution body; therefore, it is said thus. This shall now be explained.
This Bodhisattva has merely described the matters concerning Bodhisattvas who have transcended the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
Above this, the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) Bodhisattvas speak solely from the perspective of abiding in the true position of non-retrogression.
Now, it is said that for a single person who explains the Dharma of the true position to a Bodhisattva of non-retrogression, the merit is immeasurable.
Furthermore, the following sections shall all be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Because the field of merit is great," if we discuss it in terms of the field of the mind, then regardless of whether the recipient is an animal, a bodhisattva, or a Buddha, they are all entirely equal;
thus the meaning of *pāramitā* is fulfilled without any discrimination. Now, this shall be compared and evaluated.

[Answer: It is because this is the occasion for discriminating between the superior and inferior qualities of dharmas. Therefore, the discussion is framed in terms of the "field" (*kṣetra*) to characterize its excellence, so as to make it known to others. This shall now be explained.
The phrase "For example, as follows" introduces a metaphor to explain the meaning of superiority and inferiority. This shall now be explained.
Regarding the passage "At that time, Śakra clearly understood the power of the Dharma," each point shall be explained in turn.
Regarding the explanation of the thirty-eighth chapter in the sixty-first fascicle of the *Śāstra*: this constitutes the third major section among the various divisions.

It clarifies how the Bodhisattva Maitreya and Subhūti further reaffirm their positions through the causes of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It explains why, within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, [this follows] next.

After the section on comparative evaluation, the meaning of rejoicing (*anumodanā*) and so forth is elucidated. Regarding rejoicing: it must necessarily take all merits as the object of one's rejoicing.

Since it was already established in the preceding section on "Comparative Evaluation" that merits are inconceivable, the following section—situated after the comparative evaluation—is explained in order to universally dedicate all the aforementioned merits toward the Buddha-way for the sake of all beings. Thus, after the comparative evaluation, rejoicing is clarified.

Regarding the meaning of "joy" (*muditā*) and so forth: according to the commentary in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* on the "Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication" (*Anumodanā-pariṇāmanā-varga*), this should be titled the "Commentary on the Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication.
That treatise states: "As it is explained in the Mahāyāna 'Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication,' here [in this work] it is abbreviated;
therefore, it is simply called the 'Treatise on the Chapter on Rejoicing. Now, wishing to provide an explanation, it is cited as the 'Explanatory Commentary on the Thirty-eighth Chapter.'"

Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva" onwards, the treatise itself explains: after the section on the exposition of the life-span, much was said regarding merits.
Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to recover the Buddha’s original intent, therefore returns to the fundamental principle and further engages with Subhūti.
Regarding the meaning of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), this elucidates *prajñā*. Within this chapter, although there are four noble ones who speak, broadly speaking, there are only three parts.
First, it clarifies how Maitreya Bodhisattva initially explains *prajñā* through five meanings;
next, there are two questions from Subhūti and two answers from Maitreya. Second is the discourse of Subhūti; likewise, [the discourse] of the Lord of Devas (*Devendra*).
After Subhūti had posed three questions and likewise provided three answers, Maitreya then posed one question, to which Subhūti replied with seven successive points of meaning.
Next, another question was asked, again answered with successive points of meaning. The third [set of questions] consists of what the Buddha himself spoke at the end of the chapter.
This first section is the initial elucidation of the five meanings; thus, this opening portion belongs to Maitreya.
Regarding the fact that [the teaching] was first spoken by [Śāriputra], then by Subhūti, and finally by the Buddha himself:
