this clarifies that since Maitreya has succeeded to the position of the Honored One as the Regent (Kṣāntipratilabdha), the Buddha knew that the measure of the preceding instruction had concluded; therefore, he spoke to Subhūti, wishing to once again establish the fundamental principle according to the meaning of rejoicing (anumodana).

Regarding the teaching on *prajñā*: although the second [discourse] was spoken by Śubhūti, and people may already know it, Maitreya’s virtue transcends that of those in the stage of being next to Buddhahood (*saptamabhūmi*).
Nevertheless, the great assembly now truly relies upon Śubhūti for its teaching.

Although this is what these two sages have spoken, if it were not heard from the Tathāgata himself, it might be difficult to inspire faith. For this reason, the Buddha subsequently spoke of it himself; this is the first statement [of that].
There are five meanings: first, sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); second, sharing with all sentient beings; third, dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);
fourth, by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*); and fifth, the comparison of the abundance of merit. As for why sympathetic joy is clarified at the beginning:

one must first express sympathetic joy toward all the roots of goodness and all the merit belonging to the three vehicles of all ordinary and holy beings. Once one has expressed sympathetic joy, then one attains...
Having heard of those merits, once one has attained this merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one then takes up these merits and shares them with all sentient beings.
Having shared them with sentient beings, one again takes up these shared merits and dedicates them toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Although one is able to dedicate them, if it is not a dedication free from signs (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*), then it is not [true dedication].

Because it is the meaning of true and correct dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is followed by "attaining through non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*), which brings about the dedication of signlessness (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*).
If one can practice these four dharmas in this way, one will obtain immeasurable merit. Therefore, in the subsequent comparison within the first chapter, it says:
"If all the merit of giving, upholding the precepts, and practicing meditative concentration belonging to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas... [The Bodhisattva’s merit is far superior].
O Mahāsattva, if one wishes to surpass [others] by means of a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Now, this chapter is introduced here specifically to reaffirm the fundamental tenet and expand upon its meaning.

One should practice these four dharmas day and night, six times each, with the right shoulder bared. Within this context, since the vow has already been fully established, it is universally applicable.

These four are not discussed separately; rather, filial piety toward the Emperor, Father, is placed last so as to complete five dharmas that are practiced by the entire world. Each shall now be explained in turn.
The section beginning with "If the śrāvakas and others... follows the previous explanation of the five meanings, which first set forth the intention of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and so forth.

Now, following this, it further sets forth the method of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) employed therein. This refers to the merit of the beings of the three vehicles—such as giving, observing precepts, and cultivating meditative concentration;
these three are cited as representative examples to encompass all wholesome dharmas.
The passage beginning with "This bodhisattva" identifies the person who performs the dedication.
The passage beginning with "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" identifies the destination of the dedication.
The passage beginning with "That merit is supreme" evaluates the meaning of its great abundance. It is solely by means of such skillful means as these [that it is so].
By virtue of this power, one can attain immeasurable merit. This is like the case where another person performs a task for oneself;

although the laborer receives little money, one obtains much benefit nearby without actually expending effort, simply because of skillfulness. The same applies to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). This shall now be explained.
At that time, from the passage beginning with "The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya" onwards, it next clarifies the objections raised by Subhūti.

Although there are two questions, within this first question, the intent of the subsequent questions is also contained. It says: "If one says that a bodhisattva, from the initial generation of the mind until reaching nirvāṇa..."

Even until these merits are exhausted, once they have become dark and silent and one has entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, if one suddenly uses a mind conditioned by circumstances to forcibly grasp these merits and perform a dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), this gives rise to the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Within the eternal Dharma, one conceives the notion of impermanence; this constitutes falling into the four perversions, such as the views of perception, mind, and insight.
Indeed. This question is posed because the meaning of taking signs and dedicating [merit] is as such. Each shall now be explained.
Regarding the section beginning with "all the śrāvakas and below," the treatise states that there are four sections herein;

these constitute the causes and fruits of the three vehicles, as well as the four divisions of roots of goodness belonging to noble beings and ordinary persons. Their merits and so forth will be explained in the treatise. One says it is...
1. Rejoicing; 2. sharing with all sentient beings; 3. dedicating toward Bodhi; 4. employing the principle of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Herein, the mention of "the roots of goodness of the śrāvakas" refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) from the stage of worldly dharmas onward.

The mention of "those in training and those beyond training" clarifies the roots of goodness of the sages of the three paths and those who have attained the higher fruits. As for "the Buddha," this refers exclusively to the various [Buddhas] at the pinnacle of fruition.
This refers to "wholesome [roots] and so forth," which shall now be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "and the fruits such as the stage of Srotāpanna attained within the teachings expounded by the Buddhas," the preceding section discussed the wholesome roots of the various fruits during the Buddha’s lifetime;
the present section clarifies how one practices in accordance with the teachings during the Semblance Dharma (*saddharma-pratirūpaka*) after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the acquisition of the roots of goodness that lead to the various fruits: since Pratyekabuddhas appear in worlds where no Buddha exists, this is clarified herein.
Some say that Pratyekabuddhas exist during the Semblance Dharma (*dharmapratirūpaka*). However, the *Āraṇyaka-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"Only when there are no Buddha-dharmas, sūtras, or disciples of the Buddha do Pratyekabuddhas first appear. This shall now be explained.

"From 'all these are conditioned by phenomena' onwards, these constitute dedication with the grasping of signs (*nimitta*). Because they accord with what is conceptualized, they cannot be called true dedication.
It is only when it does not accord with what is conceptualized that it is true dedication. This shall now be explained."
Subhūti addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "If all things and all conditions are non-existent," and so forth—this constitutes the second question.
The intent of the question is as follows: Speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality, all things, all conditions, and all roots of goodness are entirely non-existent;
both persons and phenomena are empty. Yet, the bodhisattva suddenly, with a mind of conceptualization, takes as objects the noble ones of the three vehicles and the three... [the text continues].

If one takes all accumulated merits and the like, and employs them as a means for dedication, yet gives rise to the perception of characteristics within the dharma of signlessness, would this not be a perversion?
It is like the meaning of taking what is impermanent to be permanent, and so forth; this shall now be explained.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Because they are signless": since these dharmas are signless, the Bodhisattva nevertheless performs dedication;
does this not mean that the Bodhisattva is falling into error?

From the section "Inversion of perception" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) onwards, this clarifies the meaning of how the four inversions arise from the three inversions; this shall be explained in the main treatise.
"As for the object" (*yathālambana*) refers to the merits and so forth possessed by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of the Three Vehicles;

this shall be explained in the main treatise. "As for the phenomenon" (*yathāvastu*) refers to things such as the merits of the persons of the Three Vehicles; this shall be explained in the main treatise.
If that is so, what is it that serves as the condition? Below this, the objection is concluded by stating: "All these dharmas are non-conceptual (asaṃjñika).
How then can one speak of "dedication" (pariṇāmanā)? This shall now be explained.
The commentary states: From this point onward, the initial master of the treatise first analyzes the scriptural text by citing what precedes and generating what follows.

First, the section up to "extensively explaining the matters of merit" constitutes the citation of what precedes; now, the passage beginning with "Maitreya, following the Buddha’s original intent... and so forth, constitutes the generation of what follows. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "Śakra and those below" onwards, the intention for the arrival of this sutra is explained.
From "The meaning of Bodhisattva-mahāsattva as previously explained" onwards, the text of the sutra itself is explained.
From the section "Those who rejoice in merit" onwards, the text next explains the meaning of the preceding five points; each shall be explained in turn.
If one is unable to rejoice in merit, then one is no different from animals, as both equally possess these three matters.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Although all untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*) have no karmic reward for merit" and below: this is an interpretation based on the perspective of the Hīnayāna.
It states that because there is no worldly karmic reward for merit, it is said to be "non-existent. This shall be explained point by point.
The section beginning with "shared with all sentient beings" is next an explanation of the second meaning mentioned above.

It shall be explained point by point. Regarding the statement that the cause is spoken of within the fruit: this clarifies that while the fruit can be shared, the cause cannot. That which is now said to be "shared" refers to the sharing of the fruit.
To say that merit is shared with sentient beings is a matter pertaining to the time of the fruit; for the fruit arises from the cause. Thus it is.
This explains the cause within the context of the fruit.
Regarding the passage beginning with "By means of non-apprehension," although this constitutes the fourth sense, the meaning of dedication will be discussed extensively separately later on.
Furthermore, as it follows from what was previously stated, it is not mentioned here; it shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "Compared to all śrāvakas and others" below explains, in turn, the fifth meaning of the comparative evaluation (*tulanā*). This shall be explained point by point.

Furthermore, the section beginning with "Those who discipline themselves" indicates that the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) practiced by those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) serve only for their own self-discipline and deliverance.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s mind of sympathetic joy surpasses those [previous states] immeasurably and boundlessly.

Regarding the previous reference to the "three trainings" (*tri-śikṣā*) to clarify one's own self-discipline and so forth, this was based on the *prātimokṣa* and other forms of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Here, however, "right speech" (*samyag-vāk*) and the others are based on the ethical discipline within the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣa-dharma*). These three divisions—the right [aspects] and the eight [factors]—correspond once again to the meaning of the aforementioned three trainings. Right...

Expedient means (*upāya*) is precisely right effort (*samyag-vīrya*). Although effort is common to all practices, it is specifically [emphasized here] because within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), concentration (*samādhi*) is quiescence, whereas effort is a mental factor (*caitta*) that arouses vigor and accords with the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, it is subsumed under the category of wisdom.
As for the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), it is merely the path; it is not the path itself. It is exclusively the untainted (*anāsrava*) morality within the Eightfold Right Path.

Because these are the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), they constitute the essence of the path from the very beginning. This is for the sake of establishing one in the precepts (*śīla*), as they reside within the Eightfold Path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Among the factors of the path, there is no impure (*sāsrava*) precept; there is only the pure (*anāsrava*) precept. Although prior to this there may be a semblance of precepts associated with the path (*mārgasamprayukta-śīla*), this is not the intended meaning of the factors of the path and does not enter into them.
It can only be termed a "preparatory factor of the path" (*prayoga-mārgāṅga*), which belongs to the category of preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Virtue refers to morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.

This shall now be explained. Regarding the passage "because [other practices] such as giving and maintaining morality are obstructive, they are not explained," this means that because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and others are the proximate causes for proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*, only untainted (*anāsrava*) morality is discussed here; other forms of giving and conventional restraints (*saṃvara*) are excluded because they are obstructive. Therefore...
Within the *Mārga-varga* (Chapter on the Path), there is no mention of the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint); there is only the equipment for the path (*mārga-pariṣkāra*).

This shall now be explained. The answer given below clarifies that while the power of a single Buddha is indeed truly capable of delivering all sentient beings, it must wait until causes and conditions are fully assembled before this can be achieved.
It is like a newborn infant in a royal household: although the King truly possesses the power to provide [for him],...

Regarding matters such as the horses, carriages, wives, and concubines of the provinces and commanderies, if one lacks internal causes and conditions while possessing only external ones, there is nothing that can be done.

If you say, "I myself possess the causes and conditions for attaining liberation; what need is there for a Buddha? it would be like saying that because one has eyes, one should see even in the darkness of night;
or like saying that because one is capable of eating, one should be satiated without needing rice; or like saying that because one is oneself... [the text continues].
It means that one who is able to cross water does not require a boat or the like; this is the point to be explained.

At that time, after Subhūti has raised an objection based on the wisdom of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), Maitreya next explains the meaning of the preceding discourse by Vimalakīrti (Śāriputra) through two matters, inferring and answering that [Subhūti’s] understanding is not as he had conceived it. This is the first point.
First explanation:

From the words "one who rejoices" (*anumodaka*) onwards, the meaning of the initial question and answer has already been explained; next, the meaning of the text within the difficult passages will be explained.
This shall be explained point by point.
The passage beginning with "It is also thus, being without discrimination" concludes and explains the meaning of the preceding refutation. What is to be explained is as follows:
starting from Subhūti’s question below, each point shall be explained in turn.

From "from the initial generation of the mind" onwards, this explains the preceding passage beginning with "from the initial generation of the mind" up to "until the exhaustion of the Dharma, the various merits are harmoniously integrated," and so forth. It shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "That which is associated" clarifies that all other virtues beyond the six perfections are subsumed within these six perfections.
This follows the dedication [of merit], which is why it is said that they are "associated" and "conjoined" with the six perfections. This shall now be explained.
"Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and so forth" and below explain the inferiority of those individuals' giving and other virtues, as well as their resulting merit; this shall now be explained.
First, regarding "the exhaustion of outflows," each point shall be explained in turn.

From "The Buddhas entreat them to preach the Dharma" down to "Having studied this Dharma," the preceding section concludes the explanation of the period when the Buddha was in the world, covering the matter of all ordinary and holy beings.
Now, following this, the subsequent section explains the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, concerning those who practice according to the teachings and attain the Way;

these constitute one group. As for the explanation of the aforementioned four sections, they correspond to the time when the Buddha was present in the world, as well as the three [periods] following his passing.
Regarding the phrase "the roots of goodness of those who ride the vehicles and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) etc.," the Four Masters say:

"If one were to discuss the causes and fruits of the three vehicles according to the categories of *śaikṣa* (learner) and *aśaikṣa* (non-learner), then these roots of goodness of ordinary persons and so forth should constitute seven sections.

However, because they are discussed here in combination, only four are mentioned. One interpretation states that among the five aforementioned meanings, the roots of goodness constitute four sections. [This concerns] the practitioner’s mind.
"Below," it shall be explained.

This refers to the passage beginning with "That is, actual merit. This clarifies that since these [practices] are identical to the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) and the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), performing these practices truly generates actual merit; therefore, they are not empty. From "The object of focus" onwards, it explains the above.
This refers to the passage concerning "the objects of focus, the conditions, the entities," and so forth;
it shall now be explained. From the point where Subhūti speaks to Maitreya onwards, the meaning of the second question above shall next be explained. It shall now be explained.

Regarding the threefold classification of the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*): this clarifies that from the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) arise the perversions of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
This is because these three perversions give rise to the four perversions; this shall now be explained.

This is an analogy. It clarifies that by means of these meanings such as "inversion" (viparyāsa), one gives rise to the perception of a Buddha within the absence of a Buddha, recollects the Buddha’s merits, and dedicates the mind—this is the meaning of the analogy.
If this is so, then because one gives rise to the perception of permanence within the impermanent and so forth, these textual passages concerning inversion and the like are introduced.
Question: Regarding the passage beginning with "view is a perversion," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains: Among the three perversions, only view constitutes the nature of perversion;
it is only from the perversion of view that the four perversions arise. This means that because view contradicts reality (*yukti*), it is designated as the nature of perversion.

The two inversions of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) arise merely by taking objects as their condition; because they are a portion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), they are not themselves the actual inversions.

The answer below states: according to the various doctrines of the Mahāyāna, it is all said that the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*) arises from the inversion of perception, the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*) arises from the inversion of mind, and the four perversions arise from the inversion of view. Since this is the case where views arise from craving, one must sever the views.

At that time, the four inversions are forever extinguished. If, within the Hīnayāna, it is said that all afflictions arise from the pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), this means that craving arises from views.
Since this passage here supports the Mahāyāna doctrine, it is said that "the time of arising is different from the time of abandonment.
The Master’s commentary states: "Craving arising from views" refers to the sequential arising [of craving] from views; "views arising from craving" refers to [the same].

It arises based on the characteristics of the underlying ground (*āśraya*). This meaning shall now be explained. If one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they possess all three inversions (*viparyāsa*).

Since those in training (*śaikṣa*) have already abandoned [the inversion of] views, they possess only two inversions; this shall now be explained. If a person in training gives rise to perceptions and thoughts, these two inversions are like drops of water upon a red-hot iron—they are extinguished immediately. This shall now be stated.
Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, all things are ultimately empty according to reality" onwards, this subsequent section provides a further summary and explanation.

It brings forth the meaning of the second question posed by Subhūti above, saying: "If all phenomena are thus ultimately empty, what purpose do acts such as dedication (pariṇāmanā) serve? This shall now be explained.
From the point where Maitreya Bodhisattva speaks to Subhūti onwards, it correctly clarifies Maitreya’s response. It explains the second question above as follows:
"If bodhisattvas are able to perform such signless dedication, this is called dedication that does not follow the three inversions.
This shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "By means of the dharma of non-duality" and following, its meaning all pertains to what precedes and shall be explained in the context of the text.

The section beginning with "If bodhisattvas" and following clarifies that dedicating while grasping at signs is not true dedication; this is explained by way of completing the contrast with the preceding section on non-correspondence.
This shall now be explained.

Regarding the phrase "this mind is extinguished, transformed, and detached," the commentary explains: First, one enters the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) through the gate of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) in order to investigate and clarify the dharmas;

hence it is said that "moment by moment, it is exhausted, extinguished, transformed, and detached. Next, it clarifies that this mind enters ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) without any remainder;
hence it is said that "exhausting this mind is itself [the state of] sleep. Therefore, it is said that "extinguishing the mind is identical to the true mark. Thus.
The self-nature of clouds and transformations cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is said they are "detached. If this were the case, what would there be to dedicate?
This is not based on the meaning of impermanence, arising and ceasing, transformation, and so forth. Each of these points shall now be explained in turn.

The commentary states: From the point "Maitreya’s intention is that all dharmas are extremely profound" onwards, this correctly explains Maitreya’s fundamental intent in answering the second question. It shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "This is from previous lives" correctly sets forth the meaning of the merit of two lifetimes; this shall now be explained.

The passage beginning with "For example, the nature of iron is hard" clarifies that although the minds of sentient beings are [obstructed], if Maitreya enters into *prajñā* (wisdom), he can then obtain whatever he desires, such as realizing the various fruits of sainthood; this shall now be explained.

"That which is contrary to the above" refers to the section beginning with "not dedicating," which explains the meaning of the aforementioned relative distinctions between what is correct and what is not.
This shall be explained point by point.

For example, the passage beginning with "like a fledgling whose wings are already grown" serves as an analogy for the two types of bodhisattvas, clarifying the generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*).

Regarding the Bodhisattva of the Body (dharmakāya): because they lack the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate through the application of *prajñā*, they are unable to penetrate deeply into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and practice the path.
Below, under "Sixth, Accomplishment," it clarifies that the Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body possesses these two wisdoms and is thus able to penetrate deeply into the true mark and [practice].
One who has faith in the superior Dharma is able to practice the inferior Dharma. This shall be explained one by one.

From this point onward, following the conclusion of the explanation of the essence of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), everything from the preceding sections up to this point constitutes the essence of sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, what follows after "one should again explain by means of various different categories" is clarified in the second section, the portion spoken by Subhūti.

The passage beginning with "this mind becomes increasingly exhausted and ceases" explains the meanings of "exhaustion," "cessation," "transformation," "separation," and so forth mentioned above; this first part clarifies them initially.
This statement was made because one wishes to enter the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) by way of contemplating impermanence; it does not, however, represent the actual meaning of arising and ceasing.
Each point shall be explained in turn.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra... and following, this constitutes the second section of the chapter. Next, Subhūti speaks accordingly.
This concerns the meaning of the dedication of joy (*muditā-pariṇāmanā*). Within this section, the Devaputra first poses three questions, and Subhūti likewise provides three answers.
For the second time, Maitreya poses one question, and Subhūti answers with seven successive points of meaning.
For the third time, he again poses one question, and Subhūti again answers with four successive points of meaning. This first [section] is that of the Devaputra.
The Emperor posed three questions. The first was whether newly resolved bodhisattvas would not experience fear upon hearing of this signless dedication.
The second was how one should dedicate all roots of goodness. The third was how one should dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy. [The Buddha] explained:
After speaking thus to Śakra Devānām-indra, [the text] first explains the first question, saying: "Because one does not accept or cling to any phenomena, one has no fear.
To explain the reason for this, it says that those with "abundant faith and understanding" are of two kinds:
first, those who are complete in faith; second, those who are complete in realization. Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "First, those who are complete in contemplation; second..."
This refers to the perfection of practice. Regarding the term "faith-understanding" (*adhimukti*) used herein:

it clarifies that a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment, having thoroughly investigated the future limit, possesses the faith-understanding that enables them to realize and understand all phenomena; thus, it is simply called "faith. As for the "perfection of practice," this is the perfection of realization. This shall now be explained.
From the passage "Because this bodhisattva does not grasp at any phenomena" onwards, the meaning of being without fear as explained above is concluded.

From the passage "This bodhisattva is also never separated from the Buddhas" onwards, it answers the second question above regarding the meaning of how one dedicates all roots of goodness; this shall now be explained.

Furthermore, regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly resolved their minds, from the passage "In the past, throughout the ten directions" onwards, the meaning of how merit is rejoiced in and dedicated is answered; this shall now be explained point by point.

Regarding the passage "the path of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-mārga*) and below: if one follows the *Sūtra* circulated separately, it says "to sever the path of birth and death" (*saṃsāra-mārga*). However, in the *Śāstra*, the *Sūtra* merely states "the path of abandonment.
It is only when the *Śāstra* provides its commentary that it begins by saying: "The 'path of abandonment' refers to the severing of the path of birth and death.
This explanation within the *Śāstra* is extremely clear; each point shall be explained as we reach the relevant section of the *Śāstra*.
From the point where Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke to Subhūti onwards, the second section clarifies Maitreya Bodhisattva’s initial formulation of this one question.
Subhūti answered with seven successive points of meaning. This first part clarifies that since Maitreya intended to raise an objection, he first restated the intent of the dedication.

Regarding the passage beginning with "How is it that a bodhisattva does not follow the inversion of signs," this question also addresses the second inquiry posed by Subhūti to Maitreya within the preceding section. Now, Maitreya again raises this objection and returns the question to Subhūti,
because previously the Tathāgata had commanded Subhūti to explain the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, Subhūti is the primary interlocutor, while Maitreya merely provides supplementary explanations.

Now, at this assembly, since the true intent lies with Subhūti’s teaching on signless dedication (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*), its meaning is difficult to clarify; therefore, these two serve as host and guest to elucidate this principle.
This is intended to lead the assembly to understand that what was previously stated by Maitreya was merely a concise summary. It is for this reason that he now asks further questions.
"Śubhūti, wishing to provide a detailed explanation of the meaning of signless dedication, he poses this question:
'Since these merits and roots of goodness are signless, how can one forcibly create conditions for signs within that which is signless?
Would this not follow the three inversions?'"
From the words "Subhūti said" onwards, this constitutes the first of the seven points of meaning in response.

It first clarifies that regarding the Three Jewels, roots of goodness, and so forth, not giving rise to conceptual thoughts is the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); it does not follow the three inversions. This shall now be explained.
Following the sections on "having grasped the signs" and "having dedicated," this intention now arises to successively present what is not [explicitly] manifest;
thus, it establishes the meaning of the aforementioned correct dedication. This shall now be explained.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having used this mind to bring to mind all the Buddhas [as stated below], dedicates all roots of goodness with the second intention—that they are "inexhaustible" (akṣaya)—this constitutes the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). In each of the following intentions, there should likewise be the sense of making clear what is "not" in contrast to what "is";
however, because the compilers of the sūtra could not afford the burden of prolixity, only the first intention is explicitly provided.
This being so, it can be understood that [the former] is not required. Each point shall now be explained in turn.
Furthermore, from "Next" onwards, the third intention clarifies the response by means of the meaning of dedicating the realization of self-nature emptiness and so forth.

The meanings of "exhaustion," "cessation," and so on shall be explained; these are all as explained above. This is stated according to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*), and does not refer to actual arising.
It is extinguished.

Furthermore, from the passage "If a bodhisattva, having known thus... onwards, the fourth intention clarifies the answer by means of the fact that there is no dharma capable of being dedicated as a dharma.
Although seven intentions are presented in the explanation of this question, the commentator [proceeds]...
These four subsequent sections have already been explained as a single unit. As for the intent of the remaining three subsequent sections, they are elucidated by means of an intervening discussion.
From the point where the treatise asks "... onwards, it is said that Maitreya has already stated: "One should not speak of this before a newly initiated bodhisattva."
The explanation of the meaning of the signless dedication and so forth has already been completed above. Why, then, does the Lord of Devas ask this question again?
This first section clarifies the underlying intention for his inquiry.

The answer states: "I shall explain each point one by one below. The passage beginning with "One does not grasp this prajñā, because there is nothing to be obtained" explains the wording of the first question above; I shall explain it one by one.
Furthermore, from "Next, this newly resolved bodhisattva" onwards, the meaning of the response to the second question is explained; each point shall be explained in turn.
As for why, from "Now Maitreya asks" onwards, the text of Subhūti’s response to the three questions posed by the Lord of Devas is explained.

The section on "Intention" is concluded. Next, we shall now explain the four subsequent intentions within the response to Maitreya’s questions; this first one is the explanation of the intent of that question.
Following Subhūti’s reply, we next explain the initial intent of Subhūti’s (Śāriputra’s) response regarding the Three Jewels, roots of goodness, and so forth.
"Not giving rise to conceptualization" is the meaning of dedication; this shall now be explained.

The passage beginning with "contrary to what was stated above" explains the preceding text concerning the intention of refuting the incorrect in order to establish the correct. This shall now be discussed.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning "Next, the Bodhisattva, having thus brought to mind the Buddhas and so forth," the text explains the second point of the previous response.
First, it addresses the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*) by way of impermanence (*anitya*). Next, it enters into reality.

Regarding this section beginning with "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*), the entire intent must be traced back to correspond with each of the points in the original response; the textual flow arrives here to provide a detailed explanation. This is how it should be understood.
"Explaining each one: 'The characteristic of exhaustion is also like this' is the summary. All the dharmas mentioned above are thus;
they lack the characteristic of dedication. This shall now be explained.

Question: From "It is asked" onwards, this intention is as follows: because some people, seeing these words and phrases, might cling to the notion that the Buddha is impermanent, this question arises. This shall now be explained.
The answer will be explained below.

Furthermore, regarding the passage "neither correct nor deviant dedication" and following, the intent of the third response above is now explained: because it employs signless dedication (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*), it is said to be "neither correct nor deviant.
If one were to cite what is not [correct] as a formal example, this would be the initial establishment of the categories of "deviant" and "correct. This is how it should be understood.
This summarizes the meaning of the preceding text; herein, each point is explained in correspondence with its respective section.
Furthermore, from the passage "If a bodhisattva knows that all phenomena arise from conditions" onwards, the fourth [point] mentioned above is explained next.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the response: one should also take the aforementioned intention and apply it here as the explanation.
Furthermore, from the passage "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the merit that has arisen" onwards, there are seven instances of "furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) within Subhūti’s response;
four of these intentions have already been concluded above, and the Master of the Treatise has already explained them. Now, this...

The phrase "the text arrives" refers to the fifth section. Having already answered it from the perspective of the door of the intrinsic nature of the merit, roots of goodness, and so forth that arise, this is termed the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Each point shall now be explained in detail.
Furthermore, regarding the section following "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having rejoiced in merit... and so forth: this is the sixth section.
Above, it was explained by way of the departure from the merit that has arisen to clarify the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Now, by way of the mirror-like reflection upon the merit of rejoicing and its departure, the meaning of dedication is answered and clarified. This shall be explained point by point.
Furthermore, following the roots of goodness of all the Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa, the seventh section addresses the gate of *śānti* (quiescence).
It answers by clarifying the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The commentary explains: "It clarifies that all phenomena share the same characteristic as nirvāṇa—they are entirely quiescent.
However, the translators of the sutra rendered this as "parinirvāṇa" (*mie-du*). Although the translation is not precise, it is nonetheless acceptable.
This is for the purpose of citing the passing into parinirvāṇa to clarify quiescent extinction; thus, there is no contradiction. Each point shall be explained in turn.
All people see this text, which teaches this doctrine of impermanence.
From "Having taken up the roots of goodness of all Buddhas and dedicated them" onwards, in each successive section above,

one should at the end of each instance likewise cite what is incorrect as being contrary to what is correct, and clarify the meaning of the three inversions and so forth; however, this has not been done because it would have complicated the text,
though it shall now be explained.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, together with Subhūti and those below him, and Maitreya above, established the first section.

Subhūti employed seven further turnings to complete the broad exposition. Now, in this second [section], because sentient beings are attached to the substantiality of beings and find it difficult to understand the absence of marks (*animitta*), and to clarify that the assembly has not yet attained realization, he again poses this question. Subhūti then answers with four further turnings.
Therefore, the four noble marks are provisionally linked to the wholesome.
From the words "Subhūti said: For this reason... onwards, this initial section constitutes the first further turn [of the discourse].
It provides an answer by means of the principle of skillful means; specifically, it does so on account of this very matter of signless dedication within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
There is the power of skillful means (upāya) that can effect such dedication; this shall now be explained. Regarding the phrase "it ought to exist":
it is said so because for all bodhisattvas there exists such skillful means, whereas those who lack it do not.
The section beginning with "For what reason" explains the three meanings of why there is no conceptualization (*nimitta*) in dedication.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas do not permit it": this clarifies that because one forms conceptual conditions (*nimitta-pratyaya*) within these dharmas of quiescence (*śānta*), the Buddhas do not permit it.
As for the phrase "this dedication is mixed with poison," this is the basis for establishing the analogy.

The passage beginning with "For example" establishes the analogy. Regarding the statement in the main treatise, "One who does not truly grasp characteristics," it means that because one does not perceive them truly, one is unable to discern and grasp the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*). This shall be explained point by point.
The passage beginning with "Those who have attained the Dharma" below shall be explained.
The section beginning with "These sons and daughters of good family [who have already] entered the Buddha-way" below constitutes the second intended answer;
it clarifies the meaning of dedicating [merit] through the supreme wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*). This shall be explained point by point.
The commentary states: "The merit that has arisen is detached from the five aggregates," and so forth. This explains the answer given by Bhadrapāla to the fifth point of Maitreya’s initial inquiry.
Regarding the merit that has arisen, it clarifies the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) by showing its detachment from the five aggregates and all other phenomena. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from the passage "If a bodhisattva knows [the merit of] sympathetic joy" onwards, the sixth section is explained.
The intent of the response is to clarify the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) by way of its essential nature (*svabhāva*) being free [from conceptual proliferation].
Having already explained rejoicing in merit (*anumodana-puṇya*) in general, the following clarifies the meaning of the separation of these two intentions through brief analysis.

The previous statement that "the merit produced is separated" refers to the gate of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Now, the statement that "rejoicing and so forth are separated" refers to the gate of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which clarifies the meaning of rejoicing.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the merit of rejoicing is separated from the Buddhas and the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). And: [and so forth].
This refers to the dedication of those who have given rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
From the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva, based on what he himself seeks," the text explains the meaning of the aforementioned bodhicitta and its qualities, such as detachment and so forth.

From the passage "This bodhisattva, having [rejoiced in] the fruit of merit... onwards, it clarifies that the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) is the fruit of the mind of rejoicing (*anumodanā-citta*), and that awakening (*bodhi*) is the fruit of the mind of dedication, and so forth. This shall now be explained.

"Having provisionally designated [them] as 'bodhisattvas'" and below explains the aforementioned "bodhisattva-prajñā" and so forth; it is also the meaning of detachment (*viveka*). This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, "the bodhisattva recollects the past" and below successively explains the aforementioned seventh section, concluding the response regarding abiding in tranquility (*śamatha*).
This is the meaning of mutual dedication; it shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "Next" onwards, the meaning of the preceding passage—which sets aside the non-existent to confront the existent—shall be explained.
Because it is free from the two extremes, it is called the Middle Way. When considering its ultimate convergence, even the "Middle" cannot be apprehended; this shall now be explained.
From the words "Because this matter is difficult" onwards, the explanation of the seven successive points in Maitreya’s initial question by Śubhūti is concluded.
Now, the meaning of Maitreya’s second question will be explained, as it is difficult due to its meaning concerning signless dedication and so forth.
This is Maitreya’s second inquiry.
From the passage beginning with "Subhūti’s non-definitive answer herein" below, the text next explains the meaning of the four successive replies given by Subhūti.
This first section explains the meaning of the reply in the first successive turn. As for why it is called a "non-definitive answer":
The preceding scripture states: "For this reason, within the Prajñāpāramitā there is the power of skillful means (upāya).
Those who possess skillful means are able to perform dedication without signs (animitta); those without skillful means perform dedication by grasping at signs.

Because these two matters are not fixed, it is said that one should [respond] by means of these two matters; thus, it is called an "indefinite answer" (avyākṛta). This shall now be explained. Not... [text ends].
The path that is non-deceptive is called *prajñā-bodhi* because it is the cause; this is precisely the fruit of the non-deceptive path.
Therefore, it is said that "one dharma is real. This shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "For what reason? explains the meaning of why there is no dedication characterized by signs (*nimitta*).
If one is separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is not because of the absence of signs; yet it is also not a correct dedication.
If one is not separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is because of attachment to signs; yet it is also not a dedication. This shall now be explained.
"From 'The Bodhisattva should form this thought' onwards, [the text] next explains the scriptural passage beginning with 'The Bodhisattva forms this reflection.

It should now be explained that from 'He will not quickly attain Buddhahood' onwards, it clarifies that this is a dedication based on grasping at signs (*nimitta-pariṇāma*), because it results only in worldly fruits."
"Attaining weariness means attaining Buddhahood. This shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "This is great birth" and following clarifies that within the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), one gives rise to conceptualizations based on conditions;
because these are dedicated toward awakening, it is called "great birth."
The passage beginning with "For example, like food mixed with poison" is the original text for the preceding analogy.
The passage beginning with "This is the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*)" and so forth, wherein each point corresponds to the meaning of the preceding analogy, is extremely clear;
these shall be explained one by one as they occur in the text.
"Having not received [the teaching] with careful attention," and so forth, explains the meaning of the preceding passage on "not receiving with careful attention.

"If one were to explain it as such, that would constitute slandering the Buddha," and so forth, explains the meaning of the preceding passage stating that if one teaches taking signs and dedicating [merit], it is the sense of slandering the Buddha.
From "That which corresponds to this" onwards explains the meaning of refuting the incorrect to reveal the correct as raised above.

Furthermore, from "Next, the bodhisattva of right dedication should form this thought" onwards explains the meaning of the second subsequent response, namely that one should apply the dedication through unsurpassed knowledge. Each shall now be explained in turn.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning "Next, the sons of good family who seek the Buddha-way," etc., is the answer given by Subhūti.

This is the third response within the second question, clarifying that the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of form is neither bound to the three realms (*tridhātu*) nor subsumed within the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*).
Since all phenomena are likewise thus, how could there be any characteristic of dedication (*pariṇāmana*) to be apprehended?
And it is said that there is dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). All dharmas are likewise so; each shall be explained in turn.
As for the passage beginning with "For what reason," etc., it explains the meaning of why there is no characteristic of dedication. This shall now be discussed.
The section beginning with "Next, having taken up the signs and attained the Dharma" and below clarifies the refutation of the incorrect in contrast to the correct;

this shall be explained. Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover" and below constitutes the four subsequent sequential responses, clarifying the meaning of the non-conceptual dedication as known by all Buddhas; this shall be explained.
At that time, the Buddha said to Subhūti, "Excellent, excellent," and so forth.
This is the third section of the chapter, the extensive exposition of the Tathāgata’s praise and description. Why is this?

It is because there may be doubts among the assembly regarding the fact that although Maitreya and Subhūti are not omniscient, they have spoken on the meaning of signless rejoicing and dedication; thus, it is possible that errors might exist.
If it were not corroborated by the subsequent accounts of the Tathāgatas, it would likely be difficult for genuine faith to arise.

Therefore, the three successive Tathāgatas provide their descriptions and praises to establish what was spoken by the two preceding Sages. As for the questions posed by the Lord of Devas, they are already subsumed within these [accounts] and thus are not discussed separately.
Within this praise and exposition by the Tathāgata, there are two cycles. The first clarifies the brief praise, the brief explanation, and the brief comparison;
the subsequent part clarifies the detailed explanation and the detailed comparison, specifically elucidating the various heavens of the two realms to complete the aforementioned discourse.
Thirdly, Subhūti further clarifies the Tathāgata’s extensive explanation and detailed comparison. All of these should be understood accordingly.
Each shall be explained.
From "Excellent, excellent" onwards is the language of praise;
from "That which should be dedicated" onwards is the language of exposition. Since the meaning has already been touched upon previously, each shall now be explained in detail.
From "If [the merit of] the three thousand great [worlds]" onwards, it is next the section on comparative evaluation (*tulanā*).

This clarifies that although the retributive fruits of making offerings and practicing giving to those such as *srotāpannas* are inexhaustible, because these are blessings derived from grasping at signs (*nimitta*), one only obtains worldly retributive fruits that exhaust themselves within the cycle of existence.
Now, by means of signless dedication (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*), these become *pāramitās*, whereby one reaches the other shore. Furthermore, this is the retribution for the grass.

This inexhaustible attainment is dedicated [to enlightenment]; therefore, it cannot be compared by means of analogies. Each point shall be explained individually, without relying on dedications characterized by marks (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, from "Subhūti" onwards is the second comparison; it shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from "Subhūti" onwards is the third comparison; it shall now be explained.
From "The Buddha having thus spoken" onwards, it clarifies that Subhūti once again offers praise and further elaborates upon the superior excellence [of this teaching]. This shall now be explained.

As for the passage beginning with "Why is this?", it cites the merit derived from grasping at signs to explain the reason why dedicating [merit] through signlessness results in the acquisition of greater merit.
At that time, from the passage "the four heavenly kings and those below" onwards, it sequentially clarifies how the various devas praise and confirm what was previously stated.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by the power of skillful means," since there is a discrepancy between the initial question and the text concerning the seven subsequent repetitions,
the devas and others herein merely acknowledge and repeat Subhūti’s answers to Maitreya regarding the second question and its four repetitions.
Next, the intention [of the text] comes to praise and complete it. "By the power of skillful means" refers to the meaning of the first reiteration;
"because of non-apprehension" refers to the meaning of the second reiteration; and "by way of the signless dharma" refers to the meaning of the fourth reiteration.
These shall now be explained.
From "together with a thousand devaputras and below," the deities omitted from this list will be explained in the main treatise.
At that time, from "the various Brahmās and below," the various devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are listed in succession;
they do not merely offer praise, but also preach the Dharma, and their assembly is again very large—this shall be explained.
At that time, the Buddha had already addressed the Four Heavenly Kings and those below them. From this point onward, the text again cites non-material forms;
this clarifies the extensive comparative analysis. This shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, it is next the extensive exposition and comparative evaluation by Subhūti (Śāriputra) regarding all Tathāgatas;
each section of the text shall be explained one by one.
"Equal to liberation" and below clarifies unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), which is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Since the dharma of the true mark is such that all dharmas are equal and without differentiation, it is stated below that clearly realizing all dharmas as equal to liberation is called "right dedication" (*samyak-pariṇāmanā*). This shall now be explained point by point.
Furthermore, from "Subhūti, [regarding] those in the ten directions who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges... and following, there is a detailed comparative measurement (*pramāṇa*).

This shall be explained one by one. Regarding the section beginning with "The explanation says...", this first part is the explanation of the answer given by Subhūti (Śākyamuni) to Maitreya’s second question. First...
This is the third repetition concerning the intention. Regarding "always practicing relinquishment without error" and so forth, this meaning is based solely on [the teachings] given by the Buddha;
it shall be explained in the chapter on the Practice of Mutual Interpenetration (*xiāng xíng pǐn*). To rejoice in the merits of all Buddhas and their disciples is called the "mind of sympathetic joy.
The various merits thus obtained are called the "method of dedication. Unsurpassed Bodhi is called "dedication."
Regarding the stage: a bodhisattva is called one who practices dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) because they dedicate all these merits to all sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed enlightenment;
this is called the mind of dedication. Because it is characterized by non-apprehension, it is called signless dedication (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*);
this is known as correct dedication.
From "At that time, the Bodhisattva, having formed this thought... onwards, it shall be explained.
From "For what reason... onwards, it explains the meaning of why form transcends the three realms and the three periods of time, and so forth; each point shall be explained in turn.

The passage beginning with "Bodhicitta, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" and so forth is a summary that explains the meaning of the preceding extensive textual passages;
it is the meaning of the signless dedication (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*).

The section beginning with "Those mixed with poison" below explains the meaning of the aforementioned refutation of the incorrect and the adoption of the correct regarding the dedication of marks (*nimitta-pariṇāmanā*).
This shall be explained. Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, a bodhisattva should form this thought" below explains the intent of the fourth response above;
it clarifies the meaning of dedication by means of the dharma that is without conceptualization (*nirvikalpa-dharma*). This shall be explained.

This concludes the brief explanation of the various chapters on dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Regarding the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā*, it states that four categories are established here, whereas only three are established in this [text].
As for the four categories: they clarify the bodhisattva’s prostration to the Buddha, consisting of: first, repentance; second, [homage to] the Buddhas;
third, sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); and fourth, dedication. This is because the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) permeates all four, as each of the four is fully present therein.
It is not explained separately. Here, the *anumodanā* (rejoicing) and *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) are combined into a single chapter because this follows the structure of the sutra.
However, since the sutra itself combines them, they are not discussed individually. Furthermore, there is no harm in the Buddhas residing [in this manner].
This is a brief explanation; if it were explained extensively, there would be immeasurable chapters.

"Excellent, excellent! and so forth. This concludes the third major section of the chapter, which is the extensive explanation by the Tathāgata in two cycles, consisting of the text that praises and completes [the teaching].
Regarding the passage "you perform the work of a Buddha": if one were to teach the śrāvakas or engage in dedications based on grasping at signs, these would not constitute the work of a Buddha.
Since this is now being taught for the sake of the bodhisattvas, it concerns signless dedication and so forth.
The Dharma is the work of the Buddha.
From the passage "having opened the path of the bodhisattvas" onwards, the reason he causes the śrāvakas to speak is solely to cause them specifically to resolve upon the Great Mind (mahācitta).
Because all bodhisattvas cultivate superior practices, they cause the śrāvakas to speak of skillful means to deliver them,
leading to the Tathāgata’s repeated praise.
Furthermore, from the point where the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions below, it shall be interpreted.
The section beginning with "Contrary to the above" explains the meaning of dedication characterized by grasping at signs (*nimitta*).

The section beginning with "There are three kinds of signs" further explains the meaning of the aforementioned "contrary" state. Although signs are infinite, they are all subsumed within these three types;
this will be explained as we reach the signless sign (*animittanimitta*).
As with the example of the chariot, each point shall be explained in turn.

Regarding the passage beginning "Having departed from these two characteristics," this clarifies that although one has departed from these two conventional designations—namely, the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and so forth—one nevertheless returns to forming characteristics again because of being attached to the characteristic of signlessness (*animittalakṣaṇa*). This shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "In this, there is nothing to be attained" explains the preceding passage on "signlessness," "non-emergence," and so forth;
each of these shall be explained in turn. Thus, regarding the praise beginning with "Excellent, excellent," there are two cycles of praise within the initial section of the Buddha’s teaching. This...
This explains the meaning of the second praise mentioned above; it shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning "If a trichiliocosm... onwards, it explains the preceding text on comparative measurement; it shall now be explained.

Question: From "The following" onwards, the text next explains the passage concerning the intermediate devas praising and completing [the teaching], and further analyzes such matters as the number of devas who come.
It should be explained that because the fourth heaven has few [devas], it is said that they do not come.
Question: Following the various causes and conditions explained above, the text next provides an exposition of the second cycle of Subhūti’s questions to the Buddha.
This section consists of the extensive explanations and detailed comparisons provided by the Tathāgatas; it shall now be explained point by point.
Question: Regarding the passage beginning with "The six pāramitās, etc.," the intention here is as follows:
Since among the six pāramitās, ethical discipline (*śīla*), generosity (*dāna*), and so forth are also form (*rūpa*), why is it said that they are equal to liberation (*vimukti*)?
This question arises because [the author] intends to explain the Tathāgata’s extensive discourse on liberation and the like.
The answer begins as follows: Now, regarding the discussion on the signless liberation (animitta-vimokṣa), all true marks (dharmatā) are entirely equal.
They cannot be perceived as they are by the physical eye; therefore, one clings to the notion that they are unequal. This shall be explained point by point.
"Those called 'persons of the Way' and below" introduces a metaphor to clarify the meaning of "equality," which shall now be explained.

"The Buddha, within this, explains through differentiation" and below is the subsequent explanation of the passage concerning comparative evaluation (*tulana*). If one clarifies the meaning from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then they are no different;

yet if one discusses them from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), they are as far apart as heaven and earth. This is because the One Suchness (*tathatā*) is without duality. Therefore—

The nature of form (*rūpa*) is not different from the nature of the Buddha; therefore, it is said above that they are equal to liberation. This is because [otherwise] heaven and earth would be as far apart as they are.
Form is distinct from omniscience (*sarvajñā*); form is but an insentient, stubborn vessel, whereas omniscience is the spirit of the sage. How could they be compared?
At present, this is for the purpose of providing a conventional, mundane analysis and comparison; thus, one must...
This clarifies the meaning of superiority and inferiority and so forth;

it shall now be explained. As for the passage beginning with "Why is this? and following: it explains that the merit derived from grasping at signs mentioned above is limited, whereas the merit of rejoicing and so forth is immeasurable because it is a merit free from signs (*animitta*). This shall be explained point by point.
Regarding the thirty-ninth chapter of the sixty-second fascicle,
it is titled "The Chapter on Great Deliverance. The reason this chapter appears is that, as the Buddha has already extensively explained the principles of signless dedication,
comparative evaluation, and so forth for Maitreya, Subhūti, Śakra, and others, [the Buddha now addresses] Śāriputra...
The reason for this joy is that one admires the profound virtue of Prajñā. Below this are several chapters;
the scriptural text in all of them praises the great efficacy of Prajñā. Now, as this treatise is about to provide an exposition, it cites the commentary on the thirty-ninth chapter.

From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha," and continuing through this chapter, although there are many dharma-gates, they generally comprise three parts.
The first clarifies how Śāriputra and the assembly praise and expound upon the profound meaning of the superior sense.
The second [section] is the Tathāgata’s own discourse; the third is Subhūti’s praise, which is precisely this first part.
It clarifies how Śāriputra first praised Prajñāpāramitā with eighteen phrases, demonstrating that Prajñā illuminates all five dharma-treasuries and so forth, such that they are all ultimately pure.
The commentary explains this very clearly; each point is addressed and explained in detail according to the respective sections of the treatise.
The passage beginning with "having eliminated all darkness" refers to the elimination of the two wheels of views and craving, as well as the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).

This establishes [the overcoming of] the sixty-two types of views regarding the self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), which shall be explained in the main treatise. Because it can eliminate the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*), it is called "peaceful and secure. This shall also be explained in the treatise.

"Regarding the passage 'the wheel of Dharma with twelve aspects' and below: this refers to the demonstration, the exhortation, and the realization, which together constitute the twelve aspects, as explained in the first chapter.
Regarding the passage 'because of non-retrogression and non-return,' the preceding phrases and so forth have all been explained one by one in the treatise."
From "How, World-Honored One, should one... how should one make offerings? onwards, it clarifies that since Prajñāpāramitā is signless (animitta), making offerings to it is likewise difficult;
therefore, this inquiry is made so that future generations may understand.
From the words "As for the Buddha’s statement, 'as in making offerings to the World-Honored One'" down to the commentary on the term "equal," [the text] explains.

From the words "For what reason" onwards, it explains that *prajñā* (wisdom) is not only non-different from the Buddha, but is also superior because it can give rise to the causes and effects of the five vehicles;
this shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, having reflected... down to the discussion on what is meant by *prajñā*, it is explained as follows:

this is true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), which leads people into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The power of *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means) is expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), which leads people out of emptiness.
Because the bodhisattva possesses these two types of wisdom, he does not realize [the ultimate] emptiness, nor does he dwell in existence (*bhava*). This shall now be explained point by point.
From "Śakra Devānām Indra spoke to Śāriputra as previously stated" onwards clarifies the discourse on the meaning by the Lord of Devas;
this shall be explained point by point.
From "Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, 'Venerable One, how should one give rise to... onwards constitutes the second section of the chapter, which clarifies [the teaching] based on the body.
The question posed by Zifa concerns the Tathāgata’s extensive exposition, which shall now be explained.

From the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" onwards, it clarifies the Tathāgata’s extensive exposition; specifically, the statement that "because form (*rūpa*) is unarisen, the *prajñāpāramitā* arises" clarifies *prajñā*.
It indicates that if wisdom can contemplate the non-arising of form and so forth, only then is it called true illumination.
The color of clouds does not arise; yet when one discusses Prajñā, there is also arising. However, this is spoken of as "arising" in the sense of its true illumination.
Even the meaning of "arising" cannot be apprehended. All subsequent meanings should likewise be explained according to this same principle.
"How is it that form does not arise? This shall be explained below.
From the words "The Buddha said" onwards, it clarifies form: since it has never arisen from the beginning, what arising could there be that might arise?
To know these meanings is what is called *prajñā* (wisdom); therefore, [the sūtra] speaks of "arising."
Regarding the passage beginning with "With what does it conjoin? and so forth: the intent of this question is to ask, "If that is so, with what kind of phenomena does Prajñāpāramitā conjoin?

The Buddha’s reply beginning with "There is nothing with which it conjoins" clarifies that all phenomena lack dual characteristics; they possess but a single characteristic, which is the absence of characteristics (*animitta*).
Therefore, there is nothing with which it can be conjoined. This shall be explained one by one; it is not like names and so forth.
Below, this shall be explained one by one. Having formed this thought, [the text] clarifies that when such conceptualizing minds arise, then Prajñā arises.

How could this be [otherwise]? Therefore, it says "abandoning. This shall be explained: if one says that Prajñā is empty and not solid, then the impermanence of Prajñā arises. This shall be explained.
Commentary:
From the passage "To have faith in what dharma... onwards, it clarifies that this principle is profound and subtle, such that it cannot be known by those of shallow understanding;
therefore, Subhūti inquires into the meaning of generating faith so that others may attain comprehension.

From "The Buddha having thus spoken" onwards, the statement that one does not believe in form up to all aspects (*sarvākāra*) and so forth is extremely clear due to the Buddha’s adherence to the Vinaya;
this shall now be explained.
From "The commentary says" onwards, this first section clarifies the established order in which the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) introduces the Sūtra; this shall now be explained.
"Joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha," and so forth—this explains the meaning of the initial passage.
"Because it is ultimately pure, it is able to shine everywhere," and so forth—this explains the first sentence of the present eulogy.
Regarding the "five kinds of Dharma-treasuries": these clarify the *prajñā* (wisdom) of all Buddhas and their disciples throughout the succession of past lives.
It is also inexhaustible. Although the *prajñā* of all Buddhas and their disciples who will arise in the future is not exhausted;
the *prajñā* that elucidates all Buddhas and their disciples currently arising in the present is also not exhausted;
and the *prajñā* already realized by all Buddhas and their disciples of the past is likewise not exhausted. It neither increases nor...

[The term] "reduction" [applies to] the disciples of all past, future, and present Buddhas; since the meaning of those who have now realized and those who will realize is likewise so, these three exclusions constitute the Three Dharma Treasuries (*dharmapiṭaka*).

Because the wondrous nature of the Dharma, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), inconceivable nature, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and so forth, are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma Treasuries that cannot be spoken of. There are two kinds of Dharma Treasuries: first, as follows...
In the *Vātsīputrīya-abhidharma*, it is taught that the person (*pudgala*) is subsumed within the "teachings that cannot be spoken of.

This means that one cannot say there is a person apart from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor can one say that the person is identical to the five aggregates. Furthermore, one cannot say that the person possesses the five aggregates, nor can one say that the five aggregates possess the person.
Thus, by examining each phenomenon (*dharma*) in this manner, it is stated that in every case there is a person. However—
It is ineffable. This is the Dharma-treasury of the ineffable within the Tripitaka.

Now, in the Mahāyāna, that which clarifies the ineffable Dharma-treasury clarifies that all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent and cut off from the path of language; they cannot be cognized by consciousness, nor can knowledge be produced regarding them.
One cannot say they exist, nor can one say they do not exist. Thus, the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on the True Mark) says: "The Sage..."

That which the mind can know cannot be distinguished by the divine voice; it is not that the divine voice is incapable of distinguishing it, but rather that there are no dharmas within the sutras to be distinguished.
That which one hopes the mind can know is not that it is incapable of knowing it, but rather that there are no marks to be known.

Since this is the teaching of ultimate reality (*tattva*), it is called the "Ineffable Dharma-Treasury" (*anabhilāpya-dharmakośa*). Because the establishment of the Dharma-treasury encompasses all things, the Dharma is thereby exhausted. To explain this point, it is now said:
It illuminates the treasury of all dharmas.

Therefore, from this point onward, the sutra passages are cited and explained. Once the interpretation of the meanings in works such as the *Dilun* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* has been completed, each instance likewise cites the sutra to provide its explanation. Since there are many such sutras and treatises in this section, [the method is applied accordingly].
Since it is not possible to cite each instance one by one in this manner, I shall only mention their presence or absence from time to time.

Regarding the section beginning with "capable of guarding," the text below states that these are all restatements of the current eighteen [categories]. One should extract each point from the sūtra text within the *Praise* (Zàn).
My present citation of the intent here is for the purpose of providing a detailed, point-by-point commentary; these shall be explained in the relevant passages of the main text.

The passage beginning with "not turning within birth and death" explains the meaning of non-retrogression and non-returning. Because one does not depart from birth and death, it is said that there is no "turning";
because one does not enter nirvana, it is said there is no "returning. Therefore, the text reiterates: "Because of non-arising, there is no turning; because of non-delusion, there is no returning.
If one understands it in this way, only then can it be called the turning of the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
"The wheel. From "Thus, etc.
onwards, the explanation having been completed, this serves as a general conclusion.
Regarding the section beginning with "Next, that which shall be expanded," it will be further praised at length within the chapter titled "The Thousand Buddhas Sutra" and its equivalents.
The commentary states: The following section is the Buddha’s explanation of the meaning of Śāriputra’s current question regarding "making offerings.

This shall now be explained. Regarding the phrase "as if making offerings to the Buddha" and so forth: in the previous section on comparative evaluation, it was stated that making offerings to Prajñāpāramitā is itself Prajñāpāramitā.

However, because sentient beings currently have many attachments to signs (*nimitta*) and hold the Buddha in high esteem, it is here simply said to be "as if [offering] to the Buddha. This shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "identical, thus there is no difference" explains the text stating that [the Bodhisattva] is not different from the Buddha.

Following this, the section beginning with "When the Buddha had explained the causes and conditions" further cites the Buddha’s own words as proof that Prajñāpāramitā is superior because it can bring forth the five vehicles and so forth.
At that time, after Śakra had formed this thought, he descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inquire about the intentions of Śāriputra and the others;
each point shall now be explained.

For example, regarding the passage beginning with "Just as the four great elements": just as within trees all four great elements are fully present, yet they are designated according to which element is most predominant.

They belong to the same stage (*bhūmi*). The same applies to the five *pāramitās*: if, due to the predominance of the characteristic of relinquishment (*tyāga*), they specifically receive the name of the *dāna-pāramitā*, yet within each individual *pāramitā*, there is always the integration of *prajñā*, such that they do not become separated from one another.
This shall now be explained.
From "After Śakra had asked" onwards, the text of the present discourse by Śakra is next explained.

As for the passage beginning with "For example, when a mixture has been compounded," there are thirty or twenty kinds of grasses and leaves, yet they receive their names based on the five stones, three stones, and so forth.
The medicinal herbs are a metaphor for the five matters; the stones are a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom).
Furthermore, the soldiers that descend from the great city are a metaphor for the five matters, while the general is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom). Each of these shall be explained in turn.
From the passage beginning with "Śāriputra has already asked regarding making offerings" onwards, the second major section is now explained.

Regarding the text in which the Tathāgata, prompted by Śāriputra’s inquiry, speaks extensively, it says: "*Prajñā* is the womb (*garbha*) from which all things are born. This shall be explained point by point.
At that time, following Śāriputra’s inquiry, the text next explains the present Prajñāpāramitā and with what dharmas its meaning accords;
this shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning "Whether wholesome or unwholesome" onwards, one should understand that it does not accord with worldly or supramundane dharmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
The meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth arises here; it may be cited and explained within this context. Now, as for "having nothing with which to conjoin":

first, it clarifies that all phenomena are in reality without marks and that Prajñā is without substantiality. Therefore, it is said that within the teaching of Prajñā, there is nothing with which one can conjoin.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "For those of overweening pride, the Buddha teaches that by departing from lust, anger, and delusion, one attains [liberation]."
Liberation. Because the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is liberation itself, the terms "wholesome" and "unwholesome" mentioned herein are all included within the category of *prajñā*.
Śakra, having placed great weight on the *bodhisattva-prajñā*, asked this question because he thought that since *prajñā* is the cause, it ought to be conjoined with its fruit.
The Tathāgata’s answer was likewise that they are not conjoined. This shall now be explained; herein, the Buddha refutes [this position].

Because it is clearly seen that [all things] are severed, it is said that they "conjoin below. This shall now be explained. As for "conjoining with the Buddha-mind," this clarifies that within the Buddha-mind there is no mark of conjoining, nor is there anything to be conjoined.

The section beginning with "The answer says" clarifies that if one can refrain from grasping at signs, not receiving them, and not being attached to them, this is called "conforming to the Buddha-mind.
The section beginning with "Śakra rejoiced" is the text consisting of the praises and expositions of the present Lord of the Devas.
