As for the "one who sees," they immediately realize the Buddha-nature and perceive the Buddha-nature before them.

Furthermore, one should not say that the wisdom which contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as ultimately empty is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If it is said that this true knowledge was originally existent but is only now manifested and made functional, then it accords with reason;
however, there would be only a cause of manifestation (*vyañjana-hetu*) and no cause of production (*janana-hetu*). This is also the case for the *vipākaja-buddha* (the Buddha of retribution).
The fact that there is no cause for its arising in the present also establishes the meaning of its being primordially existent (*mūla-bhava*).
Why is this? Because it is primordially existent. Since true knowledge and the Dharma-Buddha are both primordially existent, they are merely manifested today;

thus, when it is said that they have "begun to exist," it refers to their commencement of function. The five perfections practiced together with Prajñāpāramitā are equal to the eternally abiding Prajñāpāramitā; all are primordially existent.

There is. In both cases, the essence is manifested for the first time now, and its function is attained for the first time now; there is no difference whatsoever between them. This is the emergence through the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*);
what meaning is there in a producing cause (*janana-hetu*) producing a dharma? This shall now be explained.
"If a person, for a short time, should practice... and so forth below clarifies the meaning of what ought to be externally protected.

"As with the *kara* yakṣas... and so forth below clarifies the meaning that, regarding the realization of the matter, those on the higher stages do not require external protection. Each of these shall now be explained in turn.
At that time, having expressed his longing for and esteem of this wisdom that is like a dream and so forth, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, posed four questions.
Subhūti answered them with four responses that use the difficult to illustrate the easy. Each of these passages from the sūtra shall now be explained one by one.
The remaining metaphors are also like this. Regarding the single metaphor of the dream above, it says:

"To think of the dream, to think that this is a dream, to think by means of the dream, and to ride upon the dream"—since these four aspects are thus, the four characteristics in the other nine metaphors, such as the reflection, the mirage, and the transformation, are likewise so;
this shall now be explained.
At that time, Subhūti’s reply to Śakra, beginning with the words "If a practitioner has already... and so forth, clarifies how Subhūti returns to form and the other aggregates.
He does so by employing the four characteristics as analogies to explain the preceding meaning; each point should be explained in correspondence with its respective counterpart.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, [the section] below the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds—namely, the second part of this chapter—clarifies the Dharma of Prajñā.
It is honored because its exposition is no different from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Within this, there are further two intentions:
first, to clarify the sameness of the ten directions; second, to clarify the sameness of the three periods of time. These exist...
There are two intentions [in this passage]. First, it clarifies that the various devas, upon hearing the teaching of the true reality (bhūtatathatā), have understood it with perfect clarity;
therefore, the offering is described.
Regarding the phrase "it has such characteristics and such names," this clarifies that the manifest teaching is no different [from the ultimate truth].
From the passage beginning "All were named Subhūti" onwards, it is intended to discuss how that which is spoken by all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise.
However, because the discourse here is made according to what was perceived by those in the assembly at that time, it merely mentions "ten directions each with a thousand.

This refers exclusively to ten thousand Buddha-lands. When the *Prajñāpāramitā* is clearly expounded, it must always be addressed to the foremost person who understands emptiness; therefore, [the text] concludes [with this].
The name "Subhūti" is spoken. Since the Lord of Devas (Śakra) is a lord who dwells upon the earth, he must also keep in mind that the heaven of Prajñā is named "Pure" (*śuddha*).
All that is spoken by the Buddhas requires the purification of the person who presides over it; thus, he asks about this Dharma of purity.

Therefore, the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to Śakra Devānām Indra. This shall now be explained. If the *Avataṃsaka* says, "All throughout the ten directions, they speak of the characteristics of the Ten Stages," [it is for this reason].
All Bodhisattvas are named Vajragarbha, and all those who inquire are named Vimukticandra.

This clarifies that the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) are eternally abiding, profound, and difficult to elucidate; therefore, all Bodhisattvas who explain the characteristics of the stages share the name Vajragarbha, while those who are liberated are designated as Vimukticandra.

This is based on the "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) which is free from bondage; it illuminates what was previously obscured during the dark night. Through the practice of this stage, one performs wholesome deeds.

It removes the blackness of bondage; because it can provide illumination within the profound darkness of prior birth-and-death, those from whom one seeks instruction are all named Moon of Liberation (*Vimukticandra*).
This is because the principle of the Mahāyāna is profound and differs from the texts and principles of the Hinayana teachings.
It is thus because the Buddhas of the ten directions are eternally one and truly have no differing doctrines, and what all the sages receive is not distinct. Therefore, it is so.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and those below them.

This second section clarifies that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise identical and without difference. Previously, the ten directions were cited to establish the principle that their teachings are the same;

now, by mentioning Maitreya, it is clarified that the three periods do not differ. The reason for citing Maitreya is the desire to use the future to provide corroboration that the teachings are the same.
Regarding the meaning of the present: since the future is the same as what the Buddha taught concerning the present, one should know that it is the Buddha’s teaching of the present.
However, because it is identical to the past, [the text] brings this forward in order to use it as proof.
However, from this point downward, the subsequent explanation of the "burning" is identical. This section clarifies that all Buddhas are eternally constant;
it is here that the *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as being consumed by fire."
He is always present on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and in all other dwelling places; for whenever he expounds the Mahāyāna, he clarifies the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Thus, according to this pure land of the true mark, he has never been otherwise.
"By what characteristics, by what causes, and by what meaning... and so forth, clarifies that Subhūti, based on this, further poses three questions.

"The Buddha said... and so forth, is the direct answer to the first question, clarifying that when Maitreya appears in the world, he will preach the characteristics of Prajñāpāramitā in exactly this way, no different from now.
Furthermore, because form is at times non-form, it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither bound nor liberated, and neither defiled nor pure.
...and so forth. This shall now be explained.

From the passage where Subhūti addressed the Buddha onwards, the second question is answered. Above, the meaning of the purity of form (*rūpa*) and so forth was clarified based on the purity of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Now, when it is said to be "pure," this refers to the purity of its cause (*hetu*); for the true nature (*dharmatā*) within form serves as the cause that gives rise to [purity].
Regarding *prajñā*, it is therefore called "equal. Each of these shall be explained in turn.
As for the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One said: 'Because form is pure,'" this clarifies that Subhūti asked again based on this [previous teaching]; this shall now be explained.
Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is pure... [and so forth]. Above, the Venerable Subhūti established three questions and answers; two questions have already been concluded.
Now, the third question is answered, clarifying the time of Maitreya’s appearance. This is done by means of such meanings as these.

This concerns the teaching on *prajñā*. It shall be explained point by point. Form (*rūpa*) is originally without defilement; therefore, it is said that one does not "practice" it. This shall now be explained:
space and so forth may be employed, yet they cannot be employed; therefore, it is said that *prajñā* is pure, and thus it is so.
The passage beginning with "Space can be described" clarifies that the essence of emptiness is beyond description. Even if it were described, its essence remains inherently pure;
since the essence of prajñā is likewise thus, even if it were described, it would remain pure as well.
The passage beginning with "Because two sounds have emerged from within empty space" clarifies that sentient beings are formed by the six great elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*).

The four great elements enclose empty space, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) dwells therein. The mind is the *ālayavijñāna*. When the retributive wind issues from the navel and strikes the seven locations [of the body], sound emerges.
Because sound arises from the emptiness of sound, there is resonance. If the internal and external were not empty, there would be neither sound nor resonance.
Therefore it is said that because of space, the two sounds emerge; yet although the two sounds emerge because of space, space itself does not act.
Although because of Prajñā there is that which can be called Prajñā, its nature is unstained and eternally pure, and thus it cannot be apprehended.
It is as luminous as the appearance of empty space because it is ungraspable; pure *prajñā* is pure because it is signless (*animitta*).
This shall be explained one by one.
Regarding the section beginning with "The Explanation states" and below: in the first chapter above, because the Tathāgata himself spoke, the various assemblies of devas and others were enumerated.
Next, the Chapter on the Marks of the Tongue is introduced in order to provide the teaching. Next, the Section on the Request is introduced because it is the initial request for the teaching.
It is introduced here again in order to clearly and fully reveal the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Question: The following response states "already arrived" and so forth. Its meaning is that all the newly manifested devas and others have come.

The passage beginning with "In each of the ten directions, a thousand Buddhas appear" explains the aforementioned point regarding the commonality of the ten directions. Each of these shall now be explained in turn.
From "The Buddha, wishing to verify this matter, has already descended" onwards, the general meaning of the preceding ancient and modern [teachings] is explained.

Those who wish to know that what all Buddhas have taught throughout the Bhadrakalpa is no different, and those who wish to establish a causal connection with all Buddhas, should understand it within this context.
This shall now be explained.
From "In the city of Rājagṛha" onwards, the meaning of the commonality of the aforementioned locations will be explained in succession. This shall now be explained.
From "As stated in the Maitreya Sūtra" onwards, it clarifies that the author of the treatise establishes proof from the sūtra that the Buddha formerly resided at this place.
This explains the meaning of Prajñā. Kāśyapa was the second Great Master; he maintained and upheld the Buddha-dharma for over twenty years.
Having begun at Wolf’s Foot (Vṛka-pada), he entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Next, he entrusted it to Ānanda, who maintained and upheld it for over twenty years.
He then entrusted it to Śāṇakavāsin, who maintained and upheld it for over twenty years. He entrusted it to Upagupta. Upagupta...
Kumārajīva maintained the lineage for over twenty years and entrusted it to Tiṣya.
Following Tiṣya were Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Vasubandhu, Siṃha, and others—twenty-three individuals in total. Among these, Nāgārjuna was the most eminent.

The circumstances regarding these twenty-three Dharma masters, as well as the entry of Kāśyapa into the meditative absorption of cessation and Maitreya’s deliverance of sentient beings, shall be explained in detail herein.

The Master said: "If one with a body sustained by physical food enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and remains there for more than seven days, they will die upon emerging from that absorption.
However, this Kāśyapa is a Dharma-body Bodhisattva; because he does not crave the physical body, he is able to emerge from the absorption in such a manner. There is an interpretation which says:
"If one dwells in the constant state of having entered the absorption of cessation and exceeds the allotted time limit, they must die upon emerging. But if it is one sent by the Buddha..."
Regarding "the messenger entering into equanimity": even if it were not a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body who acted as the messenger, they would not die upon emerging;

rather, they must first accomplish their task, and only then would they pass away. Thus, the *Treatise on the Ten Powers* states: "It is impossible that a messenger dispatched by a Buddha would not reach his destination.
If it were the case that a non-Dharma-body Bodhisattva died upon emerging from meditative concentration, then there would be no such thing as a messenger dispatched by a Buddha who failed to arrive.
This is the underlying intention because the meaning has been reached; it shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning "By what characteristic, by what cause, and by what practice... onwards, the sūtra text from among the three questions and three answers above is explained in sequence.
The previous statement used the term "by what meaning" (*kena arthena*); here, it says "by what gate" (*kena mukhena*). This indicates that the meaning itself serves as the gate.

The passage beginning with the Buddha’s words, "As I have taught, form and all phenomena are neither eternal nor impermanent," etc., explains the scriptural text concerning the answer to the first question mentioned above. It shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Subhūti, having rejoiced," the following explains the sūtra text that answers the second question above.
Herein, "condition" (*pratyaya*) is used as the name for the cause; it serves as the causal condition. This shall now be explained.
"By means of parables, so that the matter may be made clear," and so forth, is the subsequent explanation of the sūtra text answering the third question above.
"The eighty-four thousand clusters of dharmas are all but the single matter of Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth, clarifies that what is taught herein is all taught within Prajñā;
it is a single matter that is explained through differentiation as many clusters of dharmas.
This is why it is said that all dharmas arise from *prajñā*. This shall now be explained.
Regarding the passage beginning with "There is a sound that issues from the emptiness within the mouth," this has already been explained above and shall now be discussed.
Various minor bodhisattvas regard such things as the noble dharmas and nirvana as real— just as a person regards sound as real—
and they regard the dharmas of birth-and-death and ordinary worldlings as unreal— just as a person regards an echo as unreal.
If one says that worldly dharmas exist only in name but lack reality, while supramundane dharmas possess reality, this is all spoken for the sake of the various minor bodhisattvas.
Indeed. This shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "Question" is the inquiry;

the section beginning with "Answer" is the response. As for the statement "it exists spontaneously," this means that because the cause has already produced the result, there is no need for further production.
Yet one attains it spontaneously; thus it is said that it is "natural," like when no sound is intentionally produced, yet sound emerges of itself.
This shall be explained point by point. Space is a non-conditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); this merely explains the preceding passage stating that space is without grasping (*anupādāna*).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Just as space has the characteristic of being unapprehendable" explains the preceding sūtra text on non-apprehension.
For example, although immeasurable things are produced by means of space, space itself lacks the characteristic of producing anything, nor does it possess any characteristic that can be grasped.
Because things are produced by means of space, space is therefore not non-existent; yet, because no characteristic of space can be apprehended, it is therefore not existent.
Neither existent nor non-existent; thus it is with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and *prajñā* as well. This shall now be explained.

The Commentary on the Fifty-Seventh Chapter, titled "The Pure Land. Why does the "Pure Land" chapter follow the "Wick of the Lamp"?

The treatise itself states its own origin: it clarifies that non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas possess the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Since their own practice is already...

It is sufficient. One should simply take the adornment of the land as one's task in order to receive and transform sentient beings; therefore, the "Pure Land Chapter" is explained immediately following this.
As the treatise is about to introduce it, it says: "This is the commentary on the fifty-seventh chapter."
At that time, from the passage beginning with Śāriputra downwards, within this chapter, there are two major intentions.

First, it clarifies that following the previous chapter, one enters the three samādhis and extensively transforms sentient beings; thus, based on these beings, the discussion of doctrine proceeds, equating dreaming and waking.
Second, from the passage where the Buddha says to Subhūti, "There is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, when practicing the dāna-pāramitā... and so forth.
The final section concludes. This clarifies the conduct of the Bodhisattva and the vow to purify the Buddha-fields; this opening [section] is the first.
As for why Śāriputra poses this question at the very beginning, his intention is as follows: he considers that dreams are deceptive phenomena while samādhi is real.
Furthermore, there are other passages stating that within dreams there are both good and evil; if there is something good, one may practice this samādhi within a dream.
One should also accumulate and augment *prajñā* (wisdom); therefore, this question is posed.
From Subhūti’s response below, it is intended to discuss that within a dream one can only obtain the cause for the accumulation of karma, but cannot accumulate the retribution of karma.

However, Subhūti’s intention is to equate dreaming and waking as being one and the same, so that right and wrong, hidden and manifest, and the convergence of the real and the unreal may be understood; thus he provides this response in accordance with reality.
Answer: Because one practices *prajñāpāramitā*, one sleeps peacefully in dreams and the body is harmonious and joyful; even within dreams, one performs wholesome deeds and benefits sentient beings.
Now, as one is about to enter into actual realization, it is said that there is no difference [between waking and dreaming]. This shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "If one performs actions in a dream" constitutes the second round of the objection.

Since Subhūti has answered according to reality by stating that waking and dreaming are equal—because if daytime practice can be beneficial, nighttime practice is likewise beneficial, and thus it can fully augment *prajñā*;
whereas if daytime practice is not beneficial, nighttime practice is also not beneficial—the intent here is that within the true nature (*dharmatā*), even daytime practice does not increase.

How much less so when acting within a dream? Furthermore, since even acting during the day with a mind possessed of signs (sanimitta-citta) does not bring benefit, how could acting while the mind is shrouded by sleep possibly bring benefit?
One should know that dreaming and waking are of one kind. Now, Śāriputra, he proceeds further to pose this question specifically:
"Karma" (karma) means "action" (abhisamskāra); "accumulation" (upacaya) means "gathering together" (samudānaya); and "accomplishment" (pariniṣpatti) means "completion" (niṣpatti). If it is said...
In that case, one would cite the Buddha’s words as a challenge: since a dream is not real, there should be no accumulation therein.
It shall now be explained. From the passage beginning "Why is this? onwards, it returns to explain the meaning that there should be no accumulation within a dream. It shall now be explained.
From the passage beginning "He said to Śāriputra" onwards, it clarifies that once Subhūti was questioned, he answered by means of a counter-argument. It shall now be explained. Śāri...
From "Pu said" onwards, it clarifies that once Śāriputra was cross-examined, he replied: "If there are no causes and conditions, karma does not arise and volition (*cetanā*) does not sit.
Here, "karma" refers to the karma of body and speech, while "volition" refers to the karma of mind. If there are no causes and conditions, volitional karma does not arise at all;
it must have conditions to arise. Since volitional karma and the like first arise during the day, [it follows that they do so] in dreams at night as well.
Furthermore, because there are conditions, volitional karma and the like arise; because they do not arise in the absence of conditions, one should know that they are of one kind.

From the passage "In such and such a way" onwards, it clarifies that since the principle of the wholesome is already established, it is confirmed by showing that its factual nature and underlying logic are identical.
It clarifies that daytime karma also arises from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and so too does the karma created within a dream.

Therefore, these four dharmas arise; thus, there is no difference. Regarding the statement that within this mind there is both purity and defilement, this refers to the mind during dreams, as explained in the treatise.
"Once all volitions (*cetanā*) have ceased and their characteristics are separated," and so forth, constitutes the third rebuttal of Śāriputra, which shall now be explained.
"Because one grasps at characteristics, there is karma with an object (*sālambana*), and thus birth occurs," and so forth, is Subhūti’s response. His intention is this:

although one might discuss how all phenomena (*dharma*) are in reality devoid of intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*)—such that there is no object, no karma, and no factors such as volition—it is simply that sentient beings do not understand this within the context of phenomena that are devoid of intrinsic characteristics.
Because of grasping at signs (*nimitta*), one transcends all karmic actions by leaping across them. [Karma] arises from causes and conditions; if there are no conditions, it cannot arise.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In a dream, [one performs] giving, observing precepts, and so forth," this is the fourth objection. Its meaning is as follows:

Since it was stated above that karma arises because there are conditions within a dream, and that such things may also constitute mental karma (*cetanā-karman*) and so on, then even if a Bodhisattva spends the entire day with a mind that grasps at signs...

If even practicing such dharmas as these six pāramitās does not constitute a truly real dedication, how could there be a dedication achieved through the practice of a dream-state mind that is obscured and deluded?
Therefore, this question is posed. If one dedicates one's own roots of goodness, it should properly be called the "dedication of roots of goodness.
If one dedicates by taking the roots of goodness of others as an object, it is called "following [them]."

This is the dedication of joy. Regarding the passage beginning with "Maitreya Bodhisattva is now present," if it were as previously stated—that Subhūti’s spirit was so exalted that he was one whom all the sages submit to—the reason he now defers to Maitreya is this:

since Subhūti above has already personally attained the reality of answering that dreaming and waking are simultaneous, he wishes to cause the multitude of sages to be equally aligned from afar, so that there may be no difference among them.

Therefore, Maitreya is recommended for two reasons: first, as Maitreya is the successor to the Teacher, he is recommended so that the teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the present and future may be identical;
second, he is recommended because the four noble beings collectively and earnestly expound [the teaching] on his behalf.

However, regarding the main intent of the treatise: because it seeks to manifest the superiority of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, it states that the answer was difficult to provide, thereby leading to the referral to Maitreya.

Furthermore, since it also says that Maitreya bestows the prediction of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), one should know that the name "non-retrogression" applies throughout both the higher and lower stages.

Therefore, in the "Chapter on Certainty" (*Niścaya-parivarta*), three sections are established to clarify the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*): the first refers to the initial generation [of the mind].
There are three kinds of Bodhisattvas: first, those who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment]; second, those who possess the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and third, those in their final existence (*carama-bhavika*). Maitreya now returns once more to the ultimate benefit.

It shall be explained that the place where he receives his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is the city of Rājagṛha, specifically the dwelling place of the Brahmā-like King Brahmadatta. It shall be explained starting from the words "As you, O worthy one," since [the Buddha] has already seen Maitreya.
The statement that one "should attain the profound Dharma" is made because this question has been posed.

The passage beginning with "not yet having realized" clarifies that when a Bodhisattva enters into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it is like a bird flying through the sky whose tracks cannot be found;

it is not as with the two vehicles, which have a point of realization within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). The section beginning with "At that time, the Buddha said" next clarifies how the Tathāgata finally brings this meaning to completion.
It shall now be explained.

each point shall be explained in turn. From "Subhūti’s intention was as follows" onwards clarifies that within the true mark (dharmatā), day and... [the text continues].
Even practicing [in this way] would be of no benefit; how much less could practicing in a dream be beneficial?

Since there is no discrimination within Prajñāpāramitā, why do you pose questions based on the distinction between dreaming and waking? This is intended to cause Prajñāpāramitā to increase.

This shall now be explained. The passage beginning with "For what reason" below explains Subhūti’s statement that the minds of dreaming and waking are equal.

It shall be explained that śrāvakas do not attain the Dharma-eye; thus, they are not discussed here. All shall be explained in turn.
From "The Buddha said to Subhūti" onwards is the second section of this chapter, which clarifies the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the buddha-field through vows.
Within this text there are thirty repetitions; within these thirty repetitions, there are further three underlying intentions.
The first section consists of six successive expositions (*paryāya*), which clarify that within each of the individual *pāramitās*, the Bodhisattva gives rise to its respective vow;

therefore, these are called "distinct practices and distinct vows. From the seventh exposition onwards, there are twenty-three successive expositions, which clarify that the Bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās* collectively while giving rise to the vow for purifying the Buddha-land; these are termed "collective practice and collective vow. — *Śāstra*.
The commentary states: Among the six *pāramitās* mentioned above, that which clarifies their distinct practices and distinct vows explains how a single cause extinguishes a single effect.

Within the second [section], which clarifies the collective practice and collective vow, it explains how multiple causes produce multiple effects, as well as the principle of a single cause producing multiple effects and so forth.
Thirdly, the thirtieth section clarifies the instructional contemplative practice for bodhisattvas; this present first [section] is precisely that.
This is the first [section]. First, regarding the cause, beginning with the *dānapāramitā*, one gives rise to the vows and practices for purifying the Buddha-land.
The phrase "there is no such thing" and so forth clarifies what is absent; the passage from "robes and food and drink" onwards clarifies what is present.
This same principle applies to each of the *pāramitās* respectively. Furthermore, the following section is the second, concerning the *śīlapāramitā*.
Within the *pāramitās*, it clarifies only that which is absent and does not set forth that which is present. It shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from here on, the third [section] clarifies the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). It shall now be explained.

Furthermore, from here on, the fourth [section], within the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), clarifies the practice and vows for purifying the Buddha-land. It shall now be explained. "To be able to act thus" is the summary. Furthermore, from here on...

Below, the fifth [point] clarifies this through the *dhyānapāramitā*. Although these five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) belong to the category of afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), even those who have attained liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) regarding the first *dhyāna* cannot attain that *dhyāna* because they are unable to eliminate the obscurations to meditative concentration (*samādhy-āvaraṇa*).

There is an interpretation which states that since the obscurations to meditative concentration are established as the fifth dwelling, the followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*) are unable [to transcend them].
[They are] severed; however, they are merely suppressed. There is an interpretation which says: although these belong to the fifth dwelling, there are two kinds:

first, the obstruction of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and second, the obstruction of existence (*bhava*). As for the obstruction of emptiness, because it belongs to the obstruction of wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it must be severed by the realization of emptiness.
The second is the obstruction regarding objects (*vastu-āvaraṇa*). This refers to the fact that, regarding objects, one either clings to them or resolves them through understanding.

For example, although both views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are equally afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because the portion of craving obstructs objects, it is severed through the resolution of objects; whereas because views obstruct principles (*tattva*), they are removed through the resolution of principles.
This is because their functional applications and the paths that treat them differ respectively. However, this does not concern the meaning of the nature of views themselves. It is merely...

The path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) severs [afflictions], yet because the root is for the most part not exhausted, and because the power of the path with outflows is dull, what is severed by it often possesses the sense of being subject to rebirth;
it is not that they are severed entirely. This shall be explained below, starting from "Furthermore.
Sixth, this is clarified by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*. This shall now be discussed.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he observes sentient beings falling into the three categories [of those destined for hell, animals, and hungry ghosts].

From this point onward, there are twenty-three further sections that clarify the meaning of practicing collectively and making collective vows, such as the principles of "many causes producing many fruits" and "one cause producing many fruits. Since these are not treated individually here...
The various *pāramitās* are explained separately, yet they are collectively referred to as the six *pāramitās*. All wholesome qualities are entirely subsumed within these six *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, below, various types of karmic results are clarified; thus, many causes produce many fruits.
Just as a single *dāna-pāramitā* can also bring about results such as physical beauty, wealth, and long life, this represents the principle that a single cause can produce multiple effects.
This was not discussed previously, but is clarified here; hence, it is stated thus.

Although the meanings of the Pure Land are immeasurable, we shall now discuss twenty-three types of pure lands categorized into the True (Dharmakāya) and Responsive (Nirmāṇakāya) aspects. This encompasses all [others].

There is no country whatsoever that is not completely pervaded. If the Dharma-body of true wisdom and the Reward-Buddha abide in the Pure Land of the True Mark, they manifest immeasurable forms and images, immeasurable radiance, and immeasurable sounds, accompanied solely by Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
For the sake of the assembly, it is as when a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground receives the office of a Buddha. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The circumference of that Bodhi tree is equal to ten trillion times the number of atoms in a Buddha-land. This refers to the Pure Land of Realized Reward (*vipāka*).
However, such places as the Bodhi tree not far from the city of Gayā, or the Pure Lands in the West, are all lands of response (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). Now...
Among these, the retribution of the correct teaching is not discussed here because the Dharma-Buddha is neither cause nor fruit and is intrinsically pure.
Nevertheless, there are three great types of pure lands resulting from response and resonance: first, those brought about by the performance of practices; second, those through the power of vows;
and third, those through the roots of goodness, practices, and vows of sentient beings. Although these also depend upon the wholesome power of sentient beings, [the former two are distinguished].

However, when a bodhisattva has fulfilled the power of their own practice and vows and further transforms sentient beings externally, only then can this land be accomplished so that sentient beings may be reborn therein.

For this reason, the title of this section is "Purifying the Buddha-land" rather than "The Land of Sentient Beings. Regarding the three groups (*tri-niyata-rāśi*), both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess them.
If one is at the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) or above, one belongs to the group of right determination (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) in the Hīnayāna. [The stages of] "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)...

In the midst of the "Summit" (mūrdhan) stage is the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) of the Hīnayāna. Therefore, the *Aṣṭaskandha-vibhāṣā* all state that one who regresses from the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) severs the roots of goodness;
prior to the stage of Heat, it is called the "wrong group" (mithyā-rāśi). In the Mahāyāna, prior to the "tying of the jewel," it is called the wrong group;
in the midst of tying the jewel, it is called the indeterminate group; and from the "lineage" (gotra) stage upward, it is called the right-determined group (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi). Now, this...
The pure lands clarified herein are all those into which beings of right concentration (samyaktva-niyata) are born; therefore, they are called "pure lands.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Buddha-lands," states: "One should cultivate a mind of generosity, patience, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth;

these are the pure land of a bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, [the beings there] will be free from flattery, possess great wealth, enjoy long life, be of handsome appearance, and possess undisturbed wisdom."

Sentient beings with wisdom and other virtues will be born in that land. As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, those born in that land all enter the stage of the "Certainty of Attainment" (*niyata-rāśi*).

Furthermore, as in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, when the Buddha manifested two hundred billion pure lands for Vaidehī, he stated that those of the three grades and nine levels—even those who have committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes—shall all be born in that land. Regarding the highest grade among these, there is...

There are three grades: namely, the highest grade of the highest birth, the middle grade of the middle birth, and the lowest grade of the lowest birth. Within the middle grade, there are likewise three grades:
namely, the highest grade of the middle birth, the middle grade of the middle birth, and the lowest grade of the middle birth. Within the lowest grade, there are also three grades:

namely, the highest grade of the lowest birth, the middle grade of the lowest birth, and the lowest grade of the lowest birth. Among these, only the highest grade of the highest birth is [the most excellent].

It is difficult to attain. If one who has committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes can repent with a sincere heart, they may only achieve birth in the lowest grade of the lowest level.

Those born in the highest grade of the highest level likewise enter within the lotus flower; as soon as it opens, they behold the Buddha and immediately abide in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
As for those of the lowest grade of the lowest level, once they have entered the flower, they must pass through the duration of many kalpas before they can finally behold [the Buddha].

After the Buddha has passed through the full duration of kalpas, the flowers finally bloom and he beholds the Buddha, thereby attaining the stage of the *samyaktva-niyāma* (the certainty of rightness).
Now, within this land during the Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas appear in the world; four have already passed away, and nine hundred and ninety-six remain.
If one dwells with these remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas, one shall together abide for half a kalpa to teach and transform sentient beings. The Tower...

When the Buddha Lohita remains alone for half an eon, if one has established a karmic connection with the previous nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas, that single Buddha Lohita will deliver them all completely and exhaustively.

One should diligently establish a karmic connection with these thousand Buddhas, prostrating, making vows, and practicing their teachings, so that this eon passes without being wasted; this matter is most excellent and supreme.
"Excellent. It should be like those who attain rebirth in the lower grade of the lowest level; yet even that is not necessarily the best. This shall now be explained.
Furthermore, from the section below, the third further explanation also differs. One interpretation states: Generally, when discussing the various lands..."
Thus, the perception of purity and impurity arises from the fact that the same substance is perceived differently by different views.
It is like the gold and jade seen by Māṇava, which are but shards and rubble to the poor; this pertains solely to their differing views, while the substance itself has no distinction.
Now, according to the interpretation of the Dharma Master Shi Dao’an regarding the scriptures: "Excessive desire leads to the retribution of deep chasms; arrogance leads to high [precipices]."
The mountains are the corresponding result [of karma]. Double-tongued speech results in thorns; false views result in the retribution of hell.

If you say that while the substance is the same, the appearances differ, then the Pure Land should likewise possess golden mountains, jeweled thorns, and exquisite wonders, while hell should consist of deep ravines made of the seven treasures.
If you say that such things do exist [in the Pure Land], then since the sentient beings of the Pure Land are free from desire, arrogance, and double-tongued speech, [how can there be such features?]

Regarding the karma of wrong views and the like, by what cause do they exist? If one says they exist, then in the end one cannot avoid the thorny ravines, the deep valleys, the hells, and the high mountains.
What, then, is called a "Pure Land"? It is like being bound by golden chains; in the end, it results in confinement—how does this differ from iron?
If one were to say that it does not exist, how could this be the case of "identical substance but different perceptions"?

Therefore, what Maṇibhadra sees and so forth are all instances of "different substances and different perceptions within the same location," such as the vision of Śikhin, for whom this land is like the palace of Maheśvara, while Śāriputra beholds only hills, mounds, and thorns.
This is because [the object] appears according to my own karma; it corresponds to me, whereas for others it is empty. Thus...
What Śāriputra sees is absent in the presence of Śikhin, and what Śikhin sees is entirely absent for Śāriputra;
this is because they do not obstruct one another. The *Anjingtu lun* (Treatise on the Peaceful and Pure Land) explains: "Because that [land] is empty, there is no mutual obstruction.

Therefore, by means of these words, the ground is said to be as level as the palm of a hand; that which exists in the defiled land is made non-existent in the pure land, while that which exists in the pure land...

There is nothing that exists in the defiled land which is not present in the Pure Land. Therefore, the Bodhisattva makes a vow to cause [the defiled land] to possess all that exists in the Pure Land, except for those things absent from the defiled land.
The meaning of the "Pure Land" should be explained extensively here; thus, regarding the nature of the pure and the defiled, they are both real when real, and both empty when empty.
Why is this so? It is not only that the Pure Land is empty for Śāriputra alone; the defiled land is likewise empty for Śaṅkha-śikhin.
They are both empty. That which is the emptiness of Śaṅkhakuñjara is precisely the reality of Śāriputra; that which is the reality of Śāriputra is precisely the emptiness of Śaṅkhakuñjara.
Therefore, one should know that where there is reality, both are real, and where there is emptiness, both are empty; each does not obstruct the other.

If this is so, then when the precious pillar of King Maṇibhadra exists, the precious palace naturally follows; and when the wooden pillar of the poor man exists, his thatched hut naturally follows. This is possible.
In one location there are two houses and two pillars; because they are produced by two distinct karmic conditions and perceived by two different views, they do not obstruct one another.
Now, I say: if it were as Śāriputra and Śikhin perceived—where each sees something different according to their own [karma]—that might be acceptable.

However, since it is now stated that the tiles and stones held by Māṇava were transformed into gold and jade, this seems to be a case of the same substance being seen differently, like water being transformed into ghee (*sarpis*). How can this be?
One obtains distinct water; it does not necessarily share the same meaning as a "Pure Land" (*śuddhakṣetra*). This shall now be explained. When Maṇināman grasps it, it first undergoes transformation;
before he has grasped it, it is still earth and stone. Regarding the meaning of a Pure Land, it is simply that one does not see it; if one sees it, it appears as something different.

As for those who hold that there is either total existence or total non-existence—this refers to the case where the substance is the same but the perceptions differ—or those who hold that there is partial existence and partial non-existence, then...
This is to address the different views held by those of similar nature. Within this, each successive section appears as if there were a distinct bodhisattva making a different vow;
it may also be that a single individual makes many vows. This shall now be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "There are those who should be attached": this clarifies that because there are sentient beings who ought to be attached to the five desires, when a Bodhisattva perceives them, he gives rise to a great vow to teach and transform those beings, causing them to practice non-attachment. When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, there will be no sentient beings who are attached.

Regarding "coming to be born in that land": the passage beginning with "having seen the four castes" and below shall be explained. Regarding "seeing sentient beings as superior, middling, or inferior":

this refers to the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of human beings; "family" refers to their place of residence. This shall be explained. Regarding "seeing sentient beings of various different complexions" and below: [this shall be explained].

It is explained that within the pure lands manifested by the vows of Bodhisattvas, there is only what is induced by purely wholesome karma; such mixed retributions do not exist there. It shall now be explained:
"Seeing that sentient beings have a master" and so forth. At the beginning of the kalpa, sentient beings had no master.

Later, there were sentient beings of light conduct who, because they were largely greedy for the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-fungus), collectively established one person of excellent character and integrity to serve as the lord of the land for the purpose of distribution. After that, there were again...
The people were light-handed in their conduct; they did not take what was their own, but instead greedily seized the portions belonging to others.
Because of this matter, they went together to the place of the lord of the earth and rebuked him. From that time onward, regulations were established and handed down in succession;
thus, the noble lineage of the Kṣatriya kings began here. At that time, the king knew only his subjects and imposed no labor upon them.
In former times, the people knew only the existence of the king and offered him nothing at all.

From that time onward, human sentiments have grown increasingly base, and because people have committed many evils, the king has consequently imposed labor services upon the people, and the people have thus come to perform these duties of service.
Now, the Bodhisattva, seeing this, vows that sentient beings shall have no ruler, nor even the shadow of a ruler. This is what should be explained.

This spirit has already descended. Because there are superior, middling, and inferior grades of wholesome existence (*kuśala-bhava*), there exists the Way of Spirits (*deva-mārga*); this textual interpretation is correct.
If one were to say that it belongs to the Way of Ghosts (*preta-mārga*), then evil would have only three grades while the wholesome would have only two, which would be logically untenable.

Although humans may not equal spirits in terms of karmic retribution (*vipāka*), their reception of the Dharma is superior; this is what is esteemed in the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, it is produced by a middling grade of wholesome karma.
Furthermore, those born from a womb suffer many afflictions; therefore, one vows for birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).

It shall be explained that if one follows the scriptural passages such as these, the sentient beings born in the Pure Land likewise seem to possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) obtained as a result of their karma.

It shall be explained that although the various gods of the desire realm all consume solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), it is all digested and eliminated, and they have no excrement or urine, unlike [humans].
The five viscera and six腑 (fu) of a person interact with one another; the large and small excretions are discharged through their respective openings. It shall now be explained:

from the passage "There is no light" onwards, it refers to how Bodhisattvas teach and transform sentient beings by bestowing lamps and candles, thereby attaining such retribution as being born in a Pure Land.
From the passage "Seeing the sun and moon" onwards, it refers to how Bodhisattvas observe sentient beings during the heat of summer and the cold of winter.

"Cold" refers to the fact that [the environment] is not harmonious or comfortable. "Wishing for there to be no seasons" means that all sentient beings possess their own radiance, and thus there is no need for the sun and moon.
One interpretation states: because there are no seasons, days and months, or years, it is said that there are no days or months.
"Having departed from all roots of goodness" and below refers to being free from the three types of roots of goodness—namely, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

"Having seen that sentient beings possess the three poisons," and so forth: the Bodhisattva sees that sentient beings have the three poisons as diseases of the mind, and the four afflictions of wind, cold, heat, and their combinations as diseases of the body.
Therefore, regarding the Bodhisattva’s pure land, he makes a vow that these two types of disease—of both body and mind—shall not exist there.
If one argues that all sentient beings possess the three poisons, yet it is now said that they do not, the preceding treatise explains:
this means there are no three poisons accompanied by wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), but it does not mean that there is an absence of direct anger, greed, and so forth. The Master says:

in the Pure Lands of the Three Vehicles, for the most part there is only this first category; in the Pure Lands of the One Vehicle, there are often both categories, because [the afflictions] are light.
This is because the Bodhisattva Māluṅkyaputra was able to give rise to the Great Mind (mahācitta).

The reason it is so is as explained in the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*: there is a land in the eastern direction consisting entirely of the seven treasures, wherein all are great Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha’s lifespan there is seven hundred koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas; he is also one transformed by Śākyamuni. There is no increase [in his number].

Those below the stage of overweening pride (*abhimāna*) do not include those who have not attained [realization] yet claim to have attained it, and so forth. Regarding the statement "if my radiance and lifespan were limited," etc.:
for example, Śākyamuni’s constant radiance is one *zhang* and his lifespan is only eighty years; Maitreya’s radiance is ten *li* and his lifespan is eighty-four thousand years.

This is because they still possess the faculties of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). However, because the merit of the sentient beings in this Bodhisattva’s pure land is profound, [the radiance and lifespan are immeasurable].

May the Buddha’s lifespan be boundless and his constant radiance immeasurable. While Śākyamuni is always followed by a retinue of only one thousand two hundred and fifty, these bodhisattvas vow that their constant following of disciples and the number of the Sangha shall be boundless—not limited to the conversion of those within a single region—and this includes the emission of light and other such qualities. This shall now be explained.
If one were to say that my own land has a limit, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states: "The categories of sentient beings are the pure land of a bodhisattva.
Because the sentient beings transformed by the bodhisattva are numerous, the land is vast; because the sentient beings are pure, the Buddha-land is also pure.
Since those now being transformed are so great in number, the land is boundless. This is true for all Buddhas. This shall now be explained.
"One should form this thought: 'Although the path of birth and death is long,' and so forth. This is the thirtieth section, which clarifies the third aspect:

the Bodhisattva’s correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). If a Bodhisattva perceives that the nature of sentient beings is vast and that they cannot all be delivered, they may give rise to indolence and a mind that ceases their pursuit.
Therefore, it is necessary to instruct them in this correct contemplation in order to eliminate such indolent thoughts."
It shall now be explained. The question, "What is the sequence? and so forth, is raised to first interpret the purpose for which the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* was composed; thus, the dialogue begins.

The answer, beginning with "As for... and so forth, states that if one is a Bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), then there is the transcendence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the transcendence of the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*). First...

Because the Bodhisattvas of the [first] stages have surpassed others by contemplating the Great Dharma, and because the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage, who realize non-arising, have now exhausted the five abodes [of afflictions], they have surpassed others both in practice and virtue; thus, they should only adorn their lands, which is why this matter is explained.

If one were to say that the four abodes are first completely severed at the seventh stage, one could only say they are "equal" to others; how could one say they have "surpassed" them? One should speak of the three kinds of fruits of merit.
Regarding the "retribution" [of the Pure Land]: if one refers to Wheel-Turning Kings or Heavenly Kings, these are categorized as the transformation of retributive fruit (*vipākaphala-nirmāṇa*).
If they act as divine beings or sages, they belong to the teaching of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and *dharmakāya* (dharma body).

It should be explained that while the Pure Land is actually superior to the sixth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the phrase "like" (*yathā*) is used to convey the sense of being at will. This is why it is said to be "like" a stone.
The flavor of honey is like nectar (*amṛta*), yet it cannot equal nectar.
Furthermore, from the passage "Sentient beings, having broken the *śīla*... onwards, the second successive exposition is explained by means of the *śīlapāramitā*.
This is the aspiration for the establishment of the Pure Land.
It should be explained that the remaining aspirations are likewise so forth. Within this text on the Pure Land, there are thirty repetitions of the scriptural passage;
for now, I shall explain one or two, while the rest may be understood by the reader. Therefore, it is said thus.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Finally, because the meaning of the vow is not clear," this is the third explanation of the thirtieth "Furthermore.

It is taught so that Bodhisattvas who suffer from the arising of regressive or despondent thoughts may practice correct contemplation, thereby generating diligence and seeking to transform and guide others without ceasing. This shall now be explained.
The passage beginning with "Although birth and death are long" clarifies the destruction of their appearance as something distant and protracted.

It is like a person who, while dreaming, exerts themselves in performing various deeds and perceives everything from birth until old age; yet upon waking, this occurs within the space of not even a single sentence. This matter is likewise so:
because one is obscured by afflictions within the cycle of birth and death, one perceives it as long-lasting. However, if one realizes and awakens to its true principle, then—
There is no characteristic of permanence; therefore, one should not give rise to weariness, for one must deliver sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the "future": above, the past and present were refuted; now, the future is refuted. The passage beginning with "Although sentient beings are many" refutes the characteristic of multiplicity.
The passage beginning with "The Buddha’s wisdom is also immeasurable and boundless" clarifies immeasurable wisdom.
Wisdom returns to deliver immeasurable sentient beings; therefore, there is no weariness.
As for the fifty-eighth chapter, this chapter is named after a person; it is titled "The Chapter on Gaṅgadevā.

The reason this chapter is explained immediately following the "Pure Land" chapter is that, as mentioned above, the Tathāgata has already, in relation to the ocean-like assembly, clarified the purity [of the land].
Regarding the "Chapter on Vows for the Pure Land": this woman has now, in the presence of the Buddha, generated vows for the pure land.
Therefore, the compiler of the sutra established it as a chapter title. As the treatise is about to provide an explanation, it cites this, stating: "The Commentary on the Fifty-eighth Chapter."
At that time, the woman descended [from her seat]. Within this chapter, there are four major sections.

First, it clarifies how the woman Gaṅgā addressed the Buddha and gave rise to vows for the practice of a pure land. Second, it clarifies her making offerings to the Buddha. Third, it clarifies the Buddha bestowing upon her a prophecy.
Fourth, it clarifies her generating the resolve and practicing the path; the text here is concise. This initial section is the first. As the treatise itself states:
The commentary states: At that time, there were immeasurable people who conceived the thought of generating the aspiration for a Pure Land;

however, because this woman alone spoke [of it], she is singled out as the leader. From "As taught by the Buddha in the Prajñāpāramitā" onwards, this sutra clarifies two sections concerning the Pure Land:
one section here, and another section below that clarifies the practices and aspirations for the Pure Land. This is extremely...
It is wondrously exhaustive; therefore, it is said, "I shall practice them all to their end.
From the passage concerning the woman below, the second part clarifies her undertaking of offerings.
At that time, this woman also gave with a mind of non-arising (*anutpattika-citta*), just as the Māṇava gave to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and thereby attained the *dāna-pāramitā*. If...
One can give the three kinds of gifts with the threefold purity. Even giving a single coin to an animal is the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*;

thus, its merit is equally difficult to surpass. If it were otherwise, although one might give the wealth of the four oceans to a Buddha, it would merely be called "giving" and not a *pāramitā*, let alone giving to other persons.

At that time, the World-Honored One descended; thirdly, this clarifies that the Tathāgata bestows a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) upon them. That [the light] returns and enters through the crown of the head signifies the bestowal of the Buddha-prediction.
It corresponds to the prediction for the nine paths; if all were to receive the Buddha-prediction, [it would be so].
These are all records of the provisional fruit of empowerment; they are also merely the conferral of a prediction by a single Buddha.
If it were a record of the actual fruit of realization, then all Buddhas would gather together. This is the Dharma-body of merit, a prediction conferred by the Reward-Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*);
its meaning and characteristics are inconceivable, and it is received only by the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body of merit. The Master said: "If one cultivates the Reward-Buddha..."

Regarding the "actual fruit," it is also said that one cultivates practices such as the six pāramitās; likewise, the cultivation of the provisional wisdom of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is also said to be the cultivation of the practice of the six pāramitās.

This is because there is only a difference in their virtuous functions, and thus no distinct causes. This shall now be explained: since there are no distinct causes, one should know that there are no distinct forms.
From the passage beginning with "The Buddha told Ānanda" onwards, these are all called "women" because they conform to the secular customs of the Western Regions.
"To act as an elder sister" expresses the meaning of having no heart of enmity. Regarding the passage "The kalpa is named Star-Constellation (Tārakā)," the *Mahāmegha Sūtra* states:
"After this present Bhadrakalpa, for sixty-eight thousand kalpas, there will be an emptiness in which no Buddhas appear.

After these sixty-eight thousand kalpas have passed, the Star-Constellation Kalpa begins, in which five hundred Buddhas appear. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says that after one hundred and three [kalpas]...

"The ten kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha" likely refers to the period of one hundred and thirty kalpas prior to the ninety-one kalpas of the past, during which time passed fruitlessly without a Buddha;
now, within this Bhadrakalpa, there is a Buddha—this indicates the place where he attained Buddhahood.
"The name of the Buddha" and what follows indicate his name. "He shall be born in Akṣobhya" means that this [land] is named "Immovable."
The Buddha’s land is named Wondrous Joy (Miaole), and it is also called Wondrous Goodness (Miaoshan). From the passage "From one Buddha-land...

onwards, it clarifies that Dharma-body Bodhisattvas are born through the manifestation of the Dharma-body. If one discusses their merit as the Dharma-body, they simply enter into a profound resonance with the Dharma-nature.

Because there is a sublime wisdom that increases and becomes luminous, it is called the "body born of the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-nirmita-kāya*). Furthermore, it is not a matter of traveling from land to land;

one constantly beholds the *saṃbhoga-buddha* preaching the Dharma. This should be explained as follows: the passage beginning with "should be like the assembly of the Buddha" clarifies the meaning of the scripture concerning Ānanda’s vow for the Pure Land.
It clarifies that this buddha-land is like the aforementioned Pure Land; therefore, it says, "should be like the assembly of the Buddha."
The passage beginning with "From where did this woman plant the roots of virtue? explains, fourthly, the duration of her cultivation of the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
The commentary in the Tripiṭaka states: from the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until the time of Vipaśyin Buddha is one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa;
from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until the present Śākyamuni Buddha is ninety-one kalpas. This meaning is also consistent with...
This accords with the Mahāyāna. It should be explained that since this woman first resolved her mind [upon enlightenment], a very long time has passed.
From the question below, the text intends to explain the reason why the women of a certain heaven gave rise to the practice of vows for a Pure Land in the presence of the Buddha;
thus, the roles of host and guest are established. This shall be explained. From the answer below, each point will be explained in turn. If the Buddha remains silent...
From here on, it is like the case of the woman Śrīmālā, who requested a prophecy from the Tathāgata and he granted it to her;
this woman is likewise, for she must first speak out. It shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "Question" and following explains their names.
The passage beginning with "It should be said: this woman... and following explains the second text concerning the offering.

In the preceding sutra, it was only mentioned that flowers grown on land and water, as well as rain, were spread out; here, however, it speaks of upper and lower garments as well as bodily ornaments. Upper and...
"Robe" refers to the *saṃghāṭī* and the *antarvāsaka*.
From "The Buddha replied, 'She has already received the prediction'" onwards, this explains the third section, the text concerning the bestowing of the prediction upon her.

It clarifies that because this woman has offered with a mind of non-arising (*anutpattika-citta*), she must receive the prediction. From "As previously explained" onwards, it concerns the sevenfold meaning of the smile. As [stated]...
This was explained in the first chapter. Regarding the "five obstacles," these refer to being unable to become a Wheel-Turning King, a Śakra King, a Māra King, a Brahmā King, or a Buddha.
The passage beginning with "She should long transform her female body" follows as a detailed analysis, which shall now be discussed.

At that time, this woman had already received the manifest prediction of enlightenment and had completely exhausted the five stages of abiding; yet, it is said that her "afflictions were broken and thinned. This meaning of "broken and thinned" is broad in its application.
Now, based on the fact that residual habits are thin, [the text] asks from what point downward this woman [has practiced];
this explains the scriptural passage concerning the duration and proximity of the fourth arousal of the mind (cittotpāda). This shall now be explained.

Regarding the fifty-ninth chapter of the seventy-sixth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, it is titled "The Chapter on Learning Emptiness Without Realizing It. For what reason is this chapter explained immediately after the "River Goddess" chapter?
It is to clarify that the Golden Flower is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva, and therefore she is pure before the Tathāgata.
Regarding the "Cloud of Vows" (Ghanavyūha) and the attainment of the prediction of manifest realization (*abhimukhī-vyākaraṇa*):

because one skillfully enters the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) yet does not dwell in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one is thus able to become a Bodhisattva of great virtue. Therefore, this chapter is elucidated immediately following that [preceding section].
Since the treatise intends to provide an explanation, it is called the "Commentary on the Fifty-ninth Chapter."
From the passage beginning with "Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, this chapter consists of three major sections.
First, through two cycles of both dharma and parable, it clarifies that the bodhisattva skillfully enters the three gates of liberation yet does not dwell in emptiness.

Second, it clarifies that the three samādhis each have their specific benefits and each has its specific object of treatment. Third, it clarifies how these serve as verification for recognizing an avaivartika (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva.
This opening section is the first. It clarifies Subhūti’s inquiry as to how a bodhisattva can skillfully train in the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*).
Although they train in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), they do not take realization [of them] as their goal, and so forth. Below, the Buddha will explain:

because the bodhisattva does not transform within the city [of saṃsāra] and merely takes up a limited nirvāṇa, it is said that "there is no remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*); because they do not abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is said that "there is no existence."
[This is] a division.
From the passage beginning with "Subhūti addressed the Buddha" onwards, this is the second question. It shall be explained:

whereas the preceding text stated that one does not allow the mind to become distracted, here it is said that one does not exclusively collect the mind and bind it to an object. As for the previous statement that one does not allow the mind—
Regarding "distraction": it refers to the Bodhisattva’s skillful understanding of learning emptiness and entering the three samādhis.

The present statement that one does not exclusively collect the mind and bind it to the object of focus refers to the Bodhisattva’s non-exclusive dwelling within the realization of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) of emptiness.
It should be explained as follows: "I am now at the time of learning, not the time of realization"—this constitutes the accomplishment of the great, excellent, and wondrous Dharma.

This is the meaning; it shall be explained. To think, "Now is the time for training, not the time for realization," is the meaning of the accomplishment of the great, excellent, and sublime Dharma; this shall be explained.

The passage beginning with "Having learned the contemplation of emptiness and abiding within emptiness" clarifies that although the bodhisattva trains in the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) within emptiness, they do not realize them.
If they were to realize the various fruits [of the path], that would constitute abiding in emptiness [as a fixed state].
"Suppose there were a strong man," and so forth. Next is the explanation by way of analogies. Within this explanation of analogies, there are three analogies that arise sequentially from one another:
first, the analogy of the strong man; second, the analogy of a bird flying through the sky;
and third, the analogy of a skilled archer. This initial section is the first, which first establishes the analogy of the strong man. As for the "strong man": because...

This is illustrated by the analogy of a bodhisattva being like a strong man of the three periods of time—one who is powerful, courageous, and robust; skilled in the sixty-four arts of military strategy;

capable of subduing enemies and bandits; able to cross over dangerous difficulties; and one who supports the elderly and the weak, reaching every destination in safety and security, free from all fear.
"Jing" (勁) also means "mighty" (*zhuàng*). It is also said to mean "firm" (*jiān-jìn*). This clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is firm and mighty, surpassing a gale;
he skillfully knows the Dharma, destroys the thieves of affliction (*kleśa*), and possesses fierce and robust supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that proceed directly without obstruction.

He leads all those who are old, weak, and afflicted—beings capable of being transformed—across the fearsome and perilous difficulties of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and establishes them in the state of Nirvana where there is nothing more to attain.
This refers to a place of fear. As for the current mention of being skilled in the sixty-four arts of military strategy (*bīngfǎ*) and so forth, this is based merely on worldly matters;
it is intended as a metaphorical explanation. One should understand that the Bodhisattva corresponds to a heroic man of the world, and each point should be explained accordingly.

For instance, in this region, there is much talk of the "six arts" (*liùyì*), namely: ritual (*lǐ*), music (*yuè*), archery (*shè*), calligraphy (*shū*), mathematics (*suàn*), and the sixth—these also belong to the category of sixty.
Regarding the sixty-four skills, those who understand them are very few. Although the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* provides an extremely extensive commentary, I shall now explain it briefly.
Within Jambudvīpa, only the Prince, at the time of his birth, possessed a full understanding of these sixty-four skills;
next, Āmrapālī also understood them; and then Jīvaka—these two, mother and son, both understood them. At that time, the Buddha had first appeared in the world.

Only three people understand this. The first is one who well knows celestial phenomena: namely, the eclipses of the sun and moon, the movements and transformations of the lunar mansions, deviations from their proper degrees, the good and bad qualities of the seasons, and calamities, changes, misfortunes, and declines; this constitutes one capacity. The second is one who well knows terrestrial phenomena.
There are treasures hidden in the earth; there are the hundred grains produced from the soil; there are the plants and trees suited to the land;
and there are the winds and rains that reach it—all such things belong to a single capacity. Skillfully knowing all medical formulas and medicinal herbs belongs to one capacity.

Skillfully distinguishing all diseases belongs to one capacity. Skillfully knowing the methods of calculation belongs to one capacity. Understanding and interpreting all systems of writing belongs to one [capacity].
He is capable. He is capable of the art of archery; this constitutes one capability. He is capable of skillful training and management;

he is skilled in ritual, music, craftsmanship, technical arts, military strategy, advances and retreats, gains and losses, and so forth—each of these is a distinct capability. There are sixty-four such types in total.
It encompasses all worldly laws and arts without exception; these constitute the sixty-four skills within the secular sphere.

As for the sixty-four skills within the Buddha-dharma, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, they consist of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*). By means of these sixty-four types, [one attains] the thirty-two marks.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth—these thirty-two kinds constitute internal adornment.
Because both internal and external adornments are fully perfected, there are sixty-four capacities.
Now, in this context, because one wishes to provide an analogy for what the Bodhisattva has undertaken, these sixty-four capacities are brought forward. They shall now be explained.

The passage beginning with "Having firmly grasped the weapons" is a metaphor for how Bodhisattvas extensively deliver sentient beings through their various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom, yet remain in immediate quiescence.
They do not depart to the ten directions; rather, they manifest all manner of dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Therefore, it is said that "they move while remaining established. This metaphor illustrates the vastness of the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*), which is why it is said they are "skillful in all arts and techniques. Thus, the Bodhisattva...

Because they are fully endowed with wisdom, skillful means, and virtuous conduct, they are called "handsome. Because they skillfully eliminate all afflictions and burdens, they are called "pure and clean.

Since the Bodhisattva’s inner virtues are already fulfilled, they are outwardly capable of benefiting sentient beings; thus, humans and devas revere and look up to them, which is why they are said to be "loved and respected by others.
Through the Bodhisattva’s skillful means and ingenuity, even by cultivating small merit, one obtains vast rewards and benefits. Such is the cause.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Because of causes and conditions": because he has previously accumulated many causes and conditions, he is revered by the multitude.

When a Bodhisattva wishes to gather and transform sentient beings, and those beings already hold him in high esteem, it accords with his own mind’s aspiration for effective action; therefore, they give rise to joy. Regarding the passage beginning with "Due to few causes and conditions":
it is like a worldly strongman who possesses many skills; yet due to a minor cause and condition—such as a famine—...
In times of urgent distress, one can assist the elderly, the weak, kinsmen, and friends until they reach the land of peace and security.
The Bodhisattva, possessing various skillful means, wisdom, and functional powers, leads those sentient beings who are to be saved to the land of great nirvana and bliss.
Because sentient beings possess the sixty-two kinds of views and so forth, they are called "old"; because they possess the one hundred and eight kinds of afflictions, they are called "weak."
Therefore, it is called "weakness. For those in the two vehicles of birth and death, it is called a "perilous and fearful place.
Because the Bodhisattva takes these beings who are ready for conversion, delivers them, and leads them to Great Nirvana, it is called "crossing over.

Because the Bodhisattva’s universal love regards all beings in the Dharma-realm as their own kin, and because he compassionately pities and guides them, it is said that he "comforts his parents, wife, and children."
Because Bodhisattvas are able to bring about deliverance through skillful means, it is said that one should not have fear or anxiety.

From the passage "In the midst of perilous paths" onwards, it clarifies that within the cycle of birth and death there are many four māras who watch for opportunities to afflict and harm sentient beings.

The wisdom and power of such persons are already inferior. It is because the Bodhisattva possesses both wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*) that he is able to manifest such vast and unhindered great functions to widely transform sentient beings, delivering them from the perilous path of birth and death and the difficult ground of the two vehicles.

He is simultaneously active and quiescent, yet never departs from ultimate emptiness; therefore, it is said that he returns to his original place. Since the Bodhisattva’s skillful means are so great, and his wisdom-power...
It is boundless. Because no afflictions, demons, or heterodox views can invade or harm it, it is said that "one does not encounter thieves or injury.
Having reached nirvana, one is tranquil and joyful; hence it is called "rejoicing. It is eternally and perpetually cool; hence it is called "peaceful bliss.
The passage beginning with "The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this" corresponds to the "mighty man" mentioned above. Regarding the one...
The passage beginning with "Among all sentient beings" below corresponds to the aforementioned points:

employing many arts and crafts, firmly grasping weapons, remaining steadfastly established, and assisting the elderly and the weak across places of terror; this section serves as a comprehensive summary that perfectly completes the analogy.

This shall now be explained. The passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" and so forth refers to abiding in the aforementioned dharmas and entering the three gates of liberation. And...
It is not realized. It shall now be explained.
For example, as with a bird possessing wings that has already descended... Next, the simile of a bird flying through the sky is presented. Why does this simile recur?
