Regarding the passage beginning with "Because ignorance and space are inexhaustible," the following section explains the second point above: the meaning of inexhaustibility in relation to the twelve links of dependent origination;
this shall now be explained. Regarding the passage beginning with "As it is said in the sutra," this explains that delusion arises from causes and conditions.
This is the meaning of "arising. It shall be explained one by one.
The section beginning with the question intends to distinguish the differences among the three types of twelvefold dependent origination; thus, this question is first raised.
The answer begins as follows: First, it clarifies that which is created and perceived by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which accords with the principle of arising. Ten...

The second [section] concerns the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) which construct afflictions, ignorance, karma, and formations, leading to the cycle of birth and death;

this shall now be explained. Regarding the phrase "the second" and below: this refers to the twelve links of dependent origination as observed by the noble ones (*ārya*). Within the observation of the noble ones, there are two types:

first, that based on Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and second, that based on Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of non-arising. Among these, [the first...]
Previously, it was explained that the Lesser Sages (śrāvakas) were unable to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as being all-pervasive like space and inexhaustible;

therefore, the principle of seeking them cannot be found. This shall now be explained. Thus, the text of the aforementioned sutra states: "Even when sitting at the site of enlightenment, one contemplates in this manner.
The Master of the Treatise, wishing to provide a broad explanation so that they may understand, has set forth these three kinds [of contemplation]. This shall now be explained.
Regarding the section "aging is a non-associated formation" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) below: this correctly clarifies the analytical investigation of the twelve links of dependent origination.

For now, within the context of the Hīnayāna, among the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), aging is identified as the characteristic of difference (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is said to be a non-associated formation. Regarding the passage "the graying of the hair" and so forth:
these are not themselves the characteristic of aging, but rather belong to the secondary attributes (*dharmas*) of the characteristic of aging; they are not the characteristic of aging itself. (2)
"Because the phenomenon cannot be apprehended" means, as stated above, that both the subjective and objective aspects are unapprehendable;
how, then, could there be aging? Furthermore, from the passage "As for worldly people," it shall be explained point by point.
"If there were abiding, there would be no impermanence," and so forth. This clarifies that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) must necessarily possess [all characteristics] in their entirety.

If there were only the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) such that it could abide, yet the other characteristics were not present, then because the conditioned phenomenon would be incomplete, it would follow that it is impermanent.
Because it is impermanent, there is no aging; if it were permanent, there would likewise be no aging. How much more so in emptiness, where these two phenomena do not exist—how could there be aging?
This shall now be explained. From the passage "yet one does not cling to this matter" onwards, it clarifies that although the Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness, [he does not abide therein].
Because one does not abide in emptiness, great compassion arises. Regarding the passage beginning with "Because sentient beings are deluded," this shall be explained below.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Thus deeply contemplating the law of dependent origination and departing from all extremes and inversions," this is the second section of the chapter, clarifying the skillful means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattva.
The scriptural text states that there is both that which is eliminated and that which is attained. As for "departing from all extremes," this is the explanation.

Because he contemplates in this manner, he is able to abandon the six afflictions, such as the extremes and inversions. Now, regarding this first [section], we shall first explain the passage concerning the general abandonment. This shall now be discussed.
First, regarding "the heterodox views of non-Buddhists" and below: non-Buddhists also possess perversions (*viparyāsa*), and other people also possess heterodox views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);
however, the Master of the Treatise analyzes and explains them separately here. These two kinds of afflictions are what are called the various extremes (*anta*) and perversions (*viparyāsa*).

From this third section onwards, it is clarified that this bodhisattva actually possesses no such delusions to be severed; rather, by citing the "remedies" (*pratipakṣa*), it clarifies what is to be remedied.
Therefore, it says "removes. Regarding the passage beginning with "arising repeatedly," the *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra* asks:
"Why did the Buddha laugh so greatly immediately after his initial attainment of enlightenment? The explanation states: The Buddha said, "I and these immeasurable multitudes..."

They were born at the same time and received birth together; yet, because they were indolent and did not practice diligent effort, they now wander to and fro within saṃsāra, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
Because they have now attained Buddhahood and come to make offerings to me, I smile for this reason.

If one were to discuss the profound compassion of all Buddhas toward sentient beings, one should not smile; however, it is said thus because I wish to urge them on so that they may cultivate themselves.
The passage beginning with "Surpassing the two vehicles and those below" explains the first point above: the meaning of being free from the afflictions of the two vehicles.
The passage beginning with "If there are those who regress from the Buddha-way" explains the second point above: the meaning of being free from the affliction of turning back.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Again, if one can contemplate in this way" explains the third point above: the meaning of being free from all extremes, inversions, and false or non-existent causes.

Furthermore, regarding the point that "atoms and below" are explained in the *Sāṃkhya-sūtra* as being eternal—namely, that atoms and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) are eternal, and all phenomena arise from them—as for the statement that "space does not act as a cause for things," this treatise does not treat it as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), nor does it discuss it under the category of causes and so forth.
From "not sovereign" onwards is the explanation of the fourth section, which refutes the view of a self (*ātman*). Thus it is said.
The passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva, having dwelt securely in ultimate emptiness" explains the fifth section on the elimination of views regarding phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*).
The passage beginning with "At that time, all the Māras" explains the sixth section on the elimination of the activities of Māras. The fisherman is a metaphor for Māra;
the single fish is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva; and "entering deeply into the great waters" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva entering deeply into the reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

This refers to the water. That which is not reached by the net is a metaphor for that which Māra cannot obtain despite his efforts. "Despair" is a metaphor for Māra’s cessation of the agitation of the mind.
Furthermore, it shall be explained below. Regarding the passage beginning with "There are two kinds of people," it shall be explained below.
The sixty-seventh chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Six Perfections Encompassing One Another. It is the second chapter within the section on the Gate of Skillful Means (*upāya*).

The preceding chapter correctly elucidated the essence of skillful means; this chapter clarifies that by virtue of the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva both eliminates certain things and attains others.
It demonstrates how each single perfection (*pāramitā*) is fully endowed with all six perfections, thereby establishing the meaning of skillful means. From here...
The following section contains several chapters of sutra text that further elaborate upon the meaning of the aforementioned skillful means (*upāya*).

This is because it clarifies that by having something to eliminate, one is able to fulfill all the *pāramitās*. Therefore, immediately after this chapter, there follows the "Chapter on the Mutual Inclusion of the Six *Pāramitās*."
The Treatise is about to provide an explanation; therefore, it is cited as "the commentary on the sixty-seventh chapter.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Subhūti addressed the Buddha," the Master says: "Since this section clarifies how the six pāramitās mutually encompass one another..."

However, by taking one *pāramitā* as the head, the other five *pāramitās* are subsumed; thus, there is no need for a separate summary. Within this subsumption of characteristics, there are generally five types:
namely, subsumption by stage, by practice, by ground, by identity, and by mutual arising within a single mind.

The subsumption of characteristics has already been explained above. However, in the "Chapter on the Fulfillment of Vows" (*Pūrṇapraṇidhāna-parivarta*), the meaning of the Great Adornment (*mahā-vyūha*) is taught. Now...

Regarding the explanation of how those of the same essence mutually encompass one another, it says: "When a bodhisattva practices giving, they share this gift with all sentient beings and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this is called the 'giving within giving' (*dāna-madhye-dāna*). When practicing such giving, [the three wheels are purified].
Not mixing with the minds of those of the two vehicles is the *śīla-pāramitā*. Being able to endure this is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.
Not perceiving the three factors [of giver, recipient, and gift] is the *prajñā-pāramitā*. Within a single act of giving (*dāna*), these six *pāramitās* are fully present.
Six times six makes thirty-six *pāramitās*, which are mutually inclusive as a single essence. Now, in this chapter, it clarifies the Bodhi...
Giving with the dedication toward Bodhi is the *dānapāramitā*. Abiding in compassionate physical, verbal, and mental actions toward sentient beings is the *śīlapāramitā*.
This clarifies that, based on the *dānapāramitā*, three types of compassionate action arise; thus, these are mutually generated and mutually inclusive.
In this way, the five and six [pāramitās] together constitute the mutual inclusion of thirty pāramitās.
Because there is no giving within non-giving, the treatise discusses *śīla* (ethical discipline), taking the ten wholesome paths of action as its essence.

Here, we take its fundamental basis as our subject of discourse, clarifying that the arising of the ten wholesome paths has compassion (*maitrī*) as its root. Thus, it first cites the compassion of the three karmic actions to characterize the *śīlapāramitā*, which constitutes two types of precepts.
If these are of an inferior grade, they clarify the mutual inclusion [of all factors] within a single moment of thought; this shall be explained in the relevant passage.

The meaning of how the stages, practices, and grounds mutually encompass one another has already been explained above. Now, regarding this first [stage], it takes *dāna* (generosity) as its head to encompass the other five *pāramitās*.
This shall be explained one by one. As for the "Stage of Ambrosia" (*amṛtabhūmi*), it is the stage of immortality.
The commentary below shall explain each point in correspondence with the preceding text. "Not seeking nirvāṇa" refers to the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
"For what reason," and so forth, explains why there is no sense of benefit or lack of benefit being perceived.
"Extensive learning, reflection, maintaining the precepts," and so forth—these dharmas are all fully present within this *śīlapāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline); however, [only...]
"Taking precepts as the head. Why is this?

The following explains the meaning of "emerging" through that which is to be observed. As in the *Abhidharma*, even in the Lesser Vehicle it is taught that precepts are the dharma of emergence—meaning emerging from the fetters of the desire realm, such as the trainings of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*). Therefore, this is appropriate. It shall now be explained: "Internally attached to the most..."

From "Deeply" (*shen*) onwards: if we discuss this in terms of stages (*wei-ge*), the ten minds of the "Light Fur" (*qing-mao*) stage constitute the level of relinquishing kingdoms, cities, wives, and children;
from the "Cultivated Seed" (*xi-zhong*) stage upwards constitutes the level of relinquishing one's body, flesh, head, eyes, and so forth.

This is because in the past, when Śāriputra, the Dharma Prince, and the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra practiced superior giving, they relinquished internal things during the six minds of the Light Fur stage, and consequently, they fell back [from higher attainments].

This mostly refers to those below the level of renunciants, clarifying that because renunciants possess immeasurable disciplinary codes (*vinaya*), even if they later receive the Bodhisattva precepts,
they cannot remain as householders. As for laypeople who have previously received the Bodhisattva precepts, there is [no such restriction] afterwards because they lack...

"Because of immeasurable restraint. This is explained as it appears herein. It shall now be stated that these three types of precepts refer to the precepts of the three karmas and the three branches, and so forth.

From the passage "Although the afflictions have not yet been severed, they have already been suppressed," onwards, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is clarified. If the afflictions belonging to the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)...
It is indeed severed. Since the ignorance and afflictions that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*) belong to the fifth stage (*vihāra*), they are merely suppressed.
For this reason, even though all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions have been severed, there may still be regression from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
This is the scriptural passage from the sixty-seventh chapter of the eighty-first fascicle of the *Śāstra*.
From the point where Subhūti addressed the Buddha onwards, it is the third time that [the text] clarifies how taking patience as the foremost encompasses and gives rise to all the *pāramitās*.
The meaning of *pāramitā*. If one speaks of the severing of limb from limb and so forth, this is the meaning of patience (*kṣānti*).
From "the bodhisattva abiding in patience thinks: 'I should practice giving, etc. onwards, it clarifies how generosity (*dāna*) arises on account of patience.
From "maintaining these merits until not even a single dualistic thought arises" onwards, it clarifies the meaning of *pāramitā* for each individual perfection. Each *pāramitā*...
Within the inclusion of mutual production, all [factors] are fully present; thus, there are these three meanings. These shall be explained one by one.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the three kinds of mind do not arise," the two minds were clarified above, whereas the mention of "three kinds" here is intended to provide an expanded enumeration for the sake of analysis.
This is done because, although the intent of the preceding section was different, it was not without the presence of three as well. The Bodhisattva dwells...
Regarding the *kṣānti-pāramitā* (perfection of patience): "Detached from desire, evil, and so forth" clarifies the meaning of the cause of *kṣānti*.
From "having entered up to the fourth dhyāna" onwards, it clarifies the meaning of the arising of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

The passage beginning with "all are dedicated toward" and concluding with "the various dhyānas and their factors are unobtainable," etc., clarifies the meaning of the *pāramitās*. [This applies to] all the *pāramitās*.
This is indeed so.
The passage beginning with "without slackening or ceasing" clarifies that diligence (*vīrya*) universally pervades all practices.

Since the sense of diligent exertion exists within all practices and they are entirely comprised of diligence, this statement is made. The subsequent scriptural text will clarify this pervasive meaning quite distinctly; it shall now be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Form is like a mass of foam," if one refers to the *Mahāvadāna-sūtra* where the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are explained as being like the five *caṇḍālas*, this statement was made for the sake of those who have just begun their practice, in order to engender a sense of revulsion.

The present statement here, that they are "like the dharmas," refers to those who have practiced for a long time and perform this contemplation of emptiness; therefore, it is said thus. From grasping at signs, various [conceptualizations] arise.
From "The supernormal powers, etc. below, it clarifies the meaning of the various practices through the power of diligence; this is precisely where [the meaning] resides. It should now be explained.

Regarding the passage "Having dwelled in these fourteen emptinesses," it should actually state eighteen; however, when the Noble Ones preach the Dharma, they do so solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus, herein only fourteen emptinesses are taught, beginning from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and extending to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
This is sufficient for the matter; nothing further is required, and thus it is simply stated as "fourteen.

From the passage "having entered the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*" onwards, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, enters the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
By means of the liberations and the nine attainments, one enters the *vijṛmbhita-samādhi*. By means of the *vijṛmbhita*...
[The text] is obscure. It enters the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (leap-over samādhi). One wishes to discuss the *vikrīḍita-samādhi* (sporting samādhi) herein;

it is also said that one enters the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) from the first dhyāna in successive order. The *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* is also described in this way. What is the difference between these?

Yet it is said that by means of the *vikrīḍita-samādhi*, one enters the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*. Now, regarding the interpretation: at the beginning of the sūtra text, [one] enters in successive order, as if...
It is not different. As in the *Vikurvaṇa-samādhi*: having entered sequentially from below to above, and having returned sequentially from above to below, one then leaps directly to the bottom.
One should simply practice according to the scriptural text; there is no need for self-constructed ritual applications.
As for the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*, one ascends sequentially from below; once having entered from above, one then leaps from above into the lower levels.
Furthermore, to descend from below and leap into above, entering and exiting in successive leaps, is called the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (leap-over samādhi).

The followers of the Two Vehicles can only leap over one stage, but cannot do so as this [Bodhisattva] does. That he "attains the equal characteristics of all dharmas" clarifies the meaning of his *pāramitās*.

Question: Why is it that when one *pāramitā* alone is taken as primary? Below this, the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*), wishing to explain the scriptural text, first provides an exposition taking one *pāramitā* as the head, which subsumes all the *pāramitās*. For this reason, he raises this question and answer.
Answer: Below this, it clarifies that within the causes and conditions for cultivation, the Dharma must be such that within a single *pāramitā*...

There are these five meanings. For example, within a single *dāna* (giving), there are four kinds of the meaning of relinquishment; likewise, within a single *śīla* (precept), there are three kinds of the meaning of precept, and so on for all of them.

If, as in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), the ten *pāramitās* are mutually inclusive such that one *pāramitā* serves as the head to encompass the other nine, this can also be understood by subsuming them through their primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, it is said that the hundred *pāramitās* are mutually inclusive.
All of these are the causes and conditions for practice; one must fully possess these meanings.

Regarding the passage beginning with "There are two kinds of bodhisattvas," since this first section intends to explain that patience (*kṣānti*) is the foremost, and because the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) presides over the meaning of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), these two types of bodhisattvas are first presented in order to clarify what they practice.
Because the dharmas [of these categories] differ. If one were to discuss them collectively, one would simply speak of the ordained and the laity.
However, within these two types, there are generally seven assemblies (*saptasaṃgha*): namely, the five assemblies of the ordained and the two assemblies of the laity.

Among these seven assemblies, a bodhisattva must necessarily belong to one of the seven assemblies, yet those in the seven assemblies are not necessarily bodhisattvas. Therefore, the aforementioned treatise states: "A bodhisattva must be among the seven..."

Within the assembly, the seven groups of followers are not included among the bodhisattvas; this is because those who wish to emerge [from the mundane] and those who practice the two types of giving are distinct.
To clarify these two kinds of bodhisattvas, within the mutual inclusion of each individual *pāramitā*, all three types are present.
Thus, within the mutual inclusion of this single *pāramitā*, there is the meaning of patience (*kṣānti*), the meaning of giving (*dāna*), and the *pāramitā* itself.
Regarding the meaning: within the mutual inclusion of each individual pāramitā, all three meanings are fully present; this is the case for all of them. One should distinguish their characteristics.
This distinction will be explained in contrast to what has preceded. It shall now be set forth.
If, at the time of death, one wishes for the power of two pāramitās to cause rebirth in a favorable realm: through the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla), one obtains a human body;
by means of these two pāramitās of patience and generosity, one attains a favorable realm. This refers to the bodhisattva in the state of birth (janmakāya).
It shall be explained below under the section on taking up śīla. It shall be explained.

The response beginning with "It is answered as follows" clarifies that what is to be explained here is the meaning of how the various *pāramitās* mutually encompass one another and the distinction between the characteristics of patience (*kṣānti*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Therefore, it says, "ethical discipline arises from patience. This does not mean that the treatise is definitively establishing a sequence of successive production;

rather, this shall be explained. The passage beginning with "Ethical discipline is named the non-inflicting of harm upon others" will next analyze and explain the distinct characteristics of ethical discipline and patience. This shall be explained.
The passage beginning with "Holding the precepts is a material phenomenon" (*rūpadharma*) clarifies that non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) arises from body and speech;
because it is a phenomenon that can be maintained, one receives it through the possession of all faculties. However, patience (*kṣānti*) is not a phenomenon that is received;

it must be practiced internally by oneself, and for this reason, it is distinct [from the precepts]. Furthermore, patience can give rise to the precepts, and the precepts can also give rise to patience; this is simply due to the distinction between internal mind and external form.
These serve as distinctions; they shall now be explained.

From "having departed from the three types of mind" onwards, the second section clarifies that both person and phenomena are empty. Regarding the "point of dedication," this clarifies the quiescence of its fruit.
From "having taken up *vīrya*" onwards, it clarifies that with patience as the head, one subsequently gives rise to the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). This shall [now be explained].
It is said:
following the section on taking up dhyāna, it shall be explained; following the section on taking up prajñā, it shall be explained.
Following the section on abiding in vīrya, next the five pāramitās that gather sentient beings are clarified, with the pāramitā of vigor as the primary focus.
This is the meaning of "honey. It shall now be explained. Regarding the passage beginning with "there is no separate essence," the preceding treatise’s commentary states:

Just as ignorance (*avidyā*) pervades all five categories yet is established separately as the "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇika-avidyā*), and diligence (*vīrya*) pervades all practices yet must be established separately as the "perfection of diligence" (*vīrya-pāramitā*) because it is so predominant—so too, here, because the characteristics of existence (*sanimitta*) are so numerous, they are established separately. If...

If one clarifies the essence (*tattva*) by means of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it can be said that there is a distinct essence. If one clarifies the essence by means of the essence itself, there is no distinct essence.

Furthermore, if one follows the essence by means of its characteristics, one may also say that there are no distinct characteristics. However, in the present case, because we rely on the meaning of its universal pervasion, it is said that there is no distinct essence.
Question: If that is so, then by relying on the meaning of its pervasion, one could also say that there are no distinct characteristics. Answer: That is indeed possible.
This has already been explained above.
It shall now be discussed, as follows from the passage "At the end of the kalpa" and so forth. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "It is not without cause and condition; namely, the fire calamity.

At this time, because all sentient beings are pressed by the urgency of the fire, they are naturally able to leave desire behind, remain awake, and so forth, thereby attaining the first dhyāna. If their offenses are heavy..."
Those [who fall away] go to the hells of other regions; the rest all attain the state of a bodhisattva and no longer require these dhyānas and so forth.

There may be some who, having attained it, subsequently regress. This clarifies the untainted (anāsrava) dhyāna, which is attained in two ways: namely, attainment through the abandonment of desire (vairāgya-lābha) and attainment through regression (parihāṇi-lābha).

Furthermore, it is said that when one regresses from a contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyāna, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dhyāna is accomplished and not lost; therefore, it is called "regression of attainment.
There are two types of pure (*śuddha*) dhyāna: those obtained through birth and those obtained at the time of becoming free from desire, as already explained above in the *Dhyānapāramitā*.

Alternatively, regarding the case where one born in a higher stage obtains a lower stage: this refers to when one is born into the second dhyāna, one accomplishes and attains the first dhyāna without losing it.
Furthermore,
there are those who say that from the passage "not taking the five dharmas as primary" onwards,

it clarifies that a bodhisattva does not practice dhyāna solely for the purpose of eliminating the aforementioned conditions of the five desires and so forth. If one were to practice dhyāna merely for the sake of eliminating the conditions of the five desires...
To cultivate dhyāna for the sake of eliminating the causes and conditions of the five desires is merely to act for one's own benefit; it is not true diligence.

Only when one cultivates wisdom with single-minded devotion for the purpose of extensively delivering sentient beings and eliminating all afflictions and entanglements can it be called the diligent cultivation of dhyāna.
Therefore, the treatise says: "A bodhisattva does not practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) merely for the sake of destroying stinginess and greed."
It is solely for the sake of teaching and transforming stingy and greedy sentient beings that one practices *dāna*. It should be explained as follows:

"Suppose there is a person of merit," and so forth. This is intended exclusively for those of dull faculties who are difficult to restrain and for whom the cultivation of *dhyāna* is difficult to attain.

This is made as an analogy; it is not an analogy for one who practices diligence. Regarding the statement "due to two matters and conditions," this refers to the two matters of dhyāna (meditative concentration) and vīrya (diligence).
Regarding the phrase "excluding four pāramitās," this refers to dāna (generosity), kṣānti (patience), and dhyāna itself.
From the passage beginning with "abiding in the dhyānapāramitā as the primary" onwards, the text next explains the meaning of taking dhyāna as the head to encompass all other pāramitās.
From "Once the mind is disciplined" onwards, it clearly explains the function of dhyāna, such as the arising of true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) and so forth; this shall be explained.
Furthermore, from "Having added compassion" onwards, it clarifies the meanings of *dāna*, *kṣānti*, and *vīrya* within that dhyāna; this shall be explained.
From "Abiding in prajñā" onwards, it next interprets and clarifies that *prajñā* is the essence; this shall be explained.
The answer begins with "As stated below. The eighteen kinds of emptiness previously explained apply universally to all phenomena and were taught for the sake of all people;
they are complete in these eighteen aspects. Now, however, because this is intended only for those who practice it, it is explained according to what is attained through specific matters.
Alternatively, from "practicing the two kinds of emptiness" onwards, it clarifies that one practices only the emptiness of beginninglessness and ultimate emptiness. This is...
This is because it is fully endowed with both the emptiness of birth and the emptiness of phenomena. Why is this so? From "Why is this so?

onwards, if [this teaching] were intended generally for all non-Buddhists and others, eighteen [emptinesses] would have to be taught in order to eliminate views such as existence and non-existence. However, since it is now taught solely for the sake of the practitioner, there is no fault in explaining it according to their needs.
The passage beginning with "Why is it said that the bodhisattva is like all Buddhas... and following is an explanation of the text.

It should be explained why it says "the patience of compliance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) and so forth, since above this it did not mention the "patience of compliance," but only spoke of the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is merely the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] grand classification.

They are distinguished as superior and inferior: the "patience of compliance" (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*) is taken as the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is taken as the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Since it was previously stated that there is no one who receives abuse and no such thing as a phenomenon, it is therefore said here that he "preaches the patience of compliance. This shall now be explained.

The section beginning with "Question: Regarding the samādhi of transcendence" and following is the commentary on the passages concerning the samādhi of transcendence and so forth; this shall now be explained.
The section beginning with "By the power of prajñā" and following begins the sequential and individual explanation of the meaning of how the various pāramitās arise within prajñā;
this shall be explained one by one. The section beginning with "When a bodhisattva practices giving, various wholesome thoughts arise" and following clarifies the [meaning of] prajñā.

If it is the middle *dāna*, then it fully eliminates all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as explained in the first chapter. Furthermore, from the section below, the precepts within *prajñā* (wisdom) are clarified;
the remainder shall be explained one by one. The passage beginning with "although separated from wisdom" clarifies that there is no wisdom without *dhyāna* (meditative concentration).
It is not that there is no meaning in non-wisdom and non-meditation.
Furthermore, from the passage "This bodhisattva, for the sake of the Buddha-way, has planted roots of goodness over immeasurable kalpas" onwards, we have reached this point.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of cessation. From here on, the Master of the Treatise, having already [discussed] these six...

The *pāramitās*. Because these constitute the fundamental practices of a bodhisattva, another interpretation is provided here to clarify how the meaning of the six *pāramitās* is fully present within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). This point will be further elucidated below in the "Inferior Chapter" (*hīnabhūmi*).
However, the Master, taking this opportunity, provides an explanation here so that others may practice them as well; he analyzes each *pāramitā* individually.
This clarifies each individual pāramitā. Within a single thought-moment, all six pāramitās are fully present; this does not clarify the meaning of their sequential arising.
I shall explain each one individually when we encounter the relevant passages in the text.

Regarding the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*): this is the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) which is exclusively impure (*sāsrava*) dhyāna. The restraint of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) pertains to both the impure and the pure (*anāsrava*).

As for the pure restraint of ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla-saṃvara*), it is exclusively the restraint concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*) found within the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*); this shall now be explained.
"From 'All wholesome dharmas arise because of evil' onwards, it is as explained in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:
all afflictions, unwholesome states, and neutral states are called Buddha-nature. Why is this? Because Buddha-nature is their cause.
Although this section clarifies that within a single thought-moment the meaning of the six *pāramitās* is fully present, it also explains each one by taking them individually as the primary focus."

It is the fulfillment of six meanings. As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*: "In a single thought-moment of the first stage, one fulfills the meaning of eighty-four thousand pāramitās. This shall be explained point by point.

Regarding the sixty-eighth chapter of the eighty-second fascicle of the *Śāstra*, it is titled "The Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṭala*). This is the third chapter within the section on the Gates of Expedient Means.

As for why this chapter is explained immediately after the chapter on the Mutual Inclusion of the Six Perfections (*Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃgraha*), it is because the preceding section clarified how the Bodhisattva, regarding a single...

Regarding the section on "Transcendence" (*pāramitā*), it explains how one can fully perfect all the *pāramitās*. To clarify why this is so, it is due to the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
For this reason, following the chapter on the Mutual Inclusion of the Six Perfections, the next chapter clarifies Skillful Means.
It is raised here because it is about to be explained. It is stated that this is the commentary on the sixtieth-eighth chapter.
From the passage beginning "At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha," there are four major sections within this chapter.

The first concerns the discernment of skillful means (*upāya*) with respect to persons; therefore, Subhūti asks regarding the duration of accomplishment and the extent of offerings made to the Buddhas. He then...
The temporal aspect of the mind: the bodhisattva is the person of skillful means (*upāya*), and *prajñā* is the dharma of skillful means.
Second, following the analogy: just as the sun and moon revolve around and illuminate the four continents, this clarifies how *prajñā* and skillful means guide and bring to completion all practices.
Third, it clarifies that by cultivating the cause one attains the fruit; this is termed the "skillful means of cause and effect. Fourth, it clarifies the excellence of the bodhisattva.
Studying Prajñāpāramitā involves the simultaneous illumination of the two truths; this is termed "the skillful means of illuminating and penetrating.
There are four such intentions, and the present one is the first. Each shall now be explained in turn.
For example, as stated below regarding the sun and moon, they serve as an analogy for illumination.

Just as the sun and moon revolve and the Yin and Yang circulate, benefiting the four quarters in many ways, so too are the two dharmas of *prajñā* (wisdom) and *upāya* (skillful means). They are like the sun and moon that encompass all other phenomena;

this shall now be explained. Regarding the passage "If there were no wheel-treasure," etc., the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states: "Although one possesses the six treasures and is endowed with a thousand sons..."
It is complete. If one lacks the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), they are merely called a "semblance" of a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) and rules over only a single continent.

The corresponding analogies and meanings shall now be explained. Regarding the Three Jewels mentioned previously: [the remaining treasures] refer to the gold, the wheel, the military commander, the precious pearl, and so forth.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the six pāramitās and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
[The passage continues from here. This third section clarifies the skillful means regarding cause and effect.
Within this gate of cause and effect, there is also an elucidation of the two kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of arising and the emptiness of dharmas. Subhūti offers praise.

The meanings of demonstrating what is the path and what is not the path, as well as exhorting to study and so forth, are all addressed in their respective passages; they shall be explained one by one.
Regarding the section beginning with "Except for wisdom, one cannot deliver sentient beings by means of other dharmas," it is like the land of the Buddha Siṃhaghoṣa:

its various precious ornaments are all superior to those of the devas, yet there are no practices such as observing the precepts or performing acts of giving; rather, it is only those trees [that perform these functions].

All of these can produce the sound of the true mark (*dharmatā*), enabling sentient beings to attain understanding and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), reaching up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
In this land, one attains Buddhahood solely through wisdom. Just as with the various devas and others, although they possess merit and virtue, they cannot reach Buddhahood;
only through wisdom is there the principle of attaining Buddhahood independently. Therefore, it says "excluding wisdom. If, in this world...
Regarding the "land" and so forth: initially, one must attain Buddhahood through both merit and wisdom. As for that land, it is attained through wisdom alone.
The Master also explained that the six *pāramitās* are of the nature of causes, as stated in the *Maitreya’s Rebirth Above Sūtra*.
Within Maitreya’s crown, there are the words of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Śūraṅgama*, clearly inscribed;

this symbolizes the nature of the cause (*hetu-bhāva*). Furthermore, the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: "The buddha-nature possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is like milk mixed with blood, impossible to distinguish.
That of the śrāvakas is like milk; that of the pratyekabuddhas is like curd; that of the bodhisattvas is like fresh and refined ghee; and that of the Buddha is like clarified butter (*ghṛta*)."

Regarding the statement that the Buddha-nature of śrāvakas is like milk and so forth: this is based on the śrāvakas within the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao) of the Bodhisattvas—those who hear the sound of the Buddha-way and cause all others to hear it—and does not refer to the śrāvakas of the Distinct Teaching (pieh-chiao). In the Distinct Teaching, such śrāvakas do not possess this nature.
One interpretation holds that even if they possessed it, it would not be an obstacle; this shall be explained later. All four types of troops have now followed me.
"Below. Regarding the "fourfold army," this refers to chariots, cavalry, infantry, and elephants; these shall be explained.

From "There is much that is studied, yet in reality there is nothing studied" onwards, the fourth section clarifies how the Bodhisattva skillfully studies Prajñāpāramitā by simultaneously illuminating the two truths, thereby penetrating the skillful means (*upāya*);
this shall be explained. From "Whether in brief or in detail" onwards, the "brief characteristic" is as follows:

This is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); the extensive characteristic is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Both the Great and Small Vehicles possess these two characteristics, the general and the specific.

This shall now be explained. From the passage where the Buddha says to Subhūti, "So it is, so it is," and below, because Subhūti (Śāriputra) had just offered high praise, the Tathāgata approves of it.
He clarifies that by means of *prajñā* and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), a bodhisattva is able to know the specific within the general.
This refers to the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
From the passage "How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena?
onwards, this question is posed in order to explain these matters in detail.
